World.title: Court rules on Chongwe East MP
World.content:
The Lusaka High Court has declared Anita Kamanga as duly elected Member of Parliament for Chongwe East, dismissing the election petition filed by Former Chongwe Member of Parliament Sylvia Masebo, challenging her victory in the August 13 election.

Delivering judgment, High Court Judge Evaristo Kapengele held that the petitioner had failed to prove the allegations contained in her petition to the required standard of a fairly high degree of convincing clarity.

The petition was anchored on allegations of coercive and defamatory statements, including facebook publications and statements allegedly made at a ward rally.

Justice Kapengele said it would be unsafe to assume that because the statements were made at two meetings, the majority of the electorate were exposed to them, especially as no attempt was made to demonstrate that this was the case.

The Supreme Court had noted that public meetings where verification took place were of modest attendance, there was no evidence that all those who attended were registered voters, and the numbers given for the rallies were too few for one to conclude that the majority of voters were influenced.

Applying that principle, Justice Kapengele found that the petitioner in the Chongwe East case did not adduce any evidence whatsoever of an estimate of the number of registered voters, or even the general community, who attended the rallies where the alleged coercive and defamatory statements were made.

He further found that the petitioner did not adduce evidence to show how a single ward-level rally could have swayed the majority of voters across all the 11 wards of Chongwe East.

The judge also found that the petitioner had failed to prove that the majority of voters in Chongwe East were, or may have been, prevented from electing their preferred candidate as a result of the alleged statements.

In light of his findings on both the contested facebook publications and the statements made at the ward rally, Justice Kapengele held that the entire ground of coercive and defamatory statements had failed, and dismissed that ground.

He accordingly held that the first respondent, Ms Kamanga, was validly elected as Member of Parliament for Chongwe East Constituency and dismissed the petition.

He said he had found no basis for holding that the petition was either frivolous or vexatious, and therefore ordered that each party shall bear their own costs.

“Any dissatisfied party may appeal to the Constitutional Court,” he said

World.title: Nkana edge Zanaco to extend lead
World.content:
Record 13-time champions Nkana tightened their grip at the top of Stream A of the MTN Super League after edging Zanaco 1-0 in the away matchweek 9 fixture played on Wednesday at Sunset Stadium in Lusaka.

Forward Charles Zulu scored the only goal of the game in the 2nd minute to hand Nkana all three points and take them to 19 points from nine matches.

Zulu, the former Zanaco star, intercepted a back pass before round up keeper Lameck Siame before slotting the ball inside the net.

This was Zulu’s third goal of the season.

Nkana lead Stream A on 19 points, followed by FC MUZA on 16 points and Konkola Blades also on 16 points. Nchanga Rangers are fourth on 14 points.

At the bottom, Trident FC on 6 points and Makeni All Stars on 1 point occupy the relegation places.

Elsewhere in Stream A, Napsa Stars were held to a 1-1 draw by Konkola Blades.

Benjamin Saeli gave Blades the lead in the 31st minute, but Carlos Kaoma levelled matters from the penalty spot in first-half added time.

Nchanga Rangers and Kansanshi Dynamos failed to find the back of the net in a goalless draw, while Trident FC and FC MUZA also settled for a 0-0 stalemate.

In Stream B, Kabwe Warriors drew 1-1 with Nkwazi FC.

Matthews Mashimikilo gave Nkwazi an early lead in the 5th minute, before Richard Ngoma restored parity for Warriors in the 55th minute.

Roan United and Mufulira Wanderers also shared the spoils in a 1-1 draw at Kafubu Stadium in Luanshya.

Alex Ngonga put Wanderers ahead from the penalty spot in the 8th minute, before Clifford Hamunkoyo equalised for Roan, also from the spot, in the 17th minute.

In Stream B, Green Eagles remain top on 17 points from eight games, followed by Zesco United on 13 points and Green Buffaloes on 12 points.

Mufulira Wanderers on 5 points and Mutondo Stars on 3 points are in the relegation zone.

World.title: 33 cases a day: NPAZ records 9,020 sexual and gender-based violence cases in nine months
World.content:
THE National Prosecuting Authority of Zimbabwe (NPAZ) received 9,020 sexual and gender-based violence cases in the first nine months of 2026, translating to about 33 cases per day, NewsDay Live has learnt.

Of this, 3,678 of the cases involved minors, with more than 2,000 still pending.

Prosecutor-General Justice Loyce Matanda-Moyo shared the chilling statistics in a statement this Wednesday as the country joined the global 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence campaign.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Where are PSL junior players? – Bunjira questions Young Warriors selection
World.content:
Former Warriors striker Alois Bunjira has questioned the commitment of Zimbabwe’s Premier Soccer League and Division One clubs to grassroots football development, expressing concern over the absence of players attached to professional clubs in the national Under-17 squad.

Bunjira believes the composition of the Young Warriors squad exposes glaring gaps in the country’s football development structures, particularly the failure by top-flight clubs to invest in junior development and establish clear pathways for young talent into professional football.

His concerns come after ZIFA on Tuesday announced a 20-member squad for the Under-17 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers scheduled for December 4-13 in Maputo, Mozambique.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: USD inflation accelerates as annual rate rises to 3,4%
World.content:
ZIMBABWE’S United States dollar (USD) annual inflation rate increased to 3,4% in November from 3,2% in October, as monthly price pressures also gathered pace, according to the latest figures released by the Zimbabwe National Statistics Agency (ZimStat).

The USD month-on-month inflation rate rose to 0,3% in November, gaining 0,2 percentage points from the 0,1% recorded in October.

“The USD month-on-month inflation was 0,3% in November 2026 gaining, 0,2 percentage points on the October 2026 rate of 0,1 percent,” the agency said.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: A democratic path of development: India’s poverty reduction story
World.content:
AFTER its independence from more than 200 years of colonial rule in 1947, India faced severe, widespread poverty and very low human development indicators a life expectancy of 32 years reflecting high mortality and vulnerability to disease and famines; a roughly 12% literacy rate; weak infrastructure; 85% of the population relied on rain-fed agriculture.

Today, as the world’s most populous country and home to one-sixth of humanity India has emerged as the fastest-growing large economy. In its path of progress, India has always been mindful of spreading the gains of socio-economic development among the masses.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Christmas pass bypass targets mid-2027 completion
World.content:
THE construction of the 31.2-kilometre Christmas Pass Bypass in Manicaland is 36% complete, with government targeting completion by mid-2027, the 2027 National Budget has revealed.

The project is expected to provide an alternative route for heavy haulage trucks currently using the steep and accident-prone Christmas Pass, while easing traffic congestion in Mutare’s central business district.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Africa faces climate fallout as COP31 collapses without fossil fuel deal
World.content:
AFRICAN leaders and climate advocates have warned of dire consequences for the continent after the COP31 summit in Antalya, Turkiye, ended Sunday without an overarching agreement on moving away from fossil fuels.

The talks, which ran for more than two weeks, broke down over the central question of how quickly the world should phase out coal, oil and gas. For Africa, which contributes only about 4% of global emissions but suffers some of the harshest climate impacts, the failure is a serious setback.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Zimbabwe Gender Commission urges ministries to resource survivor services as 16 Days of Activism campaign begin
World.content:
THE Zimbabwe Gender Commission (ZGC) has called on government ministries, departments and agencies to invest in services for survivors of gender-based violence, as the 2026 16 Days of Activism kick off.

In a statement, the commission said the country must move beyond awareness and take concrete action to prevent violence and end impunity in practice.

The commission called for collective action by government, institutions, communities and individuals to strengthen access to justice, protect survivors and ensure accountability for perpetrators of violence against women and girls.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Grade 7 results out Friday
World.content:
THE Zimbabwe Schools Examinations Council (ZIMSEC) says it will release the 2026 Grade 7 results on Friday.

Primary and Secondary Education Minister Torerayi Moyo announced the development in a social media post this Wednesday.

“As I celebrate my 57th birthday today, I’m pleased to inform parents, guardians, development partners and all stakeholders that ZIMSEC will release the 2026 Grade 7 examination results this Friday (27 November 2026).”

World.title: Africa: Push for Safer Surgery to Reduce Maternal Deaths
World.content:
Nigeria has the highest estimated maternal death rate. Almost 29% of the global total of 75,000 women who died in 2023 from complications of pregnancy and childbirth died there. That is roughly one woman every seven minutes.

Many of these deaths can be prevented, but limited access to quality health care, shortages of skilled personnel, and inadequate medical resources mean that complications can quickly become fatal. Emergency surgical care, particularly in the event of a caesarean section, can mean the difference between life and death for mothers and their newborns. In low- and middle-income countries, women are up to 100 times more likely to die after a caesarean than in wealthy nations.

As countries work towards the global target of fewer than 70 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030, closing the surgical care gap must become a greater health priority.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"I don't believe in doing nothing. Let us do something."

In Kano, Dr Olusegun Samuel Spaine has witnessed the struggles of mothers and health workers. He once donated his own blood in a desperate attempt to save a mother experiencing a life-threatening childbirth complication. Despite his efforts, she died.

"It remained with me because that was the first patient I lost on the operating table," he said.

Spaine said shortages of equipment and limited resources often make it difficult for healthcare workers to respond quickly to obstetric emergencies, forcing teams to balance the urgency of treatment against patient safety. "When you have a patient that you need to take care of immediately, and there's this delay one way or the other, it's very frustrating," he said.

"We don't want to lose the patient's life, and we don't want to take unnecessary risks," said Spaine.

Dr Geoff Ibbotson, Executive Director of the Global Surgery Foundation (GSF), said that the gaps run from community awareness and antenatal care to safe birthing in well-staffed facilities and follow-up after delivery. "Safe caesarean section is one of the biggest gaps, and it is where our work focuses," he said.

"A caesarean section is meant to save two lives. It can only do that if it is safe."

John Schaeffler, President of the GE HealthCare Foundation, which supports the work, said that urgency is why surgery should not be treated as a specialist extra. "For a woman experiencing an obstetric emergency, there's nothing optional about it," he said. He pointed out that in Africa and other parts of the world, surgical care is usually provided in larger cities, while practitioners and equipment are lacking in rural and less accessible areas where a surgical intervention is most likely to save a life.

"We believe that a woman's chances of surviving childbirth should never depend on where she lives or whether her local hospital has the resources to save her," said Schaeffler.

"Surgical care requires more than equipment."

Schaeffler said that one of the biggest challenges in global health is that surgery depends on far more than equipment: trained staff, reliable infrastructure and the means to keep standards high. He said the funding for these needs is often fragmented or insufficient.

Through GSF's SURGfund, the GE HealthCare Foundation brings together funding partners to strengthen surgical services in areas where needs are greatest. He said that in Nakuru, Kenya, this support is helping clinicians adopt safer surgical practices, monitor patient outcomes and share their expertise with colleagues. He said the aim was to make these improvements part of everyday hospital operations, ensuring mothers and families have better access to safe surgery.

"By investing in both the people delivering care and the systems supporting them", he said, "we can help make safe surgery more accessible to the mothers and families who depend on it."

Schaeffler said building lasting local capacity requires foundations and private-sector partners to strengthen healthcare systems rather than focus on individual interventions.

"The real measure of philanthropy is its lasting impact," he said. "That's why we're helping healthcare systems become stronger and more self-sufficient, so they can provide quality care for generations to come."

He said this requires understanding the daily challenges facing healthcare professionals, including limited access to training and equipment, infrastructure gaps and difficulties providing safe emergency care, while identifying existing practices that work and areas where additional support could have the greatest impact. He said that as international health funding becomes less predictable, this approach is more important than ever. "Investing in the system holistically allows for sustained improvements that will serve communities well into the future," he said.

The funding squeeze has hit many organisations hard.

A news survey by PMNCH, covering partner organisations in 67 countries, shows that nearly 80% are dealing with reduced or uncertain funding. Meanwhile, 77% say global disruptions have moderately to severely affected their ability to advance the health and rights of women, children and adolescents. The survey also found that 69% have already been forced to scale back, temporarily suspend or permanently close programmes.

The findings point to a growing crisis in service delivery, as organisations struggle to maintain programmes, reach vulnerable communities and sustain essential health services amid financial uncertainty.

Ibbotson acknowledged that funding cuts have affected many organisations but said GSF had seen an increase in funding, which he attributed to its collaborative funding model and partnerships with organisations such as the GE HealthCare Foundation.

"There is a real appetite, because surgical care, and safe caesarean section care in particular, is so clearly a neglected area with great potential for impact, and we are now seeing the results of these investments," he said.

The projects GSF supports are now expanding to more facilities in Nigeria, Kenya and Nepal.

However, Ibbotson said the programme is designed to ensure local healthcare professionals take ownership of improvements through training, mentorship and the transfer of skills to other teams.

In Kano, the initiative is led by the Association for Clinical and Professional Health Advancement (ACEPHAP) at Bayero University, in partnership with the Kano State Ministry of Health. GSF mobilises funding from several partners and accompanies the teams through mentoring and quality improvement. "They own, and they deliver the training, and it is then their choice whether to continue it," he said.

"The costs to do this are minimal because the skills are incorporated into the usual routines, and therefore there are really no additional ongoing costs. The cost of not continuing is far greater," said Ibbotson.

Strong teamwork and coordination deliver impact

GSF reports a 45% drop in newborn mortality and surgical complications across its Nigerian programmes. Similar efforts in Kenya have reported a 72% reduction in newborn mortality, further highlighting the potential impact of strengthening surgical services.

"Strong teamwork and coordination deliver impact," said Ibbotson.

A new operating theatre without a trained team is useless, and sometimes dangerous.

Ibbotson said the results in Kano demonstrate the importance of strengthening existing healthcare teams through better coordination, teamwork and training. The gains came from teams already working in those hospitals, not from new buildings. New operating theatres are welcome, he said, but "a new operating theatre without a trained team is useless, and sometimes dangerous."

He said that unsafe surgery is increasingly linked to maternal deaths and to injuries such as fistula. He cited a national study in Malawi which found that 52% of maternal deaths following childbirth occurred after caesarean sections, despite the procedure accounting for about one in six hospital births in the study.

"We're seeing encouraging results in both countries," added Schaeffler.

Caesarean sections can save lives, he said, but complications such as severe bleeding, hemorrhaging and infections following surgery can put mothers at serious risk, sometimes requiring emergency treatment or prolonged hospitalization. In the most serious cases, these complications can be fatal.

In Kenya, GSF has reported a 45% reduction in newborn unit admissions, while in Nigeria, surgical site infections following Caesarean sections have fallen by nearly half. But the impact goes beyond individual procedures, he said. In Kenya, clinicians who have completed their training are now helping train the next cohort, allowing their knowledge and experience to benefit more patients.

"The lesson for scaling this work is that we can't simply replicate the same model everywhere. We need to work with local healthcare professionals and governments to understand each community's needs and incorporate successful practices into their health systems," said Schaeffler.

He said that the ultimate measure of success was ensuring improved care became standard practice across hospitals.

Ibbotson said the model could be expanded to other countries, provided it was adapted to their local healthcare needs, adding that the same approach is also working in Nepal.

He said that additional funding through SURGfund could help extend the programmes to more locations. GSF has expanded its supported projects over the past year and is prepared for further growth.

Close 

Hub-and-spoke model

Ibbotson explained that the hub-and-spoke model is designed to extend surgical skills and mentorship beyond major teaching hospitals to more remote facilities. "The key is to get these skills out to the more remote areas, where the people are and where access is limited. This will show the biggest impact," he said.

In Kano, two hospitals act as hubs that mentor the teams in eight other hospitals. This builds a strong community in which teams can support each other. "We strongly recommend not working in isolation but as part of a supportive community," he said. "The hubs can support the spokes, and even spokes support each other. That will deliver success. We focus on the more remote areas, not the big teaching hospitals."

He said African governments must take primary responsibility for financing and prioritising surgical care, with external organisations supporting locally led health systems rather than replacing government efforts.

"The ultimate responsibility remains with governments," he said. "This is not a cost; it is an investment. Lives will be saved, disabilities will be avoided, and communities will grow stronger, which strengthens the economy. It is a win-win investment."

He sees reasons for hope.

Ibbotson said that surgical care has been largely ignored by global health actors over the past several decades, and nine out of ten people in low- and lower-middle-income countries still cannot access basic surgical care. "But there is now an increasing awareness that surgical care systems are the backbone of the entire health system, particularly at the district hospital level, where the lion's share of the patients are treated," he said.

He added that local teams have shown how quickly care can become safer when they are trained and supported through a platform and funding that give them stability.

"If we can change the current situation and ensure that safe surgical care is available across Africa, then communities will have a better chance to thrive. What we are seeing at the project sites gives me hope, because the model is replicable," he said. "What is working in Kano and Nakuru can work in district hospitals across Africa. We are ready to grow it."

World.title: Kenya: What Does It Mean to Be 'On SHA'? a Guide to Kenya's New Health System
World.content:
Millions more Kenyans are now protected from the cost of falling ill, Kenyan president William Ruto said in his 2026 state of the nation address.

"Today, 33.7 million Kenyans are registered with the Social Health Authority, compared with approximately eight million registered under NHIF in 2022," Ruto told a joint sitting of parliament on 18 November.

"That is 25.7 million Kenyans, more, brought into the national health financing system," Ruto said.

He presented that growth as evidence that families were increasingly protected from medical bills that could otherwise force them to borrow, sell assets or abandon treatment.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He gave the example of a mother of three and small-scale farmer who underwent a kidney transplant and who was paying KSh840 to SHA a month. In turn, the pooled health financing scheme had paid in full a bill of KSh966,000 excluding dialysis. "Is that not a beautiful thing?" he posed.

Is registration the same as active health cover? This guide took a closer look at what the 33.7 million figure says about who can access care, who is paying for it and what the various terms and numbers mean.

The Social Health Authority manages Kenya's new public health financing system. It replaced the National Hospital Insurance Fund, or NHIF, in October 2024 as part of the government's push towards universal health coverage.

Universal health coverage, or UHC, means that people can get the health services they need without being pushed into financial hardship by the cost.

Kenya's new SHA system has three main funds.

The Social Health Insurance Fund (SHIF) is the contributory fund. It receives payments from households and other contributors, as well as government funding for people who cannot afford to pay.

The Primary Healthcare Fund pays for specified basic care mainly at lower-level facilities such as dispensaries and health centres.

The Emergency, Chronic and Critical Illness Fund covers emergency treatment and the management of chronic illnesses once a person's SHIF cover has been exhausted.

Because the three funds cover different types of care, the rules for accessing them also differ.

Ruto's comparison has two early problems. First, official records do not support the figure of eight million NHIF registrations in 2022." The available data put NHIF membership at about 15.5 million principal members and 14.5 million dependants as of June 2022. In addition, the two schemes do not count people in exactly the same way, as we will explain.

Second, being registered with SHA is not the same as making contributions or having active insurance cover.

But government officials have used the terms interchangeably:

On 10 September 2026, health cabinet secretary Aden Duale told a visiting World Bank delegation that "32.6 million people, equivalent to 68% of the population" had been "onboarded" onto SHA.

President Ruto only days later said more than 33 million people were "now covered" by SHA. This, he said, had brought the goal of Universal Health Coverage in Kenya by 2030 within reach.

On 20 September interior principal secretary Raymond Omollo reportedly described "more than 33 million Kenyans" as "registered" with SHA.

At the time of writing, SHA had not published an administrative breakdown. State House spokesperson Hussein Mohamed only told Africa Check the numbers came from a "realtime dashboard with limited access".

"It is fed from the ground as registrations happen countrywide at homes and hospitals. It is real time at the dashboard maintained by DHA (Digital Health Agency) on behalf of SHA," he said.

Every Kenyan is required to register as a member of SHIF. Children are to be registered at birth. Non-residents can also be registered.

Government officials sometimes refer to this collection of a person's details so that they can access services as being "onboarded", although the term is not defined in the Social Health Insurance Act.

Registration therefore shows how many people are entered in the SHA system. But it does not tell whether contributions for that person or household are current.

It also does not say if a registered person is a contributor or a dependant covered through somebody else. SHA's report for the period to 31 March 2026 recorded 30.13 million registered beneficiaries. It also said 16.81 million were principal members, with 12.6 million being from the informal sector and 4.2 million from the formal sector.

It also says active contributors number 4.78 million.

In other words, the registration figure contains several different groups.

For salaried households, their employers deduct their contributions from their pay. The rate is 2.75% of gross pay, with a minimum monthly contribution of KSh300 (about US$2.3 at current rates).

Households without salaried income are assessed differently. SHA uses a means test, which is a questionnaire designed to estimate household income and what premium the household can afford.

The assessment, which is answered at registration, looks at factors such as housing, access to basic services and household composition. The resulting estimate is used to calculate a contribution of 2.75% of household income, again subject to the KSh300 monthly minimum.

Households assessed as unable to afford their contributions can have these paid by the national or county government or by other sponsors.

This is important in Kenya because most employment is informal. In 2025, there were 21.6 million people in recorded employment, excluding small-scale agriculture and pastoralist activities. About 18.1 million of them, or 83.8%, were in the informal sector, according to the 2026 economic survey.

For many households, contributions cannot simply be deducted from a monthly salary and keeping them up to date can become complicated.

No. A registered person may have access to some services but not necessarily the full range paid through SHIF. The Social Health Insurance Act says that access to SHIF services is tied to contributions being "up to date and active".

People who fall behind can face penalties. In a July 2026 notice, SHA said unpaid contributions attract a 2% monthly penalty and that arrears and penalties must be cleared before a member can use SHIF-funded services again.

People paying in instalments under SHA's "Lipa Pole Pole" arrangement must first pay the equivalent of four months of their annual contribution before their cover is activated.

In other words, someone may be registered and still not have access to all SHIF-funded services. But this does not mean an unpaid member has no access to healthcare at all, as the various services are paid for through the three different funds.

Primary healthcare is funded separately from SHIF. The Primary Healthcare Fund pays for basic care at dispensaries and health centres, generally level 2 and 3 facilities. The regulations say that every person resident in Kenya is entitled to primary health care services. In August 2026, SHA said that more than 10 million people had used free services at these levels.

The Emergency, Chronic and Critical Illness Fund pays for emergency treatment. The Act defines this as the immediate care needed to prevent death or stop a medical situation getting worse.

The Social Health Insurance Regulations give every person the right to emergency treatment, and they list stabilising the patient as part of it.

The official tariffs say emergency stabilisation and an ambulance to the nearest emergency centre are available regardless of registration or contribution status.

But this cover is limited. It applies for up to 24 hours, after which SHIF takes over for members whose contributions are active.

Most hospital care, including many admissions, is paid for through SHIF.

But even when emergency care is covered, SHA pays hospitals a fixed amount. The media has reported that if a hospital charges above the KSh95,200 (about $730) set for treating a stroke, for example, then the patient pays the difference.

That means being registered but not paid up does not leave someone completely without care. But it can limit the services available once treatment moves beyond primary or emergency care.

The president's broad figures are the latest from the government.

The most recent detailed administrative figures publicly available put the paying number far below the total registered. SHA's impact report recorded about 4.78 million active contributors at the end of March 2026, and 30.13 million registered beneficiaries.

But this does not mean only about one in seven people had cover. A contributor can also cover dependants. SHA's annual report for the 2024/25 financial year, for example, recorded 24.7 million registrations at the end of June 2025, including more than 8.4 million dependants.

Under the law, a beneficiary can include the contributor, their spouse, children under 21, full-time students under 25 and some dependants with disabilities.

A teacher contributing through her salary, for example, may also cover her spouse and children. The reverse is also possible. Several people in a household may be registered while the household's contribution is not active.

That is why dividing five million contributors by 33.7 million registrations does not tell us the proportion of Kenyans with active cover.

The number needed to establish actual active coverage is therefore how many registered people are currently beneficiaries of an active contribution. SHA has not published that figure. Africa Check has asked the ministry of health and the agency for this data. Neither had responded at the time of publication. We will update this guide if they do.

A separate source gives a useful picture of what coverage looked like earlier in 2026.

The 2025-26 Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey, carried out by the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) and several other organisations, visited nearly 30,000 households between November 2025 and February 2026.

The nationally representative survey found that 39.4% of Kenya's household population reported having SHA health insurance. Overall, 40.3% reported having some form of health insurance.

This is not directly comparable with the later administrative registration total. The survey measured reported insurance coverage at an earlier point in time, while SHA's registration number counts everyone entered into its system.

But the survey provides another useful measure.

Among people registered as contributing members, only 43.9% said their SHIF premium had been paid for the current month. Another 52% said it had not been paid, while 4.1% did not know.

These figures support the need to distinguish registration from active participation and also show why a single headline number cannot describe the whole system.

The number of people contributing also matters because SHIF depends partly on those contributions to pay claims.

According to the KNBS Economic Survey 2026, SHIF collected KSh57.7 billion (about $440 million at current rates) from members in the 2024/25 financial year. This was against claims of KSh91.5 billion.

That is equivalent to about KSh1.59 in claims for every KSh1 collected.

Mwangangi said the 32,180,494 registrations in July were "equivalent to 67.7 per cent of the national population". And in September 2026, Duale said the 32.6 million registrations represented 68% of Kenya's population. Duale used the same base again on 18 November, the day of Ruto's address, putting registrations at "more than 33 million" and representing "70% of the population".

While the government is yet to respond to our query on this, those calculations closely match Kenya's 2019 census, which counted 47,564,296 people.

Dividing 32.6 million by the census total gives about 68.5%. But the country's population has grown since 2019. KNBS puts the projected population at 54,227,015 in mid-2026.

Against that estimate, 32.6 million registrations represents about 60% of the population, not 68%. Ruto's later figure of 33.7 million people would represent about 60% of the population.

While the 2019 census is still the most recent, using a current official population projection to describe the share of the current population gives a more meaningful comparison.

Put another way, to really have 68% of Kenyans registered today, SHA would need about 36.9 million people on its books, more than any number cited so far.

Officials often compare SHA registrations with its precursor, the National Hospital Insurance Fund (NHIF).

In his address, Ruto said 33.7 million people were registered with SHA, compared with about eight million under NHIF in 2022. In his June 2026 budget statement, Treasury cabinet minister John Mbadi also gave the eight million NHIF figure.

Close 

But this figure does not match official NHIF membership data. A health sector report published by the treasury recorded 15.517 million NHIF members at 30 June 2022, of whom 6.7 million were active members.

Parliamentary and KNBS figures have also variously put NHIF membership as reaching more than 16 million, as did the defunct agency and its board at separate points.

In August 2026, Mwangangi, said NHIF's highest registration had been 16.9 million.

The eight million figure is therefore neither the official total membership nor the reported number of active members.

Using the 2022 total, the simple difference between 15.5 million NHIF members and 33.7 million SHA registrations is about 18.2 million, rather than 25.7 million.

But the two schemes also counted membership differently.

NHIF's historical figures largely recorded principal members. SHA's registration total includes principal members and dependants. Its own 2024/25 annual report separates the two.

The totals therefore compare different populations and cannot be a direct measure of how many additional Kenyans have gained health insurance.

When SHA launched in October 2024, NHIF members were moved across to the new scheme. At the time, Dr Thuranira Kaugiria, then the technical lead for the transition in the president's office, told Africa Check that the number moved was 12 million.

But being moved across did not mean a person could get care. They still had to complete registration and pay.

The Mini DHS also found a large difference by household wealth. Among people in the poorest fifth of households, 24% reported SHA coverage, compared with 49.2% in the wealthiest fifth.

The difference was even wider among contributing members whose premiums were paid for the current month. Only 17.9% of contributing members in the poorest fifth were paid up, compared with 65.9% in the wealthiest fifth.

The government's means-testing and sponsorship systems are intended to prevent inability to pay from excluding poorer households.

But the means test has itself faced scrutiny. In February 2025, only 3.1 million of about 19 million registered people had completed means testing.

A 2026 investigation by Lighthouse Reports found that the model overestimated spending for 80% of the poorest households in the data it examined, meaning many could be asked to pay more than they can afford.

A separate February 2026 assessment by the Institute of Economic Affairs, a Nairobi think tank, linked weaknesses in means testing to low contribution rates, with only about 18% of registered members reportedly paying.

SHA says it has expanded ways through which the government and other sponsors can pay contributions for vulnerable people. In August 2026, the Standard daily reported fewer than 300,000 government-sponsored members, such as orphans, widows and the very poor.

But in the same month Ruto said the government had "sponsored nearly 560,000" vulnerable households, covering about 2.2 million Kenyans. SHA itself gave a figure of 453,729 sponsored beneficiaries through 249 sponsors, covering 4,235 teenage mothers and 449,494 indigent persons as of March 2026.

World.title: South Africa: South Africa Refuses to Drop Empowerment Laws Over U.S.Tariffs
World.content:
Trade Minister Parks Tau says South Africa will not give in to pressure from the United States to abandon its economic empowerment policies.

The government wants its empowerment policies to help more black business owners manufacture products, supply goods and sell them to other countries.

South Africa will not give up its black economic empowerment policies to secure lower tariffs from the United States.

Minister of Trade, Industry and Competition Parks Tau made this clear during the Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment (B-BBEE) Practice and Policy Conference in Johannesburg on Monday.

Relations between South Africa and the US remain strained, with Washington raising concerns about the country's economic empowerment policies.



Tau said the government was reviewing its empowerment policy to make it stronger, not to please its critics.

"We will not trade transformation for tariff relief. We believe that this policy is rooted in our Constitution and our Human Rights policies as a country," he said.

Tau said President Cyril Ramaphosa had committed the government to reviewing the empowerment policy.

He insisted that the review was not a sign that South Africa was giving in to pressure from Washington.

In February 2025, the US issued an executive order against South Africa, which listed the country's empowerment requirements among its concerns.

Tau said Washington followed this up with a list of demands in March this year.

Among these was a demand for South Africa to end what Washington described as compulsory surrender of business ownership or control as a condition of doing business.

Tau said the next phase of black economic empowerment must focus on creating successful black-owned businesses rather than simply handing out compliance certificates.

The government wants to see more black business owners running factories, supplying goods and selling their products overseas.

"Our direction is clear. We are moving from compliance to outcomes. From transactions to industrialisation," Tau said.

He said the policy review was aimed at creating meaningful economic opportunities and ensuring that black business owners owned assets that could produce goods and generate income.

World.title: East Africa: Somalia's Parliament Speaker Accuses Kenya, Ethiopia, Uganda of Colluding With Al-Shabaab
World.content:
Addis Abeba — Somalia's parliamentary speaker Abdulkadir Mohamed Nur, also known as Jaamac, has accused Kenya, Ethiopia and Uganda of colluding with Al-Shabaab, alleging that Israel had brought together the three countries, the militant group and forces loyal to former South West State leader Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen in a coordinated front against the federal government.

Nur made the accusations on 24 November while closing a conference on Somalia's productive resources organized by Magan Forum in Mogadishu. He warned that unnamed foreign powers were seeking to recolonize Somalia and urged Somalis to defend the country's sovereignty. The allegations, which remain unsubstantiated but were reported widely by Somali local media, risk further straining relations with regional partners involved in Somalia's security efforts.

The remarks build on Nur's earlier accusations against neighboring countries and the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM). In October, amid escalating fighting in South West State, he questioned why Al-Shabaab continued operating in areas where Ethiopian troops serving under the AU mission were deployed. He also accused Kenya of harboring individuals whom Mogadishu associates with militant activity, specifically referring to Laftagareen, who has been based in Nairobi since federal forces ousted him from Baidoa earlier this year.

Nur urged the federal government to demand explanations from Nairobi and hold Ethiopian forces accountable for the security situation in South West State. Kenyan officials said at the time they had received no formal diplomatic complaint from Mogadishu.



The accusations come amid an escalating political and security crisis in South West State. Federal forces seized Baidoa in March, ousted Laftagareen and installed Aden Mohamed Nur "Madobe." However, Laftagareen-aligned forces retained an armed presence and launched attacks, later capturing several towns in the Bay region, including Buurhakaba, Qansahdhere and Berdaale, in October. The fighting has complicated federal efforts against Al-Shabaab and contributed to displacement.

In October, Somalia's federal government imposed financial sanctions on Laftagareen and nine others over alleged links to Al-Shabaab financing. The committee responsible said the decision was based on information and evidence it had assessed, but did not publicly detail the evidence against each individual.

Nur's accusations also come as Mogadishu's relations with the United Arab Emirates deteriorate. Somalia annulled its agreements with the UAE in January, citing sovereignty concerns, and tensions escalated in November after President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud accused Abu Dhabi of interfering in Somalia's internal affairs, supporting political divisions and armed groups outside federal control, and pursuing unauthorized port arrangements. On 19 November, the Council of Ministers ordered the UAE ambassador to leave within 72 hours and recalled Somalia's envoy from Abu Dhabi. The UAE denounced the decision as escalatory and hostile.

Close 

Kenya, Ethiopia and Uganda have all contributed troops to AUSSOM, which replaced the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS) in January 2025 to support Somali forces in combating Al-Shabaab, secure key areas and facilitate the gradual transfer of security responsibilities to Somali forces. The mission's mandate has been extended through 31 December 2026, amid persistent funding shortfalls and shifting troop deployments. Uganda, AUSSOM's largest troop contributor, began withdrawing its bilateral contingent in late October, while the mission assumed responsibility for several bases in Lower Shabelle in November to prevent security gaps that could be exploited by Al-Shabaab.

At the conference, Nur also accused Al-Shabaab, Israel and the UAE of activities threatening Somalia's sovereignty. He called for greater economic self-reliance, urging the country to strengthen domestic production across agriculture, livestock, fisheries, manufacturing and mineral resources, and reduce dependence on imports. He argued that improved security and the elimination of Al-Shabaab were essential to attracting investment and advancing economic development.

Nur, a former defense minister, signed Somalia's 2024 Defense and Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement with Türkiye, which provides for Turkish support in developing Somalia's navy and protecting its maritime territory. He subsequently served as minister of ports and maritime transport. His close ties with Ankara have drawn criticism from some observers, while supporters portray the partnership as strengthening Somalia's sovereignty.

World.title: Africa: Rwanda's Return Hub Plan Risks Making Africa Europe's 'Drop-Off Zone'
World.content:
Rwanda's Minister of Interior Vincent Biruta (third right) joined senior officials from the five EU countries at a press conference announcing the new migration partnership.

analysis

Offshore deportation deals will produce opacity, shield authoritarian governments and drive more political signalling than reduce migration pressures.

On 16 November at the Vienna Migration Conference, five European Union (EU) member states - Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands - announced a plan to set up an offshore 'return hub' in Rwanda for rejected migrants. Ministers would not disclose financial details.

The plan, not yet formalised, would see 100 people sent to Rwanda from 2027. They would stay in a 'reception centre' before deciding whether to remain, move on or return to their home countries.



It would be the first scheme to apply the EU Return Regulation, adopted by the European Parliament in June and the Council of the EU in October. The regulation expands the definition of where a person can be 'returned' to include third countries with which they have no connection and to which they have not agreed to go, provided that country consents.

This allows deportation centres to be set up outside the EU for people with no legal right to remain, including families with children.

Critics such as Amnesty International compare it to the discarded 2022 United Kingdom (UK)-Rwanda deal, although the hubs are intended for those whose applications to remain in the EU have been rejected - not for people who intend to claim asylum. Rwanda sued the UK for over £100 million in unpaid funds from the deal, but lost. The UK had already paid about £290 million, yet only four people were transferred.

The five EU countries say the hubs will deter irregular migration and dismantle smuggling networks. 'We will break down the business model of human smugglers. We will take back control of our borders,' said Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.

They insist that return partnerships will be mutually beneficial, fully comply with international law and involve only countries that uphold 'Europe's shared values and human rights.' However, the regulation does not provide for comprehensive human rights monitoring.

In October 2025, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights issued a resolution criticising migration externalisation and extra-regional migrant transfers to Africa. It called for transparency and urged states to avoid policies that turn Africa into a 'drop-off zone' and degrade international law.

Forty-seven civil society and trade union groups signed a statement decrying the plan, saying it did not adequately safeguard human rights, and citing Rwanda's record, including the 2023 UK Supreme Court finding that sending asylum seekers to Rwanda was unsafe. For its part, Rwanda presents itself as a humanitarian actor offering second chances to migrants with no other options.

Rwanda's Interior Minister Vincent Biruta told the Vienna conference that the decision aligned with Rwanda's own history 'that made many of refugees' and its commitment to free movement. He cited the Africa Visa Openness Index, which rates Rwanda as the most open country, and the Emergency Transit Mechanism, through which Rwanda has received 3 097 migrants stranded in Libya since 2019. Over 2 600 of them have since been relocated, including to Europe and North America. He said Rwanda worked closely with the UN Refugee Agency, the African Union (AU) and other international partners.

Asked about concerns raised by non-governmental organisations, he said: 'We were not surprised by these comments by some ... who want to say that in Rwanda nothing is working and everything is bad. We are here to contribute to global solutions.'

Rwandan journalist Samuel Baker Byansi, in exile after receiving death threats for investigating Rwanda's military actions in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, told Al Jazeera: 'This partnership buys their silence.'

Since the 2015 migration 'crisis', migration has become deeply politicised in the EU. Where member states have failed to agree on internal solutions, the EU has focused on externalisation - extraterritorial measures to stem arrivals to its external borders.

The Rwanda plan continues a long-standing trend of disproportionately targeting Africa, even though between 2014 and 2024, Africans accounted for only a quarter (one million of about four million) of irregular migrants.

There is ample evidence that externalisation has undermined democracy and the rule of law and led to serious human rights violations in Africa. In Libya, for example, the EU-funded Libyan Coast Guard has been reported to ignore distress calls and run extortion schemes.

The EU and its member states have strengthened authoritarian governments through ad hoc, often secretive bilateral deals with repressive leaders, giving them tacit political and financial support irrespective of their records.

The 2023 EU-Tunisia Memorandum of Understanding committed €700 million in funding despite credible evidence that President Kaïs Saïed was threatening democracy and orchestrating expulsion campaigns against sub-Saharan African migrants.

Informal arrangements intentionally bypass EU accountability mechanisms required by formal agreements, compromising European oversight and the ability of African voters, taxpayers and institutions to hold their governments accountable.

Such deals are driven more by political signalling than by workable migration solutions. To date, there is no evidence that enforcing return orders to third countries or building return centres has deterred migration.

Between March 2025 and August 2026, Italy's government transferred only 'hundreds' of men with expulsion orders to Albania. With only 100 people initially earmarked for Rwanda, the plan is unlikely to be much of a deterrent.

While some restrictive measures have slowed irregular migration along specific routes in the short term, they often worsen long-term drivers. Demand for migration does not diminish, and smugglers quickly adapt, opening more dangerous and expensive routes.

Close 

The EU is under political pressure to manage migration and demonstrate that it can maintain border integrity and enforce its immigration laws, for both legitimate and politicised reasons. But member states must resist the instinct to offload internal political pressure onto Africa.

At a minimum, the EU should insist that any such deals are formal agreements, publicly available to its citizens, with independent monitoring and a review clause. The AU and member states should develop a common position on deportations that sets minimum negotiating terms, requires full transparency and ensures the terms and conditions that agreements serve African interests.

It is not in Africa's interest to become an arena for other countries and continents to externalise solutions to their internal problems. These arrangements strip African agency, put true equal partnerships at risk and have lasting negative effects on Africa and Africans.

Read the full ISS Policy Brief 'EU Return Regulation outsources migration problems to Africa' by Aimée-Noël Mbiyozo here.For permission to re-publish ISS Today articles, please email us. Aimée-Noël Mbiyozo, Senior Research Consultant, Migration, ISS

World.title: South Africa: SA Company Prepares to Make the Monthly Anti-HIV Pill. But Will the Govt Buy It?
World.content:
South African drug maker Aspen is preparing to manufacture alimatravir, a new monthly HIV prevention pill, before scientists have proved it works. But the government could still buy it from a cheaper supplier outside South Africa.

South African drug maker Aspen is preparing to manufacture a new monthly HIV prevention pill before scientists have proved it works. But the government could still buy it from a cheaper supplier outside South Africa.

The South African drug maker, Aspen, is preparing to manufacture a new monthly HIV prevention pill before scientists have even proved it works.

But there's a catch: the South African government may not buy the locally made pill if it can get cheaper versions from outside South Africa, for instance, from Indian manufacturers instead.

Aspen is one of seven companies licensed to make the pill, alimatravir. Four have manufacturing operations in India, where production could be less expensive.

Final study results will become available in mid-2027.

The dilemma: South Africa wants to grow its local pharmaceutical industry, but government medicine tenders often favour cheaper suppliers. Will Aspen's investment pay off?

Six months into South Africa's roll-out of lenacapavir, the injection that protects against HIV for six months , the local drug maker Aspen Pharmacare is preparing to manufacture alimatravir , a pill you'd swallow just once a month .

It's the first time the company has started preparing to make a medicine before the final trial results are in, says Aspen executive Stavros Nicolaou.



Aspen is one of seven generic manufacturers that MSD , the company developing the pill, licensed in July , to make cheaper versions for 129 low- and middle-income countries if the drug is approved.

MSD granted the generic licences before recruitment for the final-stage trials was complete, a move the company says is a first in HIV prevention .

The aim? To get the pill to people faster if it works.

But making the pill here doesn't mean the health department will buy it from Aspen. We don't yet know what any of the manufacturers would charge for this pill. But the government has a history of awarding its medicine contracts to cheaper suppliers, often from India.

That's a concern for Nicolaou, who says the government encourages local medicine manufacturing but doesn't always support it when awarding contracts, as has happened with recent HIV treatment tenders .

Meanwhile, the science is moving fast.

On 2 November, MSD, known as Merck in the US and Canada, announced that adult recruitment had been completed for two large, final-stage trials . Results could be available in the second half of 2027.

Early studies and modelling suggest that alimatravir reaches potentially protective levels in the body within about an hour of taking it. That's much faster than lenacapavir (LEN), which, according to South Africa's health department , starts protecting against HIV on day three, provided the injections and oral loading doses have been taken as prescribed.

But whether this translates into protection against infection in the case of alimatravir still needs to be confirmed in large clinical trials.

Why start making a pill that may not work?

Usually, manufacturers wait for final trial results before investing in production. But that can delay access to new medicines by months, even years, because it takes a long time to get the technology, equipment and facilities in place to make a particular medicine.

MSD wants to change that.

It's giving manufacturers technical information on how to make alimatravir — what Paul Schaper, MSD's associate vice president for global public policy, calls a "recipe book" — and helping them prepare applications for regulatory approval.

MSD learnt this approach during COVID-19, when it licensed manufacturers to prepare production of its treatment, molnupiravir , before the treatment was approved for emergency use.

If alimatravir passes its trials and receives regulatory approval, MSD plans to supply it until generic manufacturers are ready .

Schaper told Bhekisisa MSD would supply it at a no-profit price in the 129 countries, including South Africa, covered by the licences. The company hasn't announced what price that would be.

Aspen wasn't among the companies initially licensed by Gilead Sciences, the company that makes lenacapavir, to make generic LEN and has since stopped pursuing a licence .

Its caution comes partly from COVID-19. Aspen manufactured Johnson & Johnson's vaccines and secured the right to supply its own branded version , Aspenovax, across Africa. But production for Johnson & Johnson ended and no orders for Aspenovax materialised .

Nicolaou says the monthly pill is a smaller gamble and makes more sense for Aspen because tablets are easier and cheaper to make than injections. Injections need specialised equipment and extra care to keep them sterile.

"Once bitten, twice shy," Nicolaou says.

Will SA buy the locally made pill?

A published estimate puts the cost of making a generic version of alimatravir at as little as $4.49 (roughly R77) per person per year to make, including a profit margin.

But that's not the price governments would necessarily pay. And Aspen hasn't said what it would charge.

But when the national health department chooses which supplier to buy from, price is only one factor, spokesperson Foster Mohale told Bhekisisa . If South Africa's medicines regulator approves and registers alimatravir, the department would consider buying it under its usual rules. Mohale said the department gives priority to local manufacturing but also weighs affordability, how well a medicine works and whether it can be provided over the long term. That still leaves Aspen without an answer on whether making the pill here would give it an edge in a tender.

A recent court case illustrates the difficulty local manufacturers face.

In October, the Pretoria High Court ordered the health department to reconsider suppliers for two HIV treatment medicines after Cipla Medpro Manufacturing , the Durban-based subsidiary of an Indian drug maker, challenged the tender process.

The ruling put Cipla back in contention, but didn't guarantee it a contract.

The case raises a wider question: how much should making a medicine here count when the government decides who to buy from? The government and drug makers are looking at that question through a joint task force set up at President Cyril Ramaphosa's request.

One of its priorities is giving preference to locally made medicines .

Nicolaou, who leads the industry's delegation, hopes the task force will help the government support local manufacturing while keeping medicines affordable.

Until then, Aspen can't be certain that government orders will justify its investment.

How can one pill protect someone for a month?

When HIV prevention activist Yvette Raphael heard about the monthly pill, she had a question: "Where is the medicine sitting?" After someone swallows the pill, the medicine travels through their bloodstream into your cells, where it becomes active. When HIV gets into a cell, it starts making copies of itself. Alimatravir stops the virus mid-copy .

In experiments involving primates , none of the animals given alimatravir weekly became infected, even when scientists repeatedly tried to infect them with a virus similar to HIV.

Studies in people have also found that the medicine remains inside cells for a long time. In one study, it took about nine to 12 days for the amount to fall by half after repeated doses.

That doesn't mean it stops working after 12 days. Researchers believe enough medicine could remain to protect someone until their next monthly dose.

A Phase 2 trial also investigated the medicine's safety and how long it remains in the body.

But none of this proves that one pill a month will prevent HIV infection in people.

That's what the final-stage trials, EXPrESSIVE-10 and EXPrESSIVE-11 , are testing: whether alimatravir prevents HIV infection and how it compares to existing daily HIV prevention tablets.

Will people remember to take a pill once a month?

Raphael, co-chair of the African Women Prevention Community Accountability Board , thinks a monthly tablet could appeal to people who struggle to take daily medication. "I may struggle by a daily, but I will not struggle by a monthly," she told Bhekisisa .

But taking a tablet less often creates another challenge: remembering when the next dose is due.

MSD's calculations suggest that after several monthly pills taken on time, people might have up to seven extra days to take their next pill. Researchers still need to verify that they would remain protected during that time.

In Tshwane, researchers at Wits RHI are already investigating whether people would choose the monthly pill.

They've received approval to add questions about alimatravir to their LEN4PrEP study . The study looks at what people choose when they're offered either LEN or the daily pill at government clinics in Tshwane. From the second half of November, they'll ask HIV-negative participants finishing the study whether they'd consider monthly oral HIV prevention.

They expect responses from about 1 500 people.

Study leader Saiqa Mullick calls this "planning for success": preparing for a new medicine while researchers are still establishing whether it works.

There's good reason to investigate people's preferences.

In LEN4PrEP , more than half of those who chose the six-monthly injection had never used HIV prevention medicine before. And Bhekisisa's analysis of early LEN roll-out data found that about one in three recipients were new to HIV prevention medication.

Close 

But preferences can change. In the INSIGHT study , young women initially preferred a monthly pill, then chose the six-monthly injection a month later — without having tried either.

Community representatives have also helped shape the alimatravir trials . HIV prevention advocacy organisation Avac supports groups of about 15 people for each trial.

Now they're considering practical questions, including where people could collect the pill and what would help them remember their doses.

Would the monthly pill be worth the money?

An early modelling study that hasn't yet been checked by other scientists , compared what might happen if health services in South Africa and Western Kenya offered alimatravir, LEN or both.

It suggested LEN could prevent more HIV infections, while the monthly pill could cost less to provide. Offering both might prevent the most infections, but would also cost the most.

The researchers assumed people would take only two of every three monthly pills and that the pill would cut their risk of getting HIV by 95% during the months they took it.

Health economist Lise Jamieson of South Africa's Health Economics and Epidemiology Research Office (HE²RO) calls that assumption (the 95% figure) "brave".

HE²RO is conducting its own calculations, but the results aren't available yet. For now, neither the pill's effectiveness nor its eventual price is known.

What is clear is that getting manufacturers ready, understanding what people want and planning how to deliver the medicine needn't wait for the final trial results. By granting licences early , MSD gave generic manufacturers a head start.

"We shouldn't be doing those things sequentially," Mullick says.

The stakes are high. In 2025, an estimated 360 people acquired HIV each day in South Africa, according to UNAids .

If alimatravir works, preparing early could shorten the wait for another choice of HIV prevention medication.

But for Aspen, success in the laboratory won't necessarily mean success at the factory. Even if the pill works, the South African government may buy it elsewhere.

This story was produced by the Bhekisisa Centre for Health Journalism.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 25, 2026
World.content:
press review

Zambia Opposition Leader Indicted on Treason Charges

Zambia's main opposition leader Brian Mundubile and 12 others have been formally indicted on treason charges over an alleged plot to overthrow President Hakainde Hichilema's government. Prosecutors allege the group planned the operation between April and August 2026, with Mundubile and a businessman accused of funding military training in Russia. Mundubile, who challenged Hichilema in the August election, has denied wrongdoing. The case comes amid growing concerns over political repression. Rights groups have accused Zambian authorities of political repression in the wake of the August election, which international observer missions said was marred by irregularities. If convicted, Mundubile faces up to life imprisonment. Hichilema's first term also drew concerns over political freedoms, with opposition parties and civil society groups accusing his government of curbing dissent, allegations the government has rejected.

Veteran Nollywood Actor Pete Edochie Dies



Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Nollywood's most celebrated stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced. He died in the south-eastern city of Enugu. The cause of death has not been disclosed. Edochie rose to international prominence in 1987 for his portrayal of Okonkwo in the television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart. His career spanned several decades, with film appearances including Igodo, Rituals, and Lionheart. He received Nigeria's Member of the Order of the Niger honour in 2003. He is survived by his wife and six children, including actors Yul and Linc Edochie. In recent years, his memorable film scenes and distinctive expressions also gained popularity among younger audiences through social media memes.

UNAIDS Warns Funding Cuts Threaten HIV Progress

UNAIDS has warned that decades of progress in the fight against HIV and AIDS could be reversed by international funding cuts and growing attacks on human rights and gender equality. Its latest report highlights a $4.3 billion funding gap in low- and middle-income countries, despite 32.1 million of the estimated 40 million people living with HIV receiving treatment. Prevention services have been particularly affected, with 446,000 fewer people accessing pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in 2025 compared with the previous year. The agency warned that reduced funding for testing, treatment and community organisations could drive up infections and deaths, threatening the global target of ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030. UNAIDS said that achieving the target could prevent 3.2 million new infections and avert 1.3 million AIDS-related deaths by the end of the decade.

Amnesty Urges Egypt to Reverse Mada Masr Closure

Amnesty International has urged Egyptian authorities to reverse the closure of independent news outlet Mada Masr and drop charges against its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, ahead of an appeal hearing scheduled for 25 November. Attalah was convicted in October of operating a website without a licence, fined three million Egyptian pounds and ordered to close the publication. Amnesty says the case forms part of a wider crackdown on independent journalism and freedom of expression in Egypt, where journalists and human rights defenders face arrests and prosecution over their work. The organisation has called on international partners, including the European Union, to pressure Cairo to protect press freedom. Attalah also faces a separate case involving allegations of publishing false news, which could carry a prison sentence of up to one year.

Women's Rights Network Sounds Alarm Over Abductions and Sexual Violence in Sudan

The Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa (SIHA Network) has reported the abduction of 28 women and girls fleeing fighting in Sudan's Blue Nile state, alongside 15 cases of conflict-related sexual violence against girls under 18. The organisation alleged that Rapid Support Forces (RSF) fighters and allied militias were responsible for the abductions as civilians fled renewed clashes. More than 7,000 families are reportedly heading towards Damazin, with many facing shortages of food, safe drinking water, transport and healthcare. SIHA has warned that the withdrawal of international aid organisations is placing additional pressure on local responders and called for urgent protection and humanitarian assistance for displaced communities. The International Organization for Migration estimates that Blue Nile state was hosting about 443,494 internally displaced people by the end of October.

Malawi Denies Receiving Request From Pakistan to Deport Fake Honorary Consul Suspect

Pakistan is facing accusations of misleading the public after Malawi denied receiving any formal request from Islamabad to arrest and deport businessman Mahmood Azhar Chaudhry. An investigation by Nyasa Times found that Pakistan claimed to have engaged Malawian authorities over Chaudhry, who allegedly posed as its honorary consul in Malawi between 2018 and 2022, despite Pakistan denying he ever held the position. Malawi's Foreign Affairs Ministry said that it received no diplomatic note or official communication seeking his deportation. The controversy is linked to land disputes in Lilongwe, where more than 15,000 households claim to have lost land through transactions involving companies associated with Chaudhry. Critics said that Pakistan must produce documentary evidence of its alleged diplomatic engagement with Malawi to demonstrate that it took action.

Close 

Morocco Threatens Legal Action After Senegal Reinstated as 2025 AFCON Champions

Morocco's football federation has rejected the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling restoring Senegal's 2025 Africa Cup of Nations title, alleging irregularities in the arbitration process and threatening further legal action. The Moroccan federation questioned alleged communication between German arbitrator Ulrich Haas and the Senegalese Football Federation president shortly before the verdict. CAS overturned the CAF Appeal Board's decision to award Morocco a 3-0 victory, reinstating Senegal's original 1-0 win in the January final. It ruled that the match had resumed under the referee's authority and was completed, meaning Senegal had not forfeited. CAF has said it respects the ruling and will take the necessary steps to implement it. The unanimous CAS decision brings Senegal's title dispute to a close at the arbitration level. Morocco's threat of further legal action leaves the possibility of another challenge open.

World.title: Nigeria: Fabricated Newspaper Front Page Falsely Claims Nigerian President Bola Tinubu Promised Petrol At N200 Per Litre If Re-Elected
World.content:
Fabricated newspaper front page falsely claims Nigerian president Bola Tinubu promised petrol at N200 per litre if re-elected

IN SHORT: According to this newspaper-style graphic, Nigerian president Bola Tinibu promised to reduce the price of petrol to N200 per litre if he won a second term. But we found no evidence that such a newspaper exists or that Tinubu made the promise.

Fuel prices remain a major political issue in Nigeria ahead of the general election scheduled for 16 January 2027.



On 29 May 2023, his first day in office, president Bola Tinubu announced the removal of the petrol subsidy. Prices subsequently rose from around N200 to above N1,000 per litre, driving up the cost of living for many Nigerians.

Against this backdrop, a graphic resembling the front page of a newspaper called "The Daily Tribune" began circulating on Facebook.

Dated 1 September 2026, it carries the headline: "Tinubu: I will reduce Petrol Pump Price to N200/ltr after 2027 Election."

The graphic also claims Tinubu promised to make N1 equal to $1 before March 2027, and that Nigerians would no longer pay for electricity.

Tinubu is seeking reelection under the All Progressives Congress (APC).

The same claim also appeared here and here. (Note: See other instances of the claim at the end of this report).

But is this front page genuine? We checked.

Graphic is fabricated

Africa Check found no Nigerian newspaper, print or online, called "The Daily Tribune".

We also found no credible media reports or statements from the presidency or the APC supporting any of the three promises attributed to Tinubu.

The graphic contains inconsistent fonts and layout, raising further doubts about its authenticity.

Tinubu's administration has consistently rejected calls to reinstate the petrol subsidy. In May 2026, finance minister Taiwo Oyedele said the government would not bring back the subsidy because it created economic distortions.

In August 2026, Tinubu defended his administration's decision to remove the subsidy, describing an opponent's subsidy proposal as "serious ignorance" of the economy.

There is no credible evidence Tinubu made any of the promises attributed to him. The claim is false
