World.title: Trump's birthright citizenship restrictions struck down again by DC federal judge he called 'hater'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A DC federal judge, previously dubbed by President Donald Trump as an "anti- Trump Hater," blocked Trump's second attempt to restrict birthright citizenship in a Wednesday ruling.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who was recently in Trump's crosshairs after ruling against efforts to shut down the Kennedy Center for renovations and add Trump's name to the cultural institution, issued a 67-page ruling striking down an August executive order that barred U.S. -born children whose parents are suspected terrorists or gang members, or children born through surrogacy to foreign parents, from citizenship eligibility.

Cooper's ruling comes months after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's initial executive order, signed on his first day back in office. The order attempted to deny birthright citizenship to U.S.-born children whose mothers were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor green card holders.

WHITE HOUSE RIPS ‘ACTIVIST’ BIDEN JUDGE WHO UPENDED TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP ORDER

"As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws," Cooper ruled.

Trump's second executive order was already partially blocked on Sept. 2 by U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland, whose injunction protected U.S.-born children of mothers who were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor lawful permanent residents.

Cooper's ruling expanded protections beyond that class to include additional children born to certain foreign government and international organization employees, parents deemed "alien enemies" by the administration and foreign parents who used commercial surrogacy services in the U.S.

"The merits in this case are clear-cut. The Supreme Court has twice confirmed that all children born in this country are U.S. citizens, save only for the small handful who are not subject to U.S. law," Cooper wrote.

In addition to the Supreme Court's June ruling in Trump v. Barbara, Cooper referred to the high court's ruling in United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which determined that a man born to Chinese immigrants was a protected U.S. citizen under the 14th Amendment.

SEN ERIC SCHMITT SEEKS TO END BIRTH TOURISM, REVOKE CITIZENSHIP FOR BABIES OF FOREIGN DIPLOMATS

Cooper noted that Wong Kim Ark established narrow exceptions to birthright citizenship, including for children of foreign diplomats, children born aboard foreign public ships and children of enemy forces occupying American territory.

"While the Fourteenth Amendment may theoretically permit new exceptions beyond those listed in Wong Kim Ark, Congress has not authorized any such exceptions," Cooper wrote.

Cooper argued that membership in a terrorist organization alone does not satisfy the historical exception to birthright citizenship for children of enemy forces occupying U.S. territory. He criticized the Trump administration's contention that foreign invaders could occupy American territory without actually holding it as an "outside-the-box understanding" of what constitutes an occupation.

"To recap, a parent’s purported status as an alien enemy, standing alone, cannot strip a U.S.-born child of his right to birthright citizenship," Cooper wrote. "The alien-enemy exception, properly understood, applies only to children born to hostile enemy forces in temporarily occupied U.S. territory."

Cooper also rejected Trump's attempt to deny birthright citizenship to children born through commercial surrogacy arrangements involving foreign parents, finding that the circumstances of their birth do not exempt them from U.S. jurisdiction.

"Indeed, foreign parents choose surrogacy arrangements in the United States precisely to have the child be governed by U.S. law and have the surrogacy process ‘supervised by a court.," Cooper wrote.

TRUMP TO ASK SUPREME COURT TO REHEAR BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CASE AFTER 'INSANE DECISION'

He noted that, prior to Trump's second executive order, the State Department recognized the citizenship of children born on American soil regardless of whether they were born through surrogacy.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal the decision and request that the executive order be temporarily enforced while the litigation works its way through the courts, a process that could take months.

"This is just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by Obama attempting to thwart President Trump’s commonsense agenda," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The birthright citizenship executive order is consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court."

The Justice Department could seek temporary relief from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit or seek intervention from the Supreme Court. Fox News Digital reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE WITH TIES TO ANTI-TRUMP CONSPIRACY THEORY HIT WITH MISCONDUCT COMPLAINT

In addition to ruling against Trump's Kennedy Center renovation efforts, Cooper ruled that Trump's Department of Government Efficiency must turn over records requested in a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Trump has called Cooper one of the "Radical Left Democrats."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Cooper is also married to Amy Jeffress, who was Biden’s personal lawyer in 2025 and previously did some work for the Jan. 6 committee.

World.title: UConn head coach Geno Auriemma goes scorched earth on his team after loss to South Carolina
World.content:
UConn women's basketball coach Geno Auriemma has never been shy about speaking his mind.

The fiery legend recently took his entire sport to task over the rampant NIL paydays being awarded to incoming freshmen, showing that he still won't hesitate to empty the tank and tell it like it is.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Auriemma's sights were turned inward today, though, as he went scorched earth on his own team following their defeat at the hands of the South Carolina Gamecocks.

GENO AURIEMMA, DAWN STALEY SHAKE HANDS AFTER HOSTILE SCRAP LAST SEASON, AS NCAA MAKES HANDSHAKE RULE CHANGE

The loss dropped the Huskies to 4-3 on the season, and in his postgame news conference, an exasperated Auriemma clearly wasn't happy with the results so far.

"I'm having a really hard time coaching this team. You might be able to tell that," Auriemma said at the podium. "I've got to figure it out. But it would be nice if I could get a little help."

DUKE COACH JON SCHEYER SAYS BLUE DEVILS' UPSET LOSS TO MICHIGAN STATE FELT LIKE AN 'OUT-OF-BODY EXPERIENCE'

While all of their losses have come against top-ranked teams, UConn has never lost three games in the month of November, and Auriemma is clearly not handling this skid (or his team's demeanor) very well.

"It's just so out of character for anybody that's watched UConn play for 30-some years," he said. "I don't even recognize it."

IS IT WEIRD FOR A COACH TO NOT TALK TO HIS TEAM AFTER A GAME, OR IS IT EXTREMELY WEIRD?

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Auriemma bemoaned his team's inability to handle any sort of adversity, something his eight championship-winning teams were clearly adept at.

The 18 turnovers certainly didn't help, nor did shooting 27% from the field.

Now, Auriemma is faced with a turnaround that he isn't used to, and although there's plenty of season left, this is uncharted territory for a program that has become accustomed to winning and winning big.

I don't doubt a coach like Auriemma's ability to right the ship, but he's clearly fed up with the current iteration of his team, and it's hard for anyone to blame him.

World.title: 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed: What to know
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed ahead of a nor'easter in New York City, marking the first time the parade has been moved because of weather.

The parade has been moved from Thursday to Saturday, amid a forecast of strong winds and heavy rain, according to The Associated Press.

"With severe weather expected on Thanksgiving Day, and out of an abundance of caution, in partnership with the City the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will be postponed," Macy's said in a statement.

"Our team is now working through the complex operational logistics required to bring the Parade to life on Saturday, and we will share additional details as they are finalized," the statement continued. "We are incredibly grateful to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who make this extraordinary tradition possible. We can’t wait to celebrate 100 years of Parade magic together on Saturday."

A Thanksgiving storm is expected to hit New York City, as well as the tri-state area, with heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding in some places expected.

The iconic parade draws thousands of spectators along the 2.5-mile route, which begins in Manhattan's Upper West Side to Herald Square on 34th Street, the site of the Macy's department store.

An area of low pressure developing off the Southeast coast will push northward into the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast beginning Wednesday night. The storm is expected to intensify through Thanksgiving Day before clearing out on Friday, according to the FOX Forecast Center and the National Weather Service.

This story is breaking. Please check back for updates.

World.title: Shane Gillis wishes ex-girlfriend 'the best' after tell-all essay accusing him of cheating and 'red flags'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Comedian Shane Gillis’ ex-girlfriend wrote a lengthy piece this week about their yearlong relationship, saying his controversial "Saturday Night Live" joke about women at the gym reflects how he treats women behind closed doors.

In an essay published by The Cut, content creator Grace Brassel wrote that the comedian pressured her into quitting her job, isolated her from friends and family and cheated on her before their split in August 2025.

Speaking to Fox News Digital, Gillis responded to Brassel’s claims, saying, "Grace and I had some good times together. Breakups are tough, and I wish her the best."

'SNL' CAST MEMBER MICHAEL CHE SHRUGS OFF SHANE GILLIS' MONOLOGUE JOKE SAYING, 'THAT'S COMEDY'

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Brassel said she wrote the essay to help other women.

"I wrote this essay to help other women, and for them to know there is a life past it, these kinds of relationships. The beautiful DMs I am receiving mean so much to me. No matter what age you are, this can happen to you, and I always wished someone could have told me sooner. I hope it can help more girls speak out and stand up for themselves," Brassel said.

Brassel referenced Gillis’ recent controversial comments regarding women’s gym attire on "SNL" being that of "whores," writing that she wasn’t the "least bit surprised."

"Until last August, I was in a yearlong relationship with Shane, and his comments didn’t faze me. After our time together, how do I think he feels about women? He doesn’t like them much," Brassel wrote.

The pair began talking in May 2024 after Brassel sent him direct messages on Instagram, and she initially described their whirlwind romance as a "dream." However, she explained that when they eventually moved in together, it was a "nonstop party," which made it difficult for her to keep up her day job as a social media manager.

She claimed Gillis encouraged her to quit, and when they moved to Pennsylvania to shoot his Netflix series "Tires," she felt as though his expectations of her changed.

"I felt like I was turning into a 25-year-old housewife, someone who cooked, cleaned, did the laundry, and waited for her man to come home from a long day at work. I never said I was capable of all that, but it felt like an expectation," Brassel wrote. "When things weren’t exactly to his liking, he would tell me that I wasn’t ‘being good.’ You know, the way you would talk to a dog."

'SATURDAY NIGHT LIVE' STAR WOULD SIT SHANE GILLIS DOWN 'LIKE A LITTLE KID' OVER PROVOCATIVE MONOLOGUE

She added that she ignored many "red flags," claiming he would say something "remarkably cruel" and play it off as a joke, and noted she felt she needed to start dressing more "conservatively."

"I cried every day. I would call my mom in tears, telling her that I didn’t know if I was meant for this life. My six-month free trial of Sweet Shane Gillis had run out, and it was time for me to start paying," she wrote.

Brassel alleged that things came to a head on the Fourth of July, when she said she discovered Gillis’ infidelity after going through his phone and finding explicit messages with another woman that had been going on for months.

"I scrolled and realized they had been sexting for months and had probably had in-person encounters as well. The floor seemed to give way beneath my feet," she recalled.

Brassel admitted she "snapped" when confronting him. She described punching a hole in the bathroom wall and throwing her phone and a chair before the two eventually went through an on-and-off breakup. She claimed they had considered reconciling, but that Gillis said they could never mend things after she began telling others how he treated her.

BROADCAST BIAS: FEMINIST FREAKOUT OVER SHANE GILLIS COMMENT IS THE REAL JOKE

Brassel added that the outrage over Gillis’ recent monologue on "SNL" gave her "some kind of closure."

"He had flown too close to the sun, and people were finally seeing the man I knew. I had spent so long protecting this part of my life, afraid to speak publicly about it, and then he just did it himself. Finally, some initiative," Brassel wrote at the end of the essay.

She also addressed the attention the essay has gotten in a video posted to her 124,000 followers on Instagram, saying she’s been working on the essay for a month and was fully aware of the "discourse" it would cause.

"I'm well aware of the discourse that was going to happen," Brassel said. "And I weighed out my options, and I think that it is a net positive, no matter what. I can handle the heat. I'm in the kitchen, girl. I can handle the heat."

SWIFTIES CLAIM TRAVIS KELCE DID THE UNSPEAKABLE BY LIKING SHANE GILLIS' 'SNL' MONOLOGUE & THEY'RE NOT HAPPY

Gillis addressed the controversy he spurred on "SNL," telling host Joe Rogan earlier this month that he had promised the show’s producers "no controversy."

"Not to defend ‘SNL,’ they don't approve it. I mean, they could shut it down," Gillis said on "The Joe Rogan Experience."

"But you don't write your set and give it to them," he added. "Unless you’re not a comedian. I’m sure non-comics, they write the set for them. They have writers that write the monologue for them."

"The funniest part was... they were like, ‘What’s going on with the monologue?’ And I was like, ‘It’s not great, but I don’t say anything bad.’ The whole time, I was like, ‘Fellas, I’m giving you a solid C-minus of a monologue, but I promise there’s no controversy. I’m calling myself fat for f---ing 10 minutes. That’s it.'"

Gillis drew criticism from entertainment figures, including actor Dan Levy and former "SNL" cast member Ego Nwodim, after joking during his opening monologue last month that women at gyms "just dress like whores now."

The appearance marked his third time hosting the NBC sketch seies, which briefly hired and then fired him in 2019 as a cast member over a podcast appearance where he made jokes deemed offensive.

Fox News Digital’s Taylor Penley contributed to this report.

World.title: Thanksgiving flights booked after key hour face double the risk of major delay
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

As U.S. airports brace for a brutal Thanksgiving rush, travel analysts are warning passengers about a common scheduling mistake that raises the odds of a disrupted trip: booking a flight after 9 a.m.

"Flights departing after 9 a.m. are generally twice as likely to be delayed as those departing between 5 a.m. and 8 a.m.," according to Hopper data.

The alert lands at an uneasy moment for American flyers, with 69% now ranking delays and cancellations as their top booking concern, according to a Hopper consumer survey.

TSA DETECTS SUSPICIOUS MOVEMENT IN TRAVELER'S SUITCASE DURING SECURITY SCREENING

A storm system bringing heavy rain, wind and thunderstorms has already swept across the Gulf Coast and Southeast and is bearing down on major Mid-Atlantic and Northeast hubs through Thanksgiving Day, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

Confidence has also been tested by recent technical scares.

Travelers were shaken by the Nov. 13 FAA ground stop sparked by telecommunications instability.

The ground stop halted departures nationwide, resulting in more than 12,400 cancellations, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation and the FAA.

TRAVELERS BUSTED AT AIRPORT WITH OVER 3,000 TARANTULAS HIDDEN AWAY IN THEIR SOCKS

An isolated outage also prompted a brief ground stop at Chicago O'Hare International Airport on Nov. 24, as Fox News Digital previously reported.

How the clock turns against travelers

Across U.S. domestic flights from 2023 through 2025, just 11% of departures scheduled before 8 a.m. arrived 15 or more minutes late, according to Bureau of Transportation Statistics data analyzed by DelayGuard.

CLICK HERE TO 

Because commercial jets typically fly multiple legs a day, a storm or runway bottleneck in one hub can affect later routes. Late-arriving aircraft are responsible for 41% of all U.S. delay minutes, an AirDelay analysis noted.

Sunrise departures sidestep that chain reaction.

"The aircraft has spent the night at the airport, so there is no late inbound flight to wait for," DelayGuard reported. Morning crews are also just beginning their shifts, so earlier snags on the schedule will not hold up boarding, according to DelayGuard.

Passengers whose morning flights are disrupted have far more later departures available to rebook.

Evening snags leave fewer options, according to AirDelay and CLEAR.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

In addition, travelers willing to brave a 4 a.m. alarm often score lower fares on a 6 a.m. flight than on a 10 a.m. departure, The Points Guy reported.

"Taking a morning flight gives you a greater chance of having a plane and crew ready to go," Gary Leff, a Texas-based travel industry expert and author of the blog "View From The Wing," told Fox News Digital.

"There's an opportunity to address maintenance issues overnight. So [there's] a likelihood of starting the day with an aircraft that's ready," Leff continued.

"Crew have limits in their duty day. They could run out of allowable time with late flights that get delayed," he added. "Early flights mean starting fresh, and you aren't risking your pilots or flight attendants 'timing out.'"

Why the day matters

Picking the right day of the week can sway the odds as well.

Tuesday consistently ranks as the most punctual day at major U.S. airports, with fewer than 19% of departures arriving late — followed closely by Wednesday, according to Bureau of Transportation Statistics records reviewed by DelayGuard.

Sunday sits at the bottom, with a quarter of flights running behind schedule, DelayGuard reported.

Leff said delays have a ripple effect.

"Delays stack throughout the day. If you're on the third or fourth flight operated by your crew or aircraft that day, there were several opportunities for them to get delayed during the day," Leff said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

During peak holiday windows, timing can protect a traveler's wallet, too.

Flying home on Sunday can be the costliest option, with round-trip domestic fares averaging $604 compared with roughly $350 for passengers who wait until Monday or Tuesday, according to Hopper's 2026 Holiday Travel Index.

"Early flights mean more recovery options."

Aviation officials urge passengers to build extra buffer time into their commute, to stay subscribed to airline alerts and to check real-time airport conditions through the FAA's National Airspace System status portal.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Early flights mean more recovery options," said Leff. "Not only are there more same-day options left on the schedule, but available seats are less likely to have been taken by other passengers that were delayed."

World.title: Rams star Puka Nacua's MCL completely tore off the bone as details emerge from season-ending injury: report
World.content:
The details have come out on Puka Nacua's season-ending injury, and the details are grotesque.

The Los Angeles Rams star suffered the injury on the final offensive play of the team's 20-13 win over the Washington Commanders in Week 9. The 25-year-old sustained a grade 3 MCL tear, which means the ligament completely tore off the tibia, which is the shinbone, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter.

In addition to the MCL tear, Schefter said that Nacua "had a tear off the posterior oblique portion of the MCL as well."

World.title: Steelers cut Aaron Rodgers after he blasts coach Mike McCarthy in fiery exit interview
World.content:
The Pittsburgh Steelers released quarterback Aaron Rodgers on Wednesday shortly after he described his head coach Mike McCarthy as “unhealthy” in a critical interview following the Steelers’ decision to deactivate Rodgers for the team’s upcoming game.

Speaking to ESPN’s Pat McAfee on Wednesday, Rodgers accused McCarthy of falling asleep during team meetings and missing walkthroughs in the weeks leading up to his benching.

“Last Thursday, I was in a quarterback meeting and in 10 minutes I heard snoring,” Rodgers said of his head coach. “Thursday, he misses an offensive meeting. Friday, he misses walkthrough... Saturday, he misses the team meeting.”

Added Rodgers: “If you’re sleeping in meetings, you’re unhealthy.”

Following the interview, the team announced Rodgers had been released.

The Steelers are 6-4 and have lost their last two games. On Tuesday night, the team announced that Rodgers would be inactive for the team’s game Friday against the Denver Broncos.

The Steelers did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Rodgers’ interview.

Rodgers blasted McCarthy while speaking to McAfee, alleging his coach even broke down a team huddle with a “one, two, three, Packers!” last week, confusing players. (McCarthy was previously Rodgers’s coach in Green Bay from 2006 to 2018.)

“Everybody knows what’s going on. He’s missing walkthroughs, you don’t think everybody else knows?,” Rodgers said. “Does any other quarterback have these issues?”

Rodgers added: “It’s a very delicate situation, the coaching staff is worried about their job security, the players are worried about their money and jobs security.”

Rodgers said he is willing to speak out about McCarthy because of the financial security his long career has afforded him.

Rodgers also claimed McCarthy hasn’t connected with Pittsburgh’s defense, and rebuffed Rodgers’ efforts to get him to connect with players on that side of the ball.

Rodgers also said McCarthy has not been watching film and lacks an intimate knowledge of the team’s week-to-week game plans.

“I don’t expect people to come out strong in my defense even though everybody knows the truth,” the quarterback said.

Rodgers said issues with McCarthy began in training camp, and he also accused his coach of harboring ill will over his dismissal from the Packers.

“In Mike’s mind, I got him fired in 2018. He told a staff member he still doesn’t forgive me for getting him fired in 2018,” Rodgers claimed.

In the hours before his benching, Rodgers said he brought up his issues with McCarthy in an in-person conversation and delivered him an ultimatum to either address the problems or grant him a release. Rodgers claimed McCarthy did not admit to sleeping during team meetings, and the idea of his benching was not raised.

“I found out that I was going to be inactive on a phone call last night from Pat Freiermuth,” Rodgers said, referring to the tight end.

The quarterback repeatedly said his stories are not “hyperbole” or “opinion,” but instead first-hand accounts and facts.

McCarthy spoke with reporters at a press conference in the wake of Rodgers’ comments, and refuted multiple claims. McCarthy said it was “not accurate” that he held a grudge with Rodgers over his firing in 2018, and also said he made multiple attempts to reach Rodgers to inform him of his benching.

But the coach also largely avoided getting into the finer details of Rodgers’s accusations.

“We are focused on beating Denver,” McCarthy said.

World.title: More than 700,000 Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine war, new estimate suggests
World.content:
More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in Ukraine, according to a new projection based on leaked official data, an estimate that sheds new light on the staggering cost of President Vladimir Putin’s war.

The grim assessment comes more than 4½ years after the Kremlin’s invasion of its neighbor, an all-out war that has consumed Russian society. The death toll has been mounting with each painstaking ground assault, with no end to the conflict in sight despite pressure from President Donald Trump for Kyiv to make a deal.

The leak from Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat — released by Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers earlier this month — reveals that at least 490,000 Russian soldiers had been killed in Ukraine based on registered deaths as of the end of September. That’s according to breakdowns by a range of independent media, including the BBC and others, that were published this week. But one exiled Russian media outlet, Meduza, also used the leaked mortality data to project the total number of military deaths, including those that have not yet been recorded.

Meduza estimates that number to be 720,000.

NBC News did not have access to the leaked data and could not authenticate it or independently confirm these numbers.

Neither Moscow nor Kyiv provide regular updates on their battlefield losses.

Mediazona, along with the BBC Russian Service and a team of volunteers, has been compiling a separate named list of Russian war dead using open-source data for years, given the difficulty of gauging the true impact of the war on Russian society.

In its analysis, Mediazona said it arrived at the 490,000 war dead number from the 29.7 million records it obtained from the hackers that covered nearly all death registrations in Russia from early 2021 through September this year, based mainly on records with an “explicit military cause of death” and court rulings declaring people dead.

The leaked data was cross-checked against Mediazona’s own named list and matched 95% of the records, as well as the publicly accessible national Probate Registry, a database of inheritance cases, and Rosstat’s own official mortality statistics, the outlet said.

Mediazona said it also checked against possible data tempering and fake military death injections by cross-referencing a unique vital record number that every death registration carries, and court rulings, which often cite death record numbers.

“We are confident that this data is genuine,” the outlet said, adding that fabricating a dataset of this scale from scratch would be “impossible” especially as it checks out against official registries.

The hackers shared leaked data with a number of other exiled Russian media outlets and the BBC, who all arrived at a figure close to the 490,000 reported by Mediazona. A similar estimate of half a million Russian troops killed was also shared by a senior British defense official in September.

Before the new analysis of the data in the Rosstat leak, the verified named list of Russia’s war dead compiled by Mediazona and the BBC stood at just over 289,000. It was based on obituaries, local news and official registries, and was the only publicly available database containing the fallen soldiers’ names.

The Russian Defense Ministry has not officially updated its death toll in Ukraine since the early months of the war, when then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu said it stood at nearly 6,000.

Mediazona warned that due to a considerable lag in military death registrations, Rosstat may not yet have finished capturing deaths from 2025. “That means the leaked records through late September — however authentic and reliable they are — still fall short of the true death toll,” it said.

World.title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed for 1st time in history
World.content:
For the first time in history, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed, Macy's said Wednesday.

The 100th annual parade will now kick off Saturday at 8:30 a.m.

The historic move comes as a powerful coastal storm is set to impact the area Thursday.

Safety concerns regarding the storm, crowds and the balloons contributed to the decision.

"The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our city and agency partners, we've made the decision to move the celebration due to expected severe weather," Macy's said in a statement. "Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday."

The operational challenges involved in shifting the date of the parade are substantial. The parade involves plenty of marching bands and other performers who had been expecting the event on Thursday, and now will need to make alternative arrangements.

Fans who came into New York City to see Wednesday night's balloon inflation seemed alright with the decision was made to postpone the parade.

"So much goes into the parade each year. It's like a tradition each year to watch, get up early and watch the parade with my whole family," one person said. "I'm really excited that they're changing it because so much work goes into it every year, and people come from all over to help with the balloons. So I'm really excited that they're still making an effort to do it. Even on a different day, it's still just as special."

The parade was previously suspended from 1942 to 1944 during World War II, but it has never been postponed due to weather.

This is a developing story. Check back soon for more information.

World.title: Stocks turn volatile as Jensen Huang rebound rally fades
World.content:
Stocks swung wildly on Wednesday, plunging in early trading before paring losses by the close.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite tumbled more than 1,000 points early in the session, but regained ground to close down 148 points, or 0.6%, at 23,586. The S&P 500 fell 0.2% on the day, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.3%.

Stocks have slumped in recent weeks amid concerns surrounding the health of the artificial intelligence sector. Shares of Anthropic, the AI lab that staged the largest initial stock offering in history last week, declined 7.6% to $75.66, below its IPO price of $83 per share.

Investors are increasingly questioning whether the AI sector can justify the enormous investment in data centers. Compounding those fears just before the Thanksgiving holiday are the Trump administration's plans to raise tariffs on China and other major trading partners.

"At this point, between the AI angst and the newly announced tariffs, it doesn't look like the Santa Claus rally is in store for us this year," Chris Zaccarelli, Chief Investment Officer for Northlight Asset Management, said in an email.

With Democrats set to control Congress next year and winning many state-level seats, AI companies may face more headwinds as lawmakers push back against data center construction, according to investment adviser Capital Economics. Even before the midterm elections, investors were increasingly questioning the finances of AI companies, it added.

Investors are also bracing for the impact of more interest rate hikes starting in December, with expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise borrowing costs to counter rising inflation. That could make it more difficult for businesses, including AI companies, to borrow money to fuel growth.

World.title: Maps show where Thanksgiving storms could disrupt holiday
World.content:
Various types of severe weather are expected to impact large stretches of the United States this week, potentially disrupting Thanksgiving plans and hampering travel for Americans along both coasts and into the middle of the country.

A storm developing Wednesday over Florida threatened to bring flooding to southeastern states before quickly traveling up the coast and moving into the Northeast in time for Thanksgiving. Forecasts showed the storm could generate high winds and heavy rain across the region, while areas in the Midwest, including St. Louis, could see snow around the holiday.

CBS News

In New York City, organizers of the iconic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade announced the parade is being postponed until Saturday due to the coming storm. It's the first time in the parade's 100-year history that it's been postponed, although it was not held at all from 1942 to 1944 because of World War II. In 1971, the balloons were grounded due to strong winds, but the parade still went on.

While the city isn't expected to get excessive rain, a relatively rare High Wind Warning was issued, and wind gusts could reach 60 mph.

CBS News

More than 80 million people were under alerts Wednesday as the National Weather Service warned of powerful wind gusts, potentially as intense as 70 mph, that could impact a massive stretch of the East Coast, from South Carolina up to Massachusetts.

CBS News

In addition to New York, other major cities like Boston, Philadelphia and Washington, D.C., would likely receive chilly rainfall on Thanksgiving, but forecasters expected most metropolitan hubs to be spared from the highest amounts. The weather service did note a flash-flooding threat impacting the Southeast on Wednesday could shift toward New York City by Thursday.

CBS News

Up to 5 inches of rain could fall in other places, especially in southeastern states like Florida and the Carolinas. As the storm continues to develop, those areas could also face damaging winds, tornadoes and, potentially, waterspouts, forecasters said. The storm system already brought more than half a foot of rain to Miami, causing flooding in South Florida.

Interior portions of the eastern U.S. and some spots in the Midwest could receive their first measurable snowfall of the season around Thanksgiving. The weather service issued several winter storm warnings and winter weather advisories for parts of Illinois and Missouri, including St. Louis, through Thursday evening, as sections of both states brace for up to 6 inches, or even 9 inches in certain areas, of snow.

CBS News

"Roads, especially bridges and overpasses, will likely become slick and hazardous. The weight of snow on tree limbs may down power lines and could cause sporadic power outages," the weather service in St. Louis wrote in a Wednesday advisory, which recommended that people delay travel completely, if possible.

World.title: China may have surveilled Alice Huang amid affair with Nvidia CEO
World.content:
China's Ministry of State Security may have been surveilling Alice Huang and sought information from her after her affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang began, U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staffers Tuesday, according to people familiar with the briefing.

While there are still gaps in what U.S. intelligence agencies know, there is no indication to date that Alice Huang was specifically tasked with collecting information on Jensen Huang or that she passed information of significant value to the Chinese intelligence service.

But she was known to U.S. intelligence agencies to have been in contact with an MSS officer starting at least in spring 2025, multiple sources said, and her contacts with the agency raised counterintelligence concerns among U.S. intelligence officials. China's intelligence services rely not only on trained officers and formally recruited assets but also on citizens who are obliged under Chinese law to provide assistance when called upon.

Congressional staffers were also told that Kang Wei, believed to be Alice Huang's husband, had more extensive ties to the MSS, people familiar with the briefing said.

The New York Times was first to report on the briefing.

The two-hour briefing for House and Senate Intelligence Committee staffers, which included senior analysts from across the U.S. intelligence community, came two days after President Trump intervened to secure Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, despite national security concerns raised by some of his senior advisers.

Alice Huang was a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company under U.S. investigation for potentially diverting sensitive American technology to China.

Concerns about Alice Huang were laid out in a classified memo drafted this spring by Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio that summarized U.S. intelligence, including intercepted communications involving the former Megaspeed executive. It was intended to ensure senior administration officials involved in relevant policy decisions were aware of the potential counterintelligence risks posed by her interactions with Jensen Huang.

Among those who received the memo were Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and senior White House staff. Rubio also briefed the president on intelligence.

The memo was not provided during Tuesday's briefing, despite requests from both congressional intelligence committees to see it.

China has denied allegations that Alice Huang is a spy.

Shortly after the existence of the memo came to light earlier this month, Jensen Huang acknowledged that he had an extramarital affair. He later resigned as Nvidia CEO, but after less than two weeks, the company's board of directors reinstated him.

The reinstatement came after Trump administration officials offered Nvidia assurances that Jensen Huang was not the target of a Justice Department investigation and that the government had no legal issues with him, CBS News reported earlier Wednesday. The assurances did not extend to Alice Huang.

Two criminal investigations involving potential violations of U.S. export controls by Megaspeed and another buyer of Nvidia chips, Super Micro Computer, remain ongoing. The FBI has been investigating both cases for more than a year, with the Justice Department's National Security Division leading the Megaspeed investigation. Megaspeed has denied any violations of U.S. export control laws and says Alice Huang left the company last year.

Jensen Huang is expected on Capitol Hill next week for a closed-door session with House lawmakers and public testimony before the Senate Banking Committee.

World.title: Blindsided by Iowa detonation, White House scrambled, sources say
World.content:
Washington — The chaotic lead-up to Wednesday's detonation of barrels of chemicals at a U.S. Army munitions plant in Iowa that raised contamination fears has prompted questions inside the Trump administration about what went wrong and who was to blame for not elevating the matter to senior officials sooner, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

President Trump and other administration officials praised the controlled detonation of about 5 tons of degraded lead azide at the plant in Middletown as having "exceeded expectations," saying maximum mitigation efforts were successfully achieved.

"Great job by the Army, and others, in Iowa!!! President DJT," Mr. Trump posted on Truth Social about five hours after the blast took place.

But White House officials have expressed frustration in internal conversations that they had to scramble to deal with the crisis. The situation rapidly became a national news story, with complaints from Iowa residents that they had not received sufficient notice about the potential dangers.

The Army had known since spring that the lead azide at the plant posed a threat to the public and to the environment, but then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll failed to raise the issue to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth or to other senior administration officials, according to several U.S. officials who requested anonymity to speak about a controversial topic.

A separate source familiar with the discussions surrounding the ammunition said the Army notified Hegseth's office early on. The notification never reached Hegseth directly, other officials said.

The process of coordinating the response was triggered before Driscoll left the administration, two sources said. Driscoll resigned in September amid tensions with Hegseth.

Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle learned of the stored chemicals and the risks in September, officials told CBS News, but didn't brief superiors. There have been discussions about quietly moving Telle out of the acting role in coming weeks, several sources said.

Administration leaders at the most senior levels were taken by surprise when they learned Thursday about the extent of the problem as they flew home from China after Mr. Trump's Asia trip, one U.S. official said. That forced White House chief of staff Stephen Miller to launch an intensive response from Air Force One, involving hours of phone calls, a dozen agencies and nearly every member of the Cabinet.

Mr. Trump and other White House officials in post-blast conversations Wednesday were relieved about the results of the detonation and the steps taken from Thursday on to handle the crisis. But Mr. Trump was furious about how the Army had handled the matter in the months before that, three of the sources said.

The president's plans to golf Wednesday in West Palm Beach were dashed by rain, and he watched the television coverage of events in Iowa closely, sources told CBS News.

There have also been internal administration conversations about the role in this by Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army's chief of staff, the sources said.

Other officials defended the administration action, saying the dozens of lower-level career officials who knew about the impending danger from the lead azide for months appropriately discussed how to handle it.

CBS News reached out to the White House for comment. The Pentagon referred questions to the Army, which has not yet responded to a request for comment.

In March, the Army officially notified the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency that 68 barrels of potentially unstable chemicals were discovered during a routine inspection at the Iowa plant.

Vice President JD Vance told reporters Wednesday that the administration became aware about six months ago "that it was impossible to move it — it was impossible to effectively neutralize it without causing significant danger to the surrounding community." Vance said the administration examined other options.

But other U.S. officials said the conclusion was reached only about two months ago that a controlled detonation would be the only safe way to get rid of the chemicals. A private contractor retained by the Pentagon looked into potential disposal processes, two of the sources said.

Miller worked on the problem over the weekend before the blast, calling various officials, including Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand on Monday, two sources said. The administration sought to keep the response – and the public blame – bipartisan, one of the sources said.

A federal appeals court on Monday cleared the way for the detonation amid challenges from environmental groups and elected officials about the operation's potential risks to public health. The military ultimately went forward with a controlled blast of the material, rather than letting it further degrade.

Maps released Tuesday by the Army noted that the dust cloud may travel as far as 100 miles, but the most potent effects would likely be felt within 30 square miles of the munitions plant.

Fifteen minutes after the detonation, the Environmental Protection Agency reported that zero lead was detected in the air by four monitoring stations in the area. Those sensors continued to show the same readings two hours later, according to the EPA.

The Army said it had taken steps to barricade the concrete bunkers holding the munitions and absorb the toxic dust, including with aqueous foam, which is used to extinguish fuel fires.

World.title: Group of Senate Democrats push to add freshman to leadership
World.content:
Group of Senate Democrats push to add freshman to leadership

toggle caption i Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/Getty Images North America

A group of Senate Democrats elected in 2024 sent a letter to colleagues Tuesday proposing to add an incoming freshman to the leadership ranks.

"The Freshman Representative to Leadership would be elected by members of the incoming freshman class and confirmed by the Conference," the letter said. "We intend to request a vote on this proposal."

The letter, first reported by Politico, is signed by California Sen. Adam Schiff, Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, and New Jersey Sen. Andy Kim.

The letter nods to the diverse class of incoming freshmen who helped catapult the party to controlling both chambers of Congress.

Sponsor Message

"These freshmen have their fingers on the pulse of long-time Democratic voters, those who voted for Democrats for the first time this past Election Day, and everyone in-between," the letter reads. "The deserve a seat at the table."

Senate Democrats have been signaling a desire to uplift new voices in the party.

"On election night, people voted very clearly for a new generation of leadership. That was very, very clear," Slotkin said during remarks at a conference of Democrats after the midterms.

New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker told MS NOW that leadership extends beyond the top post.

"This is a time for new leadership," Booker said, mentioning wanting to see more of incoming Sens. Annie Andrews of South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas. "I want to see them out front, I want to see them taking issues, I want to see them running on the field."

The proposed rule change comes ahead of the leadership election next week. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the majority leader.

Senate leadership is comprised not only of the top position of Majority leader but of additional conference officers. Both Van Hollen and Schumer support the idea of adding a position for a freshman to that leadership group.

Sponsor Message

"Leader Schumer was already planning to do this and is incredibly supportive of the idea," a spokesperson told NPR.

On Tuesday, Van Hollen posted to social media: "There should be a freshman senator on the Senate leadership team. As I've said, we need a new way to organize so we can deliver for the American people."

World.title: How American Thanksgiving took root -- and evolved -- in Liberia
World.content:
How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia

toggle caption i Eddie Raynes

Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.

"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."

Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.

"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."

The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.

Sponsor Message

Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.

That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.

The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.

A sacred day for all

Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."

Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well

"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff , a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving . "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."

When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.

Sponsor Message

"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.

Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.

"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."

The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.

toggle caption i Rebecca Blapoh Weah

"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."

Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."

(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")

"I'm thanking God"

This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.

Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."

Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation , an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.

"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.

World.title: What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
World.content:
What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping

toggle caption i Heather Diehl/Getty Images

Artificial intelligence is here to help with Black Friday.

This weekend, 59% of consumers plan on using AI to support their winter shopping, according to the National Retail Federation .

But AI has proven one way it is not unlike humans: It makes mistakes. The stakes of those hallucinations are much higher when your wallet – and holiday unwrapping memories – are on the line. These tools also become better shoppers when you hand over personal data, which also means giving up more information on your private life to massive tech companies.

Here are some tips – and notes of caution – before using AI as your personal holiday shopper.

Sponsor Message

Treat AI searches like a conversation with a kid

Traditional online shopping is about search terms and the infinite product scroll. AI is meant to be a conversation.

Unlike shopping on a retail website, AI platforms are designed to look more like texting apps. Prompt bars on these platforms sit on the bottom of the page, inviting a back and forth chat between user and bot about what to buy.

After all, it can be hard to know what keyword to plug in to shop for uncle before the Christmas exchange. AI instead allows for search based on a vibe – like describing that uncle's hobbies and personal style. If a shopper wants to buy a suitcase to support their uncle's European travel dreams, this makes it easier to narrow down the options.

"You can say if that bag is overstuffed, will it fit under the seat on JetBlue?" says Emily Pfeiffer, a principal analyst at Forrester who advises retailers and brands on digital commerce strategy, including for AI. "Don't give me the dimensions," she advises, "Tell me if it will suit my use case."

Pfeiffer cautions that even though AI is able to think through these nuanced shopping criteria, it works better with more hand holding.

Sponsor Message

"It's best if you imagine that it's a young child who will probably misinterpret your request," Pfeiffer said. "You want to be as specific and clear as possible."

AI Agents can shop for you. Be careful what you give them

Newer AI models can do more than talk and brainstorm. They can handle shopping tasks.

If shoppers are, for example, worried about holiday shipments arriving on time, AI can monitor an email inbox in order to track packages, even messaging a late shipper on the shopper's behalf. Beyond just suggesting a gift, agents can do the actual buying (with your money).

These are useful features, but require granting access to sensitive personal data, such as an inbox or credit card. One of the first questions Meta's AI agent platform Muse asks is if the user would like to connect their email and calendar.

Meta says its AI is highly secure. Everyone is assigned their own AI agent and the company promises that information shoppers share with it is kept private. Particularly sensitive information like credit card numbers, they say, are held separately and never viewed directly by the AI.

Yet Meta also has long been accused of violating user privacy, as in a 2022 case about improperly sharing user data . Meta did not admit to wrongdoing but settled for about $725 million.

Beyond Meta, there are cases of AI jumping guardrails that programmers set for it. Users have also reported their AI agents acting without their consent, such as sending their home address to a buyer from Facebook Marketplace and booking a hotel .

Philip Bruno, chief strategy and growth officer with ACI Worldwide, says he would share what he's shopping for with AI, but warns to be more careful with personal information.

"I'm cooking for a family of four. That is fine to be able to say," Bruno says. "I would be very careful about payment information."

On that note, experts caution shoppers to be careful with other people's information. It's easy to give most AIs loads of information about your father while brainstorming his gift. Know AI agents can also use this to build profiles of the shopper's friends and family . Being elusive and not specifying who you're shopping for during the brainstorming can help.

Sponsor Message

Just like for humans, it takes time for AI to find the best deals

One major selling point for using AI agents is that they can check multiple websites and compare prices, bringing them for human review all in one spot. That does not mean the first price it shows you is the best one.

"One of the biggest misconceptions about AI is that it somehow sees everything," Pfeiffer says. "That's just false. It gets you the best answer it can as quickly as possible."

AI agents still need time to hunt for deals. Many will often let shoppers watch along as they browse the web, rather than relying on preset knowledge.

This automating can also mean time savings for the user. Agents often can run in the background 24/7.

If users are in no particular holiday rush, they can leave the AI to continue shopping for weeks or even months, only sending a notice when a price drops into a budget friendly range.

Just know these agents don't always have access to every website. Amazon, for example, blocks Muse, arguing Meta did not alert Amazon of plans and that agents did not identify themselves while browsing.

Check the AI's work

For all the advances since ChatGPT's launch four years ago, AI still hallucinates and makes mistakes.

Visa recently released a report warning buyers to beware of AI shoppers. It tested different AI models and found they failed to recommend a product that met a customer's needs in 42% of test runs – more than half of those still recommended a product that didn't match.

That provides even more reason to click through and read up on whatever potential gift an AI recommends to make sure it's what shoppers want.

Otherwise people may find themselves turning back to that same AI agent for help making a return.

World.title: Army to detonate tons of lead azide after delays. And, Abrego Garcia leaves U.S.
World.content:
Army to detonate tons of lead azide after delays. And, Abrego Garcia leaves U.S.

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The Army will detonate a huge explosion in Middletown, Iowa, this morning to safely dispose of thousands of pounds of lead azide that could spontaneously explode. The explosive has been used since WWI and was moved to the Iowa bunker 17 years ago. The detonation is happening after officials found that the lead azide had crystallized and become unstable. Authorities have evacuated a 5-mile radius, and those within 20 miles are advised to stay indoors to avoid exposure to toxins.

toggle caption i Scott Olson/Getty Images

🎧 The U.S. Army rescheduled the detonation multiple times after the public got wind of it last week, NPR's Quil Lawrence tells Up First. Purdue University's Andrew Whelton, who has worked on disaster planning, tells Lawrence the detonation caused stress for residents, businesses and farmers. The Trump administration pushed back on the notion that this planned action was a surprise, citing town hall meetings on the topic. Lawrence says the biggest danger in the detonation is to kids and pregnant people due to the lead dust in the air or on surfaces. There are also worries about potential harm to livestock and crops, as well as the cleanup duration.

Sponsor Message

Kilmar Abrego Garcia has voluntarily left the U.S. after a nearly two-year legal battle. He is the Salvadoran immigrant who became emblematic of the challenges posed by President Trump's mass deportation campaign. Abrego Garcia was arrested in 2025 and mistakenly deported to El Salvador. He returned to the U.S. but departed for Spain yesterday. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said that Abrego Garcia boarded a commercial flight to a destination of his choice and "left the United States a free man." Sandoval-Moshenberg described the move as "a temporary departure," saying that Abrego Garcia, whose wife and child are U.S. citizens, has options to return to the U.S.



🎧 Abrego Garcia's attorney said that he will essentially spend two years waiting abroad. His case raises concerns about due process and the risks of sending individuals to countries where they could be harmed, NPR's Juliana Kim says. The Department of Homeland Security said they are delighted by his decision to leave the U.S. The agency, in a statement, said that "now this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocents." After being mistakenly deported, upon his return to the U.S., Abrego Garcia was charged with human smuggling, an allegation he has denied.

Sponsor Message

Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang, apologized to his staff yesterday for his previous behavior, according to the New York Times. He reportedly denied that Trump pressured the board for his return, despite the president saying otherwise. Huang had stepped down following reports of affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being recruited by China's spy agency. Some members of Congress still have concerns about the national security scandal.



🎧 Some lawmakers are upset with Huang, while others criticized Nvidia and its board, NPR's Maham Javaid says. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren says that Huang owes Congress answers about Nvidia's compliance with laws designed to keep advanced chips out of China. Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas is calling for a congressional investigation into Huang and urging faster action on chip-control legislation. House Democratic Committee leaders sent a letter to the president after he claimed he helped with Huang's reinstatement. They asked if he prioritizes friends and allies over the nation's economic and national security interests. They demanded a response by Dec. 8 on what he knew about Huang's ties to an alleged Chinese spy. Huang will attend a closed-door hearing with House members next week, followed by testimony before a Senate committee two days later.

Today's listen

Tatyana Alanis for NPR

NPR launched the first-ever Senior Podcast Challenge this fall, inviting people over 65 to share their stories. Unlike the NPR Student Podcast Challenge, which has attracted more than 90,000 young voices since 2018, this contest focuses on the wisdom and experiences of older voices. While the contest is still open for a few more days, the judges have already listened to more than 100 submissions. Some stories explore life after retirement, dating after divorce or the loss of a partner, and coming to terms with being a senior. Take a listen to some of their favorite early entries.

Sponsor Message

There's still time to enter. The competition will close on Nov. 30. These are the official rules for the 2026 NPR Senior Podcast Challenge and you can submit your entry here.

Life advice

Beck Harlan for NPR

If you're spending your free time ruminating about work-related issues, you're essentially still on the clock, according to psychologist and author Guy Winch. Don't let workplace woes invade your home life. Winch shares techniques with Life Kit to help you reclaim your time, energy and attention when work consumes too much of your mental bandwidth.

🧠 Instead of reliving the work issue, spend 15 minutes creating a plan to address the situation. Ask yourself, "How can I handle this? What outcome do I want?"

🧠 Adopt rituals that engage as many senses as possible to help your brain transition between tasks. For example, try changing your clothes to signal the end of the workday. The more you repeat rituals, the easier it is for your brain to shift from work to relaxation.

🧠 Do something that energizes you. Activities like screen time and doomscrolling may seem relaxing, but they aren't effective.

🧠 Ask yourself: "If my job disappeared tomorrow, what remains of me?" You might realize your worth isn't tied to your job title.

For more guidance on how to switch off your work brain, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Frailejon, a plant of Colombia's high-mountain wetlands that's vital to the country's water supply, is facing an array of threats from farmers, ranchers and climate change. Volunteers are working to save these plants, one seedling at a time. Doctors are combating disinformation about routine vitamin K shots for newborns, which prevent rare but life-threatening hemorrhaging. The rate of parents skipping these shots for their kids has increased from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025, according to new research in JAMA.

World.title: Republican wants FBI and CIA answers before questioning Nvidia chief
World.content:
Republican wants FBI and CIA answers before questioning Nvidia chief

toggle caption i Samuel Corum/Getty Images

Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia with President Trump's backing. But the questions surrounding the AI chipmaker and its ties to China are far from settled.

U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staff there is no evidence that Alice Huang, the woman who had an affair with the Nvidia chief, was a Chinese spy or intelligence asset, according to a person familiar with the matter who was granted anonymity to speak about a closed-door briefing.

There is also no evidence that she initiated the affair to collect intelligence for China's government, the person told NPR's Ryan Lucas on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the matter. She is, however, believed to have passed along information after the affair began.

Sponsor Message

Trump has said he helped arrange Huang's return as CEO, and Nvidia's board maintains that his reinstatement presents no national security risk. Some Republican lawmakers, however, want to understand how those conclusions were reached.

Speaking to Morning Edition on Wednesday, before NPR obtained the new information, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., said he wants to hear from the FBI and CIA before Huang appears before House lawmakers next week.

For Fitzpatrick, a former FBI special agent who sits on the House Intelligence Committee, the inquiry begins with what federal authorities knew and whether they warned the Nvidia chief of potential espionage threats.

"What briefings did they give? When did they give them?" he asked.

Huang's reinstatement, Fitzpatrick said, should not put those questions to rest.

"The public is rightly concerned, and they deserve answers," he said.

Fitzpatrick also wants to hear from Attorney General Todd Blanche, who on Tuesday described Nvidia as a good corporate citizen, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department faces questions over Nvidia's chip exports to China.

"Anytime you do an investigation, you follow the facts wherever they lead, and you report those facts with unimpeachable integrity," Fitzpatrick said. "You leave no stone unturned."

The debate over Huang's reinstatement extends beyond Washington.

Sponsor Message

In Silicon Valley, his return has alarmed women and advocates who have spent years pushing for a better workplace culture, renewing questions about the limits of executive accountability.

World.title: Greetings from Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest point in all its splendor
World.content:
Greetings from Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest point in all its splendor

Emily Feng/NPR

As dawn broke one recent morning over camp, we got one of our first full views of the peak of Mount Kilimanjaro, normally hidden behind clouds.

Climbing tall mountains like Kilimanjaro is a study in contrasts. The beating sun bakes you during the day, walking so close to the equator, but the nights quickly dip below freezing. Snow remains constantly in sight from humid rainforest and alpine landscapes, freshly charred from a wildfire three weeks before. And always beckoning is the peak, within sight, but seemingly never nearer; the high altitude means hikers need to walk slowly or else risk exhaustion and altitude sickness.

Sponsor Message

A group of friends and fellow hikers and I spent days camping at altitude to acclimatize before a final summit push during our second-to-last evening on the mountain. We trudged through heavy snow under the stars, cresting a massive volcanic crater rim, and leaned against drifts of what had become a full blizzard to reach the top in the early morning hours. I stood on the peak I'd seen only from a distance for the last week but saw only whiteness: all snow and ice, the absence of life and color heightened by my low oxygen levels.

Days later, having descended and decompressed and readying myself to fly back home, I looked back at the mountain one last time. For a few minutes, in the dusk light, the clouds parted and she revealed herself before disappearing again into the darkening evening, still as elusive as ever.
