World.title: Buying new things feels wonderful. But it can also be a trap
World.content:
Buying new things feels wonderful. But it can also be a trap

toggle caption i ㅤ/J Studios/Getty Images

Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. 

Buyer beware: Holiday shopping season is here. Is every sale calling your name? Is your virtual shopping cart overflowing?

Before you start buying everything, take note. There's a reason new things get us excited, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New: Why New Things Are Stealing Your Time, Money, and Happiness — and How to Take Back Your Life, published in September. Our brains are wired to seek out newness, and the retail industry is set up to keep us coming back for more as quickly as possible.

Sponsor Message

That constant consumption of novel possessions — whether they're brand-new, digital, secondhand or even free — can be problematic. "It's hard to be grateful for what you have if you're always on the lookout for something else," he says.

To break the cycle of chasing newness, we need to shop with more intention and find joy in what we already own, Athas says. In a conversation with Life Kit, he explains how. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Why are we so drawn to seeking out new things?

Our brains are programmed to find new things interesting and old things boring.

If you think about our ancient ancestors, it was beneficial [for their survival] to explore new foods to eat and new territory and eventually explore different parts of the world.

There's also research that shows when we encounter something new, we get a little shot of dopamine. You get that feeling of excitement when you first use that new app or try that new video game or bring home a new gizmo for the kitchen.

What are some of the downsides of chasing newness?

New things can steal our happiness. Everyone can relate to the feeling of tearing open that new box or putting on that new outfit. You do feel joy and excitement from that initially.

Sponsor Message

But science says those feelings can't last. So we have to go out and get something else, and that's where we can get into this cycle of constantly chasing happiness in new things.

These days, it feels particularly hard to focus on what you have. There's so much pressure to buy new things. Why is that?

Everywhere we go, whether that's scrolling our favorite shopping app or browsing the aisle of our favorite store, there are little cues driving our [shopping] decisions. These companies have designs we don't even realize are engineering our choices.

For example, at the checkout page of a website or an app, there might be a countdown clock that says, "Save 25% if you make this purchase in three minutes." That's a tactic meant to whip up anxiety.

The other part of this is that you can buy new things faster than you've ever been able to before. It's all seamless and frictionless.

toggle caption i J Studios/Getty Images

What can we do to create more friction between ourselves and the new things we want to buy?

Expand what I call "the new-thing gap." That's the time and distance between you encountering a new thing and you acquiring it.

If you've got one-click checkout with a certain company, maybe delete the app from your phone or remove your credit card information from that app.

Another easy tactic is to drop something in your cart and leave it there for 24 hours. Researchers have found that when you delay a purchase, interest in that thing will start to decline.

What happens when you use all these tactics and still feel like buying something new?

The main thing is to make intentional choices. The goal here is not to say no to all new things.

Now that I know my brain is programmed to find new things, I bring my attention to that whenever I feel drawn to something new. Is this something I want, or am I being influenced?

You can get really good at saying no to the wrong type of new things, better at saying yes to the right type of new things.

You say because we're programmed to want new things, we can be quick to set old things aside. So is it possible to get joy from old things?

Research has found that if we force ourselves to revisit old things, we may find there's untapped enjoyment in those old things.

Sponsor Message

In one study, researchers had people go through a museum exhibit. At the end, they asked participants how much they thought they would enjoy going through the exhibit again. People predicted they would get less enjoyment from the repeated experience.

But when the researchers forced them to go through it again, the participants said, "Actually, we enjoyed that just as much, if not more, the second time." They discovered details they missed the first time around or just liked seeing everything again.

How do we apply this lesson in our own life?

Reexperience old things. Books, movies, board games, your neighborhood. Go to that restaurant down the street that you love. Travel to that city that you've been to before.

What's great is you can relieve yourself of this obligation to always be spending money, time and attention on new things. You can fight against this bias that we have for novel experiences and find there's joy and excitement hiding in plain sight.

World.title: NATO's No. 2 commander strikes different tone on Canada than Pentagon
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The deputy commander of NATO said he's happy with Canada's contribution to the Western allies' deterrence mission in Eastern Europe and offered qualified praise on Wednesday for the country's efforts to rebuild its forces.

British Air Chief Marshal Sir John Stringer sat down with CBC News in Ottawa for an exclusive broadcast interview amid the ongoing political fight between the Pentagon and the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney over defence spending and military readiness.

Senior officials at the U.S. Department of War have been waging an increasingly public campaign to force Canada to spend more on defence in the short term, saying the country is not meeting its NORAD and NATO commitments because of a poor readiness among its forces.

Separately, a senior U.S. Department of War official, speaking on background, warned the Pentagon was prepared to "up the ante" on recent restrictions it had imposed on interaction with the Canadian military unless Ottawa took Washington's concerns more seriously.

WATCH | NATO's military 2nd in command on Canada's buildup: Canada 'spending well' on NATO commitments: NATO's 2nd in command in Europe | Duration closed caption 1:16 Asked by CBC News about the Pentagon's assessment that Canada isn't pulling its weight on defence investment, NATO deputy commander Air Chief Marshal John Stringer said Canada is 'a nation that is recapitalizing its investments in its air forces and its land component, in maritime.'

"I won't get drawn on what other nations may say," said Stringer.

"What I do look at in Canada now is a nation putting significant forces into Europe, most obviously, but not exclusively the multinational brigade in Latvia. I look at a nation that is recapitalizing its investments in its forces."

Asked directly whether he was satisfied with the readiness of the Canadian-led brigade in Latvia, Stringer responded: "I'm happy when I look at Canada."

At the moment, there are roughly 2,200 Canadian troops in Latvia with a plan to increase the number to 2,600 in the near term.

Aside from contributing a battle group, Canada serves as the commander of the 3,000-strong NATO multinational brigade, a deployment which Carney recently extended until 2031.

The commitment to Operation Reassurance, according to the recent federal budget, will amount to $7 billion during that timeframe.

Canada isn't alone in terms of where it is on the curve of rebuilding its forces and is making the necessary investments, said Stringer, who is next in line to NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich.

"Everybody had that wonderful moment of — we won the Cold War and it created both physical disinvestment and it also created a bit of conceptual disinvestment," Stringer said.

"A bunch of nations now are coming out of some relatively low spends and I look at Canada as one of those nations that's spending well."

On Monday, the Pentagon publicly released a "fact sheet" that said Canada is not a credible defence partner and that military spending is unfocused. The document pointed to subpar Canadian military readiness statistics and deferred modernizations of key equipment.

WATCH | Pentagon takes aim at Canada: Pentagon takes aim at Canada's military readiness | Duration 1:39 The war of words between the Pentagon and the Canadian government escalated as a senior U.S. official said if Canada doesn't focus its military investments on protecting the continent, the U.S. will start looking at 'significant mitigation measures.'

"Ottawa's prioritization of parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization introduces further uncertainty for NORAD and will further burden our Joint Force and the American taxpayer," the fact sheet said.

But Canada is hardly alone among NATO allies in struggling with military readiness, including the United States itself.

The U.S. Government Accountability Office told Congress in March that American military readiness had deteriorated over the past two decades. Twenty-five of 27 types of its army and air force aircraft failed to meet their operational availability targets in 2024.

A separate audit, published in June, found the mission-capable rate for the American F-35 fleet had plunged from 67 per cent in 2021 to 44 per cent last year. Only 25 per cent were capable of performing all their assigned missions.

Senior U.S. Navy officials said last year that readiness across their fleet of ships, submarines and aircraft hovered between 67 and 70 per cent.

Britain, meanwhile, refuses to publicly disclose detailed military readiness figures, citing national security. Parliamentary research published this year showed all three branches were below their trained personnel targets.

France has similarly restricted publication of readiness data. Its 2023 figures projected operational availability of 69 per cent for combat aircraft, 59 per cent for frigates and 87 per cent for battle tanks.

Germany has also classified detailed equipment readiness figures, making direct comparisons with Canada's military particularly difficult.

"If I look at where Canada is in that mix, it looks a lot like a lot of other nations," said Stringer.

"Readiness can always be improved. You can always be better tomorrow than you are today. And indeed that's one of the focuses we've got with all the nations in the alliance."

Going into a meeting of the Liberal caucus on Wednesday, the prime minister weighed in and dismissed the controversy with the Pentagon.

WATCH | Carney comments on Pentagon memos: Carney says Trump 'has not raised' Canada's military investments in conversations | Duration closed caption 0:55 Asked about the Pentagon saying Canada isn't pulling its weight on North American defence, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his recent discussions with U.S. President Donald Trump have focused on 'conflict resolution around the world.'

"I can assure you that in my discussions with the president of the United States, we're focused on conflict resolution around the world and he has not raised issues such as has been reported recently," Carney said.

"Canada is taking responsibility for our defence. We're at the front lines of NATO's defence, Operation Reassurance in Latvia. We're working with our NATO partners, including the U.S. but very much with the Nordics — with Germany, with France — through the High North, the Arctic."

As Canada and the U.S. debate commitment and investment, Stringer and the rest of NATO's supreme command has focused on Russia's rising campaign of grey zone warfare in Europe.

Last week, three Russian KH-101 cruise missiles crashed in southeastern Poland during a large-scale overnight Russian attack on Ukraine. There were no injuries or infrastructure damage. One missile landed about 35 kilometres from where troops from 11 allied countries were conducting military exercises to prepare for a potential postwar mission in Ukraine.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the airspace violation an "intentional provocation" by Russia.

Stringer was not prepared to go that far, saying an investigation was still being conducted.

"What we're really looking at is, why did they go there? And fundamentally … was it deliberate or was it accidental?" Stringer told CBC News.

"And by the way, even if it's accidental, what does it tell us about a recklessness in warfare five years into their three-day special military operation?"

He said Russia is always seeking to provoke. The question for NATO is how to respond.

"What we don't need to do is do Mr. Putin's job for him by overreacting," Stringer said. "What we need to do is be calm and measured and resolute in the approach to provocations. And by the way, not every military act needs, even warrants, some form of military response."

World.title: Health Canada issues warning on rare risk of vision loss with semaglutide GLP-1 drugs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Health Canada has issued a public warning about the "very rare but serious" risk of vision loss tied to semaglutide GLP-1 drugs, best known by brand names such as Ozempic, Rybelsus and Wegovy.

On the heels of similar warnings in the U.S. and Europe, the federal department announced on Wednesday that it had completed its own safety review, which found a possible link between prescription semaglutide drugs and the risk of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).

The condition causes sudden blindness or vision changes due to reduced blood flow to the optic nerve, which carries information from the eyes to the brain. NAION typically occurs more commonly in people with diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol. It's a permanent condition, with no known treatment.

"If you experience sudden vision loss or rapidly worsening eyesight while taking semaglutide … seek urgent medical attention," the new warning reads.

Multiple studies show links to vision loss

Both Health Canada and other international medical experts have stressed the rarity of NAION, even as millions of individuals around the world are now taking GLP-1 medications, including an estimated three million Canadians.

Yet multiple studies have also suggested there may be increased risk of the condition among those using these drugs, which are approved in Canada for a variety of uses, including chronic weight management and treating Type 2 diabetes.

One headline-making 2024 study in JAMA Ophthalmology found a "potential risk" of NAION associated with prescriptions for semaglutide, but the researchers stressed more research was needed to assess causality.

Earlier this year, other observational research published in the British Journal of Ophthalmology found the risk of vision loss varied between semaglutide formulations, and was three times greater among men than women. The findings highlighted a "potential dose-dependent safety concern," the authors wrote.

WATCH | GLP-1s linked to vision loss in diabetics: Ozempic, Mounjaro linked to vision loss in diabetics | Duration closed caption 2:01 Researchers at the University of Toronto have found GLP-1 weight loss and diabetes drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro double the risk of a severe form of vision loss among diabetics, affecting daily activities such as reading and driving.

Vision loss usually painless, sudden

NAION usually affects one eye at a time, Health Canada noted in its new notice, and often occurs as cloudy, blurry or worsened sight across part of the field of vision — usually in the lower half — of the affected eye.

Most people notice the vision loss when waking up, though it can also happen gradually over about two weeks.

"It is usually painless, though mild headaches or discomfort around the eye may occur," the department's warning adds.

Health Canada recommended any Canadians experiencing sudden vision loss or eyesight changes while taking semaglutide GLP-1 drugs should quickly get medical attention, while health-care providers should urgently refer those patients for ophthalmological examination and discontinue semaglutide treatment if NAION is confirmed.

The notice applies to all types of prescription semaglutide drugs used in Canada, including brand names such as Ozempic, Plosbrio, Poviztra, Rybelsus and Wegovy, along with generic offerings such as apo-semaglutide injection, aspen-semaglutide, Dr. Reddy's Laboratories Ltd. semaglutide injection, Sandoz semaglutide and Sevmia.

World.title: Montreal mayor walks back 'clumsy' Kraft Dinner comment after major tax hike
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A day after the City of Montreal unveiled a budget that featured a property tax average increase of 9.8 per cent — about three times the inflation rate — the mayor is once again on the defensive.

This time, it's over comments she made about Kraft Dinner.

The property tax increase unveiled on Tuesday was the talk of city hall, as it meant that Montreal homeowners will need to spend an average of $515 more on taxes.

Soraya Martinez Ferrada has insisted the tax increase is necessary to get the city's finances in order and to catch up on much-needed infrastructure work.

During an interview with local media outlet Urbania, the mayor talked about the city's financial struggles and made a comment that has sparked lots of social media backlash.

"We're going through every service to see what we can save. It's like when you make your personal budget: if you know you'll have less money one year, then, you have to make choices," she said.

"Sometimes, you'll have to eat a little more Kraft Dinner because we can't afford filet mignon."

Many comments online suggested the mayor and the city should've found alternative solutions to the city's financial problems instead of imposing such a hefty tax on residents.

In an Instagram story posted on Wednesday, the mayor acknowledged her comments were "clumsy."

"What I wanted to say is the city will have to make choices: Build new parks or fill potholes. I'm going to focus on filling potholes."

A large chunk of the 9.8 per cent average property tax increase will generate money for a new infrastructure fund that will help the city make more cash payments for maintenance and repair work, rather than relying on credit.

This increase means Martinez Ferrada has broken her campaign promise about limiting tax increases to the rate of inflation.

She was sworn in as mayor in November 2025 and this is her administration's second budget.

World.title: Remember when NASA slammed a spacecraft into an asteroid? We now have close-up images of the aftermath
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In 2021, NASA embarked on an ambitious mission: Sending a spacecraft to slam into one of two asteroids in a double-asteroid system to test whether the impact could change its orbit.

Why? To see if the technology could be used to redirect any potentially hazardous asteroid that was on a collision course with Earth. (Don’t panic: There’s no known asteroid on a collision course.)

The binary asteroid system consists of Didymos and its smaller moonlet, Dimorphos , which orbit a common centre of mass. The mission was to slam into the moonlet to see if it would change its orbit around Didymos.

Fast forward to September 2022, and the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) did just that. It shortened Dimorphos's orbit around Didymos by roughly 33 minutes. NASA had anticipated a change of roughly 10 minutes.

While telescopes on Earth revealed the aftermath, another mission — the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera — was planned to take a closer look.

Now, ESA has released close-up images and videos of the pair four years after DART.

Looking closely at the images and video, there is a noticeable flattening on Dimorphos compared to pre-impact.

“But now where that rounded face was, now, well, it's a big crater … that is almost as large as the body itself, which is really, really spectacular,” said Sabina Raducan, planetary scientist with the International Space Science Institute and part of the Hera mission.

“It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to finally see what happened.”

A big surprise

But there was more for Hera to discover.

“Every space mission has surprises. But there was a particularly big one in store for Hera,” said Naomi Murdoch, planetary scientist with ISAE-SUPAERO at the Université de Toulouse, and part of the Hera science team.

“Hera has observed hundreds of boulders moving around these two asteroids and ranging in size from tens of centimetres to metre-sized,” she said.

The image produced by 11 long-exposure images look like fireflies are swarming around the pair of asteroids.

This is a composite image combining 11 long-exposure Hyperscout H images, centred on the Didymos asteroid. The dot trails correspond to hundreds of boulders of differing sizes in motion around the Didymos-Dimorphos system. The two asteroids have been subtracted from the image for improved visualisation of the boulders. These images were acquired on 6 November with an approximate distance of 29.9 km from the asteroids. (European Space Agency)

But it’s not clear from where they originated. Was it a result of the 2022 impact, or were they there before, as part of Didymos?

“We're still really trying to characterize them,” Murdoch said. “So, understanding with lots of imaging what their sizes are and how exactly they're moving in the space around the asteroids. So right now, we're not entirely sure where they came from.”

Hera has been orbiting the dual asteroid system for the past three weeks. There are still six months left in its mission. And scientists are eager to discover more.

Comparing images of the Didymos system before and after the 2022 impact of NASA's DART mission with the smaller Dimorphos moonlet. The left-side image is a view from the DART spacecraft shortly before impact. The right-side image is a view from Hera, aiming to match the previous mission's view angle as closely as possible. Dimorphos appears entirely transformed, with its once-rounded face flattened into a crater that seems as wide as the impacted face of the asteroid and some weird structures inside it, including an apparent cigar-shaped structure at its centre. (NASA/Johns Hopkins APL/European Space Agency)

For example, Didymos looks like a giant walnut, with a pronounced ridge across the 700-metre wide asteroid.

“The central ridge is a very spectacular feature of this asteroid. What we know is that the asteroid is rotating very fast, and we think that what happens when asteroids rotate fast is that the material on the surface actually flows down from the higher latitudes, down towards the equatorial region,” Murdoch explained.

Another interesting thing is that, since the impact, Dimorphos is now tumbling as it orbits.

“Before the DART impact, Dimorphos was more like our own moon. So it was always showing the same face to Didymos,” Raducan said. “It was behaving quite nicely. Now it's very chaotic.”

More successful than anticipated

Not only did DART change Dimorphos’s orbit around Didymos, but it turns out it also changed the pair’s orbit around the sun.

In March, a study published in the journal Science Advances , reported that the impact changed its 770-day orbital period around the sun by a fraction of a second. A fraction of a second may not seem like much, but it marks the first time in history that a human-made object has changed the orbit of an object around the sun.

WATCH | NASA slams spacecraft into asteroid to test planetary defence: NASA slams spacecraft into asteroid to test planetary defence | Duration 3:14 NASA's DART spacecraft slammed into the asteroid Dimorphos — 11.3 million kilometres away from Earth — to alter its orbit and test whether objects that threaten Earth can be redirected.

Over the next six months, Hera will continue to collect data about the binary asteroid system to see what else may have changed. It will deploy two CubeSats (miniature satellites), to further explore both the mineral make-up of Dimorphos as well as the first radar sounding within an asteroid.

After that, the pair will descend to the asteroid’s surface. And when Hera’s mission is completed, it too will descend to the surface.

For now, astronomers are excited to see what the next six months will tell them about this little pairing, and specifically, if an asteroid re-direct mission is a viable solution to keeping Earth safe.

“We learned that from DART, that we can send a spacecraft there, we can hit it, and now from Hera, we can see this effect,” Raducan said. “We know that we can deflect it. The next question that we would need to answer as we get more data is to see how much this deflection, how efficient this deflection actually was.”

World.title: PQ urges other parties urged to sit in Quebec legislature — despite recent ruling ordering oath to King
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is encouraging his opponents to join him in taking their seats at the National Assembly next Tuesday, despite a Quebec Superior Court judge’s ruling ordering legislators to swear allegiance to the King before sitting at the National Assembly.

Justice Ian Demers warned on Monday that laws passed at the National Assembly could be rendered invalid if members do not take the oath.

The government is contesting the decision, with the appeal scheduled to be heard at 2 p.m. on Friday in Montreal.

In the meantime, the premier has sent a letter to the leaders of the three opposition parties, urging them to commit "to begin our parliamentary work on December 1, with our oaths as they currently stand."

During the swearing-in ceremonies of each party, the MNAs made their oaths to the Quebec people. It was Bill 4, passed unanimously in Quebec in Dec. 2022, that made the oath to the Crown optional.

WATCH | PQ letter calls for business as usual — despite recent ruling: PQ government seeks solidarity from other parties on oath to King refusal as it awaits court appeal | Duration 1:21 Quebec's justice minister says plans are going ahead to open a parliamentary session on Dec. 1 with many MNAs, including the premier, planning to swear an oath to the people of Quebec rather than King Charles. That's despite a judge ruling that a 2022 Quebec law allowing such an act is unconstitutional, a judgment the government is appealing.

Demers said in his Monday ruling, though, that the Quebec government had overstepped its constitutional boundaries with this law. He wrote that "the Constitution is not an à la carte menu" from which individuals can pick and choose what to follow.

Lawrence David, one of the lawyers challenging Bill 4, pointed out that unless the judgment by Demers is overturned on Friday, it is the law.

"I believe that it is extremely concerning that a public official that holds the title of [premier] of a province — and let’s be clear, a minister of the Crown … is saying that he would like to defy a court order," said David.

Where the other parties stand

All four parties with seats at the National Assembly have said they want the legislative session to start next Tuesday as planned.

But the leaders of the Quebec Liberal and Conservative parties say they're not going to sign the letter just yet. Instead, they're waiting to hear the outcome of Friday's appeal decision.

"Why are we going in front of the Court of Appeal if we want to put them in front of a fait accompli, I don’t get it," Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime said of the premier's letter.

"The priority of Quebecers right now, it’s not the oath to the King," he added. "It’s the economy."

On Tuesday, Duhaime said that making the oath to the King doesn't necessarily mean you become "a federalist and a monarchist."

Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard said on Tuesday that he wouldn't rule out taking the oath.

Meanwhile, the province's political parties have reached an agreement to change another National Assembly rule.

When the premier marks the opening of the legislative session, the new Speaker of the National Assembly will table the written speech of the lieutenant-governor, who's a representative of the monarchy.

The lieutenant-governor has traditionally delivered an opening address at the start of a new legislative session.

An adventurous hamster named Buster is back home in Arnprior, Ont., three weeks after hitching a ride inside a discarded Halloween pumpkin and ending up on a farm about 20 kilometres away.

Every November, Matthew Brearley and Tanya Sprowl collect donated pumpkins at Castlegarth Farms in White Lake, Ont., where they're used for compost.

The couple told CBC’s Ottawa Morning that they typically inspect the pumpkins for non-compostable items such as forgotten tea lights.

"We go through each pumpkin, piling it on the compost pile, and there was quite a sizable amount," Brearly said. "I was turning it over, looked down and saw what I thought was not a hamster, but [another kind of] small rodent, which does happen on farms."

But after a closer look, Brearley realized this was no typical farmyard rodent, but a domesticated hamster that's definitely not native to the Ottawa Valley.

Buster had spent an estimated 21 days inside the pumpkin, where he at least had plenty to eat.

"He was quite wet, he was covered in pumpkin guts and juice," said Sprowl. "So he was a little scraggly, but he seemed otherwise OK and didn’t have any injuries."

'That's Buster!'

Brearley scooped the hamster up and brought him into the house to be properly fed and cleaned. Figuring he was someone's missing pet, the couple took Buster's "mug shot" and posted it to a local Facebook group in an attempt to find his owners.

"He must have crawled into one of their Halloween pumpkins to have a snack and then ended up in the pile at the Nick Smith Centre bound for a dump truck that was headed to our farm for composting," the Facebook post read.

Word spread quickly.

"People followed the story all weekend looking for updates. It was kind of funny,” Brearley said.

Eventually, a family from Arnprior reached out.

"They sent us a direct message saying, 'That’s Buster!’ and they had been tearing their house apart for the last three weeks looking for their hamster," Sprowl said.

Sprowl said Buster was finally reunited with his owners after being "fluffed up" and made more presentable. Buster's family, which includes three boys, declined to comment for this story.

Brearley said it was an unexpectedly happy ending to a remarkable adventure.

"I would’ve been surprised if my hamster disappeared three weeks ago. I would’ve assumed it gone forever, but there it was, no foul and reunited with its family,” he said.

"He’s one lucky hamster that’s for sure,” the couple wrote on Facebook, thanking the online community for helping make Buster's homecoming happen.

World.title: Final Avengers: Doomsday trailer racks up over 500 million views in 1st day
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's safe to say there's a fair amount of hype around the upcoming release of Avengers: Doomsday.

Marvel released the final trailer for the upcoming superhero movie on Tuesday, and after just 24 hours it had already generated 563 million views.

That makes it the most viewed Disney trailer of all time, beating out the previous Avengers: Doomsday teaser, which hit 503 million views in the first 24 hours. It's also already the second most viewed movie trailer of all time, just below Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which has over 718 million views.

The film, directed by Anthony Russo and Joe Russo — who also directed Avengers: Infinity War and Avengers: Endgame — is set to hit theatres Dec. 18.

The trailer starts by showing Steve Rogers, played by Chris Evans, as he talks about fatherhood, and if he should tell his son about his past life as Captain America and an Avenger. He's then approached by Reed Richards, played by Pedro Pascal, and the rest of the Fantastic Four.

WATCH | Avengers: Doomsday final trailer:

That's followed by a shot of Doctor Doom, played by Robert Downey Jr., accompanied by three mysterious masked women.

More heroes meet each other (and in some cases fight) including Canadian Simu Liu as Shang-Chi, Ian McKellen as Magneto and Chris Hemsworth as Thor. Though he doesn't appear in this trailer, Doomsday will be the final big-screen role for Patrick Stewart, who plays Charles Xavier, the leader of the X-Men.

Mixed reviews

"My family and I have booked the entire movie theatre for ourselves for the premiere of Avengers: Doomsday," posted X user @JesabelRaay. "They all couldn't stop talking about the new trailer."

But not all the hype is positive.

In the final scene, many of the heroes come together on a sort of battleground, and viewers weren't impressed.

"Avengers: Doomsday looks hideous … it visually looks awful," said @constantine_james7 in a video on Instagram.

Another Instagramer, @screened_scored, said it looked like "they took a bunch of individual characters, cut them out, and placed them against a digital background."

What is hype worth?

The last Avengers film, 2019's Avengers: Endgame, made $2.9 billion US at the box office ( With a bump from the recently released slightly updated version ) making it the highest-grossing movie of all time, not accounting for inflation.

But other recent films with high trailer views have done well.

While many fans are excited for the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday movie, some took to social media to complain about some of the visuals in the latest trailer. (Marvel Studios)

The hype around Spider-Man: Brand New Day translated into box office success, with the movie pulling in $2.52 billion US worldwide

Deadpool & Wolverine's 2024 Super Bowl teaser scored 365 million views if you include those who watched the trailer during the Super Bowl broadcast, and that movie took in $1.3 billion US globally.

Possible hidden secrets

Keen-eyed viewers believe they aren't exactly seeing everything in these trailers.

At the end of the recent release, many of the heroes team up for a classic "Avengers, assemble" shot that often accompanies these big team-up movies when all the heroes unite to fight against common enemy.

But some viewers have pointed out that there are some gaps where they believe characters have been digitally edited out.

While much of the cast has been announced, there are still some unknowns around who will appear in the movie, such as three characters pictured here. (Marvel Studios)

It wouldn't be the first time.

In a trailer for Spider-Man: No Way Home, Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield playing their versions of Spider-Man were edited out of the trailer that otherwise would've shown them swinging into action with Tom Holland's Spider-Man.

In trailers for Endgame, Thor and Bruce Banner's Smart Hulk were edited out of scenes, so it wouldn't give away their appearance.

Tickets for the Dec. 18 release of Avengers: Doomsday have been on sale since July. It will premier the same day as Dune: Part Three directed by Canadian Denis Villeneuve.

World.title: 2 men charged in burglary at home of Prince and Princess of Wales stole cufflinks and a clock, police say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When it comes to matters of royal security, nothing is taken lightly in the U.K. Responsibility falls to a specialist branch of the Metropolitan Police Service, and guaranteeing the safety and protection of senior, working royals is constantly under review.

So when police in Norfolk, a rural county in eastern England, were alerted Monday evening to suspicious activity on the King’s Sandringham estate, the response was rapid and widespread. A helicopter reportedly was in the air for some three hours. Dogs and a drone searched the extensive grounds under cover of darkness.

The response was a far cry from what the average Briton might get — a visit from some police officers, sometimes several hours after a break-in, and a reference number to follow up with later. But these are the royals.

Two men were arrested and charged on Wednesday with burglary of a dwelling with intent to steal and trespassing on a protected site — in this case, Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom house gifted by the late Queen Elizabeth to her grandson Prince William, now next in line to the throne, and his wife, Princess Catherine, when they married in 2011.

Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, make an appearance at an event in Mumbai on Nov. 17. The couple are now back in the U.K., but were not at their country residence during Monday's break-in. (Rafiq Maqbool/The Associated Press)

Police confirmed the royal couple were not at the property at the time. Anmer Hall is not a permanent residence, but they are known to use it on weekends and holidays.

3rd suspect at large

The accused appeared in court Wednesday in Norwich. Both spoke through an Albanian interpreter, identifying themselves as 34-year-old Mirgen Doku and Arilen Ndoci, 32. Prosecutors revealed that another suspect remains at large.

The court heard details alleging the men stole six pairs of cufflinks — one set was described as "the Duke of Edinburgh cufflinks" — and a clock after climbing up a drainpipe into the royal property and forcing entry into a dressing room.

The Magistrates' Court was told motion sensors were triggered outside Anmer Hall at around 6 p.m. local time Monday. A game and conservation manager, who was on duty in the estate carrying out what was described as a "hare patrol" reportedly saw two men jump through a hedgerow and into the woods.

The court heard that, along with the heat-seeking equipment on the police helicopter, the estate worker helped in the search using a thermal spotter.

A police forensics van sits near Anmer Hall on Tuesday. The 10-bedroom home is often used as a country retreat for the family. (Martin Pope/Getty Images)

Prosecutors said the two men were not wearing shoes when they were detained.

Neither man entered any pleas during his court appearance, and both were remanded in custody to reappear Monday.

Anmer Hall is where the Princess of Wales spent time after her cancer diagnosis and features in a video marking the end of her chemotherapy. The location has also been a backdrop for many photos of William and Catherine with their children Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis.

Property open to public part of year

The property is a short drive from Sandringham House, King Charles and Queen Camilla’s country retreat. For six months of the year the house and gardens are open to the public for visits. Traditionally, it’s where the Royal Family spends Christmas and New Year's Eve.

The sprawling estate is also home to the King’s brother and former prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, who moved to Marsh Farm in Sandringham in April.

Security breaches at royal properties remain rare, but they have happened. In 2021, on Christmas Day, a man was found in Windsor Castle grounds armed with a crossbow. He was later sentenced to nine years in prison.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, the former prince, leaves a police station in Aylsham, U.K., on Feb. 19. Mountbatten-Windsor has lived in Marsh Farm, on Sandringham estate, since April. (Phil Noble/Reuters)

The most serious security lapse happened in 1982, when Queen Elizabeth, asleep in her bedroom in Buckingham Palace, woke to find an intruder in her room. She spoke with him for about ten minutes before the alarm was raised.

Kensington Palace — William and Catherine's official residence — has previously said they do not comment on security matters.

World.title: Colombia’s special forces liberate hostages from Cartagena supermarket
World.content:
Colombia’s security forces liberated some 20 people who were held hostage inside a supermarket in the northern city of Cartagena after a 15-hour stand-off.

The operation ended a tense situation that began around 8AM on Tuesday when the armed kidnappers entered the Exito supermarket in La Castellano, a residential neighborhood.

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who led the liberation operation, the kidnappers meant to rob an armored car that had already left with the proceeds of the day before.

The kidnappers subsequently kidnapped a group of 30 people, and demanded COP7billion ($2 million) and the possibility to escape the supermarket.

Throughout the day, at least five of the hostages were released from the supermarket cafeteria, whose windows had been covered with papers. One video showed a row of hostages sitting behind the window.

Riot police was deployed around midnight after family members and onlookers became restless.

The situation took a quick turn after 1PM when explosions were heard and special forces entered the building.

The security forces killed one of the kidnappers and detained the remaining four, De la Espriella said in a social media video.

Images that were shared on social media showed special police forces securing the Exito’s cafeteria and removing the paper from the windows.

De la Espriella said that all the hostages were released in an “extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the military forces.”

One agent would have been injured in the rescue operation, reported Caracol Radio.

The kidnappers “were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages, but they rejected that opportunity, so we took decisive action,” said the president.

In the morning, the prosecution said the kidnappers’ arms and explosives were fake and former hostages said the hostage takers spent most of the day getting drunk.

World.title: 22 injured after car bomb strikes central Colombia governor’s office
World.content:
Twenty-two people were reportedly injured and more than 80 buildings were damaged in a car bomb attack on the Governor’s Office of Meta in Villavicencio, central Colombia.

According to Meta’s Security Secretary, Franklin Olivos, the car that exploded carried approximately 100 kilograms of explosives and caused damage to buildings that were located more than 100 meters away from the blast.

Among the injured are five private security guards. One of them needed surgery, according to his employer.

Olivos blamed the attack on the 39th Front, a unit of the FARC dissident group EMC, which has opposed the peace process that started 10 years ago on Tuesday and controls large swathes of jungle territory in the south of Colombia.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said that “narcoterrorism is desperate because we are confronting it head-on. It seeks to intimidate us and force us to back down so we seek another sham peace process.”

De la Espriella, an opponent of the peace process, has been advertising an “iron fist” policy against organized crime and illegal armed groups.

The president’s alleged offensive has failed to produce any results and guerrilla groups have continued to attack State security forces and infrastructure.

World.title: Colombia strips key critics of security details
World.content:
Colombia’s National Protection Unit (UNP) has withdrawn the security details of journalist Daniel Coronell, a major critic of President Abelardo de la Espriella, after vowing to protect the freedom of the press.

Coronell’s local security detail was removed because he lives in the United States, which would make it impossible for the UNP to reassess his protection plan.

The Miami-based journalist frequently travels to Colombia for his work and was in Bogota to receive a lifetime achievement award from the national journalism prize.

While receiving the prize, Coronell sharply criticized De la Espriella for promoting self-promotion over governance. using state resources to censor critics, restricting public information to “friendly media,” and leveraging a history of aggressive lawsuits against reporters.

The journalist’s criticism triggered a clash with Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez, who accused Coronell of being angry for having State subsidies pulled.

After press freedom foundation FLIP responded to defend Coronell, Ordoñez claimed that “the freedom of the press enjoys full protection and guarantees from the government.”

We value and defend freedom of the press as a cornerstone of democracy. The press is free, but it is also responsible. It is not a license to abuse, slander, defame, fabricate stories, spread misinformation, or engage in politics. Nor is it a license to destroy democracy or its institutions with lies. Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez

Coronell played a key role in Colombian journalism since the late 1980’s and was forced to flee Colombia in 2005 after reports on the ties of former President Alvaro Uribe and paramilitary groups escalated death threats.

The journalist currently works with Noticias Uno and Caracol Radio, and has more than 700,000 subscribers on YouTube.

The UNP previously stripped former President Gustavo Petro and former presidential candidate Claudia Lopez of their security details.

World.title: Illegal armed group carries out first urban drone attack: three injured in northeast Colombia
World.content:
A couple and their 18-month-old baby were injured in a drone attack on a police station in Cucuta, the first major city to be struck from the sky by guerrilla explosives.

The attack damaged more than 60 homes near the Norte de Santander Police Department in the Tasajero neighborhood in the north of the regional capital, the province’s security secretary, George Quintero, told press.

As of now, the situation is as follows: more than 60 damaged homes located just 20 meters from the police headquarters, and three people injured. Security secretary George Quintero

The homes were hit because the police department’s signal-jamming systems reportedly caused the drones to miss their target.

An unknown number of drones were able to reach the interior of the Police Department’s compound, leaving only minor damage.

Guerrilla group ELN has been carrying out multiple drone attacks in Catatumbo, a nearby region with major coca cultivations, and exercises control in the peripheral slums of Cucuta.

The group was accused of attacking the same police department with home-made mortars in August. This attack injured seven policemen.

In a response to the guerrilla attack, President Abelardo de la Espriella in October ordered the militarization of the border city, which has been struggling with security issues for years.

De la Espriella vowed that he “will not allow narco-terrorism to continue sowing fear and threatening families” in Cucuta and the surrounding Norte de Santander province.

According to the authorities, the militarization of the city sought to “strengthen territorial control, protect citizens, and confront” the illegal armed groups that operate in and around Cucuta.

The president’s offensive against illegal armed groups and organized crime has been hampered by an increase in the use of drones that are equipped with explosives.

All kinds of illegal armed groups use the relatively new technology to push back the authorities from areas under their control.

World.title: Colombia asks X to suspend Petro’s social media account
World.content:
Colombia’s communications ministry said Sunday that it had requested social media platform X to suspend former President Gustavo Petro for “possible incitement to violence.”

In a statement that was published of X, the ministry said it reported Petro’s account to X’s Public Affairs, Safety, and Rules Enforcement Team.

According to the statement, the request to suspend the leftist former president, who has more than 9 million followers, was due to a November 21 post in which Petro asked “the people of Colombia to demand Abelardo’s resignation now.”

Petro has been trying to promote popular opposition against De la Espriella, who he has called an illegitimate president.

According to the ministry, Petro’s call to “take action in the streets” could constitute a call for violence against the government.

In a response, the former president said the De la Espriella administration sought to impose censorship on him, which is “expressly prohibited by the Constitution.”

The ministry’s request “demonstrates the extent of the current government’s illegitimacy,” added Petro.

The former president is now the leader of the Historic Pact (PH) opposition party and has actively been promoting a general strike in response to his successor’s controversial policy decisions.

Petro is a member of the PH’s more radical wing and can still count on a significant following among Colombia’s population.
