World.title: De la Espriella calls on US to prosecute Petro in response to call to “resign now”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the US Justice Department to “investigate, prosecute and hopefully jail former President Gustavo Petro after the latter called on the people to “rise up” and “restore real democracy.”

De la Espriella addressed the nation at the end of a day of anti-government marches that mobilized tens of thousands of people throughout Colombia.

Petro led the march in Cali and called on his supporters to “rise up,” call a general strike and force the president to “leave now,” less than four months after De la Espriella took office.

Reiterating fraud accusations and the president’s business ties to paramilitary warlords and drug traffickers, the former president told the crowd that “it is not about waiting until 2030; an illegitimate government must leave now.”

A government whose policy goes against the people must leave now. A government whose policy builds hunger and death for the people of Colombia must leave now. Life must be restored, democracy must be restored, and the slogan “Abelardo, resign now!” must become the slogan of the majority of the Colombian people. An agreement will eventually be made to transition back so that the Constitution of Colombia and the laws in favor of the Colombian people prevail. But from here on out—and that is why we must move to a national strike, that is why we must move to a general strike—within the people’s right of expression and decision, an illegitimate government that goes against the interests of the Colombian population must leave now. Gustavo Petro

De la Espriella told Petro that he would never accept they “attack democracy, promote a coup d’état or attempt to destroy Colombia, just as he did when he was a guerrilla fighter.”

The president claimed that the former President and congressional opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “have no moral authority whatsoever. However, as I tell you, I will not accept them attacking democracy, attacking institutionality, or promoting a coup d’état in an attempt to destroy Colombia.”

De la Espriella repeated his threat to extradite his predecessor if requested to do so by the administration of his ally, US President Donald Trump.

I make a direct call to the judicial authorities of the United States so that investigations related to acts of corruption, drug trafficking, or any other criminal conduct move forward with full rigor and the independence of the judicial system in the United States. Petro’s government was a criminal enterprise, and international laws and provisions were violated. The United States has jurisdiction to investigate him, prosecute him, and hopefully imprison him. Let the North American justice system act, let the whole truth be known, let the evidence be examined, and let those found responsible answer before the law without regard for anything other than the application of the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president has tried to criminalize the opposition and the former government ever since taking office in August without much success.

World.title: Colombia rejects US proposal to conduct joint strikes against drug trafficking: NYT
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rejected a US plan to conduct joint military operations, anonymous US officials told the New York Times (NYT).

According to the NYT, De la Espriella told the US government he supported working with the US military, but lacked congressional support invite US soldiers on Colombian soil.

The conversation would have taken place in the week ahead of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Colombia on Wednesday.

In a response, the president and the defense secretary said that the alleged US plan was “fake news.”

“I have not rejected any proposal of the Government of President Donald Trump,” De la Espriella said on social media platform X.

Colombia and the United States maintain strong and increasingly close cooperation in the areas of security, intelligence, and the fight against drug cartels and narco-terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president confirmed that congressional approval would be required for him to invite foreign troops into Colombia.

Between visits to Venezuela and Ecuador, Hegseth briefly stopped in Colombia, and met with Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora and Foreign Minister Omar Bulla.

The defense secretary expressed his support for the government’s plans to combat drug trafficking.

“You, sir, are never going to have a stronger partner than President Trump, Secretary Hegseth an the War Department,” Hegseth told Bula.

Both the US and the Colombian governments have assumed a militaristic approach to drug trafficking, contrary to their predecessors.

World.title: The Grocery Combo: Cuba’s Pantry Is Paid for Abroad
World.content:
Products paid for abroad and delivered to homes.

By Safie M. Gonzalez

HAVANA TIMES – On an iron chair and a blue sofa with worn upholstery, survival is displayed in plastic. A tray of thirty eggs, bottles of cooking oil, bags of powdered milk, Yeya pasta, Rios rice and canned goods form a pyramid that, at first glance, looks like a middle-class family’s groceries for the month. To one side sits the coveted La Excelencia toilet paper, Fox detergent and Coolwhite soap. On the floor, green mesh bags reveal malanga, sweet potatoes and plantains.

This is not the bounty from a miraculous ration store, nor the result of a carefully planned shopping trip to a local market. It is a supermarket package paid for abroad.

The transaction did not take place in Havana. It happened through a screen in Miami, Madrid or Santiago de Chile. A click, a credit card, a Zelle transfer or a cash payment at a shipping agency. Across the sea, a relative or friend put together the package, selected the brands and paid in foreign currency so that, days later, a “mule” or a delivery truck would drop off this shipment of food and hygiene products at the doorstep of a Cuban home.

This is the new anatomy of Cuba’s basic basket of goods: a household economy no longer governed by state salaries, but by the wallets of the diaspora and the exchange rate.

The Luxury of Basic Necessities

This type of grocery combo package is a barometer of the crisis. A decade ago, a shipment from abroad usually included clothes, shoes, perfumes or household appliances. Today, the priorities are eggs, cooking oil and toilet paper. The diaspora has become the de facto “Ministry of Food” for thousands of households, sending what cannot be guaranteed locally.

The irony lies in the brands. Products such as Yeya rice or La Excelencia toilet paper are notorious among Cuban consumers for their poor quality or local packaging processes. Yet when included in a package paid for abroad, they acquire the status of a privilege. Having a pantry stocked with these products means having a relative who makes sacrifices, working overtime abroad to ensure that detergent or powdered milk does not run out back on the island.

The Divide of Plastic and Cardboard

This reality also illustrates the social inequality eating away at the island. While packages of pasta and canned goods pile up in some households, in others survival depends on the informal market, where prices are beyond people’s reach.

The grocery package paid for abroad is a lifeline, but also a marker of social class. For those who receive it, it offers the peace of mind of knowing that their protein and hygiene needs are covered for a month. For those who have no one abroad, it is a reminder of their economic isolation. In Cuba today, family solidarity crosses oceans, but it also leaves many stranded on the shore.

The Business of Survival

Behind this domestic scene lies a commercial machinery. Shipping agencies have perfected the model of grocery packages known as “combos” (Combo A, Combo B, Executive Combo). They offer emigrants the convenience of choosing a preassembled package—with eggs, grains, cooking oil and hygiene products—and paying for it securely.

This model has transformed consumption. Families in Cuba no longer ask for what they need; they adapt to what the package offers. Standardization has turned grocery shopping into a lottery in which those who pay get to choose, and those who receive make do with what they get.

In the middle of the living room, the package waits to be unpacked. Every can, every roll of toilet paper is a reminder of distance and of love packaged for delivery. But it is also evidence of a country where daily survival has been outsourced abroad, and where a packet of detergent or a simple bag of root vegetables and plantains has become the most precious of treasures.

Read more from the diary of Safie M. González aquí en Havana Times.

World.title: Cuba Restricts Food Rations to Only the Most Vulnerable
World.content:
An employee distributes rationed food to a customer inside a nearly empty state-run grocery store in Havana. Food distributed through the ration booklet is being restricted to people in the most vulnerable situations. Photo: Jorge Luis Baños / IPS

By Dariel Pradas (IPS)

HAVANA TIMES – Most Cubans, except for the oldest generations, were born into a system with a ration booklet, the hallmark of a state-subsidized and rationed distribution system for food and other basic goods to which all inhabitants had access.

Today, however, almost all the bodegas, the local name for state-run neighborhood stores where these goods were previously sold, remain closed. A few are now responsible for distributing food as social assistance to the most vulnerable, while others have been leased to the private sector.

“Look, I haven’t received rice in months. Nor sugar, coffee, or beans. As for chicken, not since 2025, if I remember correctly. Now people are saying they’re going to eliminate the ration booklet, but I think that in practice they had already eliminated it,” Carlos Garrido, a 63-year-old construction worker living in Havana, told IPS while showing his household’s ration booklet.

This distribution system was established in 1962 to overcome shortages generated, among other factors, by the position taken by the United States, then the country’s main supplier, which, dissatisfied with the direction of the Cuban Revolution, severed all kinds of relations with this Caribbean island nation.

Rice, chicken, sugar, milk, eggs, cooking oil, beans, spaghetti, and cooking gas were sold through the ration booklet until about five years ago.

After the COVID-19 pandemic, as Cuba’s multidimensional crisis intensified, with rising inflation, economic contraction, and a failed monetary reform, the number of products offered through the ration booklet steadily dwindled.

In 2026, the oil blockade and new financial sanctions imposed by the United States on the island exacerbated the crisis and rations at state-run grocery stores were reduced to a bare minimum.

Cubans, who previously met part of their calorie needs through the distribution of subsidized food, now have no choice but to face the high prices of a predominantly private market governed by supply and demand, without the government-imposed price caps previously used in unsuccessful attempts to contain price increases.

The ration booklet “has disappeared in practice; it could be said that it has become extinct, and among the approved measures it is indicated that in the future it will focus exclusively on vulnerable sectors of the population,” economist Omar Everleny wrote in an article for IPS.

On the radio program *Haciendo Radio*, Marpessa Portal, general director of Merchandise Sales at the Ministry of Domestic Trade, announced that “1,913 bodegas had been selected to serve people in the most vulnerable situations,” out of the 12,000 existing nationwide.

According to Everleny, this new approach “would require the State to define who is and who is not vulnerable, so the necessary clarification must be made in this regard.”

During an IPS tour of several bodegas that remain operational, each was found to be responsible for distributing products within a community, either free of charge or at a cost of one US cent or less, mainly to recipients of social assistance or people of retirement age, which is 60 for women and 65 for men.

To a lesser extent, beneficiaries also include children with chronic illnesses or low body weight, women with high-risk pregnancies, female heads of households with more than three children, and other specific cases.

According to the store managers, who gave similar accounts, the census to identify these individuals was conducted with social workers from the Ministry of Labor and Social Security, local political delegates, and health and education authorities.

Under the new system, a person can receive rice, beans, sugar, and even sunflower oil every month, the latter being highly sought after and expensive on the private market. The World Food Program (WFP) provides that oil and other imported products, which are distributed every two months to vulnerable individuals.

Many people are therefore eager to be included on these lists of vulnerable individuals at a time when survival is becoming increasingly difficult for most of the population.

A mother of three who benefits from the new system and preferred to remain anonymous when interviewed by IPS lied during the census, claiming that she was raising her children alone when, in fact, she lives with her husband and receives his financial support.

“I had to say I didn’t have a husband because things are really bad. Our money isn’t enough for anything. The other day we couldn’t eat until we picked up the package of subsidized products at the bodega,” she acknowledged.

Customers line up outside a state-run bakery that sells rationed bread rolls to the population in Havana. Photo: Jorge Luis Baños / IPS

The Long-Standing Debate Over Eliminating the Ration Booklet

There had been talk of eliminating the ration booklet for many years.

In 2011, at the Sixth Congress of the Communist Party of Cuba (PCC, the only political party permitted in the country), former Cuban President Raúl Castro (2008–2018) already spoke of eliminating universal assistance and focusing it on the most vulnerable, advocating a policy of subsidizing people rather than products.

The then-president even reduced the number of items available through the ration booklet in an effort to eliminate extensive subsidies that, as late as 2012, represented an annual expenditure of more than US $1 billion, with only 12% of the actual value of the products being recovered.

Since taking office in 2018, current President Miguel Diaz-Canel, along with other members of the government, has repeatedly stressed the economic necessity of eliminating these subsidies.

In 2019, IPS consulted several economists, sociologists, and other specialists on the subject, and many agreed that it was indeed necessary to eliminate the universal nature of a subsidy that, ultimately, was unnecessary for more privileged groups.

However, some experts warned that its elimination should be gradual and should take place when domestic food production and the Cuban economy were capable of cushioning the blow it would deal to the diets of many families.

For those very reasons, the elimination of the ration booklet was postponed until a more favorable time that never came and that, instead, became increasingly unfavorable from 2020 onward.

Its elimination now is a consequence of the Cuban government’s financial inability to maintain that assistance, as well as the ideological backing provided by a new economic policy.

In June, 2026, the PCC and Cuba’s one chamber parliament approved a package of 176 economic and social reforms promoting deregulation, privatization, and the expansion of market-oriented practices in a historically centralized country.

One of the most recent measures accompanying the new policy was approved on Monday, November 16, which establishes that state and private entities can invest in social infrastructure such as schools, hospitals, nursing homes, cultural centers, and sports facilities in exchange for tax exemptions.

Social assistance would thus become a shared responsibility between the state and private sectors, at a time when the government has already identified some 883,000 people in vulnerable situations, equivalent to 9% of Cuba’s 9.4 million inhabitants.

Minister of Labor and Social Security Jesús Otamendiz reported that figure in late October.

However, he clarified that not all of these individuals suffer from food insecurity, since other indicators taken into consideration may include unmet family care needs, low household incomes, or a lack of housing, in a country with a housing deficit of 800,000 units.

Other independent studies, such as one conducted by sociologist Mayra Espina, estimate the number of vulnerable people at more than 1.3 million, while 66% of the Cuban population currently lives in economic poverty, with incomes insufficient to cover the approximately US $14 per month needed for a basic foods.

A white erase board displays the prices of products sold at a private neighborhood store in Havana. The new neighborhood markets have yet to offer competitive prices for most Cubans, whose incomes put these products beyond their reach. Photo: Jorge Luis Baños / IPS

New Markets

To replace the universal food distribution system provided by the ration booklet, the government will not only retain a small portion of its premises to distribute goods to vulnerable individuals but will also promote a new commercial model: “neighborhood markets.”

Legally approved in August, neighborhood markets are intended to offer certain essential products at competitive prices in exchange for tax incentives and a two-year exemption from rental payments for those same state-owned grocery stores.

“The objectives of the neighborhood market are to sell a range of essential food and personal hygiene products… at lower prices than other markets, taking into account the tax and commercial incentives designed for the project,” Marpessa Portal, the Domestic Trade Ministry official, said in late October.

In her earlier appearance on the radio program, she had mentioned that there were 47 such markets operating in the country at the time.

The major problem with the initiative is that prices, far from being more competitive, turned out to be higher than those at other nearby private markets, as many customers complained on social media.

Some explanations for this disastrous outcome point to the fact that certain vendors are not lowering their prices to reflect the savings resulting from the tax and rental exemptions offered under this system.

Others simply point out that the numbers don’t add up.

In theory, neighborhood markets should obtain their supplies from state and non-state producers and wholesalers, who sell in bulk at lower prices.

Alongside these entities, the creation of so-called wholesale supply markets was authorized, with the two types of markets designed to complement one another.

But hardly any such markets exist yet, nor do they have the capacity to maintain a steady flow of supplies capable of meeting the enormous demand and bringing prices down. Furthermore, most food is imported, and shipments are affected by restrictions imposed by shipping companies following US sanctions.

“Everything is very expensive today. Far too expensive… Yes, when I see how desperate the situation is, I do miss the days when you could at least get the basic foods through the ration booklet. There are a lot of people now who have nothing left,” said Garrido, the Havana construction worker.

First published in Spanish by IPS and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: International News Briefs for Wednesday, November 25, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Wednesday, November 25, 2026.

Army Publishes New Map Showing Lead Dust from Munitions Plant Detonation Could Spread to Missouri

Nov 25, 2026

Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds has declared a disaster emergency in three counties, as the U.S. Army prepares to detonate nearly five tons of highly unstable lead-based explosives at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa today. Environmental groups are warning of an unfolding public health catastrophe, with a detonation scheduled for 9 a.m. Central Time that could spew toxic lead dust across communities, farmland and potentially into the Mississippi River. Officials have recommended that residents of Middletown, where the plant is located, and anyone within a five-mile cone southwest of the plant evacuate, while people living up to 20 miles away have been told to stay indoors with their windows closed. This is Sean Kaufman, a disaster preparedness official with the Department of Health and Human Services.

Sean Kaufman: “Individuals that are in that directly affected area — which, again, we will continuously get updates based on the weather — if they are women who are pregnant, children under the age of 6, or children in general, and individuals who may have chronic disease, you definitely want to be out of that area. I would evacuate that area.”

The Army published an updated map estimating the lead plume could spread all the way to northern Missouri, more than 100 miles from ground zero. There is no safe level of exposure to lead, a neurotoxin that can cause permanent cognitive and behavioral harm. Ahead of today’s detonation, The New York Times published an investigation revealing the Army had initially hired a firm to turn the explosives into harmless waste, but then dropped the contract in favor of a so-called controlled blast. We’ll have the latest on this story after headlines.

Gaza Health Officials Warn of Spread of Meningitis as Israel Continues to Violate Ceasefire Deal

Nov 25, 2026

In Gaza, at least four Palestinians were killed this morning in an Israeli airstrike on an apartment building in the al-Shati refugee camp. The strike followed Israeli attacks that killed at least 10 Palestinians across Gaza on Tuesday, including a 30-year-old pregnant mother and Khaled Walid al-Jamal, a 13-year-old boy shot dead in northern Gaza City. Another Israeli airstrike killed a senior Hamas security official, along with his wife and their two teenage daughters. The relentless attacks came as Palestinians held funeral services in Khan Younis for three people killed in an Israeli strike on a police post. Rashad Abu Loli is a relative of one of the victims.

Rashad Abu Loli: “There is no ceasefire. Throughout the days, throughout the hours, there are strikes in the streets on civilians and on vehicles. We hear about a ceasefire, but this ceasefire exists only as an agreement. On the ground and in reality, it does not exist.”

On Tuesday, Gaza’s Health Ministry declared an epidemic alert over a surge in meningitis, warning that hundreds of thousands of people are at risk of contracting the deadly condition.

Yemen’s Houthis Strike Saudi Arabia’s Largest Refinery and Riyadh Skyscraper

Nov 25, 2026

Image Credit: NASA Worldview

Saudi Arabia’s biggest oil refinery caught fire following an attack by Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement, known as the Houthis. Ras Tanura is one of the largest refining complexes and oil export terminals in the world, with a capacity of over a half-million barrels per day. It erupted in flames hours after a Houthi strike on Saudi Arabia’s main financial district in Riyadh Tuesday that injured 11 people. That attack damaged Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, which is home to the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund. The Saudi-backed coalition responded by attacking the Houthi-controlled port of Hodeidah, prompting Ansar Allah to threaten Jeddah and other ports on the Red Sea.

World Food Programme Warns Wars in Ukraine and Mideast Are Jeopardizing Food Aid for Millions

Nov 25, 2026

In Moscow, President Vladimir Putin has vowed to retaliate against Ukrainian ⁠attacks on Russian energy sites. At least 14 oil refineries have been struck since the start of November, despite President Trump’s explicit request to Kyiv to halt such attacks. On Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky defended the strikes, as well as a drone attack on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland.

Meanwhile, Italy has warned the conflict has spread to the Mediterranean, after a Ukrainian drone struck a Russian ship anchored at a port in Benghazi, killing two Libyan naval officers. The Libyan National Army has vowed to retaliate.

This comes as the U.N. food agency warns the war in Ukraine is disrupting grain shipments, jeopardizing food aid for 7.3 million people. Luke Lindberg is director of the World Food Programme.

Luke Lindberg: “This is one of the world’s breadbasket regions. Its grains are vital to nations, including Somalia, which is at risk of famine, and Yemen, which imports 90% of its food today. And yet, grain silos in Ukraine and Poland are full, while families in Somalia, Sudan and South Sudan suffer catastrophic hunger. This is not a problem of production. It is a political problem. Grain is available, but it is not reaching the people who need it.”

Lawsuits Allege ICE Brutalized U.S. Citizens and Prisoners at For-Profit Jail

Nov 25, 2026

Image Credit: Stacey Wescott/Chicago Tribune/ZUMA Press Wire, Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune

Two people who were brutally arrested by federal agents during widespread immigration raids in the Chicago area last year have filed separate lawsuits against the Trump administration. Dayanne Figueroa and Luis Jesus Acosta Gutierrez were among those detained as hundreds of federal agents descended onto Illinois for Trump’s so-called Operation Midway Blitz. Gutierrez was taken into custody following an hourslong standoff with federal agents who deployed tear gas and pepper spray on community members and neighbors who had gathered to try to protect Gutierrez. Figueroa is a single mother and U.S. citizen. She had just dropped off her 5-year-old child at school when her car was rammed by ICE agents, who then dragged her out by her legs, threw her onto the pavement and pinned her face-down using their knees. According to the lawsuit, one of the agents placed a knee near an incision from a recent kidney surgery, causing grueling pain. Figueroa was arrested without a warrant despite repeatedly telling agents she was a U.S. citizen.

In related news, the family of a U.S. citizen from Pharr, Texas, is considering legal action against the Trump administration after surveillance footage showed masked federal agents detaining Domingo Vásquez at a construction site in Alamo. His mother says he has an intellectual disability and at the time of his arrest did not have his identification. Vásquez had been working in construction with his uncle.

Meanwhile, four formerly detained immigrants, including two transgender men, say they were subjected to rape, sexual assault, anti-LGBTQ hate speech and forced labor by staff at a for-profit ICE jail in Basile, Louisiana. The group has filed a lawsuit against the private prison company GEO Group and two ex-employees at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, including the former assistant warden. The plaintiffs say they were also denied medical care and were placed in solitary confinement in retaliation for filing complaints against the abuses.

Kilmar Ábrego García Leaves U.S. for Spain, Ending 20-Month Legal Ordeal

Nov 25, 2026

In more immigration news, Maryland father Kilmar Ábrego García has arrived in Spain after leaving the U.S. on his own to avoid deportation. The Trump administration repeatedly attempted to deport him to countries he had no ties to, in a legal standoff that’s lasted for nearly two years. Ábrego García, who is originally from El Salvador, became a symbol of Trump’s cruel mass deportation campaign after he was sent to the notorious Salvadoran maximum-security prison known as CECOT in March 2025. García was returned to the U.S. about two months later, following a high-profile visit to El Salvador by Maryland Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, who met with Ábrego García and advocated for his release.

Trump Says He Might Pardon Jensen Huang as Attorney General Calls Nvidia a “Good Corporate Citizen”

Nov 25, 2026

Attorney General Todd Blanche signaled Wednesday that he won’t investigate Nvidia’s co-founder Jensen Huang over potential criminal charges, following reports that Huang had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whose former company is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export rules; she was also allegedly in communication with China’s top spy agency. Blanche spoke to reporters a day after President Trump publicly proclaimed that Jensen Huang was not a national security threat. Asked if he had investigated Huang, Blanche snapped, “For what?”

Attorney General Todd Blanche: “What I will say is, yes, Nvidia is a good corporate citizen. That’s not — that shouldn’t be groundbreaking. I’m not — that’s something that — that the president has talked about, that the vice president has talked about, that everybody in leadership has talked about. And I would echo that.”

On Tuesday, President Trump told the New York Post he’s willing to pardon Jensen Huang but believes that won’t be necessary.

Meanwhile, Public Citizen called for an investigation into suspiciously timed bets on the so-called prediction market platforms Kalshi and Polymarket that Jensen Huang would be reinstated as CEO of Nvidia. That includes one account that sat idle for almost a year until mid-November, when a flurry of bets earned the trader $128,000.

Indian PM Narendra Modi Has Weakened Democratic Institutions, Human Rights Watch Finds

Nov 25, 2026

A leader of India’s Cockroach movement says he was stopped by immigration officials at the Delhi airport and blocked from boarding a flight to the United Kingdom. Twenty-seven-year-old Saurav Das has been one of the main organizers with the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party. This incident comes about a month after he was detained during mass protests demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner.

In related news, a new report by Human Rights Watch warns Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Hindu nationalist government have systematically eroded India’s democratic freedoms, human rights and civil liberties over the past decade.

The report accuses Modi of weaponizing federal and judicial agencies to target and persecute his critics.

Hollywood Stars Defend Iranian Director Jafar Panahi After Tehran Court Sentences Him in Absentia

Nov 25, 2026

Image Credit: Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images

Renowned actors and directors have rallied in support of Oscar-nominated Iranian director Jafar Panahi, who last month was sentenced in absentia by a Tehran court to five years and one month in prison. Variety reported about 200 individuals and film institutions have signed on to a letter expressing deep concern over Iran’s persecution of Panahi, but that number has now soared to nearly 2,000 signatures and counting. Signatories include Mark Ruffalo, Tilda Swinton, Michael Moore and Barry Jenkins. The Cannes Film Festival also issued a letter protesting Panahi’s prison sentence, calling “for the lifting of all restrictions that prevent him from traveling, creating and expressing himself freely.”

Far-Right Parties Lead in Polls Ahead of Sunday’s Snap Election in Spain

Nov 25, 2026

Spanish voters head to the polls Sunday in a snap election triggered by nationwide protests over the spiraling cost of living that erupted after the eviction of an 87-year-old from her lifelong home in Madrid. The Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party led by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez faces challenges by the right-wing People’s Party and the far-right, anti-immigrant Vox party.

Court Bars U.S. from Punishing People Who Liaise with International Criminal Court

Nov 25, 2026

A federal judge has permanently barred the Trump administration from punishing people or organizations who share evidence with the International Criminal Court or other Palestinian rights groups sanctioned by the U.S. Monday’s ruling makes permanent a court injunction that blocked the Trump administration from potentially imposing civil or criminal liability on the groups Democracy for the Arab World Now and the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide. The groups sued the Trump administration in July, after an executive order threatened civil fines and up to 20 years in prison for sharing evidence with the ICC, a U.N. expert on Palestine or rights groups including the Palestinian Center for Human Rights. The court ruled the executive order was a content-based restriction on speech, in violation of the First Amendment.

Celebrities Call on Sen. Chris Van Hollen to Be Elected Democratic Leader Over Sen. Chuck Schumer

Nov 25, 2026

Image Credit: Facebook

More than two dozen Hollywood superstars are calling on New York Senator Chuck Schumer to resign from his leadership role as Democrats take control of the Senate in January. Among those calling for Senator Chris Van Hollen to instead be elected Senate majority leader are actors Robert De Niro, Marisa Tomei and Jane Fonda.

Read more news here on Havana Times.

World.title: Cubans Living Abroad Are Now the Largest Group of Visitors
World.content:
The Island’s hotels are empty of tourists, although construction work continues to be carried out from time to time. / 14ymedio

For them and for all nationalities, the numbers continue to decline, and in October fewer than 30,000 visitors arrived in total.

By 14ymedio

HAVANA TIMES – The Cuban community residing abroad has surpassed Canada for the first time as the largest group of international visitors to Cuba, with a total of 132,390 compared with 130,253 for the year through the end of October. This unprecedented figure comes after a month in which Cuban emigrants accounted for more than half of all arrivals (51.1%), contributing 15,004 visitors out of the total of just 29,376 who arrived on the Island. This is the third-lowest monthly figure of the year, surpassed only by September (27,354) and June (28,100).

The figures, published in the monthly report for October and released this weekend, make clear the catastrophic state of the tourism industry. In October of last year, the Island attracted 110,299 tourists, almost four times as many, representing a year-over-year decline of 73.4%.

The change in the trend among the Cuban community had been noticeable throughout the year and is not due to an improvement in that market, which has actually also declined compared with 2025. Travel by the diaspora fell 32% in the year-to-date figures, but the absolute collapse of the other markets has confirmed this structural change.

The sharpest contrast can be seen with Canada, which went from sending 37,094 tourists in October 2025 to registering just 1,006 in the same month this year, or 2.7% of the previous year’s volume. Through the end of September, the North American country, historically Cuba’s leading tourism market, was still at the top of the arrivals list, with 129,247 visitors compared with 117,386 from the diaspora. The overwhelming majority of those visitors had arrived in January and early February, when the Island’s airports issued their first warning about a shortage of jet fuel stemming from the loss of Venezuela’s donated fuel shipments and the oil blockade imposed by the United States. The airlines devoted themselves almost exclusively to repatriating the thousands of Canadians who were on the Island.

Since then, none of the country’s airlines has resumed flights to Cuba, resulting in only a handful of Canadians reaching the Island through the United States or Mexico. This October was the first time Cubans living abroad took the lead in the year-to-date figures, after months of closing the gap. Emigrants now account for 26.1% of all tourism received in 2026, double their share between January and October 2025, when it stood at 13.2%. The continuation of flights, particularly from Miami to Havana, combined with family and personal ties, has prevented this market from collapsing like the others.

In October 2025, the 17,085 emigrants who traveled to the Island represented just 15.5% of total arrivals, whereas they now account for half, despite a 12.2% decline compared with the same month the previous year. Meanwhile, the United States ranked as the second-largest group of visitors for the month, behind the Cuban community, with 4,373 visitors compared with 6,460 in October 2025, followed by Mexico, which contributed 2,052, or 48.3% of the 4,248 recorded the previous year.

The declines in the other markets are even more dramatic. Russia and Argentina have practically disappeared from the monthly statistics: the former went from 11,002 visitors in October 2025 to just 107 last month, while the latter plunged from 3,644 to 87, even as intensive campaigns have been carried out in that country to attract new travelers. In Europe, Spain contributed 848 visitors (compared with 3,270 in October 2025), while Italy registered 639, down from 1,783. Finally, Colombia and China complete the list with 804 and 587 arrivals, respectively.

In total, during the first ten months of 2026, Cuba received only 507,083 international travelers, just 34.3% of the 1,478,146 recorded during the same period in 2025, which had already been a terrible year for the sector in its own right, representing a loss of nearly one million tourists. January got off to what was then considered a not-too-bad start, with 184,833 arrivals.

Although 2019 had the best first month in history, with 489,637 tourists, those figures were already largely a thing of the past, and the 2026 figure was not much lower than that of 2025 (196,000). But the oil blockade began to take its toll, and throughout February, the month of repatriations, only 77,663 visitors arrived. Since then, no month has exceeded 36,000.

Among the markets behind the diaspora and Canada are the United States, with 50,268 visitors (52.7% of the 95,339 recorded in 2025); Mexico, with 26,421 (55.2% of the previous 47,864); and Russia, with 21,822 (21.8% of the 99,922 recorded the previous year). One of the most serious cases, given the historical and cultural ties, is Spain, which has accumulated only 12,030 visitors this year, compared with 40,043 through October of last year. Something similar has happened with Italy: its figures fell from 26,039 to 9,917.

The tourism crisis, compounded by the departure of international hotel companies, has produced a collateral victim: the 22,000 state employees who lost their jobs, according to Tourism Minister Juan Carlos García Granda, as a result of the “progressive deterioration of activity” since the COVID-19 pandemic.

A week ago, he stated on the state television program Mesa Redonda that, at the end of 2025, there were approximately 103,000 workers employed in the sector and that currently around 83,000 continue working at its facilities.

Translated by Regina Anavy for Translating Cuba.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: An Excursion 30 Years in the Making
World.content:
Photo Feature by Fabiana del Valle

HAVANA TIMES – In the late 1990s, my school organized trips to the Jardín de Aspiro campground. These outings were supervised by teachers and a few parents who joined in the adventure. However, my mother wouldn’t let me go. For her, anything beyond familiar boundaries entailed a lurking danger.

It’s true that on one occasion, after much begging and pleading, she gave me permission. But since bad luck has followed me since childhood, the bus that was supposed to pick us up broke down along the way, and the trip was postponed until the following weekend. My mother saw this as a divine sign or some kind of omen and withdrew her permission.

I remember the innocent envy I felt toward my best friends, who never missed a single excursion. Every Monday, the classroom was filled with stories of swimming in the river and nights under the stars. My teenage imagination placed that spot on a par with London, a city I dreamed of visiting someday.

That little corner in the foothills of the Sierra del Rosario, in the municipality of San Cristobal, retained for me the allure of the forbidden and the unattainable. But I grew up and never had another opportunity to go, nor did I seek one. My life changed, and adulthood took me toward other horizons.

Still, that unfulfilled longing remained buried deep inside me, and my husband, knowing my story, was determined to make the trip happen. He made some inquiries, and a friend told him we could get there on our electric motorcycle without any problems. Although the campground remains closed to the public, we could go to the river or enjoy the natural pool.

The idea of fulfilling a wish nearly three decades in the making excited me. Since walking the damp streets of London remains a dream with no foreseeable prospect of coming true, at least I could immerse myself for a few hours in the natural surroundings Aspiro promised. We prepared some sandwiches, a bottle of soda, and some water to quench our thirst, and set off early that morning. What we hadn’t anticipated was the condition of the route. The steep hills and the road, deteriorated from a lack of maintenance, proved quite a challenge for our motorcycle.

Since the heat is less intense at this time of year, we hoped to find some privacy. But Cubans aren’t afraid of the cold, and as the morning wore on, other people began arriving at the pool, seeking to wash away their everyday troubles in the refreshing water.

We had been looking for some privacy in a place where we could breathe fresh air and disconnect for a while. Our dream refuge ended up crowded with people, their speakers blasting reparto music through the vegetation, disrupting the natural harmony and the haven of peace we had both envisioned for our getaway.

Despite everything, it was worth immersing ourselves in those crystal-clear, cold waters, so cold that our skin felt as though it were burning the moment we touched the water. Those natural surroundings brought us a revitalizing sense of relief. And we were only there for a few hours!

Before returning home, we stopped at the entrance to the Jardín de Aspiro campground, and I asked the guards for permission to take some pictures. I couldn’t leave without seeing the inside of the place I had so longed to visit as a teenager.

I did a little research and discovered that the campground opened in 1982. The site was chosen to take advantage of the river, the natural pool, its proximity to the waterfall, and the mountain trails with their numerous caves.

The name Aspiro is associated with the Spanish merchant Don Jose de Aspiro, who was one of the owners of those lands. The grounds of this enclave once formed part of several estates where agricultural activities were combined with botanical experimentation. I have read that in the early 19th century, a garden featuring exotic species and a wide variety of flora was established there, where the naturalist and botanist Jose Blaín Cervantes conducted his studies.

The facility was repaired and refurbished last year so that it could be operational this summer. But on this island, after 1959, objectivity was lost. A video room, a restaurant, a game room, and remodeled cabins with air conditioning, kitchens, and bathrooms.

All of this without water, since the blackouts prevent water from being pumped to the facility. The services the center was supposed to offer have been reduced to zero, and there is no hope of recovering the investment. The place possesses an undeniable beauty, and it is a shame that it cannot be enjoyed.

Although we returned home satisfied — once again managing to escape the suffocating reality we live in with very few resources — I cannot shake the sad conviction that there is no future for an island that sinks deeper into misery, neglect, and darkness with each passing day.

See more photo features here on Havana Times.

World.title: A Week of “Normality” Ended
World.content:
By Veronica Vega

HAVANA TIMES – Since everything that begins must come to an end, this morning the spell was broken and Cinderella’s carriage turned back into a pumpkin.

What I mean is that the seven days of DAF (Automatic Frequency Tripping) on the circuit to which our building was assigned have come to an end.

These circuits ration access to electricity in this new, nameless phase we are living through in Cuba. (There is an urgent need to give it a name to make historians’ work easier.)

I have no idea what DAF actually means, but in practice, it entails a week of uninterrupted electricity and a return to our lost normality.

A functioning refrigerator, food that you are not forced to pack into small containers crammed into the freezer among jars of ice. Because you have to make as much ice as possible to withstand the long hours of blackouts, maintaining a temperature that allows you to preserve your food.

That food, with its heart-stopping prices, robs you of your peace of mind three times: when you buy it, when you cook it — if you have no gas available and depend on an electric burner and whatever brief spell of electricity you get — and finally, when you rack your brain trying to fit whatever is left for the next day into a freezer that is no longer running.

That blessed week also means cooking in the electric cooker without fear that the process will be interrupted and the beans will remain hard. Or the rice half-cooked.

Feeling a strange peace that gradually begins to rock you like the waves, transporting you back to almost idyllic times, when the word “crisis” was still the subject of jokes rather than this constant tightness in your stomach, this bitter feeling of stagnation and of having lost your way.

Night falls, and the lights around you reassure you that there is life outside: televisions switched on, fans and air conditioners providing that minimum level of comfort and restoring the home to its status as a sacred refuge.

Some people play dance music, and the lights of small private businesses twinkle like costly harbors of hope, of other people’s prosperity.

When I go out to walk my dogs, I sense a kind of tranquility in the air, a feeling of shared goodwill throughout the area where DAF reigns, or a sense of relief that rekindles the memory of what a country can be, even amid shortages, if at least a basic level of functionality prevails.

But the full bliss of DAF is only achieved if you are lucky enough for that week to coincide with water flowing into the communal cistern.

Then there is no need to rush to fill tanks, buckets, and all kinds of containers in an agonizing race against the ever-uncertain hours of electricity.

You can do everything at the pace of nature, at the pace of life. Relax. Remember a way of living in which everyone can enjoy a glass of cold water, a hot meal, and a warm bath, even if they don’t have a solar panel, EcoFlow power stations, or gas paid for by a relative abroad.

You can feel that your time belongs to you again, face life’s other minor setbacks without experiencing them as anonymous and unexpected assaults.

“We used to live like this…” you tell yourself and immediately wonder how long ago that was and what we did (or failed to do) to lose the little we had.

Who marked us on the map of the world with an ominous sign? And why? After surviving the promises, the lies, and the disintegration of a fledgling society that never became prosperous, just, or equitable.

A disintegration all the more terrible because it is so inconspicuous. There are no bombs or explosions. No wounded people shedding that blood which assaults the eyes and which Facebook mercifully covers up as soon as it detects it, to protect its users’ visual sensibilities.

No, nobody sees us. Nobody hears us. The entire island could disappear, just as even the sharpest outlines are swallowed up by darkness.

As though we were being engulfed by the waters that separate us from the most powerful country in the world.

If an unspoken joy awakens with the arrival of DAF, a heavy sadness settles over everything when the day comes when the blessing shifts to another circuit that you will see glowing at night, while we return to the darkness and the wretched feeling of abandonment.

Then you console yourself by counting the weeks it takes for DAF to rotate through each of the circuits, like the hands of a clock, like the rotation of the Earth, until it is our turn once again to experience that fleeting season of normality.

Read more from the diary of Veronica Vega here on Havana Times.

Autumn, Toulon, France. By: Xavier Anaise (France). Camera: Canon Eos 5D mark III

World.title: Brazil's falling real and pressure on the Argentine peso are "bad news" for Uruguay's summer
World.content:
Brazil's falling real and pressure on the Argentine peso are “bad news” for Uruguay's summer

25th Wednesday, November 2026 - 17:23 UTC Full article

Argentines and Brazilians are Uruguay's main visitors during the southern summer

Currency turbulence in Argentina and Brazil is “bad news” for Uruguay's inbound tourism, just weeks before the start of the summer season, the Economic Outlook Observatory of the Catholic University of Uruguay warned in its latest report, published on Tuesday, according to the Uruguayan newspaper El País.

“Although to a large extent the summer tourist season is already 'decided', the recent turbulence in our neighbours may affect the decisions of those who have not yet made up their minds,” the document says. The observatory considers that an Argentina with country risk above 1,000 basis points and a Brazil whose currency fell after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's re-election are “bad news for our inbound tourism”.

The report analyses the evolution of prices measured in dollars in the three countries over the past 12 months. Argentina is 17% more expensive in dollars than in November 2025, which until now made it less competitive than Uruguay as a destination. However, the recent rise in the “contado con liquidación” dollar, the exchange rate the observatory regards as closest to an unrestricted market, could make Argentine prices cheaper in dollars, something the report says has already “begun to emerge”.

Brazil became more expensive in dollars during the first half of the year, then stabilised and became cheaper “suddenly” in November after Lula's election victory, and is now 3% cheaper than a year ago. Uruguay, by contrast, became cheaper in March thanks to monetary easing but then showed a slight upward trend, and in November is 3% more expensive in dollars than a year ago.

Argentines and Brazilians are Uruguay's main visitors during the southern summer. The warnings come at a time of tension in both countries: Argentina entered a technical recession in the third quarter, and Brazil's Central Bank last week sold US$1 billion from its reserves to curb the rise of the US currency.

World.title: Falklands at JMC: UK steps up security support for British Overseas Territories
World.content:
Falklands at JMC: UK steps up security support for British Overseas Territories

25th Wednesday, November 2026 - 11:20 UTC Full article

Uma Kumaran MP – UK Minister for the OTs and David Burt JP MP – Premier of Bermuda and President of the UK's Overseas Territories Association (UKOTA)

The UK government and elected leaders and representatives from the Overseas Territories are meeting in London, beginning this Monday until November 26, for the annual Joint Ministerial Council (JMC). The JMC is a chance for UKOT leaders to come together to celebrate partnerships with UK and tackle the major challenges of our time.

The UK government and elected leaders and representatives from the Overseas Territories are meeting in London, beginning this Monday until November 26, for the annual Joint Ministerial Council (JMC). The JMC is a chance for UKOT leaders to come together to celebrate partnerships with UK and tackle the major challenges of our time.

The Territories are custodians of extraordinary biodiversity and marine environments, which includes some of the most extraordinary places on Earth – from spectacular coral reefs to huge penguin populations and vast protected ocean like the Sargasso Sea. Preserving this natural heritage is not just good for Britain it is of crucial importance for the whole world's climate ambition.

In an increasingly volatile world, security is also closely connected too. Malign states, criminal gangs, cyber hackers – each seek to exploit weaknesses for their own gain. By working together to protect our communities and respond to emerging threats, the UK and Overseas Territories are more than the sum of our parts.

Working on this objective, people across the British Overseas Territories will benefit from greater protection as the UK steps up security support for the Territories. UK is committing £18m in new funding to tackle organized crime, violence and emerging security threats.

New support will focus on policing, criminal justice and prisons, maritime security, cyber and safeguarding capabilities. It will also draw on UK expertise to enable increased information sharing and cooperation between the Territories.

The four-day Joint Ministerial Council is an annual event to celebrate the modern partnership and explore closer collaboration on shared key priorities, including security, economic growth and climate.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said that the “Overseas Territories are an essential part of the British family of nations, and in a more dangerous world, our security is increasingly bound together.

”Through improved policing, justice and security, today's funding will help to protect us all from malign actors that would do us harm, from organized crime to cyber hackers and hostile states“.

Minister for the Overseas Territories Uma Kumaran pointed out that, ”The Joint Ministerial Council is an important moment for the UK and our Overseas Territories to come together and tackle head-on the key issues of our time.

“The strength of our relationship lies in our ability to tackle challenges around security, growth and climate together, drawing on our respective expertise, experience and global connections.

Furthermore ”when the Territories prosper, Britain prospers too. By standing together, we are stronger, safer and better prepared for the future”.

In effect the Territories are also crucial to Britain's prosperity by supporting investment, jobs and economic activity. Trade between the UK and the Territories is worth around £17bn. Taken together, that puts them among Britain's top 25 trading partners, ahead of major economies including South Korea, Brazil and South Africa.

This is what Britain's relationship with the Territories is about – communities standing together, protecting our shared environment and standing up to the threats we face. It is something we should all value, invest in and be proud of.

The Minister for the Overseas Territories will also use the summit to announce a new safeguarding partnership between the FCDO and the London Borough of Camden.

This will see the exchange of expertise and best practices between the UK and the Overseas Territories, strengthening safeguarding across communities through shared learning.

This year's Joint Ministerial Council is centered on advancing a modern, equal and forward-looking partnership based on mutual respect, shared responsibility and ensuring Overseas Territories voices are heard in decisions that affect them.

The event is expected to focus on wide-ranging discussions on security and resilience, sustainable economic growth, climate and nature, AI, tech and more.

Discussions are also expected on a shared commitment to tackling Violence Against Women and Girls (VAWG), recognizing the challenges of this in isolated communities and the collaboration between the UK and Territories in this area.

The meeting builds on the recently agreed Charter for UK Government Engagement with the Overseas Territories. The Charter recognizes the UK's responsibilities towards the Territories and commits to championing Territories' voices and interests.

Falklands and self-determination

The Falkland Islands as a UK Overseas Territory is represented by the Chair of the Legislative Assembly. In a brief statement MLA Ford underlined the significance of JMC and UK's support for self-determination, which is “enshrined in the UN Charter as a fundamental right, yet one we must continually defend. While our freedom was restored by the taskforce in 1982, our right to determine our own future remains challenged by Argentina.

”The cross-party support of MPs and peers is therefore invaluable and we are deeply grateful. Today, our diverse, welcoming community remains united in its determination to shape its own future“.

MLA Ford also recalled that in 2013, 99.8% of Falkland Islanders, on a 92% turnout, voted in an internationally observed referendum to remain a self-governing Overseas Territory of the UK. ”This was self-determination in action”.

World.title: British heritage in Chile, 1858 Catedral de San Pablo, refurbished in city-port Valparaiso
World.content:
British heritage in Chile, 1858 Catedral de San Pablo, refurbished in city-port Valparaiso

25th Wednesday, November 2026 - 11:17 UTC Full article

Catedral de San Pablo brought together the early immigrant British community which settled in the central port city of Valparaíso, 120km from the capital Santiago.

Chile's oldest Anglican church will be preserved as a museum to celebrate the role of the British Anglicans building religious tolerance in Chile. St Paul's Cathedral, (Catedral de San Pablo), brought together the early immigrant British community which settled in the central port city of Valparaíso, 120km away from the capital Santiago.

Chile's oldest Anglican church will be preserved as a museum to celebrate the role of the British Anglicans building religious tolerance in Chile. St Paul's Cathedral, (Catedral de San Pablo), brought together the early immigrant British community which settled in the central port city of Valparaíso, 120km away from the capital Santiago.

After years and years of attempting to repair the church which has stood since 1858, a cultural center has been transferred into management of the building.

Destino Valparaíso, which has the Immigrant Museum in their building across the street from St Paul's Cathedral on Cerro Concepción, will take over the cathedral built on a centerpiece hill in the port city.

“Chile didn't have freedom of religion when the British arrived in the 1820s, and they wanted to practice their faith, which was Anglican,” Eduardo Dib, executive director of Destino Valparaíso, told Religion Unplugged.

As the Chilean independence movement from Spain began, and free trade was declared in Valparaíso by the First Junta Government in 1811, a wave of immigration built and peaked in the second half of the 19th century.

British immigrants were the most influential immigrant group in the city, and started building a cemetery in 1823. The “Dissidents Cemetery”, as it was known, was the only place where Protestants were allowed to be buried.

St Paul's was built to be discreet with no main entrance, small windows and no spire, cross or bell tower. A Lutheran church was built later on in the 19th century by Germans 41 years after St Paul's, and became the first Protestant church in South America with a bell tower. The Church and State were later separated in Chile's 1925 constitution.

St Paul's was designed by British designer William Henry Lloyd and was a place of worship under the Diocese of the Falkland Islands, like most South American Protestant churches, until 1963. The cathedral now belongs to the Anglican Diocese of Valparaíso.

Michelle Prain, a professor at Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, said: “St. Paul's is a witness to the tensions between a clerical state that gradually became liberalized, and people of different faiths.”

It was declared a historic monument in 1979 by the Chilean government and became a cathedral in 2016. The neo-gothic cathedral will be handed over to Destino Valparaíso on 30 November, and before then, the roof, floors, pews and stained-glass windows will have been restored.

World.content:
CIA and US intelligence office suffer intrusion exposing unclassified information

25th Wednesday, November 2026 - 01:08 UTC Full article

The CIA headquarters seal in Langley, Virginia

The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the US Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a computer intrusion that exposed unclassified information from an open-source intelligence analysis system, The New York Times reported on Tuesday. Unlike the system outages of recent weeks, attributed to technical failures, this is a security breach.

The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the US Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a computer intrusion that exposed unclassified information from an open-source intelligence analysis system, The New York Times reported on Tuesday. Unlike the system outages of recent weeks, attributed to technical failures, this is a security breach.

The intrusion affected a network analysts use to draw intelligence from public, unclassified material such as social media, satellite imagery and commercial databases, according to US officials and people familiar with the incident cited by the newspaper and by Reuters. It is unclear what information was compromised or how the intrusion occurred, and data from other federal agencies was probably also exposed. Those responsible have not been identified.

The Office of the Director of National Intelligence said there had been “no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems”. The CIA did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The incident adds to a series of security breaches at federal bodies: according to Reuters, one has recently been reported at the Department of Agriculture and two at the FBI, one of them at its National Crime Information Center, while the Pentagon and the Department of Homeland Security have also been affected by cyber incidents.

It also coincides with a string of technology failures that authorities attributed to technical causes: the global Microsoft outage on November 12; the nationwide ground stop of all US flights for about four and a half hours on November 13, which the government blamed on outdated telecommunications equipment; and the outage of the National Security Agency's classified internal network on November 17, which the agency attributed to routine maintenance.

According to Uruguay's El País, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is no evidence that the failures are linked or that the country is under a systemic attack.

World.title: Job creation slows and unemployment ticks up in Mexico’s third quarter
World.content:
Mexico added 122,348 jobs in the third quarter of 2026, according to official data, down from 487,434 in the second quarter.

The slower pace of job creation coincided with a slowdown in quarter-over-quarter economic growth. Mexico’s economy grew 0.9% on a sequential basis in the third quarter, compared to 1.4% in Q2.

The national statistics agency INEGI reported on Wednesday that 60,162,442 (60.16 million) people were in jobs in the third quarter, up from 60.04 million in the second quarter.

The total number of people in jobs was 628,993 higher in the third quarter than a year earlier.

Overall, the number of women in jobs increased by 157,009 between the second and third quarters, while the number of employed men fell by 34,661.

INEGI also reported on Wednesday that Mexico’s unemployment rate was 2.9% in Q3, up from 2.7% in the previous quarter. That’s the highest rate of any quarter since Q3 of 2024. Gabriela Siller, director of economic analysis at Banco Base, said that the higher unemployment rate and the high level of employment informality were signs of a “weak” labor market.

Mexico’s employment informality rate — the percentage of total workers employed in the informal sector of the economy — was 55% in Q3, down from 55.1% in Q2.

The newspaper El Economista reported that 78% of the jobs added in the third quarter were formal sector positions, causing the informality rate to decline slightly.

Of the more than 60.1 million people in jobs in the third quarter, 6.9% were underemployed, down from 7.1% in Q2.

Which sectors added the most jobs over the past year?

According to INEGI’s data, 722,566 jobs were added in Mexico’s tertiary or services sector in the 12 months to the end of September. The secondary sector added 179,297 positions in the same period, while the primary sector shed 270,633 jobs.

The industries that added the most jobs between the end of Q3 2025 and the end of Q3 2026 were:

Diverse services: 337,440

Construction: 166,384

Government and international organizations: 152,750

Professional, financial and corporate services: 150,431

Restaurants and accommodation services: 112,475

Social services: 55,599

Manufacturing: 20,799

The composition of Mexico’s workforce

Mexico’s economically active population (PEA) — the number of people in jobs and looking for work — numbers 61.96 million, according to INEGI’s third-quarter data.

The percentage of economically active people who currently hold a paid job (i.e., not seeking employment) is 97% (35.3 million men and 24.9 million women).

Of the 60.16 million people in jobs, 64.3% (38.71 million) work in the tertiary sector, 24.7% (14.85 million) work in the secondary sector and 10.3% (6.19 million) work in the primary sector.

The informal sector workforce is made up of 33.11 million people, or 55% of all workers.

Around 68.4% (41.14 million) of all workers are employees, while 6.2% (3.67 million) are employers.

Around 22% (13.33 million) of employed people work for themselves and have no paid staff. The number of independent, self-employed workers increased by more than 386,000 in the 12 months to the end of September.

Just over 3.2% (1.94 million) of workers are unpaid, according to INEGI’s latest employment data.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: A ‘unique’ human skeleton found during AIFA airport construction may date back 13,000 years
World.content:
A male human skeleton unearthed in 2021 during construction of the Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA) outside Mexico City has now been confirmed by the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) to date back at least 11,700 years, making it one of the 23 oldest human skeletons found in the Basin of Mexico.

Foreign laboratories determined the age of the find by focusing mainly on the third molar. Isotopic Aging Inc., in Belgium, examined collagen and determined an age of between 12,987 and 13, 087 years before the present. The University of Georgia, in the United States, studied bioapatite — a non-organic substance in human bones and teeth — to come up with an age of between 11,700 and 12,050 years.

“Yotzin is one of the oldest human remains known to us from the Basin of Mexico,” said Culture Minister Claudia Curiel de Icaza, using the skeleton’s nickname from a Náhuatl word for “unique.” “Its dating brings us closer to a period in our history for which very little evidence exists, and it opens up new possibilities for investigating how those populations lived and where they came from.”

Three other human skeletons were found during the AIFA’s construction work, but according to INAH anthropologist Arturo Talavera González, Yotzin’s features are unique, as his nickname implies. He measures 1.75 meters tall and features high bone mass and a “tremendously robust” skeleton, showing characteristics of a hunter used to long-distance walking and combat.

As Yotzin’s teeth were examined, tooth wear was confirmed but there were no cavities. That absence reflects the fact that pre-ceramic hunter-gatherers did not consume sugars or simple carbohydrates. As Talavera explains it, instead they chewed many roots and tough barks, and used their teeth as a “third hand” for cutting and crushing, which accounts for the wear on its teeth.

Yotzin was discovered by archaeologist Israel Peña in the northwestern sector of AIFA, in sediments associated with ancient marshy environments and the remains of Late Pleistocene fauna – primarily mammoths and camels. Initially, Peña assumed they belonged to a camel. But as the excavation expanded, he identified them as human.

INAH expects to have the results of a genomic study from the University of Burgos, Spain, available during the first quarter of 2027. It should clarify the individual’s ancestry and provide information about the ancient populations of the Basin of Mexico, a geological region comprising four valleys, including the Valley of Mexico.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: El Jalapeño: Mexico’s new Animal Welfare Law officially reclassifies Mexico City roof dogs as municipal early-warning infrastructure
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Congress has formally approved the General Law on Animal Welfare, Care and Protection, landmark legislation that legally recognizes domestic animals as sentient beings while carefully preserving the constitutional right of second-story concrete roofs in the capital to serve as unregulated canine surveillance towers.

The sweeping reform, which amends five separate federal statutes and awaits publication in the Official Gazette, mandates that pet owners provide constant access to drinking water, suitable nutrition and shelter from harsh weather. However, legislative aides confirmed that the statute includes a critical semantic carve-out classifying a three-by-four-meter slab of sun-baked mortar in Colonia Narvarte or Santa María la Ribera as “an elevated, open-air security perimeter with panoramic street visibility.”

Under the new framework, failing to meet basic standards of pet care can result in administrative detention of up to 36 hours and steep fines. Yet legal analysts noted that the law’s enforcement mechanisms in Mexico City rely heavily on whether a territorial chihuahua barking at a passing tamales oaxaqueños loudspeaker at 3:14 a.m. constitutes “emotional distress” or “performing essential municipal infrastructure duties.”

“We are thrilled to align Mexico with the highest international standards of animal sentience,” said Hilario Padilla, a policy adviser to the Senate’s Joint Committee on Urban Ecology and Elevated Guard Dogs. “At the same time, we had to respect capital realities. If you take Solovino off a third-floor roof in Iztapalapa, who is going to alert a four-block radius that a gas truck or camote vendor has entered the neighborhood?”

The bill also cracks down on unregulated pet sales on social media platforms and prohibits aesthetic mutilations, though it stops short of defining whether an overturned plastic laundry tub wedged next to a tinaco water tank qualifies as “adequate protection from the elements.” Across Mexico City boroughs from Coyoacán to Azcapotzalco, residents reported that their local roof dogs had already reviewed the legislation and found it entirely satisfactory, largely because nobody climbed the staircase to tell them about it.

Lawmakers indicated that a follow-up subcommittee will convene next spring to determine whether a piece of corrugated fiberglass weighted down by a cinder block meets the federal definition of a “clean and safe environment,” provided the dog is left with at least some shade between noon and 4 p.m.

Sheinbaum sides with coffee growers in dispute with Nestlé

The reporter asked the president whether federal authorities would speak with the coffee producers and governor of Chiapas about the issue.
