“I agree with the campesinos, with the coffee growers,” Sheinbaum said.

“Nestlé has to pay what it has to pay for a kilo of coffee,” she said.

Sheinbaum noted that coffee producers say that Nestlé sells coffee for 580 pesos per kilo, but only pays 43 pesos for a kilo of beans.

“I think what they’re asking is for them to buy [a kilo of coffee beans] for between 50 and 60 pesos. We completely agree with what they’re requesting,” she said.

Sheinbaum said she had instructed the minister of agriculture to “support” the coffee growers in Chiapas in their negotiations with Nestlé.

“It cannot be that the international market sets the price of coffee for coffee growers through intermediaries … and that the price of Nescafé doesn’t come down,” she said.

“The coffee growers are right and we’re going to support them,” Sheinbaum said.

“And Nestlé has to pay [a fair price] and has to buy directly from the producers,” she added.

Sheinbaum questions why the US didn’t extradite Inés Gómez Mont to Mexico

Sheinbaum said that the release of Gómez Mont from ICE custody and her removal from the United States — but not to Mexico — is a “very important issue” in Mexico’s relationship with the U.S.

She noted that Gómez Mont was the subject of an Interpol Red Notice because a warrant for her arrest was issued in Mexico.

But the Red Notice — a request to law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender, or similar legal action — was “withdrawn” around a month ago, Sheinbaum said.

“So we have a very relevant complaint with Interpol. Why was this Red Notice withdrawn?” she said.

Sheinbaum said that Gómez Mont entered the United States on her Spanish passport and was consequently deported to Spain.

She questioned why U.S. authorities didn’t send her to Mexico given that “they know” there is an outstanding warrant for her arrest here.

“What we ask for in the relationship, as we have always said, is reciprocity,” Sheinbaum said, noting that her government has sent “94 criminals” — including a number of high-profile cartel figures — to the United States.

She said that “a lot” of Mexico’s extradition requests to the United States haven’t been granted, including ones for suspects in the infamous Ayotzinapa case involving the abduction and presumed murder of 43 students in Guerrero in 2014.

After reiterating that Gómez Mont’s case is an “important” issue in the Mexico-U.S. relationship, Sheinbaum said her government would send a diplomatic note to its U.S. counterpart.

She added that her administration has submitted a request to the government of Spain for Gómez Mont’s extradition to Mexico.

“We already requested it. But we’re interested in knowing why the Red Notice was withdrawn … because there is ample proof that she dedicated herself to fake invoices,” Sheinbaum said.

“So why wasn’t she extradited to Mexico?”

Sheinbaum explains why her husband didn’t accompany her to China

Asked why her husband, Jesús María Tarriba Unger, didn’t accompany her to China last week for the APEC Leaders’ Meeting, Sheinbaum explained that he had work commitments.

“My husband works,” she said before breaking into a hearty laugh.

“As you know, he works at the Bank of Mexico,” Sheinbaum said, referring to Tarriba’s employment at the central bank as a financial risk specialist.

“He goes to work every day. … That’s why he didn’t go with me,” she said.

Sheinbaum noted that Tarriba does often accompany her on her weekend working trips to different parts of Mexico.

“But on this occasion, well, he also has his job,” she said.

World.title: MND Local BCS: Enjoying film and food festivals in Los Cabos, plus a guide to whale watching season
World.content:
Celebrities were synonymous with Los Cabos long before that moniker — a reference to the shared word for “cape” in both Cabo San Lucas and San José del Cabo — was officially coined for the newly minted municipality in 1981. When tourism began in the area in the late 1950s, celebrities were among the first guests at local hotels, including movie stars like John Wayne and Bing Crosby.

It’s not surprising, really, when you consider that Los Angeles has always been Los Cabos’ primary market for international arrivals, or that before the first scheduled flight from Los Angeles to La Paz was inaugurated in 1962, one needed either a boat or a private plane to reach Los Cabos’ early hotels.

But even as Los Cabos became more accessible in subsequent decades, celebrities continued to be among the destination’s most loyal visitors, a trend that has continued into the present.

However, it is only since 2012 that Hollywood A-listers have come to Los Cabos not just for pleasure, but also for business.

The Los Cabos International Film Festival returns in December

Numerous stars have walked the red carpet for opening night at the Los Cabos International Film Festival, or appeared to receive awards or talk up their latest films, including actors Monica Bellucci, Robert De Niro, Matt Dillon, Adam Driver, Gael García Bernal, Daniel Giménez Cacho, Nicole Kidman, Jared Leto, Diego Luna, Virginia Madsen, Ewan McGregor, Liam Neeson and Reese Witherspoon, and directors such as Terry Gilliam, Spike Lee and Oliver Stone.

Despite the movie star glamor, the festival is perhaps best known internationally as an industry platform that brings together filmmakers from the U.S., Canada and Mexico for behind-the-scenes dealmaking, and as a support network for Mexican filmmakers through its Gabriel Figueroa Film Fund (named for the acclaimed Mexican cinematographer). Locally, however, it’s the screenings that are the festival’s most beloved feature, including, through the years, the Mexican premieres for films like “Jackie” and “The Killing of a Sacred Deer.”

Screenings

For those planning to be in Los Cabos from Dec. 9-13, the scheduled dates for the 14th edition of the Los Cabos International Film Festival, headline screenings include “Elsinore,” a film starring Andrew Scott, Olivia Colman and “Mobland” villain Johnny Flynn, which will open the festival with an outdoor showing at the Puerto Los Cabos Marina.

Visit the festival’s website for a complete listing of screenings and events, including a Dec. 10 tribute to Dolores Heredia presented by fellow Mexican actor José María Yazpik. Like the majority of screenings, this retrospective will take place at Cinépolis in San José del Cabo, with tickets available to the public. The closing night outdoor screening, meanwhile, will be free in Plaza Mijares in San José del Cabo, although the film has yet to be announced.

Dates: Dec. 9-13

Location: Cinépolis, Mauricio Castro 1738, Campo de Golf Fonatur, 23400 San José del Cabo, B.C.S.

Cost: Not yet announced

Whale watching season approaching in Los Cabos

You don’t need to take a cruise to see whales in Los Cabos, as transiting cetaceans can be seen from virtually every coastal vantage during winter months. However, boat tours, particularly aboard high-speed inflatable Zodiacs, do offer the most intimate encounters once the season officially starts on Dec. 15, although “intimate” is relative, since regulations prevent boats from getting closer to whales than 60 to 80 meters (depending on the size of the boat).

For the benefit of first-time visitors, whale watching season essentially heralds the arrival of 5,000 or so whales, which have migrated from summer feeding grounds in the Arctic to their winter breeding grounds around Baja California Sur. Numerous whales make this annual journey, including gray and humpback whales, as well as blue, bryde, fin, minke, orca and sei species.

Gray whales are the main attractions in Magdalena Bay and the San Ignacio and Ojo de Liebre lagoons within the El Vizcaíno Biosphere Reserve, while in Los Cabos, transiting humpbacks, known for their spectacular breaching behavior, are typically the stars of local tours.

The season runs through April 15.

Foodie fest Sabor a Cabo returns

Sabor a Cabo was firmly established as the premier food festival in Los Cabos, at least before the COVID-19 pandemic, when the annual eat, drink and be merry fête featuring gourmet fare from international chefs and more than 50 local restaurants drew thousands of attendees, as well as a wealth of world-class musical talent, from Lila Downs to Earth, Wind and Fire.

This decade, though, the event sponsored by CANIRAC Los Cabos, the local restaurant association, suffered a long absence from annual event calendars during a three-year hiatus from 2020 to 2022 — although Sabor a Cabo Rural, a smaller gastronomic get-together held each spring in organic farm-to-table farming community Miraflores, has been more consistently scheduled.

The 18th edition of the main event, themed “La Verbena Sibarita” (“The Sybarite’s Fair”), should help restore Sabor a Cabo to its former prestige, particularly if organizers reach their targeted attendance of 3,500 on Dec. 5 at EDEA Venue, just outside Cabo San Lucas.

What to expect for the 2026 edition

The food and wine attractions will be abundant, highlighted by fare from 45 restaurants and a wine garden focused on Mexican vintners, with over 40 represented (many from Baja California’s Valle de Guadalupe). A producer’s market will also be held this year, along with a mixology garden; a chef’s plaza showcasing classes and presentations; a sybarite’s market spotlighting artisanal cheeses, chocolates and other gourmet goods; and “streets” focused on everything from seafood and tacos to coffee and desserts. The musical headliner is La Única Internacional Sonora Santanera.

Date: Dec. 5, 5 p.m. to 9 p.m.

Location: EDEA Venue, behind Viveros de la Baja, Puente Salto Seco, El Arenal, 23460 Cabo San Lucas, B.C.S.

Cost: General admission tickets are 3,250 pesos; VIP tickets are 5,600 pesos

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: Why the NFL’s Mexico moment belongs to its fiercely loyal fans
World.content:
Outside of Estadio Banorte (formerly Azteca), on a side street that veered off into the surrounding neighborhood, I saw something I’ve never witnessed before in Mexico: For an entire block, a large group of American football fans, all wearing their team jerseys, sombreros vaqueros, and bandanas, danced in unison while a singer belted out regional Mexican music from a microphone and speaker.

The vibe was akin to a Mexican family taking over the corner, setting up a tent with entertainment, and inviting everyone around to join in. But instead of celebrating a quinceañera or hosting a feria, this celebration was all in the name of the National Football League.

4-year hiatus comes to an explosive end

A diverse group of Mexicanos and out-of-towners relished the moment, some wearing George Kittle jerseys, others Justin Jefferson.

That energy reverberated all around the stadium, and all over Mexico’s capital, as the San Francisco 49ers hosted the Minnesota Vikings for the 2026 NFL Mexico City Game. The 49ers — clearly the fan favorite, having played the most NFL games on Mexican soil in league history — won 35-10.

After the game, three of the 49ers’ key players, Brock Purdy, Fred Warner and George Kittle, all donned matching mariachi sombreros during their post-game interview.

But it was the fans — 85,612 of whom were present for the game itself, as well as the many more who hosted or attended watch parties around the city — who made the NFL’s return to Mexico so magical.

‘It keeps growing’

In the days leading up to the game, Mexican-born NFL fans across generations and team loyalties came together for different events and rallies throughout the city, celebrating the league’s return after a four-year hiatus. The NFL’s absence was partially due to the renovation of Estadio Banorte, which was under construction for 22 months prior to the World Cup.

The anticipation was palpable. Mexican fans partied, chanted and high-fived visiting fans from the U.S., showcasing the league’s international potency.

“I’ve been watching the NFL for 45 years,” said Alberto López Cerrón, a 60-year-old 49ers fan who attended NFL Barrio, an NFL-curated fan experience, with hundreds of others on a Thursday before the game. “I remember watching Joe Montana, then Steve Young. Ever since those times, there have been more and more Niners fanatics in Mexico. It keeps growing.”

An atmosphere to rival any soccer match

López Cerrón certainly wasn’t alone. I met Mexican fans who traveled from Monterrey, others from Veracruz. Add to that Mexican Americans and other U.S. citizens who made the trip from California and Minnesota, Illinois and Nevada, eager to experience the NFL in Mexico, even if their team wasn’t playing.

Inside the stadium, fans cheered as loudly as I’ve ever heard at any NFL game — or soccer match, for that matter.

I grew up in the San Francisco Bay Area, meaning I grew up in a dyed-in-the-wool 49ers household, having attended games at Levi’s Stadium and the now-demolished Candlestick Park. I’ve also watched major soccer matches at Azteca, including a Liga MX final between Club América and los Rayados de Monterrey.

The NFL fan experience was distinct: as boisterous and energizing as any headlining sports event, but also filled with an air of gratitude from fans who are aware that it’s not something they get to regularly do.

Cultivating a deep loyalty across generations

Being an NFL fan in Mexico can be odd. For starters, unless they choose to travel for several months out of every year, most fans will be lucky if they get to see even one game in a season. Secondly, the sport itself — violent and highly Americanized — doesn’t translate very cleanly into everyday Mexican life. It requires expensive equipment to play, and a grasp of foreign rules and sports jargon.

Those who do come to appreciate the gringo sport, though, are deeply loyal to it. And there are, according to NFL reports, more than 39.5 million of them in Mexico.

Germán Robles is among them. The 49-year-old NFL fanatic is, coincidentally, a 49ers supporter. In fact, he’s the president and founder of Club 49ers, one of Mexico’s largest 49ers fan groups, which he launched in 2014.

He claims that the group broke the Guinness World Record for the photo with the most Mexican 49ers fans in one frame, with over 850 club members gathering at the Auditoría Nacional last week. While Mexico News Daily couldn’t independently verify whether the record was broken, footage of the massive gathering is available online.

“I’ve been a fan since 1988,” Robles says. “My father was a huge fan of the Washington Redskins [now the Commanders]. He had four sons, but none of us were Redskins fans. My brothers chose the Cowboys and Steelers, but I fell in love with the 49ers.”

Robles and his club have remained on the front lines of NFL fandom in Mexico by hosting parties, organizing fan activities, and bringing 49ers supporters from all over Mexico together. It highlights a distinct segment of Mexican sports fans who, rather than wearing the jerseys and apparel of the Guadalajara Chivas or UNAM Pumas, have chosen athletes like Jerry Rice as their sports idols. Rice himself was in attendance at the game and entered the arena wearing a tri-color mariachi sombrero.

“I’ve had the honor of meeting Jerry Rice three times, and I honestly love the way he played,” Robles tells me in Spanish. “He’s the best player of all time.”

Robles and his generation represent the older vanguard of NFL fandom. But it isn’t just the veterans of the sport who enjoy it. Many younger fans — from children to Gen Z teenagers and young adults — attended the game or watched from their homes. And many of them aren’t just fans of former NFL dynasties or legendary players. They’re fans of the present.

One of my college-aged nephews, Santiago, is a die-hard Buffalo Bills fan, despite being born and raised in Veracruz. We regularly talk trash to each other, and every Sunday he posts photos of Bills quarterback Josh Allen on social media after a victory.

It’s part of an ongoing trend in which the NFL is finally reaping the rewards of its growth outside the United States, as younger generations engage with the league’s current stars.

Mexico City fandoms are decades in the making

For decades, the NFL has been carefully planning and executing its expanded footprint in Latin America, culminating in Bad Bunny’s first-of-its-kind Spanish-language halftime show during last year’s Super Bowl, which featured a groundbreaking performance from the Puerto Rican superstar.

Mexico, in particular, has long been the NFL’s biggest target, as the league has relentlessly promoted the sport south of the border, an effort that’s ramped up in recent years. It’s not uncommon to see NFL s around Mexico City — a phenomenon I never would’ve dreamed of as a young Mexican American visiting my family in Mexico — such as a major Las Vegas Raiders mural in a residential area near the TAPO bus terminal.

The efforts have clearly paid off. In 2024, Mexico topped out with 62.5 million fans tuning in for the Super Bowl, ranking second in the world behind only the U.S.

The NFL’s presence in Mexico goes through the 1970s, ‘80s and ‘90s when the league would hype up the “American Bowl” by playing preseason games around the globe, including Montreal, Tokyo, Dublin, London, Monterrey and of course, Mexico City. Of all those international American Bowl games, the largest crowd ever recorded was in 1994, when the Dallas Cowboys played the Houston Oilers in front of 112,376 people at Estadio Azteca.

This year’s sold-out game was the fifth time the NFL has been received by Mexico City’s fans, and the first since 2022, when the 49ers played against the Arizona Cardinals. Incidentally, the 49ers also played in the first-ever NFL Mexico Game, in 2005, also against the Cardinals.

In addition to the Cardinals, Vikings and 49ers, other NFL teams that have played a regular season game in Mexico City include the Houston Texans, Las Vegas Raiders, New England Patriots, Kansas City Chiefs and Los Angeles Chargers. That list grows to 16 teams when exhibition games are included, dating back to 1978, when the Philadelphia Eagles played the New Orleans Saints.

Barrio NFL combines football, iconic neighborhoods

Right now, the NFL is capitalizing on its momentum with Mexican-inspired fan experiences.

Leading the charge was Barrio NFL, an artful display of football photography, arts, crafts and memorabilia. Housed inside Casa Grande in Condesa, the four-day exhibit sought to amplify different interpretations of the NFL in Mexico.

Ovaldito 😎 se dio a la tarea de pasear por la CDMX y visitó cada uno de los 4 sitios que conformarán Barrio NFL Y tú ¿Qué Ovaldito serías? 👀 https://t.co/HUQI23WCDA — NFL México (@nflmx) November 6, 2026

Here, fans roamed the neocolonial patio and walkways while taking photos with former NFL players and Super Bowl artifacts. In addition to supplying sports nostalgia, Barrio NFL added a fresh twist by replicating some of Mexico City’s famed neighborhoods to capture what the city’s NFL fandom looks, sounds and feels like in various communities.

Gallery rooms corresponded to four designated barrios — Tepito, Condesa, Coyoacán and Doctores — with distinct features highlighting the identity of each. Tepito, for example, was set inside an urban barbershop, while Coyoacán took its cues from an outdoor plaza complete with a replica of the Fuente de los Coyotes. Signage and iconography of the 49ers Vikings match-up were presented as rótulo signs, lucha libre cartaleras and sonidero prints.

Translating the game for Mexican fans

I’ve watched the NFL since childhood, and can confidently say I’ve never seen such a significant and visible effort to bring the sport to Mexico. Not to mention, in a way that has been so culturally responsive and attuned.

Growing up, I never felt like the NFL was particularly interested in translating the sport — both literally and figuratively — to its Spanish-speaking audiences beyond the U.S.’s rigid borders. But as of late, the league has changed its approach. And Mexico is at the center of it.

Of course, there’s much for the NFL to gain. Mexico, and Latin America as a whole, are ideal markets for the league, with Mexico and Brazil ranking as the second and third largest NFL audiences in the world, behind only the U.S.

What does the NFL’s future in Mexico look like?

That said, it hasn’t been without some botches. Nick Bosa of the 49ers has fumbled his way through the NFL’s international transition, making pregame comments about Mexican fans that were largely perceived as derogatory. The Pro Bowl defensive end, who has a history of supporting President Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, implied that Mexican fans needed to be taught how to cheer for the sport. As a result, chants of “culero” (“asshole”) rang throughout Estadio Banorte when Bosa was introduced on the jumbotron.

Those instances further feed stereotypes on both sides of the border: that Americans view Mexicans as rudimentary and unable to comprehend the sport, while Mexicans view Americans as arrogant and out of touch. Nobody wins.

The NFL will never be the main attraction in Latin America. But it’s more beloved than ever; that has to count for something in Mexico’s expanding sports circuit. And with flag football set to enter the Olympics, and the prospect of Mexico’s national women’s team clinching gold as one of the world’s highest-ranked teams, the sport’s aura will likely only get brighter.

In the meantime, however, the NFL isn’t going anywhere, and last week’s carousel of colors, fandom and distinctly Mexican passion is proof.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: In Beijing, Ebrard pushes for more Mexican exports to China
World.content:
Remaining in China after last week’s close of the APEC summit, Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard took advantage of the 11th Mexico-China High-Level Group Meeting to arrange for a working group to be formed to address Mexico’s gaping trade deficit with the Asian giant.

Ebrard met with his Chinese counterpart, Commerce Minister Wentao Wang, in Beijing — a 2,000-kilometer flight from Shenzhen, the site of the APEC summit — to urge the establishment of new mechanisms to boost Mexican exports to China.

Resultados de la reunión del Grupo de Alto Nivel México-China https://t.co/YUgHILOlH0 — Marcelo Ebrard C. (@m_ebrard) November 23, 2026

He emphasized the need to change the “persistent and growing” trade imbalance between Mexico and China. While China is projected to export more than US $130 billion worth of goods to Mexico this year, Mexico will likely export only around $10 billion to China.

The hope is that the new bilateral working group will create the necessary protocols to allow the export of certain Mexican products, such as avocados, lemons, beef, pork, sorghum and processed seafood, some of which have been in the works for a decade.

“Our ability to export more to China depends on the authorization of all these protocols, so that the balance between imports and exports improves in Mexico’s favor,” Ebrard said. “That is fair and reasonable.”

Several Mexican companies are prepared to export their products if a favorable business environment can be established. For example, the Mexican state-owned company Exportadora de Sal (Salt Exporter) hopes to increase its market share in China, having provided a proposal to supply up to 10 million tonnes of salt over four years.

After attending the APEC meeting, President Sheinbaum stressed that deepening trade ties with China would not impede Mexico’s bilateral relationship with the United States.

“The economic integration between Mexico and the U.S. is very significant,” Sheinbaum said during a press conference. “What we want is greater cooperation with China on various issues, from scientific research to tourism, and everything related to this collaboration.”

At the same time, Sheinbaum ruled out for now the negotiation of a free-trade agreement with China.

With reports from La Jornada, Líder Empresarial and El Financiero

World.title: Nescafé coffee producers protest in southern Mexico over low pay
World.content:
Coffee producers from the Costa, Sierra and Frontera regions of Chiapas – Mexico’s largest coffee-producing state – marched on Monday to protest against the low prices that the multinational food company Nestlé pays them to produce coffee beans for Nescafé.

The demonstration moved through the main streets of Tapachula and concluded with a rally in front of the municipal government building.

Protestan #Productores de #Café contra la empresa #Nestlé.

En #Tapachula cerca de 400 #Cafeticultores se manifiestan frente al palacio municipal contra la empresa global #NESCAFÉ exigiendo mejores precios al producto que le venden.

Les están comprando por debajo del precio de producción. #Chiapas — Gabriela Coutiño (@GabyCoutino) November 23, 2026

“We harvest the coffee, tend to it all year round, and we get paid 43 pesos (US $2.20) per kilogram. That same coffee sells for 580 pesos ($29) in the supermarket,” the protesters pointed out.

The farmers are demanding a fair price of at least 60 pesos ($3) per kg.

Meanwhile, farmer Eduardo Camarena told the newspaper La Jornada that the discontent extends throughout at least 20 municipalities and that the issue affects 165,000 families.

He noted that the gap between the price Nestlé pays farmers and the coffee’s retail price does not result in higher earnings for producers.

Camarena added that although farmers have held talks with the company, Nestlé has refused to adjust prices in response to the cost increases producers have faced. Moreover, he accused the company of centralizing the coffee market in the border region.

Protesters requested the intervention of the Chiapas state government to facilitate negotiations with Nestlé to agree on what they consider a fair price for their coffee.

“The cost of production, plus a decent profit for the producer — that is what we are asking for; it’s only fair,” he stressed.

Figures from the Agriculture and Rural Development Ministry (Sader) revealed that in Mexico, approximately 701,735 hectares across 10 states are dedicated to growing coffee beans, with national production expected to exceed 1 million tonnes by the end of 2026.

Production is spearheaded by Chiapas, with a contribution of 392,000 tonnes of beans per year, followed by Veracruz, with 256,000 and Puebla, with 225,000.

With reports from La Jornada and Diario de Chiapas

World.title: Argentines Buy 3% Less at Supermarkets
World.content:
Argentines are paying more pesos for groceries but taking home less, and the supermarket survey shows that gap has now lasted nine months.

Photo: MewMeowth / Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

ARGENTINA · ECONOMY

Argentine supermarkets sold 3.0% less in real terms in September 2026 than a year earlier, the ninth yearly fall in a row, INDEC said on Wednesday 25 November 2026. INDEC is Argentina’s national statistics institute.

For US readers, the survey is a timely read on whether Argentine households are spending again. Peso sales rose 25.0%, yet the volume bought kept shrinking.

Key Facts Who INDEC, Argentina’s national statistics institute, published the September supermarket survey on 25 November 2026.

What Sales at constant prices fell 3.0% from September 2025, the ninth yearly fall in a row.

The total Supermarkets sold 2.45 trillion pesos in September, about US$1.5 billion at 1,602 pesos per dollar.

Prediction markets Polymarket, a crypto-based betting market, gives 30% to 34.9% inflation for 2026 a 95% chance (25 November, 15:55 ET).

Power Index Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 60.2 points (November 2026 edition).

Argentines are paying more pesos for groceries but taking home less, and the supermarket survey shows that gap has now lasted nine months.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on INDEC (Argentina) Email address Follow

INDEC counts supermarket sales twice, at current prices and at constant prices, and the second count strips out inflation. At constant prices, September sales were 3.0% below September 2025 and 0.9% below August after INDEC cleaned the data of regular calendar swings.

At current prices, supermarkets sold 2.45 trillion pesos (about US$1.5 billion at 1,602 pesos per dollar, rate of RT, a market-data provider, on 25 November 2026). That is 25.0% more than a year earlier, but INDEC’s implicit price index for the sector, which shows how much prices in supermarket sales rose, climbed 28.9% in the same year.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Argentina ranks 4th of 14 with 60.2 points. Strongest pillar: future resources (68); weakest: economic relationships (23). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Prices in supermarkets rose 1.7% in September alone, according to the same INDEC series. The gap between 28.9% price growth and 25.0% sales growth is what turns a nominal gain into a real loss.

The slide is not new. Real sales rose 2.0% across 2025, then turned negative in January 2026 and have stayed there, with falls of 2.1% in July and 3.7% in August.

INDEC’s trend-cycle line, which smooths out monthly noise, has dropped every month since April 2025. It now sits 5.2% below its March 2025 peak, a longer decline than the nine-month run in the yearly figures suggests.

INDEC sets its sales index at 100 for the year 2017. The seasonally adjusted reading for September 2026 was 79.55, against 82.77 a year earlier.

Over January to September, sales at current prices rose 23.9% while real sales fell 2.9%. The seasonally adjusted index, which is cleaned of regular calendar swings, has also dropped four months running, by 1.4% in June, 0.7% in July and 0.9% in each of August and September.

How Argentines pay at the till has shifted as well. Credit cards covered 40.7% of supermarket sales in September, down from 44.0% a year earlier, while INDEC’s catch-all category of other means of payment rose from 13.3% to 17.6%.

Online orders made up 3.3% of sales, against 3.5% a year earlier, so almost all of the money still changes hands in the shop. Cash and debit cards together account for 41.7% of sales.

For investors in Argentine bonds and shares through US funds, the message is that peso sales growth overstates demand. Retailers are selling fewer goods at higher prices, which helps revenue in pesos but not volumes.

INDEC publishes sales, not motives, so the reasons households are buying less stay open. Wholesale stores and shopping centres are covered by separate INDEC surveys that are not used here.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, shows a 95.3% chance that Argentina’s 2026 annual inflation lands between 30.0% and 34.9%. About US$117,411 has been traded across all ranges of the market (US$49,674 on this one), as of 25 November 2026, 15:55 ET.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

World.title: Kenyan Bank NCBA Profit Rises 14.5%
World.content:
A Kenyan bank under new South African ownership grew profit faster than costs, but set aside more for bad corporate loans. It is the first full set of results since the takeover.

KENYA · BANKING

NCBA Group, a Kenyan bank listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange, said on 25 November that profit after tax rose 14.5% to 18.8 billion Kenyan shillings (KES), about US$145 million, in the nine months to 30 September 2026. A year earlier it earned KES 16.4 billion (about US$126 million).

It is the first set of results since South Africa’s Nedbank took a 66% stake. Conversions use the market-data provider RT’s rate of 25 November 2026, 1 KES = US$0.007689.

Key Facts Who NCBA Group PLC, Kenyan lender, now a subsidiary of South Africa’s Nedbank.

What Nine-month profit after tax up 14.5% to KES 18.8 billion (about US$145 million).

Why Loan earnings after deposit costs rose 19.8% while costs grew only 4.3%.

When Nine months to 30 September 2026, published 25 November 2026.

A Kenyan bank under new South African ownership grew profit faster than costs, but set aside more for bad corporate loans. It is the first full set of results since the takeover.

NCBA’s profit before tax rose 14.6% to KES 23.4 billion (about US$180 million), according to the group’s results release of 25 November. The rise in net interest income, the money earned on loans minus the interest paid on deposits, did most of the work.

Net interest income grew 19.8% to KES 38.4 billion (about US$295 million), while operating expenses rose only 4.3% to KES 29.1 billion (about US$224 million). That gap between income and costs is why profit grew faster than the balance sheet, which expanded 11.8%.

File photo: the Nairobi skyline with the Kenyatta International Convention Centre (KICC) tower, seen from Uhuru Park.

Nedbank Group Limited, a South African bank listed in Johannesburg, said in October that its offer for 66% of NCBA had become unconditional. The share transfer followed in early November 2026.

NCBA stays listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange, with the public holding the other 34%. Nedbank’s stake gives it control, so NCBA now reports as a subsidiary of the South African lender.

Provisions are the one line moving the wrong way. NCBA set aside KES 8.0 billion (about US$61.5 million) for credit losses in the nine months, up from KES 5.1 billion (about US$39 million) a year earlier.

The company’s release ties the higher charge to an intention to strengthen coverage on a few large corporate bad loans. The share of loans classed as non-performing, meaning borrowers behind on payments, was 10.1% and stable.

Lending is growing at a pace the bank can fund. Loan growth was 10.7%, and customer deposits rose 13.5% to KES 554 billion (about US$4.26 billion), per the 30 September figures in the release.

Total assets reached KES 744 billion (about US$5.72 billion). The bank’s total capital adequacy ratio, a regulatory cushion against losses, stood at 21.4% against a required minimum of 14.5%.

Digital lending remains a signature of the franchise, with KES 1.3 trillion (about US$10 billion) disbursed over the period, up 27.2%. The figure is cumulative lending, not the size of the loan book.

Return on average equity, profit as a share of shareholders’ money, was 19.0%. CEO John Gachora said the figure underscored “the quality of our returns”, and that operating income improved 15 per cent year on year.

Kenya’s bank still earns most of the profit. NCBA Bank Kenya produced 86% of group profit before tax, while Uganda, Tanzania and Rwanda together added KES 2.7 billion (about US$21 million), with lending up 21% and deposits up 17%.

Non-bank units, covering investment banking, insurance, leasing and bancassurance (insurance sold through banks), contributed KES 1.1 billion (about US$8.5 million) of pre-tax profit. The group’s non-funded income, mainly fees, insurance and trading, rose 7.2% to KES 22.9 billion (about US$176 million).

The interest-rate setting helps explain the demand for credit. The central bank’s rate-setting panel, the Monetary Policy Committee, held its benchmark lending rate (the Central Bank Rate) at 8.75% on 7 October 2026, after cutting it to that level in February.

Lower borrowing costs tend to lift loan demand but squeeze margins over time. The release does not say how NCBA expects the rate path to affect net interest income.

For US investors, the result is a first read on a Kenyan lender now under South African ownership. Nedbank, not NCBA, is the group’s parent, so NCBA’s listed shares trade on the Nairobi exchange rather than as a US-listed security.

Two things are not yet public. NCBA’s release does not mention a dividend, and it gives no figure for what the Nedbank integration will cost or save.

Two dates would matter next: the central bank’s December rate decision (date not yet announced) and NCBA’s full-year results. Neither date is confirmed yet.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who owns NCBA now?

Nedbank Group of South Africa holds 66% after the share transfer in early November 2026, and the public holds the rest. NCBA keeps its Nairobi listing.

Why did loan-loss provisions rise?

NCBA says it wants stronger cover for a few large corporate bad loans. The headline bad-loan ratio was stable.

Where does the profit come from?

Mostly from Kenya, which gave 86% of pre-tax profit. Uganda, Tanzania and Rwanda add a smaller share.

World.title: Chile Power Group Owners Seek New Partner
World.content:
Two Canadian pension funds want a new partner in the Chilean power group they have owned together for years. They would keep control.

Dalcahue pier, Chiloe island. Photo: Rjcastillo / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

CHILE · POWER UTILITIES

The Canadian pension funds that own Chile’s Grupo Saesa power group have started a search for a new investor to take a non-controlling stake, a group holding company said on 25 November 2026. Inversiones Eléctricas del Sur S.A. (IESA) made the disclosure in a regulatory notice to the Commission for the Financial Market (CMF), Chile’s financial regulator.

Alberta Investment Management Corporation (AIMCo) and Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan Board (OTPPB) would remain in charge. Chilean business reporting puts the stake at about one third of the group, or one sixth from each owner.

Key Facts Who Canadian pension managers AIMCo and Ontario Teachers’ control Chile’s Grupo Saesa power group.

What They begin a process to find an investor for a non-controlling stake, reported at about one third.

When Announced 25 November 2026; formal contacts with interested parties start in the coming days.

Unknown Price, bidders and timetable beyond the coming months have not been disclosed.

Two Canadian pension funds want a new partner in the Chilean power group they have owned together for years. They would keep control.

The notice says the controllers told IESA of the “start of a process to look for a potential investor interested in acquiring a non-controlling stake” in Inversiones Grupo Saesa Limitada. That company is the group’s controlling holding, and the notice says it holds 99.99% of the shares of IESA.

The notice also sets the pace: “In the coming days formal contact with potential interested parties will begin so that they can make a preliminary assessment and eventually express interest in taking part.” The wording is the Rio Times translation of the Spanish original, and the notice does not give a price, a list of bidders or a closing date.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Chile ranks 3rd of 14 with 62.9 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (86); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (38). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Chilean business reporting names BTG Pactual, a Brazilian investment bank, and J.P. Morgan, a US bank, as the advisers who will approach infrastructure investors in the coming months.

The filing itself does not name the banks, and neither the banks nor the companies have confirmed it.

File photo: Route 5 South on Chiloé island, southern Chile.

The two sellers have owned Saesa together for years. Morgan Stanley Infrastructure, a US fund, said on 8 November 2011 that it sold its half of Saesa to AIMCo, the pension manager of the Canadian province of Alberta, and Enel Chile, the Chilean arm of the Italian utility, said on 9 December 2022 that Ontario Teachers’ and AIMCo each hold 50% of Saesa.

Saesa then grew through the grid: Enel Chile said its sale of Enel Transmisión Chile, Enel’s grid unit, to Saesa closed on 9 December 2022 at US$1.399 billion for a 99.09% stake, after a public tender offer that ran from 7 November to 6 December. The unit operated 683 kilometres of transmission lines and 57 substations.

Feller Rate, a Chilean credit-rating agency, reaffirmed the investment-grade AA- rating of IESA and its subsidiaries in May 2026. The rating sets out how the agency sees the group’s ability to repay its debts.

For readers in the United States, the story is first about Canadian pension money rethinking a large Latin American holding. It is also a test of how much appetite infrastructure investors have for Chilean regulated power networks, which earn their income from distribution and transmission rather than from selling electricity at market prices.

Several points are open. The price, the identity of any buyer, a timetable beyond the coming months and whether the stake is sold in one block have not been disclosed, and no named holder has publicly objected to the process.

The next step is the formal contact with potential investors that the notice says will start in the coming days. The notice does not say whether the controllers would sell the stake in one block or in parts.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will the Canadian owners lose control of Saesa?

No. The notice describes a non-controlling stake, so the controllers would stay in charge.

Who is advising on the process?

Chilean business reporting names BTG Pactual and J.P. Morgan. The filing does not name them and neither bank has confirmed it.

Sources: Inversiones Eléctricas del Sur S.A., regulatory notice (hecho esencial, material-event notice) to the CMF, 25 November 2026; Enel Chile press release on the completed sale of its transmission business, 9 December 2022 (https://www.enel.cl/en/meet-enel/media/press-enel-chile/d202212-enel-chile-completes-the-sale-of-its-electricity-transmission-business.html); Feller Rate rating report on IESA, May 2026 (https://www.feller-rate.com/clasificacion-riesgo/10749/inversiones-electricas-del-sur-sa). World.title: São Paulo Water Firm Denies E. coli Claims
World.content:
The main water utility in São Paulo state says a wave of Instagram posts misread laboratory results to suggest its tap water is contaminated. Sabesp calls it a coordinated campaign.

BRAZIL · WATER UTILITIES

Sabesp, the main water utility of Brazil’s São Paulo state, said on Wednesday 25 November 2026 that it is the target of “a coordinated action of spreading false information on social networks about water quality”. The posts of recent days warned that the bacterium Escherichia coli, a marker of faecal contamination, had been found in water samples.

Sabesp’s monitoring counted 89 posts from at least 32 Instagram profiles between Monday 23 and Tuesday 24 November. The company says the water it supplies in every locality named in the posts is fit to drink and can be used normally for bathing.

Key Facts Who Sabesp, São Paulo state’s main water utility, accuses Instagram accounts of false contamination alerts.

What 89 posts from at least 32 profiles claimed E. coli in water, on 23 and 24 November.

Result New network samples in all cited cases were negative for E. coli, Sabesp says.

Next Sabesp is seeking to establish responsibility in court.

As of The afternoon of 25 November 2026.

The main water utility in São Paulo state says a wave of Instagram posts misread laboratory results to suggest its tap water is contaminated. Sabesp calls it a coordinated campaign.

Sabesp, formally Companhia de Saneamento Básico do Estado de São Paulo, issued its statement on Wednesday 25 November on the afternoon of Wednesday 25 November. It says the posts “used distorted laboratory results to support a claim of generalised contamination”.

The company says new samples collected in its distribution network in all the cited cases came back negative for E. coli. It adds that those samples also met the standards for the four other parameters assessed.

File photo: a Sabesp water tower in São Paulo.

Brazil’s drinking-water rule is the Health Ministry’s Portaria GM/MS nº 888 of 4 May 2021, which requires E. coli to be absent from a 100-millilitre sample. A single positive reading in a sample therefore counts as out of standard, which is why utilities repeat the test.

Sabesp says every result is recorded in Sisagua, the Health Ministry’s national information system for drinking-water quality surveillance, including samples that fail the standard. The public can also see the results on Sabesp’s website.

According to the company, crews return to the network at once whenever an analysis is out of standard. They collect new samples, investigate the cause and act, and Sabesp says it sent the results of the new collections in the cited cases to the health surveillance authority, known in Brazil as Vigilância.

The distinction matters for readers abroad because a one-off out-of-standard sample is not the same as a contaminated supply. Sabesp’s position is that the posts took isolated readings from its own records and presented them as proof that the water in whole areas is unsafe.

We have not seen the Instagram posts ourselves and cannot say whether any single sample cited in them was positive. Sabesp has not said which localities the posts name, and the statement does not identify who runs the profiles.

The company says it is seeking to establish responsibility in court. It has not said whether a case has been filed, against whom, or in which court.

Sabesp’s water supply is a daily concern for millions of households in São Paulo state, so alarms about contamination travel fast. The utility’s answer rests on two checks that readers can follow: the Sisagua records and the public results on its own website.

Our Brazil coverage tracks how public services and companies respond to online claims in the country’s largest state; see the Brazil hub. This story will be updated if Sabesp, the health authorities or a court publishes new findings.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is São Paulo tap water unsafe, according to Sabesp?

Sabesp says the water it supplies in every locality named in the posts is fit to drink and for normal bathing. It says new samples in the cited cases were negative for E. coli.

What is E. coli and why do utilities test for it?

Escherichia coli is a bacterium that signals faecal contamination in water. Brazil’s potability rule requires it to be absent from a 100-millilitre sample.

Where can residents check water results?

Sabesp says results are recorded in Sisagua and are also visible on the company’s website. It says out-of-standard samples are included.

World.title: Brazil’s Real Rallies as Dollar Drops 1.5%
World.content:
A currency that looked fragile on Monday ended Wednesday on firmer ground. The relief rests on central bank action and talk, not on a signed spending plan.

Markets: Brazil

The dollar lost about 1.5% against the Brazilian real on Wednesday 25 November 2026, closing at about 5.82 reais, its third straight daily fall. Only two days earlier, on Monday 23 November, it had briefly topped 6 reais.

Two forces moved the currency: the central bank put dollars on the market, and the federal government kept talking about more spending cuts. Both matter to anyone holding assets in the Brazil economy, because they bear on how the country pays its bills.

A currency that looked fragile on Monday ended Wednesday on firmer ground. The relief rests on central bank action and talk, not on a signed spending plan.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Bruno Moretti (Brazil) Email address Follow

The slide did not start on Wednesday. Since President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won re-election in the runoff on Sunday 25 October 2026, investors have seen fiscal policy, the way the state taxes and spends, as the weak point of his government.

Congress recently approved a fiscal adjustment worth 50 billion reais (about US$8.6 billion) for 2027, and Lula signed it without vetoes. Investors wanted more, and on Tuesday 24 November press reports said Lula had authorised sending Congress a further proposal on mandatory spending, the outlays the law forces the state to pay.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 74.2 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Planning and Budget Minister Bruno Moretti slowed that talk on Wednesday at a press conference in Brasília, the capital. “There is no PEC; what there is, is continuous discussion of measures,” he said, using the Portuguese acronym for a constitutional amendment proposal (our translation).

Moretti added that there is “no silver bullet, no D-Day”, and that the government has “a menu” of options that must keep the president’s premise of guaranteeing social rights. He said he wants new proposals to go to Congress before the year ends, and that extra measures give “more security” for meeting the primary budget targets (the balance before interest payments).

The central bank acted first, offering dollars in two “line” auctions in mid-morning and selling US$2 billion in one. In a line auction the bank sells dollars now and agrees to buy them back later, which adds dollars to the market for a while and can ease pressure on the exchange rate.

The dollar touched 5.97 reais early, then slid to a low of about 5.80 during the session. It closed at about 5.82, which is 2.2% below its close on Friday 20 November of about 5.95 (RT, a market data provider).

The dollar in Brazilian reais, daily candles to 25 November 2026. Source: RT market data; its close-to-close change is 1.5%.

In the afternoon the move gathered speed on a rumour. Luiz Carlos Trabuco Cappi, chairman of the board of Bradesco, a large Brazilian bank, was named as a possible finance minister after he met Lula at the Alvorada presidential residence on Monday 23 November.

No offer of the job has been confirmed. The rumour is also not the whole story, because the dollar lost ground against other currencies that day, so part of the fall had nothing to do with Brasília.

For a US traveller the move cuts both ways: US$1,000 now buys about 130 fewer reais than on Friday 20 November. For investors, a firmer real raises what Brazilian profits are worth in dollars, which matters to holders of New York-traded shares of oil company Petrobras (PBR), miner Vale (VALE) and bank Itaú Unibanco (ITUB), and of the EWZ fund that tracks Brazilian stocks.

How much of the fall came from the auctions, the Trabuco rumour or the weaker dollar abroad is not known, and we found no word on more auctions. A close back above 6 reais would signal that the relief has faded, while proposals sent to Congress before 31 December, as Moretti wants, would help it last.

What Prediction Markets Say Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, leads with Rafael Fonteles, governor of the state of Piauí, at about 51% to become Brazil’s next finance minister, ahead of Vice President Geraldo Alckmin at 24.0%. Trabuco is not a listed candidate, thin trading of US$21,719 makes the prices shaky, and they are bets, not polls (as of 25 November 2026, 3:45 p.m. ET). Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did the dollar fall against the real?

Dollar sales by the central bank, calmer talk on spending and a weaker dollar abroad all helped. Which mattered most is not clear.

Does Brazil have a new spending-cut amendment?

Not yet, according to the planning minister. The government is still discussing a set of measures.

What does a stronger real mean for visitors?

Each dollar buys fewer reais, so prices in Brazil look a little higher in dollar terms. The effect is small for now.

World.title: Ecuador Campaign Ends, Silence Fines Apply
World.content:
Ecuador’s silence and alcohol rules take effect on Friday, and the penalties are tied to the minimum wage.

File photo. Voting booths marked "El voto es secreto" (the vote is secret) at the Colegio Julio María Matovelle polling station in Cuenca, Ecuador, 16 November 2025. Photo: Martín Vasco, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

ECUADOR · ELECTIONS

Ecuador’s election campaign ends on Thursday 26 November 2026, and a ban on political messages starts at midnight. Anyone who breaks it risks a fine of US$241, and that includes ordinary citizens, not only candidates.

Ecuador votes on Sunday 29 November for mayors, prefects (provincial governors), councillors and parish board members, plus members of the Citizen Participation Council, a state oversight body. The National Electoral Council (CNE), the election authority, enabled 13,827,643 voters.

Key Facts Silence Campaigning stops Thursday 26 November; silence runs 00:00 Friday to 17:00 Sunday.

Fine Campaigning during silence, or breaking the alcohol ban, costs US$241.

Alcohol No sale or consumption from noon Friday 27 to noon Monday 30 November.

Prediction markets Polymarket, a US platform, gives Pabel Muñoz 44.5% for Quito mayor (3:42 p.m. ET, 25 November).

Ecuador’s silence and alcohol rules take effect on Friday, and the penalties are tied to the minimum wage.

The CNE opened the campaign on 12 November and closes it on Thursday 26 November, under its electoral calendar. It fixed Sunday 29 November as voting day for the local elections.

The Código de la Democracia, Ecuador’s electoral law, punishes propaganda on the banned days with a fine of 50% of the unified basic salary (SBU), the national monthly minimum wage. The Labour Ministry set the 2026 SBU at US$482 in ministerial agreement MDT-2025-195 of 15 December 2025, so the fine is US$241.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Ecuador ranks 8th of 14 with 37.2 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (14). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B); 51 homicides per 100,000. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The penalty reaches citizens as well as candidates. The Electoral Disputes Tribunal (TCE), the election court, sets sanctions.

Electoral silence begins at 00:00 on Friday 27 November and lasts until 17:00 on Sunday 29 November, the hour polling stations close. During those hours the ban on political messages applies to candidates and to ordinary voters alike.

Guayaquil's riverfront promenade (file photo). photo, February 2024. Pedestrians on the Malecón 2000 riverfront promenade in Guayaquil, Ecuador's largest city. Photo: Freddy eduardo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

The alcohol ban, known as the ley seca (dry law), runs 72 hours from 12:00 on Friday 27 November to 12:00 on Monday 30 November. It bars selling and consuming alcohol, with the same US$241 fine as for propaganda.

Voting is compulsory for Ecuadorian citizens, and skipping it costs 10% of the SBU, or US$48.20, unless the CNE accepts a justification. Citizens summoned to staff a polling table who do not appear pay US$72.30, which is 15% of the SBU.

Voters choose prefects, vice-prefects, mayors, councillors, rural parish board members and members of the Citizen Participation Council (CPCCS), the state oversight body. Prefects head the provinces, mayors run the cities, and parish boards govern the rural districts.

Ecuador uses the US dollar, so every fine is payable in the currency Americans already carry, and the CNE has enabled card payment. The CNE material reviewed does not say how the silence and alcohol rules apply to foreign visitors, so travellers should confirm with the CNE.

Voting closes at 17:00 on Sunday 29 November, when electoral silence ends. The alcohol ban then lasts until noon on Monday 30 November.

What Prediction Markets Say On Polymarket, a US prediction-market platform where users bet real money, US$48,462 had been traded on the Quito mayoral race at 3:42 p.m. ET on 25 November 2026. It priced Pabel Muñoz at 44.5%, Harold Burbano at 32.0%, Jorge Yunda at 16.9% and Bernardo Jijón at 10.3%; these prices are bets, not polls. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who can be fined during electoral silence?

The rule applies to anyone who campaigns on the banned days, citizens as well as candidates. The Electoral Disputes Tribunal sets the sanctions.

When can I buy alcohol again?

Sales and consumption stay barred until midday on Monday. The ban starts at noon on Friday.

Can a voter avoid the fine for not voting?

Yes, if the CNE accepts a justification. The voter files it through the CNE’s official channels.

World.title: Bolivia’s Ex-Oil Chief Testifies Twice
World.content:
A former state oil chief spent Wednesday answering prosecutors’ questions in two cases, while a third complaint over imported crude is still being assessed.

A view over La Paz, the seat of Bolivia's government and Congress, from a cable-car line. (Photo: Rio Times library)

BOLIVIA · INVESTIGATIONS

Yussef Akly, who ran Bolivia’s state oil and gas company until he was replaced in March, appeared twice at the La Paz Prosecutor’s Office on Wednesday 25 November 2026. He went as a witness, not a suspect, in two separate criminal cases.

One is the “bad gasoline” case over poor-quality fuel that damaged vehicles across the country. The other involves Fernando Cerimedo, an Argentine political consultant accused of illicit enrichment.

Akly took over YPFB (Yacimientos Petrolíferos Fiscales Bolivianos) in November 2025, when President Rodrigo Paz appointed him. Paz replaced him on 30 March 2026 as the fuel-quality crisis grew.

His successor, Claudia Cronenbold, resigned on 22 April 2026 after three weeks in the job. Sebastián Daroca then took over the company.

Prosecutors had already questioned other former officials in the gasoline case. Former Hydrocarbons Minister Mauricio Medinaceli was arrested on 28 July 2026 in the same case and is under house detention.

In the morning, La Paz departmental prosecutor Gabriel Quiroga confirmed that Akly came as a witness in the gasoline investigation. “He has appeared as a witness, and the bad-gasoline matter is under investigation,” Quiroga said in Spanish.

Quiroga added that the office will call more people. Akly has not been charged in the gasoline case.

Plaza Murillo in La Paz, Bolivia's seat of government (file photo).

Quiroga also said that investigators are already collecting testimony. “Evidentemente se están realizando una serie de declaraciones que ya han pasado y otras que van a venir,” he said on Wednesday 25 November 2026, meaning that a series of statements has already been taken and more will follow.

At about 14:00 Bolivia time (18:00 GMT), Akly returned for a second statement, this time in the case against Cerimedo. “Now I go as a witness in the Cerimedo case,” he told waiting reporters.

He said he met Cerimedo, an Argentine political consultant, during the presidential campaigns. He said he does not know the scope of the investigation.

Prosecutors accuse Cerimedo of illicit enrichment of private persons to the harm of the state, after cash was found in a property he occupied. He is in pretrial detention, and on Friday 20 November 2026 a judge refused his release request.

Prosecutors have not said what Akly told them in either hearing. His statements are part of a case in which Cerimedo remains in custody.

A third matter hangs over Akly personally. On Monday 23 November 2026, Hydrocarbons Minister Marcelo Blanco told a news conference that imported crude oil failed the legal limits for nitrogen and mercury, and he announced a criminal complaint against Akly, a manager and others.

Blanco said the contaminated batch is sealed and came from Argentina, and that it was imported about four months ago. He promised that “not one drop of this crude” would be processed until it meets the legal standards.

The ministry did not state the volume of the crude, its cost or the laboratory test results. Without those figures, the scale of the problem and the size of any loss to the state stay unclear.

Quiroga said the Blanco complaint has “just entered” the prosecution and is under preliminary evaluation. Vice President Edmand Lara had earlier lodged a separate complaint alleging overpricing in crude purchases.

The prosecutor’s office has given no date for the further summonses Quiroga announced. Until it does, Akly’s status stays that of a witness in two cases and a named target of an unevaluated complaint in a third.

Is Yussef Akly charged with a crime?

In the gasoline case he appeared as a witness and has not been charged. A separate criminal complaint over imported crude is only under preliminary evaluation.

Why does a fuel scandal in Bolivia matter abroad?

Bolivia depends on its state company for fuel and gas, so doubts about quality and pricing affect investors and traders in the region. The cases also show how the new government treats officials it appointed itself.

What happens next?

Prosecutors say they will summon more people in the gasoline case. No date has been given for those summonses.

World.title: Court Revives Probe of Minister’s Siblings
World.content:
A federal chamber says the case was closed too soon. The Economy Minister’s brother and sister stay under investigation while judges test where a small stream of money went in 2022.

ARGENTINA · COURTS

An Argentine appeals court on Wednesday 25 November 2026 reopened an investigation into two siblings of Economy Minister Luis Caputo. Judges revoked the dismissals of Flavio and Rosana Caputo, who are suspected of helping to fund a street group tied to the 2022 attempt to kill Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, then vice president.

The ruling does not say the Caputos financed the group or took part in the attack, and no charge is proven. It matters abroad because Luis Caputo is the face of the government’s economic programme for foreign investors.

Key Facts Who Flavio and Rosana Caputo, siblings of Economy Minister Luis Caputo, are again under investigation.

What An appeals court revoked their dismissals in the Revolución Federal funding probe.

Status No charge is proven; the judges called the earlier closure premature.

Next The file returns to the first-instance court to hear witnesses.

A federal chamber says the case was closed too soon. The Economy Minister’s brother and sister stay under investigation while judges test where a small stream of money went in 2022.

Prosecutors charged members of Revolución Federal with incitement to collective violence and threats in the run-up to the attack of 1 September 2022. On that day a gunman pointed a pistol at Kirchner outside her Buenos Aires home.

Federal Oral Court No. 6 convicted the gunman, Fernando Sabag Montiel, to 10 years on 8 October 2025, and his partner Brenda Uliarte to 8 years. That trial dealt with the attack itself, while the Caputo file is a separate offshoot about money.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Argentina ranks 4th of 14 with 60.2 points. Strongest pillar: future resources (68); weakest: economic relationships (23). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Argentina’s financial intelligence unit, the UIF, detected bank transfers and cash payments of more than 6.5 million pesos (roughly US$50,000 at official 2022 rates of about 100 to 140 pesos per US$) between January and August 2022. They flowed from two building trusts, Santa Clara del Sur and Espacio Añelo, where the family firm Caputo Hermanos worked as contractor, to carpenter Jonathan Morel, his former employee Ailén Vallero and his former partner Evelyn Balboa.

A prosecutor’s opinion in October 2022 opened the offshoot probe into those payments. Morel is one of the group’s members sent to trial.

The National Congress building in Buenos Aires (file photo).

Defence lawyer Matías Cúneo Libarona argues there is no evidence linking his clients to any financing. He says the money paid for real, invoiced work on housing in Añelo, in Neuquén province, for workers in Vaca Muerta, Argentina’s main shale oil field.

Judge Marcelo Martínez de Giorgi dismissed the siblings on Tuesday 15 September 2026, writing: “No se encuentra probada una participación criminal de Caputo Hermanos en el accionar de Revolución Federal” (criminal participation by Caputo Hermanos in the group’s actions is not proven). Prosecutor Gerardo Pollicita agreed, noting “ciertas irregularidades indiciarias” (certain indicative irregularities) but not enough suspicion.

The judge also passed evidence on inconsistent invoices to ARCA, the national tax agency. Luis Caputo celebrated the dismissal on X and called the case persecution.

On Wednesday, Sala I (Chamber I) of the Federal Criminal and Correctional Court of Appeals in Buenos Aires set the dismissals aside. Judges Pablo Bertuzzi and Pablo Yadarola found the closure premature because the “negative certainty” needed to end a case for good (clear proof that no crime occurred) had not been reached, and Mariano Llorens joined them.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

The ruling states that “aún no se encuentran dadas las condiciones previstas por el art. 336 inc. 2 del C.P.P.N para sobreseer a los encausados” (the conditions to dismiss the defendants have not yet been met).

It adds that the decision must be balanced against the defendants’ right to have their position settled within a reasonable time. The chamber sent the file back to the first-instance court to complete the evidence.

That includes testimony from Vallero, Balboa and María Isabel Said, whose invoicing documents show inconsistencies, an accounting expert report using another method, and details of Morel’s other clients. The judges also want the role and pay of Rosana Caputo clarified.

The appeal came from the plaintiffs, Kirchner’s lawyers José Manuel Ubeira and Marcos Aldazábal and the legal team of Juan Grabois, a leftist leader. Separately, the first-instance judge sent five Revolución Federal members to oral trial: Morel, Leonardo Sosa, Gastón Guerra, Sabrina Basile and Lidia Casciano.

The charges are incitement to collective violence and threats against political leaders in 2022. The first-instance court now has to hear the witnesses and rule again on whether to close the case.

No date for those hearings has been announced, and until they take place both siblings remain under investigation with no charge proven.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Luis Caputo under investigation?

No. The file concerns his siblings Flavio and Rosana, and the ruling does not accuse any Caputo of taking part in the attack.

Does the ruling mean the Caputos financed the group?

No. The judges only said the dismissal came too early and that more evidence must be gathered before the case can be closed.

What happens to the trial of the group’s members?

That case runs separately and is not changed by this ruling. The Caputo offshoot continues on its own track.

Sources: Federal Criminal and Correctional Court of Appeals, Sala I, ruling of 25 November 2026; Federal Criminal and Correctional Court No. 8, dismissal of 15 September 2026; Federal Oral Court No. 6, verdict of 8 October 2025

World.title: Costa Rica Urban Bee Survey Finds 128 Species in Belén
World.content:
Costa Rica’s biodiversity is not confined to just its national parks and tropical rainforests. A scientific inventory in Belén, Heredia, has shown that even highly urbanized communities can harbor a remarkable diversity of native bees. Researchers documented 128 bee species belonging to 49 genera, coming from 3,178 records. The results highlight the ecological importance of urban gardens, parks, and other green spaces, and follow a separate survey that added 60 new species records in urban Heredia.

The findings are featured in a new book, “Plantas y abejas del cantón de Belén” (Plants and Bees of Belén), presented by the Municipality of Belén. The free publication aims to encourage residents, businesses, educational institutions, and gardening enthusiasts to take part in pollinator conservation.

Biologist Daniela Azofeifa and entomologist Manuel Zumbado led the development of the publication, with contributions from parataxonomist Enia Navarro and ethnobotanist Agustín Contreras. The research draws on fieldwork conducted between February and June 2025 across 22 locations in Belén’s three districts, San Antonio, La Ribera, and La Asunción. Previously collected scientific records were also incorporated.

Bees are an exceptionally diverse group of insects that play an essential role in plant reproduction, ecosystem stability, and agricultural production. Protecting them does not necessarily require large areas of land or specialized scientific knowledge. Something as simple as allowing certain plants to flower rather than removing them can provide valuable food for pollinators. The guide encourages residents to select native vegetation with different flowering seasons, so bees have access to food throughout the year.

It also recommends reducing intensive garden maintenance and where it is safe to do so, leaving natural materials such as fallen leaves and dead branches in place, since these can provide nesting sites. Avoiding synthetic pesticides and herbicides is another important conservation measure.

Belén officially declared itself a bee-friendly area in 2021. Since then, local authorities have promoted environmental education, native beekeeping, and the creation of green spaces that support pollinators. The municipality is also encouraging private companies and community organizations to take part through a pilot recognition program that promotes environmentally responsible gardening practices.

Residents interested in contributing to scientific knowledge can document their observations through Naturalista Costa Rica, part of the international citizen science platform iNaturalist. The book is available in Spanish as a free PDF download.

World.title: Solana Sierra and Nadia Podoroska Advance at Argentina Open
World.content:
Argentine tennis players Solana Sierra and Nadia Podoroska advanced to the second round of the WTA 125 Argentina Open on Tuesday, giving home fans two reasons to celebrate as the women’s professional tennis season draws to a close. Sierra, the tournament’s top seed and Argentina’s highest-ranked female player, overcame a difficult start against Andorra’s Victoria Jiménez Kasintseva.

After losing the opening set 6-1, Sierra won the second in a tiebreak before her opponent retired with an injury while trailing 2-0 in the deciding set. The match lasted two hours and seven minutes, with Sierra advancing by a score of 1-6, 7-6(1), 2-0. She will face France’s Carole Monnet in the second round.

Podoroska, meanwhile, delivered a convincing performance against Spain’s Leyre Romero Gormaz. The former French Open semifinalist won a closely contested opening set before dominating the second to secure a 7-6(4), 6-0 victory. For Podoroska, the result represents another encouraging step in her return to competitive tennis following an extended absence caused by injuries. The 29-year-old, who once reached No. 36 in the world, is working her way back up the WTA rankings after spending more than a year away from competition.

She will face either María Lourdes Carlé or Sol Larraya Guidi in the second round, guaranteeing Argentina at least one representative in the quarterfinals. Argentina’s Julia Riera also remains in contention after defeating Greece’s Despina Papamichail 6-2, 7-5 on Monday. Her next opponent is Turkey’s Ipek Oz.

Not all the local players enjoyed the same success. Victoria Bosio, Luna María Cinalli and Lourdes Ayala were eliminated in their opening matches. Sierra and Podoroska have been responsible for two of Argentina’s most notable women’s tennis achievements in recent years. Podoroska reached the Roland Garros semifinals as a qualifier in 2020, while Sierra made history in 2025 by becoming the first women’s singles lucky loser to reach the fourth round at

The Argentina Open, played on outdoor clay at the Tenis Club Argentino in Buenos Aires, offers $115,000 in total financial commitment and features a 32-player singles draw. Part of the WTA 125 calendar since 2021, the tournament provides South American players with a valuable opportunity to earn ranking points closer to home before preparations begin for the 2027 season and the Australian Open in January.

The tournament runs through Sunday, November 29.

World.title: Your Guide to Puriscal’s Chicharrón Fair as It Opens Friday
World.content:
If you want to taste the chicharrón many Costa Ricans call the best in the country, your window opens Friday. The Feria del Chicharrón in Santiago de Puriscal, a hill town about an hour west of San José, runs from Nov. 27 through Monday, Dec. 7. The fair takes over the Parque del Agricultor in the center of town with food stands, live music and family activities. Entry has traditionally been free, so you only pay for what you eat and drink.

Puriscal earned its reputation the slow way. Local butchers and home cooks have made Costa Rica’s favorite fried pork, along with chorizo and salchichón, for generations, and many families still guard recipes handed down for more than a century. The fair has run almost every year since 1999, pausing only during the pandemic.

Forget the bagged pork rinds sold in supermarkets. The chicharrón here is meaty, with chunks of pork belly fried with the fat still attached until the outside crackles and the inside stays tender. Locals call this style chicharrón de panzada, and it is what most stands are known for.

It usually comes with fried yuca, tortillas and a wedge of lime. Some stands add chimichurri, the Costa Rican tomato-and-onion salsa similar to pico de gallo. Save room for the local chorizo and salchichón, and for traditional dishes such as tamal de maíz and pozol that have turned up at past editions.

Vendors start frying in the morning. Go in late morning or early afternoon if you want pork fresh from the pan and shorter lines. By evening, the crowd shifts toward the main stage. The program is built for families. Past editions have included children’s shows, a mechanical bull for kids, a pet pageant, a beach volleyball tournament, a horse parade and concerts by national artists. Mornings lean toward sports and recreation, while afternoons and evenings bring music, comedy and cultural performances.

The main event for many visitors is the Mejor Chicharrón contest, where local producers put their best batch in front of judges who score it on flavor and texture. At last year’s Puriscal chicharrón festival, it was held on the final Sunday. The full schedule, including the date of this year’s contest, is posted on the fair’s official Facebook page. It can change from day to day, so check it before you leave home.

Driving from San José takes about an hour. Expect heavier traffic on Friday evenings and Sunday afternoons and arrive before lunch on weekends if you want a parking spot close to the park. If you would rather not drive, Comtrasuli buses connect San José and Puriscal from a terminal near the Coca-Cola market. Staying for the evening concerts? Check the time of the last bus back before you go.

Bring cash. Many stands are small family operations that may not take cards, and SINPE Móvil transfers only work if you have a Costa Rican bank account. Pack a light layer too, because December days in the Central Valley are usually sunny but evenings can turn cool and breezy. Portions are generous, so a group can share a few plates and try more. If you want to make a day of it, La Cangreja National Park is in the same canton and makes a good morning hike before lunch at the fair. Check its opening hours before you go.

For Puriscal, the fair is more than a food festival. It traditionally opens the town’s Christmas season with the lighting of the town tree, and it gives small producers a place to sell directly to the public. One plate of chicharrón de panzada usually explains why people keep making the drive each December.

World.title: Turtle Season Is On in Guanacaste and Playa Grande Now Closes at 5 p.m.
World.content:
If you are heading to Playa Grande before March, plan to be off the sand by 5 p.m. Leatherback nesting season is under way at Las Baulas National Marine Park, and the beach closes an hour earlier than usual so the turtles can come ashore undisturbed. The season runs from October through February, according to the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC). The park was created to protect leatherbacks on three nesting beaches near Tamarindo: Playa Grande, Ventanas and Langosta.

Leatherbacks are critically endangered worldwide. They nest at night, which is the reason for the early closing. Lights, noise and people on the sand can send a female back to the water before she lays her eggs. Do not expect to find one on your own, and do not walk the beach after dark to look. Few leatherbacks reach these beaches now. Ask the park office whether guided night visits are operating this season before you pay anyone for a tour.

Farther south, Ostional National Wildlife Refuge offers a different sight. Olive ridley turtles nest there in mass arrivals known as arribadas, when thousands come ashore at once along 7 kilometers (4.3 miles) of beach. SINAC says the arrivals happen throughout the year. Arribadas tend to cluster around the moon’s last quarter. Tuesday’s moon is full, which puts the next last quarter around Dec. 1. Treat that as a window and not a date, because the turtles keep their own schedule.

One of this year’s largest arrivals came in early September. SINAC specialists warned at the time that the heat brought by El Niño could affect nesting. Hatchlings normally emerge about 50 days after the eggs are laid. If you go, get a certified local guide, keep your distance and leave flash and white lights off. The eggs are protected by law. In September, authorities detained two people carrying 125 olive ridley eggs taken illegally from the refuge.
