Both sites are part of the public protected area system and the rules apply to everyone on the beach during nesting season.

World.title: Costa Rica Will Host Miss Universe 2027 for the First Time
World.content:
Costa Rica will host Miss Universe in 2027, the first time the pageant has come here. The Miss Universe Organization made the announcement Tuesday night during the final of this year’s competition in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The 2027 pageant will be the 76th edition. President Laura Fernández delivered the news in a recorded video message released with ¡OPA!, the television channel that holds the Miss Universe franchise in Costa Rica.

No host city, venue or dates have been announced. Nothing has been said publicly about what the event will cost or how much public money, if any, will go into it. The first details are expected in the coming weeks. Money is what stopped an earlier attempt. In 2021 the government of then-President Carlos Alvarado declined to take on the expense, and then-Tourism Minister Gustavo Segura said Costa Rica did not have the resources for an event of that scale.

At the time, organizers had asked for a venue and staff, close to 6,000 hotel nights, meals, local transport, airfare and equipment freight. The pageant went to Israel instead. Costa Rica was again among the candidate hosts for the 2025 edition, which was held in Thailand. Fernández has courted the pageant since the start of her term.

In June she received then-reigning Miss Universe Fátima Bosch at Casa Presidencial, along with former titleholders Sheynnis Palacios and Victoria Kjær, and told them she would love to see the contest held in Costa Rica and that they could count on her support. In October she met Mariale Acosta, this year’s national titleholder, and national director Yessenia Ramírez. The national organization said afterward that hosting would take planning, strategic alliances and backing from several sectors.

The announcement also follows weeks of confusion over next year’s host. On Oct. 8, a statement on the Miss Universe website said Vietnam had been selected for the 76th competition. It said the choice was made by Legacy Holding Group, operating as MU East, under an agreement dividing the pageant between two groups.

That statement was challenged within days. A message on the pageant’s Instagram account said MU East had no authority to speak for the organization, that Vietnam had not been designated, and that the next host would be named after this year’s edition. Yesterday’s announcement in San Juan followed that timeline. On stage, Acosta reached the top 30 from a field of 116 contestants but did not advance to the final 12. Costa Rica has competed at Miss Universe since 1954 and has never won the crown.

Jennifer Barreto of Puerto Rico took the title at the José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum, succeeding Fátima Bosch of Mexico. Former first lady Signe Zeikate, an economist and the wife of former President Rodrigo Chaves, sat on the final judging panel. The open questions are now where the pageant will be held, when, and who pays for it.

World.title: Guanacaste Now Builds More Large Homes Than San José
World.content:
Guanacaste registered 882 new homes of 200 square meters (2,150 square feet) or more in 2025, compared with 542 in San José, according to preliminary construction statistics from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC). The Guanacaste homes carried a declared value of 102,000 million colones (about $229 million), against 61,100 million colones (about $137 million) for those in San José. Nationwide, 2,507 homes of that size were recorded, which places just over a third of them in Guanacaste.

San José still leads in the total value of residential construction, with 194,500 million colones (about $437 million) to Guanacaste’s 181,600 million (about $408 million). Two cantons account for most of the province’s figure. Santa Cruz registered 557 large homes worth about 62,300 million colones (about $140 million), more than the 542 recorded in San José. Carrillo registered 219, worth about 27,700 million colones (about $62 million). Together they represent roughly 88% of Guanacaste’s large homes.

Santa Cruz also ranked first in the declared value of residential building permits, at 99,774 million colones (about $224 million). In Carrillo, 73.7% of the 37,540 million colones in new-home permits went to houses of more than 200 square meters. Santa Cruz includes Tamarindo, Flamingo and Playa Grande. Carrillo includes Playas del Coco, Playa Hermosa and Ocotal.

The tourism observatory at the National University (OBTUR-UNA) attributes the growth to tourism, second homes and capital that arrived after the pandemic. It reported price increases of up to 400% for some coastal properties between 2020 and 2023. At the top of the market, three of the five most expensive properties listed in Costa Rica in June were on the Papagayo peninsula, the costliest of them at $30 million.

The INEC figures are preliminary, and a home of 200 square meters or more is not necessarily a luxury property. The construction is concentrated in a province where water supply is under strain. The national water utility, AyA, estimated this month that more than 306,000 people, most of them in Guanacaste, could be affected by shortages linked to El Niño.

World.title: Mel Gibson Is in Costa Rica, Immigration Confirms
World.content:
Hollywood actor and director Mel Gibson is in Costa Rica, immigration authorities confirmed today. The General Directorate of Migration and Immigration said Gibson entered the country on Sunday, November 22, and that as of Tuesday, November 24, there was no record of him leaving. Officials gave no details about the purpose of the trip, how long he plans to stay or where he is staying, and Gibson has made no public statement about the visit.

Gibson has owned a large private estate for nearly two decades at Playa Barrigona, a remote stretch of coast on the Nicoya Peninsula in Guanacaste. He came across the land in 2006 while scouting locations for Apocalypto, his film about the decline of the Maya civilization. The production was eventually shot in Veracruz, Mexico, but Gibson bought the property in 2007 for a reported $26 million (about 11.6 billion colones at the current exchange rate).

The estate covers some 162 hectares (400 acres) of jungle and includes three hilltop villas, a dining pavilion and more than 3.2 kilometers (two miles) of shoreline. The beach below, about half an hour north of Sámara, shows no visible development and is regularly described by travel writers as one of the most secluded on the Pacific coast.

Gibson has tried for years to sell and the property first went on the market in 2010 at $35 million (about 15.6 billion colones) and was later relisted more than once at $29.75 million (about 13.2 billion colones). No sale has been reported, and it has not been confirmed whether he still owns all of it or is staying there on this trip.

His relationship with the area has not always been smooth. In 2016 a national television report accused the estate’s administrators of blocking public access to the beach and of building in violation of the Maritime Terrestrial Zone Law, which guarantees public use of the first 50 meters (164 feet) inland from the high tide line. A representative for the property called the report inaccurate and sensationalist. At the time, Gibson had not visited the country in nearly a year.

His ties to Costa Rica run deeper than real estate. In 2007 he met with then President Óscar Arias at the president’s home in San José to discuss a donation to support the Indigenous communities and he has spent the New Year holiday and his birthday here on more than one occasion.

Speculation about a longer stay grew in January 2025, after Gibson lost his Malibu home in the wildfires that tore through Los Angeles. Asked on Joe Rogan’s podcast whether the disaster might drive him out of California, he said it might and pointed to Costa Rica. He said he has a place here that he loves, and that it sits away from the tourist crowds.

The current visit comes at a relatively quiet point in his schedule. Gibson has wrapped filming on The Resurrection of the Christ, his long awaited follow up to The Passion of the Christ, which Lionsgate will release in two parts. Part One is set for May 6, 2027, and Part Two for May 25, 2028, with Finnish actor Jaakko Ohtonen in the role of Jesus. Gibson also serves as one of President Donald Trump’s special ambassadors to Hollywood.

Born in Peekskill, New York, in 1956 and raised in Australia, Gibson rose to fame in the Mad Max and Lethal Weapon franchises. He directed and starred in Braveheart, which won five Academy Awards, two of them for Gibson as director and producer. His other directing credits include The Passion of the Christ and Hacksaw Ridge.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Critically Endangered Sawfish Is So Rare Even Scientists Struggle to Find It
World.content:
Costa Rica’s rivers and coastal waters are home to a fish that can grow to nearly 6.5 meters (21 feet), yet it is so elusive that some researchers have written entire theses on it without ever seeing one alive. The sawfish, recognizable by its long, flattened snout lined with teeth, is among the world’s most threatened marine animals.

Its populations have fallen by about 70% over the past six decades, according to Mario Espinoza, a biologist at the University of Costa Rica (UCR), and researchers are still working out where the remaining animals live and how to protect them. Sawfish are rays, closely related to sharks, Espinoza said. Five species exist worldwide and two have been recorded in Costa Rica, the largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) and the smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata).

Unlike most marine species, sawfish move between freshwater and saltwater. In Costa Rica, most reported sightings come from the San Juan River along the border with Nicaragua, with others from the Térraba-Sierpe National Wetland on the southern Pacific coast. Finding one is another matter. Espinoza has studied the species for about a decade, and for much of that time his team has relied less on direct observation than on local fishermen and riverside communities. Through interviews, the researchers reconstructed past sightings and identified the areas where sawfish were most likely to survive.

Those accounts pointed the team to the Térraba-Sierpe wetlands and the San Juan River system, including waters connected to Barra del Colorado on the northern Caribbean coast. The researchers also turned to environmental DNA, or eDNA, a technique that detects the genetic traces animals leave behind in water. By sampling sites where residents reported sightings, the team could look for sawfish without having to catch or see one.

The method worked. In 2019 and 2020, the team detected sawfish DNA at several sites, mainly in rivers of the northern zone and the northern Caribbean, and the findings were published in 2025 in the journal Endangered Species Research. In 2022, UCR researchers also caught and released a largetooth sawfish near the San Juan River.

All five sawfish species are classified as critically endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List. One of the greatest threats comes from the very feature that makes them so distinctive. The saw-shaped snout tangles easily in nets and other fishing gear. Espinoza said many fishermen do not know how to release the animals safely, so accidental captures often end in death.

In northern Costa Rica, spearfishing for tarpon poses another risk. Some fishermen have killed sawfish by mistake after confusing their silhouette underwater with that of the fish they were hunting, according to Espinoza. Sawfish have been protected by law in Costa Rica since 2022, when a reform Espinoza worked on with legislators was signed. Before that, neither species had any legal protection in the country.

World.title: Belize Defence Force hosts U.S. Ambassador and U.S. Southcom Commander
World.content:
Belize Defence Force hosts U.S. Ambassador and U.S. Southcom Commander

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Belize Defence Force (BDF) hosted a special visit by the United States Ambassador to Belize, Andre Bauer, and the Commander of the United States Southern Command, General Francis L. Donovan.

The United States officials were received at Price Barracks with a welcoming parade, reflecting the military honors and formal protocol of the Belize Defence Force.

The senior United States officials held a meeting with Minister of National Security, Energy and Ports Michel Chebat; Chief Executive Officer in the Ministry of National Security, Francis Usher (Maj. Rtd.); Chief Executive Officer in the Ministry of Public Utilities, Energy and Logistics, Dr. Leroy Almendarez; Chief of Defence Staff in the Ministry of National Security, Major General Asariel Loria; Commander of the Belize Defence Force, Brigadier General Anthony Velasquez; and Commandant of the Belize Coast Guard, Rear Admiral Gregory Soberanis.

The meeting provided an important opportunity for senior United States and Belizean officials to discuss bilateral military affairs, strengthen existing cooperation, and explore opportunities for continued engagement between both nations.

The BDF says that this highlights the enduring partnership between Belize and the United States and their shared commitment to fostering collaboration, mutual understanding, and regional security.

World.title: U.S. Ambassador Andre Bauer welcomes SOUTHCOM commander on 1st visit to Belize
World.content:
U.S. Ambassador Andre Bauer welcomes SOUTHCOM commander on 1st visit to Belize

By Zoila Palma: U.S. Ambassador to Belize Andre Bauer welcomed Commander of U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM), General Francis L. Donovan, on his first official visit to Belize today.

Ambassador Bauer hosted the visit, which included high-level discussions with Minister of National Security Michel Chebat, Chief of Defence Staff Brigadier General Azariel Loria, and other senior defense officials.

“Together with Belize’s senior military and national security leaders, we had productive discussions on strengthening our partnership, combating transnational criminal organizations, and advancing security and stability throughout the Western Hemisphere,” Ambassador Bauer said.

“I am proud to represent the United States as we continue to strengthen our relationship with Belize, a valued friend and vital regional security partner,” he added.

World.title: State-of-the-art Caribbean Sugar Refinery officially opens in Belize
World.content:
State-of-the-art Caribbean Sugar Refinery officially opens in Belize

By Zoila Palma: The CARICOM region marked a historic agricultural and industrial milestone on Saturday, November 21, 2026, with the official inauguration of the Caribbean Sugar Refinery (CSR) in Belize.

Located in scenic Valley of Peace, the new state-of-the-art facility enables Belize to process the highest grades of refined white sugar. By establishing local refining capabilities, the project adds significant value to intraregional production and strengthens the Caribbean’s ability to produce its own food.

Developed through a strategic joint venture between Santander Sugar Group and Sucro Limited, the landmark US$20 million investment is engineered to meet at least 75% of CARICOM’s total refined white sugar demand.

The facility will process raw sugar sourced from Santander’s operations in Cayo alongside raw sugar supplied by ASR/BSI in the north. Leveraging Sucro’s proven refining expertise and established distribution network, CSR will deliver beverage-grade refined white sugar directly to regional manufacturers.

During his keynote address, Prime Minister of Belize John Briceño highlighted the transformative economic impact of the facility for both Belize and the wider Caribbean. He noted that the country’s abundant raw sugar supply positions the refinery to reliably satisfy regional demand while retaining greater economic returns at home. “Value-added production creates value-added opportunities,” Prime Minister Briceño emphasized, highlighting a new era for Belizean industry.

Dr. Osmond Martinez, Minister of Economic Transformation with responsibility for the sugar industry, echoed the Prime Minister’s sentiments during the event.

He stressed the critical need for Belize to move beyond traditional raw commodity exports by capturing greater value from its domestic resources.

Minister Martinez also commended Santander Sugar Group and Sucro Limited for the cross-sector collaboration and capital investment that brought the complex to fruition.

Beyond boosting domestic value, the refinery is poised to reshape regional supply chains by reducing CARICOM’s heavy reliance on refined sugar imported from outside the Caribbean.

Supported by direct shipping routes linking Belize to neighboring island markets, the facility promises manufacturers a more efficient, secure, and consistent supply of regionally produced sugar.

Building on generations of Belizean sugarcane cultivation and agricultural expertise, the launch of the Caribbean Sugar Refinery bridges traditional farming with modern industrial manufacturing.

World.title: Belize Foam Ltd announces Christmas season hours and GST free weekends
World.content:
Belize Foam Ltd announces Christmas season hours and GST free weekends

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize Foam Ltd has announced its Christmas season hours, including two GST free weekends in December.

The company’s regular schedule remains Monday to Friday, 8:00am to 5:00pm.

For the season, Belize Foam will open on Saturday, December 5, from 9:00am to 4:00pm.

The GST free weekends will be held on Saturday and Sunday, December 12 and 13, and Saturday and Sunday, December 19 and 20. The store will open from 9:00am to 4:00pm on all four days.

The company is encouraging Belizeans to shop local this Christmas.

Belize Foam Ltd is located at Mile 2.5 on the George Price Highway. For more information, call 222-4143 or WhatsApp 638-1868.

World.title: U.S. SOUTHCOM Commander meets with National Security Minister
World.content:
U.S. SOUTHCOM Commander meets with National Security Minister

By Zoila Palma: U.S. Southern Command Commander General Francis L. Donovan made his first visit to Belize today, hosted by U.S. Ambassador to Belize Andre Bauer.

During the visit, Donovan met with Minister of National Security Michel Chebat, Chief of Defence Staff Brigadier General Azariel Loria, and other senior defense leaders.

The U.S. Embassy said discussions focused on mutual support for the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (A3C), the strong bilateral partnership between Belize and the United States, and efforts to advance security and stability across the Western Hemisphere.

The Embassy said that Belize is a vital regional security partner.

World.title: Belize City welcomed regional leaders for 52nd Ordinary Meeting of the Ministers of Education and Culture of the Central American Integration System
World.content:
Belize City welcomed regional leaders for 52nd Ordinary Meeting of the Ministers of Education and Culture of the Central American Integration System

By Zoila Palma: On November 24, 2026, Belize City hosted the 52nd Ordinary Meeting of the Ministers of Education and Culture of the Central American Integration System (CECC/SICA), bringing together regional leaders to strengthen cooperation in education and promote cultural development across Central America.

Minister of Education, Culture, Science and Technology, Francis Fonseca, who was recently appointed President Pro Tempore of CECC/SICA, welcomed delegates from across the region and chaired the opening session. His appointment places Belize in a regional leadership role focused on advancing education and cultural cooperation among member countries.

Deputy Mayor of Belize City, Eluide Miller, also attended the meeting and expressed pride in the city hosting the regional gathering. He welcomed the opportunity for regional partners to come together to discuss collaboration, unity and progress in education and culture.

The Belize City Council congratulated Fonseca on his appointment as President Pro Tempore of CECC/SICA and wished him success in his new role.

World.title: International News: Trump announces new tariffs on China, EU and 12 other trading partners
World.content:
International News: Trump announces new tariffs on China, EU and 12 other trading partners

By Zoila Palma: United States President Donald Trump has announced a new round of tariffs targeting imports from China, the European Union and 12 other trading partners as he continues to pursue his administration’s trade policy.

The new duties are expected to take effect next year and follow a White House investigation into foreign trade practices after the US Supreme Court ruled that Trump’s previously announced “Liberation Day” tariffs were illegal.

According to the BBC, China faces the highest proposed tariff rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%. Other countries and jurisdictions, including Japan, India, South Korea, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Taiwan and Bangladesh, will face rates of either 20% or 25%. However, some countries may benefit from agreed tariff caps that could reduce the effective rates applied to their goods.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new tariffs are intended to create fairer trading conditions for American workers and support a more sustainable global economy. He accused several trading partners of using industrial strategies and other market practices that he said had weakened the US manufacturing sector and contributed to trade imbalances.

Economists have warned that tariffs could increase the cost of imported goods, potentially leading businesses to pass higher expenses on to consumers.

The duties could also affect international trade and increase tensions between the United States and its major economic partners.

World.title: International News: Mexico’s arrest of ‘El Chapo Isidro’ adds pressure on powerful drug cartels
World.content:
International News: Mexico’s arrest of ‘El Chapo Isidro’ adds pressure on powerful drug cartels

By Zoila Palma: Mexican authorities have arrested another major drug trafficking figure, Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” as the government intensifies its crackdown on organized crime. His capture over the weekend was welcomed by both Mexico and the United States, which has been increasing pressure on Mexican authorities to dismantle powerful criminal organizations.

The arrest comes amid significant changes in Mexico’s criminal landscape following the removal of several major cartel leaders, AP reports.

Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, one of the founders of the Sinaloa Cartel, was arrested in the United States in 2024 and is serving a life sentence. Meanwhile, Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as “El Mencho,” the leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), was killed by Mexican forces, triggering violence across several states.

Meza Flores was a prominent figure in northern Sinaloa, where he led a criminal organization involved in drug trafficking. His group reportedly maintained alliances with different factions of the Sinaloa Cartel, including “Los Chapitos” and followers of Zambada. Analysts say his arrest could provide authorities with information about cartel operations and possible links between criminal groups and local officials.

The Sinaloa Cartel has been weakened by an internal conflict between the “Los Mayos” and “Los Chapitos” factions following Zambada’s arrest. The fighting has contributed to continued violence in Sinaloa, despite the deployment of additional military personnel and hundreds of arrests.

Meanwhile, the CJNG has reportedly managed a relatively peaceful leadership transition following the death of “El Mencho,” allowing it to maintain its operations.

World.title: Kyle Butler, Vauxhall High part ways
World.content:
Vauxhall High School Head Coach Kyle Butler

Kyle Butler says his stint as head coach of Vauxhall High School’s football programme has come to an end after two seasons.

Butler made the announcement on social media, saying he was proud of what he had accomplished at the school, highlighting the team’s consistency in the Inter-Secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) competitions and his role in helping players secure professional contracts and college opportunities.

“Thank you, Vauxhall, for two seasons I’ll always be proud of. Together, we reached three quarter-finals and made one round-of-16 appearance,” Butler posted.

The development follows Vauxhall’s exit from the under-16 schoolboy football competition after their 3-2 win against Kingston College (KC) was reversed, handing KC a 3-0 victory, due to what ISSA said in a release were “irregularities”.

ISSA is yet to rule on the matter as the punishment could be severe seeing that allegations are that the school used two ineligible players in other players’ names.

Butler, in his announcement, identified player development and creating opportunities beyond schoolboy football as his biggest achievement.

“My biggest achievement was helping eight players sign professional contracts and opening doors to college for even more,” he said, while thanking the players for trusting him as their coach.

Butler explained that he had agreed to remain at Vauxhall for another season at the end of the previous campaign, but believes the time has now come to pursue a new challenge.

“At the end of last season, I agreed to stay at Vauxhall for one more year. My time at Vauxhall has now come to an end, and I’m proud of what we achieved together. Now I look forward to finding a new home,” he said.

The ambitious coach is now looking to take his experience in Jamaica to Europe, where he hopes to learn from some of the continent’s leading coaches and further his professional qualifications.

“I’m excited to take what I’ve learned in Jamaica overseas and learn from some of the best coaches in Europe. My ambition is to earn my UEFA Pro Licence, coach some of the biggest clubs in the world and one day lead Jamaica’s national team,” Butler said.

Despite his overseas ambitions, Butler made it clear that he has not closed the door on local schoolboy football, indicating that he would be willing to return to the competition when the right opportunity presents itself.

He also outlined the importance of loyalty, unity and mutual commitment in any future coaching appointment, insisting that success requires the backing of everyone involved in a programme.

“When I take on another programme, I want the board, the coaching staff and the players to know we can count on each other. That means celebrating the wins together and standing side by side when things get difficult, on and off the pitch,” he said.

— Howard Walker

World.title: PREDATOR!
World.content:
A 58-year-old Trelawny man who in 2022 dragged a 10-year-old girl into his house, raped her, and later falsely claimed that a relative had sent her to him so he could have sex with her, has been sentenced to 17 years behind bars after he pleaded guilty to the act. He had snatched the girl while she was on her way to fetch water from a spring.

The man, who already spent 10 years behind bars for incest with his own child, and who was also on the Trelawny police’s Most Wanted List for murder, was sentenced by Supreme Court Judge Justice Judith Pusey in the Portland Circuit Court on November 17 after pleading guilty.

In the matter prosecuted by Deputy Director of Public Prosecutions Malike Kellier and Crown Counsel Nyron Wright, the child — who lived next door to the man — left her home one evening in June 2022 for the spring and “took a shortcut through his yard”. The man called out to her to “come here a little bit”. The child said she told him, “No, I am going to fill my water bottle,” at which point he jumped towards her, grabbed her by the arm, pulled her into his house and closed the door.

She said he then proceeded to touch her inappropriately and kiss her all over her face, except on her mouth. According to the child, she pushed him and kicked him, telling him to stop, but he ignored her protests and threw her on a bed while trying to remove her clothing.

She said he had partially penetrated her when a knock on the door by her grandmother, who began calling her name, interrupted him. According to the child, her violator told her not to answer or make a sound or he would “thump” her in her mouth. She obeyed.

The relentless grandmother, however, pushed the door down and entered the house, at which point the man replaced the child’s underwear before attempting to push the grandmother from the house.

He further told the child to continue on her journey, ordered her to “pretend” as if she was not in his house, and further threatened to kill her if she told anyone. The matter was reported to the police that same day. He was arrested a day later and subsequently charged with rape and sexual touching of a child.

During his arrest the man, who initially refused to divulge his name to cops, when cautioned declared, “Officer a di [name withheld] send her over deh fi mi [have sex] with her.”

The man later told probation aftercare officers that his marriage deteriorated after his wife accused him of inappropriate conduct with his daughter — for which he was prosecuted and found guilty. He had lived in the community for just under a year when he struck.

A probation aftercare officer who interviewed the convicted man ahead of his sentencing said he “appeared nervous and had a disposition of unease during his interview at the Horizon Adult Remand and Correctional Centre” and that “he struggled to speak definitively about the circumstances surrounding the offences for which he was charged”. According to the officer, he admitted to touching the child on her private parts and kissing her all over her face but “vehemently denied raping her”.

According to the officer, the man expressed regret about his actions but claimed that he was “unable to resist the advances” of the child who, he claimed, was “touching him in an affectionate way”. The official said when challenged about the child’s “cognitive ability to respond from an informed position, based on her age, he retracted his claim and expressed that he could not validate his actions”.

He further told his interviewer that while he recognised the experience may have been traumatic for the child and would cause her to struggle because of memories of that day, he could not see how it would affect her in other ways. Furthermore, he said while he was aware of the embarrassment his actions would cause to his family, and particularly his estranged spouse, he did not believe what he did would affect the wider community. The man has also been accused by community members of engaging in inappropriate conduct with other minors over the years.

In a report produced for the courts in February of this year, at which point the repeat offender had yet to plead guilty, a probation aftercare officer said if the man decided to take responsibility for his actions, a custodial sentence would be a “suitable means of punishment”.

Residents from the area, in the meantime, further described him as “brazen”, alleging that he was also involved in praedial larceny and was seen taking produce from the farms of others. Furthermore, the residents, who said they did not confront him out of fear for their own safety, described his actions as “troubling” to them while expressing “relief” at his departure from the area.

World.title: Precarious position
World.content:
Jonathan Bernard’s house that sits precariously on the hillside in Spring Mount, above a gaping breakaway.

SPRING MOUNT, St James — Faced with uncertainty about the structural integrity of his house, Spring Mount resident Jonathan Bernard is hoping Government will buy the property, even as uncertainty swirls around if and when repairs will be done to the massive breakaway which threatens the building.

Bernard’s house sits atop a hillside, offering him a bird’s-eye view of the collapsed roadway that has cut off vehicular traffic along the Spring Mount and Springfield corridor since last year’s Hurricane Melissa. There had been reports that the purchase of his house was being considered as part of efforts to fix the issue, and Bernard confirmed that discussions had taken place.

“Them come to me about it. The last time I spoke to them was in August and since then there hasn’t been any contact,” he told the Jamaica Observer during a recent visit to the community.

Bernard explained that the two-bedroom, one-bathroom dwelling had been his home for the past 17 years, but he was willing to sell.

“We had made some arrangements as it relates to that, but they haven’t come forward again,” he explained.

“We’ve tried to reach out to them but we can’t get a positive response as to what is happening,” he lamented.

The proposed purchase has become even more urgent because, just over two weeks ago, he received word that heavy equipment was being used to cut into the land on which his house stands. He said the intention was to create space for vehicles to pass.

“It has made the situation worse because I can’t access the place and is there I have all of my stuff. If I need to change my clothes, anything I need to do, that’s where I go because I don’t live anywhere else,” said a forlorn Bernard.

He told the Observer that after the Category 5 storm there had been some indication of danger as the house appeared to have tilted. However, he was still able to access the property then. Now, portions of the columns holding it up are increasingly being exposed as the surrounding soil continues to loosen.

“It wasn’t in danger but a this that them come do now cause the problem. I had my place, I would sleep there,” he said.

“Them just think that my thing has no value. Them want them road and that is the most important thing to them,” Bernard added.

He explained that he began building the house 17 years ago after landing a job at a call centre.

“Most of the material, a me carry them there, most of the blocks a me carry them up there,” he said.

“It’s not like I have money or whatever, it’s [from doing] a 9-5 I work,” he told the

Observer.

Bernard now farms for a living and he has put together a makeshift shelter while he awaits word on his precariously perched house.

“I have a hut in the bush so this is all I have,” he lamented.

Bernard said he has reached out to political representatives in the area and was told that efforts would be made to assist him.

“The councillor said them going to try build up a place where I can store my things, for now, and then he is going to talk to the member of parliament to see if I can get one of the social house them, something to that sort; but I need somewhere to live now,” he appealed.

Initial indications that nearby land would be bought and the Spring Mount breakaway repaired were dashed after the Government said it would be unwise to spend US$250,000 on a fix that likely would not last more than five years. The focus is now on repairing other routes.

World.title: Curtisay the Bessout turns dubplate job into a bouncy single
World.content:
Curtisay the Bessout .

Emerging dancehall artiste Curtisay was supposed to cut a dubplate and remix a track for Latin pop singer Natalie Q. Instead, the talented rhyme-spitter flipped the script and formulated a whole new song.

The producer, Psycho Pablo, loved the song so much it was released as a separate single, Back it Up Senorita, and he still recorded another verse for Natalie Q.

“All of that happened because of my philosophy of doing more than what is asked. I have a mindset centred on initiative, ownership, and value creation; I always try to go above and beyond,” Curtisay the Bessout said.

Released earlier this month, the song is already putting up impressive streaming numbers.

Curtisay the Bessout is excited about the early feedback. The record reflects the pulse of the streets, built for the dancers, with a Spanish lilt in Psycho Pablo’s instrumental and a chorus that tells you what to do with your waist.

As the sing progresses, the verses get more specific. Curtisay uses his lived experiences in the streets to pen songs about DMs, and the ‘genie wine’ to paint portraits with his music.

“Each line in this song is about someone and a real experience. My babymother, after all, is a dancer,” he said.

The first version was raunchier. Then Curtisay took it to Tuff Gong, where the association with Bob Marley made him think twice about just how far to push it. He dialled back the explicit lyrics and came away thinking the edit made the song easier to take abroad.

The studio changed his approach to the vocal, too. He spent years honing his craft to construct the right sound out of his voice. At Tuff Gong, he could relax and let the lower register do its job.

“All I had to do there was be myself,” he said.

When Curtisay drops into those deep tones he remembers Baby Cham passing his gate in a topless luxury car alongside the Topless Crew.

“Nuff Baby Cham influence is in my style,” he said.

He points to Sean Paul and Shaggy for a different lesson in delivery. Both showed him how far a Jamaican cadence can carry when listeners around the world can follow the words.

On Back It Up Senorita he deejayed with a Spanish touch inspired from the beat. The rest comes from nights out in the dancehall, where selectors, dancers, and the crowd let you know quickly whether a chorus works.

Curtisay has spent enough time in other people’s sessions to appreciate having his own voice out front. He contributed Stay With Me to Jah Cure’s Grammy-nominated album The Cure.

Working with Ahzee on Way You Whine, he recalled going through roughly 20 cuts before settling on lyrics. Curtisay usually likes to walk into the booth and leave with a finished song. Ahzee made him sit with the melodies first, a habit he took back to his own work. Writing for other artistes taught him a tougher lesson about what happens when the paperwork comes around.

These days he demands a substantial advance before taking on that kind of job.

For Back It Up Senorita, Curtisay wrote and performed, Psycho Pablo produced the instrumental, and Ramjam handled the mix.

Once it was time to make the video, Curtisay lined up the dancers, helped organise the shoot, and edited the footage after Driz N8 and Great Devoted Generation filmed it.

The artiste who turned a remix brief into his own single had apparently found a few more ways to make himself useful.

Now comes the litmus test: The walking gauntlet that is the essence of dancehall. He wants to see what dancers like Shelly Belly and others do with the chorus at Boom Sundays.

“I can’t wait to see what the reaction will be inna the dances…It’s going to be epic,” he said.

World.title: ‘TIME TO TALK!’
World.content:
Match officials (from left) Ojay Duhaney, Oshane Nation, Stephanie-Dale Yee-Sing, Okeito Nicholson, and Kemar Gayle receive tokens after officiating the Jamaica Premier League football final between champions Cavalier FC and Mount Pleasant Football Academy on May 19, 2024.

MONTEGO Bay United Chairman Yoni Epstein has called for an urgent meeting involving the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF), the Jamaica Football Referees Association (JFRA) and Jamaica Premier League clubs to resolve the dispute over outstanding payments to match officials and get the competition back on track.

Epstein says all parties have a responsibility to find a solution as the continued suspension of games is hurting the sport, its sponsors, supporters and players.

Last Sunday’s Jamaica Premier League games were postponed after referees withdrew their services over outstanding payments. The JFRA and Professional Football Jamaica Limited (PFJL) — organisers of the competition — were still uncertain up to yesterday about when the games would resume,

JFRA President Valdin Ledgister told the Jamaica Observer that the association was still awaiting more than $2 million promised by the JFF. Ledgister said that as of 1:45 pm on Tuesday, the outstanding amount had not reached their accounts.

The referees had received approximately $3.2 million from the PFJL but were still awaiting the balance, Ledgister said.

“The referees are not in a position to turn out for the games,” he said, adding that the outstanding money had reportedly been sent since Friday.

Ledgister said the dispute had not affected games in the Inter-secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) competitions, as the referees were not owed any money for those matches.

“We are not owed anything from the ISSA games, and we have clear communication and arrangements with them,” he said.

PFJL Chief Executive Officer Owen Hill, however, says his organisation had fulfilled its responsibilities and was seeking clarification as to why the referees were still withholding their services.

In a letter to JFF General Secretary Gregory Daley dated November 23, Hill said the PFJL had advanced approximately $3.29 million between November 21 and 23 to the referees’ standard payment account, THE RA Limited, to settle the outstanding claims.

Hill said the payments were made without a formal invoice or the complete supporting documentation normally required, as the PFJL sought to prevent the disruption of the competition.

“The PFJL’s position is that all monies brought to its attention in connection with the current payment dispute have been advanced and settled accordingly, and that no further amounts have been formally established as outstanding in relation to the claims presented,” the letter stated.

Hill also questioned why the referees continued to withhold their services without providing an explanation or a reconciliation of any further amounts being claimed.

The PFJL chief executive said there were no new developments regarding the dispute and that the organisation was still awaiting word on when the next round of games would be played.

“We are yet to hear from the parties involved as to when the next scheduled round of games will be played,” Hill said. “The PFJL has a responsibility to its core stakeholders to protect their investment so we continue to seek a resolution.”

Epstein described the situation as a “real travesty” and says the parties need to put aside their differences and find a solution.

“I understand their concerns, and I think that we are all at fault. At the end of the day, the one thing that is suffering is the football. The sponsors, the supporters, the players trying to progress their careers are all suffering because of this situation,” he said.

Epstein says the clubs, JFF, and referees need to meet within the next 24 hours to understand the concerns and resolve the matter, whether in person or virtually.

“The referees feel disrespected, and as stakeholders we need to understand why, and we need to rectify this. Without them, the game cannot be played,” he said.

Epstein says the dispute is damaging the reputation of the JFF and the Jamaica Premier League while also hurting clubs, referees, players, fans and sponsors.

He is urging all parties to work together to find a solution and have the league back on the field by Sunday.

“There is nothing in life that is insurmountable, but we have to get into a room, and we have to get into a room fast in order to solve this situation to get football back on the field come this Sunday, no questions asked.”

World.title: BOJ moves to unlock farm credit in inflation fight
World.content:
Governor of the Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) Brian Langrin addresses journalists during the central bank’s quarterly monetary policy press conference on Monday at its headquarters in downtown, Kingston. Looking on is Wayne Robinson, senior deputy governor of the BOJ.Garfield Robinson

BANK of Jamaica (BOJ) is proposing to halve the regulatory risk weights applied to loans for climate-resilient agricultural projects, seeking to draw more bank financing into a sector whose exposure to droughts and hurricanes has repeatedly fed food-price inflation.

The proposal would cover qualifying investments such as solar-powered drip irrigation, water storage, hurricane-resilient greenhouses, cold and dry storage facilities, farm roads, drainage and other post-harvest infrastructure.

Governor Brian Langrin said the measure is intended to strengthen domestic food production before another climate shock occurs, rather than relying mainly on interest rates to contain the inflationary fallout afterwards.

“Interest rates cannot prevent a drought, restore damaged crops, or repair a disrupted food supply chain.We must therefore look beyond interest rates and examine whether complementary measures can help to reduce the economy’s vulnerability to these shocks.” Langrin said during the BOJ’s monetary policy press briefing on Monday.

The proposal is still at an early stage. No framework has been agreed, and the measure remains subject to internal assessment, legal review and the required approvals. The central bank has also not yet held detailed discussions with deposit-taking institutions, although Langrin said they had been alerted to the initiative.

Under the proposal, a qualifying agricultural loan carrying a risk weight of 100 per cent could be assigned a 50 per cent weight. Reducing the risk weight would lower the amount of capital a bank must hold against the loan, giving financial institutions more room and an incentive to lend to approved projects.

Current risk weights on the loans range from 50 per cent to as much as 150 per cent.

Still, the BOJ is not proposing to relax the credit checks applied to borrowers. Eligible investments would have to be physical, independently verified assets with a clear resilience component, while the adjustment would be narrowly defined to ensure capital requirements continue to reflect the underlying credit risk.

Langrin acknowledged that the central bank would have to monitor whether financial institutions translate the regulatory benefit into increased lending on more favourable terms.

“We will have to watch: Do they in fact pass on these incentives to climate-resilient agricultural production? And they ought to, because now more loans in that area actually have a smaller charge on the capital,” he said during the question-and-answer segment.

The initiative comes amid renewed concern over the willingness of financial institutions to lend to agriculture and other productive sectors, particularly where borrowers lack the property or other readily marketable assets traditionally accepted as collateral.

Langrin said banks have historically preferred to lend against real estate and motor vehicles, which can be sold more easily if a borrower defaults, rather than assess businesses principally on their cash flow.

“They have to lend against cash flow,” he said, noting that farmers and other underserved borrowers may operate viable businesses without possessing the type of collateral banks typically demand.

The BOJ is examining how technology could allow financial institutions, with the borrower’s permission, to assess the cash flows of small and medium-sized businesses more efficiently. Langrin said this could reduce the cost of monitoring smaller borrowers and give banks greater confidence to lend based on the income generated by a business.

The agricultural initiative forms part of a broader attempt by the BOJ to expand its response to inflation beyond its traditional monetary policy tools. Food accounts for approximately one-third of Jamaica’s consumer price index, giving agricultural disruptions an outsized effect on the cost of living.

Research conducted by the central bank over a 25-year period found that global food-price shocks had a larger and more persistent effect on domestic inflation than comparable movements in oil and alumina prices.

Jamaica’s vulnerability has been reinforced by successive weather events, including hurricanes Beryl and Melissa and the intensifying El Niño conditions now affecting agricultural production.

Langrin said more resilient infrastructure could reduce crop losses, improve the reliability of domestic food supplies and lower the risk of agricultural loans becoming non-performing after a disaster. It could also strengthen farmers’ ability to supply the tourism industry, reducing some of the country’s dependence on food imports.

The governor argued that Jamaica’s agricultural sector has not been able to supply the tourism industry reliably and at sufficient scale, leaving the country exposed to both domestic crop failures and increases in international food prices.

“We would love for the industry to be able to supply the demand, especially from the tourism sector, but it simply cannot do so on a sustainable basis,” Langrin said.

“A large part of this impulse from food is from imported food. Prices have increased significantly abroad,” he added.

The BOJ has offered to convene a symposium involving government agencies, financial institutions and other stakeholders to examine the obstacles to agricultural financing and resilience. Langrin said several public agencies were already working in the area, but greater coordination was needed.

The proposed measure was unveiled as the BOJ increased its policy rate by 50 basis points to 6.50 per cent, its second consecutive increase of that size since September.

Annual inflation stood at 8.2 per cent in October, down from 8.6 per cent in September but above the BOJ’s target range of four to six per cent for a fifth consecutive month. The central bank now expects inflation to remain above target for most of the next four quarters and return sustainably to the range by late 2027, later than previously projected.

Food prices, transport costs and electricity rates were among the main contributors to the October out-turn. Business expectations for inflation 12 months ahead also rose to 8.3 per cent in September, from 7.3 per cent in July, increasing the risk that companies will adjust prices in anticipation of higher future costs.

The BOJ said the rate increases were intended to prevent those expectations from producing a self-reinforcing cycle of price increases. However, it believes the adjustments made to date should be sufficient to return inflation to target if current conditions do not deteriorate.

The proposed agricultural measure will take longer to produce results and is not expected to lower food prices immediately. Its objective is instead to reduce the severity of future supply shocks, which could lessen the need for the central bank to repeatedly use interest rates against inflation originating outside the financial system.

World.title: Fi Wi Land: The fight to save Jamaica’s dying lignum vitae
World.content:
A symbol of Jamaica’s natural beauty and national identity, the lignum vitae holds a special place in the island’s heritage. But despite its significance as Jamaica’s national flower, this treasured species is facing growing threats to its survival, raising concerns about the future of one of the country’s national symbols.

Renowned for its exceptionally hard and durable wood, the lignum vitae has faced years of overexploitation, habitat loss and land degradation, contributing to a decline in its population.

With the species subject to international trade restrictions under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), protecting and restoring its population is an important conservation priority.

In this week’s episode of Fi Wi Land, Environmental Officer for Flora at the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA), Ashleigh Sanderson, sheds light on the threats facing Jamaica’s national flower and the efforts being made to safeguard its future.

From population surveys revealing concerns about its decline to conservation action plans and environmental protection measures, discover how NEPA is working to preserve the lignum vitae and other threatened plant species across the island.

Catch the latest episode on the Jamaica Observer’s YouTube channel and other digital platforms.

World.title: From ‘Bulbie’ to ‘Blackman’, the evolution of the Klansman gang
World.content:
The United States has designated the St Catherine-based Klansman gang as a transnational criminal organisation (TCO), a move that will bar purported members of the criminal group from entering the country.

Prime Minister Andrew Holness disclosed the development following a recent meeting with US Assistant Secretary of State for Western Hemisphere Affairs Juan Pablo Segura and members of his delegation, who were visiting Jamaica.

The TCO designation is a formal US government label placed on criminal groups that operate across international borders, and includes major criminal outfits and terrorist organisations such as the Sinaloa Cartel and Hezbollah.

During the 2000s and 2010s, the Klansman gang’s violent turf wars in Spanish Town, resulted in police crackdowns like Operation Kingfish, and the arrests and deaths of reputed figures such as Donovan “Bulbie” Bennett and Tesha Miller.

READ: US designates Jamaica’s Klansman Gang as transnational criminal organisation

ORIGINS OF KLANSMAN

Based in the southeastern parish of St Catherine, west of the capital Kingston, despite the name, the Jamaican gang has no connection to the Ku Klux Klan, an American white supremacist group whose members are called “Klansmen”. Anecdotal tales say the local gang was formed when young men met in a house in Dela Vega City and decided to become one ‘clan’, and set up an extortion racket in the Old Capital of Spanish Town.

The history of the Klansman gang is like a top ten Netflix movie: rival factions, secret burial sites, homicidal bosses.

The recent trials of dozens of members of the gang in Jamaica is shedding light on how criminal groups function on the island. At one time, police said the gang was raking in J$1.8 million weekly from extorting mainly business owners and transport operators. The gang also reportedly made money through targeted killings and weapons trafficking.

The gang’s status and organisation also helped rake in the cash. Its primary means of revenue, according to prosecutors, is extortion. One witness said that extortion payments from a section of the bus park in Spanish Town ranged from $80,000 to $100,000 a day.

One popular loan company, Torpedo, also paid up to $150,000 a month to a splinter faction of the gang, claimed one witness. The witness revealed that another organisation, which he refused to name due to security concerns as it includes “powerful individuals”, paid $200,000 a month.

Fifteen members of the One Don splinter faction of the gang, including leader Andre “Blackman” Bryan, were in March 2023 convicted under Jamaica’s anti-gang legislation. Meanwhile, 25 alleged members of the reputed Tesha Miller faction are now before the Supreme Court answering to 16 offences – including murder and robbery – allegedly committed over the span of five years between August 2017 and November 2022.

According to prosecutors and witnesses in the Klansman trial, the criminal outfit is now firmly a third-generation gang. The testimony of two former gang members stated that the Klansman reportedly had some 400 members within its different factions. The gang also had clearly defined roles, corrupt links with the police, international criminal connections and even allegedly carried out hits ordered by a celebrity musician.

Here are some of the generational figures that have defined the history of the Klansman, a firmly established third generation gang with tentacles in St Catherine, Clarendon and even Manchester.

BEFORE ‘BULBIE’: THE ‘PUPPY STRING’ CHAPTER

Derrick “Puppy String” Eccleston was an early leader of the Klansman, before Donovan “Bulbie” Bennett assumed control.

Eccleston was killed on May 12, 1993. His death marked a change in the gang’s leadership, with Bennett subsequently taking over.

Although some accounts alleged Bennett’s involvement in Eccleston’s killing, that allegation was never proven in court.

BALLAD OF ‘BULBIE’

Donovan “Bulbie” Bennett, the leader of the Klansman gang and Jamaica’s most-wanted man for over a decade, was fatally shot on October 30, 2005, during a joint police-military raid in Clarendon.

Bennett gradually built up a criminal empire through murder and extortion whose assets included 80 motor vehicles and heavy equipment used in construction and hauling industries throughout Jamaica.

Authorities believe he gained leadership through the murder of then leader Eccleston in 1993.

During the early 1990s, Bennett led the gang against their rivals, the One Order Gang, resulting in numerous gangland shootings and other violence in Spanish Town.

READ: From ‘Bubba’ to ‘Thickman’: The ill-fated leadership of the One Order Gang

He later established an elaborate extortion operation targeting local business, particularly taximen, in both the central and south central regions of St Catherine. He would later be connected to criminal activities in Old Harbour and Portmore, St Catherine and May Pen.

He was thought to have briefly fled from authorities in Kingston to Great Britain under a false identity in 2001.

In 2005, security forces under Operation Kingfish cornered the 43-year-old Bennett at a lavish, seven-bedroom hideout he had built in the secluded hillside district of Tanaky (near Rock River), Clarendon.

According to police reports, security forces came under gunfire as they approached the compound in the pre-dawn hours. In the ensuing gun battle, Bennett and his driver, identified only as Nathan, were killed.

Police recovered a .50-caliber Desert Eagle pistol from Bennett, a Ruger pistol from his driver, and a large cache of cash and jewelry. At the time of his death, his wealth—amassed through extortion, construction equipment, and heavy haulage—was estimated at over J$100 million.

News of Bennett’s death triggered immediate violent reprisal across Spanish Town. Gang members mounted roadblocks, burned effigies of then-National Security Minister Dr Peter Phillips, and launched a gun attack on the Spanish Town Police Station, injuring two officers.

Following his elaborate funeral in De La Vega City and burial in Goshen, Clarendon, leadership of the Klansman gang allegedly passed to Tesha Miller, a welder by profession.

THE RISE OF TESHA

Tesha Miller, who grew up in Spanish Town after being born in De la Vega City, gained national attention in 2005 when he was charged with four counts of murder and three counts of shooting, for which he received bail.

Miller however, allegedly absconded to the United States.

He is also known on the streets by the nickname “Rat” (sometimes spelled “Ratt”). He has allegedly also used the alias Marlon Andre Williams (or Marlon Williams) on travel documents during past immigration incidents in The Bahamas and Jamaica.

Authorities linked the organisation under his alleged leadership to widespread extortion networks targeting transport operators, bus terminals, and businesses across Spanish Town and St Catherine.

He became even more notorious, attracting national attention over the June 2008 killing of JUTC chairman Douglas Chambers outside the company’s Spanish Town depot. Sentenced in January 2020 to more than 38 years for being an accessory before and after the fact, Miller had those convictions overturned in March 2026 because of jury-selection errors. The Court of Appeal ordered a retrial.

His history also includes capture and deportation from The Bahamas, where he reportedly travelled under a false identity. He is separately standing trial alongside 24 co-accused on an anti-gang indictment concerning alleged offences across several parishes between 2017 and 2022. Miller maintains his innocence and denies leading a gang.

MILLER HAS A LONG RAP SHEET

On May 3, 2007, after being caught by US officials, he was deported to Jamaica and was slapped with a nine-month prison term for absconding bail.

On March 5, 2008, Miller was fined $100,000 for breaching his curfew order.

On July 7, 2008, a cell phone was allegedly found in Miller’s rectum during a search of his cell at Horizon Remand Centre after the device reportedly rang. Miller strongly refuted the claim.

On November 21, 2008, Director of Public Prosecutions Paula Llewellyn took the decision not to proceed with a triple-murder case against Miller, as the police were having difficulty locating the sole eyewitness in the matter. He had been charged with the murder of Orane Jackson, Jeffrey Johnson and Nicole Allen who were shot in Braeton, St Catherine, on January 14, 2005.

On March 25, 2009, Miller was back before the court, and was denied bail, as he awaited trial for the murder of Rohan Haughton, who was fatally shot on St John’s Road, Spanish Town in April 2004. The eyewitness in the case was reportedly shot dead in St Elizabeth in August 2008.

After being in custody for almost a year, Miller was found not guilty for the murder of Haughton on June 10, 2009 as the Crown offered no further evidence against him as there was nothing to link him to the offence.

On December 26, 2009, Miller was arrested while at the Boxing Day show, Sting, after he allegedly breached a curfew order imposed by the court.

On May 2010, Miller turned himself in to the police after being listed among 25 men wanted for allegedly being gang members and area leaders.

On June 2010, Miller was detained under a State of Emergency. October 15, 2010, Miller was taken into custody for questioning in relation to an upsurge of shootings and other crimes in the St Catherine North Police Division.

On December 21, 2010, Miller was charged with robbery with aggravation involving a motor car and illegal possession of a firearm. Not long after, his 23-year-old sister Renase James was shot and killed while she was a passenger in a taxi in Spanish Town, St Catherine, in December 2011.

On April 15, 2011, Miller was sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment for robbery with aggravation. He was also sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment for illegal possession of firearm with the sentences to run concurrently.

Miller’s conviction for illegal possession of a firearm and robbery with aggravation was quashed and his sentence set aside on March 22, 2013 by the Court of Appeal.

He left Jamaica for the United States of America in April 2013.

Five months later, he was arrested there and charged with illegal re-entry, having previously been deported, and for having an identification card in another person’s name. Miller was convicted of the offences and sentenced to two years and eight months in prison. He was subsequently deported in March 2016. While Miller was in custody in the US, two of his brothers were shot and killed in 2015.

On August 7, 2016, Miller was listed by the police as a person of interest with claims being he could assist with investigations into several murders recorded in Spanish Town and Portmore, St Catherine.

On April 4, 2017, Miller was deported from The Bahamas after illegally entering the country. Fifteen days later, Miller was fined the $100 maximum fine under the law after he pleaded guilty to making a false declaration to Jamaican immigration officials.

THE RISE OF ‘BLACKMAN’

The One Don gang, led by Andre “Blackman” Bryan, emerged as a breakaway faction of the Klansman following a power struggle with reputed leader Tesha Miller around 2017.

Prosecutors alleged that the faction carried out murders, extortion, arson and firearms offences across St Catherine between 2015 and 2019, particularly in Spanish Town and Jones Avenue.

In March 2023, Chief Justice Bryan Sykes convicted Bryan of leading a criminal organisation and facilitating serious offences in a landmark anti-gang trial. Fifteen of the 33 defendants were convicted. Bryan was subsequently sentenced in October 2023 to 39 years and six months in prison.

Bryan was allegedly once the top hitman for reputed Klansman boss, Tesha Miller. The split dates back to at least 2017, when Bryan appears to have rebelled against Miller and began killing his associates.

Bryan’s ability to operate freely was significantly enhanced in 2016 when both men were on trial for the 2008 murder of senior transport official Douglas Chambers. While prosecutors said Miller ordered the hit and Bryan was the gunman, Miller was sentenced to over 38 years in jail for being an accessory before and after the fact, and Bryan was exonerated. Miller’s conviction was subsequently overturned due to jury selection errors.

Witness testimony has painted Bryan as an incredibly violent individual who laughed upon learning targets had been killed. State witnesses said they were forced to join the gang out of fear for their lives.

During sentencing hearings in late September and early October 2023, Bryan addressed the court and openly acknowledged his leadership role, showing his sense of fearlessness and growing hubris.

World.title: Tusk government ‘facing armageddon’ as European court resumes cases against Poland
World.content:
ND - NOVEMBER 7: Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk holds a press conference after a deadly shooting took place on November 7, 2026 in the Main Market Square of Krakow. | Omar Marques/Getty Images

The country faces millions of euros in potential compensation payments over its former nationalist government’s judicial overhaul.

Europe’s top human rights court resumed proceedings against Poland on Wednesday, putting fresh pressure on Prime Minister Donald Tusk to deliver on his promise to restore the independence of the country’s courts.

The European Court of Human Rights said it has around 1,600 cases pending over judicial changes introduced by Poland’s former nationalist Law and Justice government. It suspended proceedings in 2023 to give Warsaw time to restore judicial independence.

Tusk’s promise to restore the rule of law helped unlock billions in frozen EU funding following his return to power in 2023. But his efforts have been hampered by two successive PiS-backed presidents, most recently Karol Nawrocki.

World.title: “Les COP, c’est une blague” : les critiques enflent contre les sommets climatiques après l’échec à Antalya
World.content:
“Si nous parvenons à donner le meilleur de nous-mêmes, à nous organiser, au cours des douze prochains mois, la COP31 nous paraîtra rétrospectivement comme un moment cathartique de prise de conscience”, a positivé Rachel Kyte, envoyée spéciale du Royaume-Uni pour le climat, lors d’un entretien accordé à POLITICO, ajoutant que les pays devaient corriger le processus qui, ces dernières années, a peiné à produire des résultats.

Ceux appelant à une refonte du processus réclament une réforme du format COP, voire sa suppression pure et simple, sans que l’on ait réellement d’idées sur la manière de mettre en œuvre l’une ou l’autre de ces options. Reste que l’échec des organisateurs à négocier un accord final a libéré un flot de critiques.

Selon ses détracteurs, le processus actuel, dans lequel les pays pétroliers font obstacle aux initiatives visant à mentionner explicitement les énergies fossiles, n’est plus viable dans un monde qui se dirige à toute vitesse vers une aggravation des conditions climatiques.

“Nous avons tous été pris en otage par les producteurs de pétrole, mais aussi par les plus grands consommateurs de pétrole”, a pointé auprès de POLITICO le ministre panaméen du Climat, Juan Carlos Navarro.

La faute aux producteurs d’énergies fossiles, mais pas que

Ces négociations chaotiques en Turquie interviennent onze ans après que, pour la première fois, tous les pays se sont mis d’accord sur la nécessité de lutter contre le changement climatique en signant l’Accord de Paris. Depuis, des progrès poussifs ont laissé les pays à la traîne par rapport à leurs objectifs. Au point que l’ONU a annoncé le mois dernier qu’il n’y avait plus aucun espoir d’éviter un réchauffement de 1,5 °C.

L’échec de ce week-end contraste fortement avec les négociations de l’année dernière au Brésil, où les gouvernements étaient parvenus à un accord malgré les attaques à distance contre le processus du président Donald Trump, et sa décision de retirer les Etats-Unis de l’Accord de Paris.

World.title: Don’t ‘backslide’ on defense spending, senior US lawmaker tells Europe
World.content:
His comments come as EU leaders prepare to discuss the bloc’s next seven-year budget at a summit Thursday and Friday. The latest draft defense budget tabled by European Council President António Costa would see tens of billions cut from the European Commission’s earlier proposal, drawing the ire of some EU countries — though the total is still double the previous seven-year budget.

Boyle said he was “heartened” that all NATO allies were now spending more on defense than the alliance’s longstanding 2% of GDP target agreed at the 2014 Wales summit. “I’m glad that that is a floor and no longer considered a ceiling,” he said, while acknowledging that European governments face “similar budget constraints” to the U.S.

He said Europe building up its own defense industry after decades of relying on American weapons was a net positive for the NATO alliance, but warned against the bloc breaking that dependence too fast. EU countries are currently only spending about 15% of their defense procurement budgets on European-made equipment, despite calls from the Commission to raise this to at least half by 2030.

“Where it would become a negative is if suddenly there was a hard turn away from totally buying U.S. systems,” Boyle said. “That would be a mistake.”

World.title: French presidential hopeful Teddy Riner says Ukraine is ‘not our war’
World.content:
"If I become president tomorrow, I would like to be the kind of person who brings people together, who smiles and shakes hands to put an end to this war," Riner added about Russia's war in Ukraine.

Russian leader Vladimir Putin also practices judo and was honorary president of the International Judo Federation before launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The 37-year-old Riner has unveiled few policy proposals and had not yet weighed in on foreign affairs since announcing his candidacy earlier this month. The two leading candidates for next April's election in France — far-right chief Marine Le Pen and far-left veteran Jean-Luc Mélenchon — have both been critical of current President Emmanuel Macron's Ukraine policy. Macron's government has sent funds and weapons to Ukraine and co-led the coalition of the willing, a group of Kyiv's most significant allies and supporters.

Riner, however, had been more closely associated with the pro-Macron camp based on early campaign statements, making his Ukraine comments more surprising. Early surveys have shown him polling at about 4%, drawing mostly from voters who opted for Macron in the last presidential election.

Center-right MEP Nathalie Loiseau, who handles foreign affairs policy for presidential candidate Edouard Philippe, seized on Riner's remarks to attack the election rival.

"Teddy Riner's world would be so simple: you don't get involved in anything, you shake hands with everyone, and there's peace and love all over the world," she wrote on X.

Riner was speaking from the French mayors' congress currently taking place in Paris, where he was seeking out endorsements needed to run for president.

He still has a long way to go before actually getting onto the ballot: Riner said he had obtained more than 100 signatures from local officials in support his candidacy — far from the 500 needed to confirm his candidacy under French law.

World.title: Macron threatens to stop negotiating EU budget after December
World.content:
Macron is leaving office in spring next year because he cannot constitutionally run for a third consecutive term. He has already told fellow leaders that he would not be in a position to continue negotiating the bloc's 2028-2034 budget in the new year.

Marine Le Pen, the far-right candidate leading the polls for the 2027 presidential election, has repeatedly accused EU institutions and the French president of deliberately speeding up budget negotiations to leave her out of the process. She pledged to drastically cut France's contribution to the EU budget and transform the European Commission into a "secretariat" of member countries, if she is elected.

Macron's office openly criticized Costa's proposal to shave another €44 billion off the EU’s planned seven-year budget, even if it shields some of France's favoured spending items like subsidies to farmers from cuts. Macron had lunch with Costa on Tuesday in Paris.

On Wednesday afternoon, Macron hosted representatives of the country's top farmers' organizations at the Elysée. He promised them that “the CAP will be the number one subject and the number one goal for France” at this week's European Council meeting.

The Elysée official quoted above, who in line with the French government’s communications practices was not named, predicted that the EUCO meeting would not be conclusive and stressed that Costa's proposal was not addressing French demands, including on raising more own resources levied by the EU directly to finance the budget.

In addition to the cuts, Macron's office warned that Costa's proposal offers little certainty that new-EU wide taxes would see the light any time soon, as they would have to be adopted in a separate vote after budget negotiations. While France backs the new digital levy proposed by Costa and the European Commission, it warned that it would be hard to convince all EU countries to get on board.

World.title: EU weist Trumps Argumente für neue Zölle zurück
World.content:
Das Büro des US-Handelsbeauftragten unter der Leitung von Jamieson Greer hatte festgestellt, dass 14 Handelspartner, darunter die EU, China und Japan, Preise künstlich gedrückt hatten, indem sie die Märkte mit Industriegütern überschwemmten. Die Entscheidung folgte auf eine im März eingeleitete Untersuchung nach Abschnitt 301 des US-Handelsgesetzes von 1974

Greer schlug einen Zollsatz von 15 Prozent für die EU vor. Er entspricht der Obergrenze, die im Juli 2025 im EU-US-Handelsabkommen von Turnberry vereinbart wurde.

Greer wird voraussichtlich am Montag per Video an einem Treffen der europäischen Handelsminister teilnehmen. Die EU-Minister dürften dabei mangelnde Fortschritte bei der Senkung der Zölle auf EU-Produkte mit Stahlanteilen zur Sprache bringen. Für einige davon gelten nach wie vor US-Zölle bis zu 50 Prozent.

Die Untersuchung gemäß Abschnitt 301 die zweite abgeschlossene Handelsuntersuchung der USA gegen die EU seit dem Frühjahr. Die US-Regierung hatte bereits einen Zollsatz von 10 Prozent gegen die EU verhängt, weil die EU die Einfuhr von Waren nicht verbiete, die unter Einsatz von Zwangsarbeit hergestellt wurden. Es werde aber nur der höhere der beiden Zollsätze gelten, anstatt dass beide addiert würden, erklärte ein hochrangiger US-Beamter. Außerdem werde die Turnberry-Grenze von 15 Prozent eingehalten.

Der Vorsitzende des Handelsausschusses des Europäischen Parlaments, Bernd Lange, bezeichnete die Schlussfolgerungen des USTR-Berichts als „absurd“.

„Wer nach den Zwischenwahlen ruhigere Zeiten erwartet hatte, hat sich getäuscht. Das hatte ohnehin kaum jemand ernsthaft erwartet“, erklärte Lange. Bei der Wahl vom 3. November hatten die Demokraten im Senat und im Repräsentantenhaus deutliche Mehrheiten errungen.

World.title: UK will not offer equal tuition fees for EU students, says Burnham
World.content:
The issue of tuition fees has become politically fraught since Friday, when contradictory briefings from London and Brussels left it unclear if the agreements reached at the U.K.-EU summit on food, emissions and youth mobility were contingent on a deal for students.

Burnham insisted that the university deal was not linked to the other agreements. "The deal on tuition fees is not done," he said. "It's on a separate piece of paper, a separate deal."

Under the current scheme, EU students pay international fees — which can sometimes be £20,000 higher than the rate British students pay.

Last week, two EU diplomats, granted anonymity to discuss the plans, told POLITICO London had so far offered fees of £12,000.

In a joint statement released Friday, EU and U.K. leaders said they would "work towards" an agreement on tuition fees. "We will conclude the negotiations within six months from the date of the summit," they added.

Universities have warned that giving EU students a better deal on fees could impact the financial health of higher education institutions — many of which are already facing a cash crisis.

World.title: EU rejects Trump’s case for new tariffs
World.content:
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, led by Jamieson Greer, found that 14 trading partners, including the European Union, China and Japan, had artificially deflated prices by flooding markets with manufactured goods. The decision follows a trade investigation launched in March.

Greer on Wednesday proposed a 15% tariff on the European Union, in line with the ceiling agreed in the transatlantic trade truce struck in July 2025 between U.S. President Donald Trump and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

Greer, who is expected to dial in next Monday to a meeting of European trade ministers, can expect pushback on the excess capacity probe. EU ministers are also expected to bring up the lack of progress on lowering tariffs on EU products containing steel — some of which still face U.S. duties of as high as 50%.

The overcapacity investigation, launched under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, is the second of two trade probes initiated in the spring as part of the Trump administration’s mission to rebuild its tariff wall.

After the “reciprocal” duties Trump imposed in 2025 were invalidated earlier this year by the U.S. Supreme Court, the administration imposed a 10% tariff on the European Union, citing concerns that Brussels had failed to ban the import of goods made using forced labor. The higher of the two tariff rates will apply, rather than the two being added together, a senior U.S. official said.

The official added that the proposed duties would likely take effect in January at the earliest, after USTR holds hearings and receives public comments.

World.title: One EU budget. Too many priorities? MEPs join The Ring in Strasbourg
World.content:
The European Commission is proposing a new €45 billion loan to Ukraine as the country continues to face Russia’s war. But who ultimately bears the cost and how will the money be financed?

 

With the EU debating the scale and conditions of its long-term commitment, the proposal raises difficult questions about European solidarity, financial responsibility and the path towards peace.

At the same time, the stakes for the EU budget have risen sharply as the German chancellor Friedrich Merz tied the deal to approving the €45 billion loan for Kyiv.

EU lawmakers Marcos Ros (S&D) from Spain and Ondřej Kolář (EPP) from Czechia, discuss whether the EU can continue its aid to Ukraine without cutting funds from other areas such as the EU's cohesion policy.

Is a deal on the EU budget in sight? And how will the EU continue its support to Ukraine?

Watch The Ring in the player above.

World.title: Wrongly deported Salvadoran arrives in Spain after US legal battle
World.content:
