World.title: What’s Changing for Cash Payments in Croatia in 2027?
World.content:
November the 25th, 2026 – The EU is tightening its rules for cash payments across the bloc, and as such in Croatia in 2027. Here’s what it means for the general public.

As of the 10th of July 2027, much stricter rules for cash payments will start to apply across the entire European Union. While the cash payment limit of €10,000 already exists in Croatia, the novelty is the introduction of a lower general threshold for mandatory identity checks on cash transactions. Index reports that according to the new European Union regulation on preventing money laundering and terrorist financing, certain business entities will have to establish and verify the identity of clients already for occasional cash transactions of €3,000. The regulation was adopted back in 2024 and begins to apply in July next year.

what’s changing for cash payments in croatia in 2027?

Under the current Croatian law, banks, financial institutions and other obliged entities under money-laundering prevention regulations are required to carry out customer due diligence for occasional transactions of €10,000 or more. This analysis includes identity verification. For certain activities and types of transactions, lower thresholds already apply. Checks are also mandatory when establishing a business relationship and when there is a suspicion of money laundering, regardless of the transaction amount. The new European Union regulation introduces an additional obligation to verify identity for occasional cash transactions of €3,000, while the general threshold for full customer due diligence remains €10,000.

This does not, however, mean that every trader in Croatia will have to ask for the customer’s identity card when a bill of €3,000 is paid in cash. The obligation applies to business entities covered by the regulation, including banks, financial institutions, traders in precious metals, precious stones and certain categories of luxury goods.

croatia actually already has a cash payment limit

The European Union is also introducing a common upper limit for cash payments for goods and services of €10,000. Member states will be able to retain existing stricter limits or introduce new ones. In Croatia specifically, natural and legal persons who perform a registered activity are already not allowed to accept or make cash payments of €10,000 or more. The ban also covers several interrelated transactions whose total amount reaches that limit.

what about buying a car from a private individual?

The European Union limit will not apply to payments between natural persons who are not acting within the framework of their business or professional activity. This means that a person who buys a used car from another member of the public, and not from a car dealership, can, according to the European regulation, pay more than €10,000 in cash. The limit will also not apply to deposits and payments at bank branches and other payment service providers, for which separate supervisory rules apply.

working to prevent money laundering

The new rules are part of a broader package of European measures aimed at making it more difficult to use the financial system for money laundering and terrorist financing, and at harmonising regulations among member states. Until now, cash payment limits differed significantly among EU members, and some countries did not have them at all. The European Union wants to prevent criminals from exploiting these differences to transfer and conceal illegally obtained money. As part of the same package, a new European Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) with its seat in Frankfurt has also been established; from 2028 it will directly supervise selected high-risk financial institutions.

World.title: Major Airlines Are Leaving Zagreb. The Airport Has Announced New Plans
World.content:
November the 24th, 2026 – With major airlines like British Airways and Austrian Airlines leaving Zagreb, the airport has announced new plans.

Zagreb Airport has issued another statement today following the announced withdrawals of British Airways and Austrian Airlines, as well as flight reductions by other carriers. Index reports that they state that the departure of individual airlines isn’t good news, but they have still emphasised that the airport will not lose direct connections to the destinations affected by the announced changes. They also announced the start of the next phase of airport development during 2027.

“We’re aware that the withdrawal of an individual airline or a reduction in flight frequencies is not positive news for the airport, and we take every such business decision seriously,” they stated in the press release. They emphasised that a distinction must be made between the departure of a specific carrier and the complete cancellation of a direct connection to a given destination. “According to currently published flight schedules, all markets affected by the recently announced changes remain directly connected to Zagreb,” they said.

flight cuts and reductions

In recent days, Index has written about the problems facing Zagreb Airport, which has been left without two major European carriers. British Airways removed flights between Zagreb and London Heathrow from sale for the 2027 summer season, while Austrian Airlines will cease operating its route to Vienna at the beginning of next year. At the same time, Iberia, Qatar Airways, and several other carriers have reduced the number of flights or abandoned planned capacity increases. Despite this, Zagreb still has direct flights to London and Vienna. Croatia Airlines continues to fly to Heathrow and Vienna, while Ryanair connects Zagreb with London Stansted.

traffic growth has almost stalled

Zagreb Airport achieved a record 4.72 million passengers last year, but growth has slowed significantly this year. In the first ten months, only 0.6 percent more passengers were recorded compared to the same period last year, and every month from July to October was weaker than in 2025. However, the airport emphasized today that after the pandemic, they achieved one of the strongest recoveries among comparable European airports. Passenger numbers grew from approximately 3.4 million before the coronavirus pandemic to an expected 4.8 million by the end of this year, representing a growth of nearly 40 percent. They state that airlines adjust their operations due to demand, the profitability of individual routes, aircraft availability, and their own strategic priorities. They add that the European aviation industry is suffering the consequences of rising fuel prices and operating costs, delays in the delivery of new aircraft, and geopolitical uncertainty.

no drop in passenger numbers is expected in 2027

Despite the announced departures and flight reductions, Zagreb Airport does not expect a drop in total passenger numbers in 2027. “Based on currently available information, we do not expect the number of passengers in 2027 to be lower than the level achieved in 2026,” they stated. They admit, however, that flight schedules for the 2027 summer season have not yet been finalised and that the final picture of capacity will only be known once airlines finish their planning. They also claim that while some carriers are reducing the number of flights, others are increasing capacities and expanding their presence in Zagreb.

is the terminal expansion happening?

This latest statement also comes after reports circulated about a possible postponement of investments in expanding the passenger terminal. As a reminder, the airport is managed by a private concessionaire, the international consortium ZAIC. According to the concession agreement, when annual traffic reaches five million passengers, the concessionaire is obligated to initiate the expansion of the western part of the existing terminal, including three new departure lounges and an expansion of the apron. The final contractual deadline for the start of works is January the 1st, 2032.

It was previously reported that the concessionaire is asking the government for the possibility of reopening the old Pleso passenger terminal, to which it would transfer the traffic of low-cost carriers. According to unofficial information obtained by the media, the proposal also includes counting passenger numbers separately at the old and new terminals, which could delay the obligation to expand the new terminal. Such a calculation method is not foreseen in the existing concession agreement.

development plans remain unaltered

“The next phase of the airport’s development program begins during 2027 and will include preparatory, technical, and planning activities necessary for further increasing passenger and operational capacities,” they stated. This, however, does not mean that construction work on the terminal expansion will begin next year. The statement refers to preparatory activities, with no concrete deadline for the start of construction. Zagreb Airport did not directly comment on the possible reopening of the old Pleso terminal or the proposal to change the way passenger numbers are counted.

not a single word about fee increases…

This larest statement also made no mention of the increase in airport fees that took effect on June the 1st of this year. As was previously reported, certain fees for airlines were increased by between 10 and 24 percent. According to fee comparisons, Zagreb is more expensive than most competing airports in the region, with the exception of Budapest.

So far, there is no proof that the fee increase was the decisive reason for the departure of individual airlines. Zagreb Airport states that it continues negotiations with existing and potential carriers regarding new routes, the return of certain flights, and increased frequencies. They announce that any new destinations and carriers will be made public only after official confirmation from the airlines.

World.title: the Gap Between Europe’s Rich and Poor – Croatia is Below the Average
World.content:
November the 24th, 2026 – The gap between the rich and the poor across the European Union narrowed slightly last year, with Croatia being below the average.

Despite the aforementioned narrowing, significant differences remain among countries. Poslovni reports that Croatia is below the European average, while among the major economies, Germany, France, Spain, and Italy are more unequal than the EU as a whole, according to Euronews. According to the latest Eurostat data, the Gini coefficient for the EU back in 2025 stood at 29.2, down from 29.4 the year before. This is the lowest value in the current European data series, which began in 2010.

Croatia finished at 28.5, below the European Union average, after recording a coefficient of 29.8 in 2024. The Gini coefficient is one of the most commonly used indicators of income inequality. A value of zero would represent complete equality, meaning a situation where everyone has the exact same income. A value of 100 would represent the opposite extreme, where all income belongs to a single person.

In its calculations, Eurostat uses disposable household income after taxes and social contributions, adjusted for household size and composition. The lower the number, the more evenly income is distributed.

the highest level of inequality in the eu is in bulgaria

Among European Union countries, Bulgaria had the highest income inequality in 2025 with a Gini coefficient of 37.7. It is followed by Latvia at 35.6 and Lithuania at 35.5. If non-EU European countries are included, Turkey stands out by far with a coefficient of 43.9. Also near the top are Greece at 31.6 and Italy at 31.0, while Switzerland is also at 31.0 according to the latest available data. Eurostat emphasises that differences between countries cannot be explained by wages alone, as they depend on a combination of the labour market, tax system, social transfers, unemployment, and economic structure.

slovakia is home to the most equal income distribution

At the other end of the scale is Slovakia with a coefficient of 23.0, the lowest in the EU. It is followed by Belgium at 23.4, the Czech Republic at 24.0, Slovenia at 24.6, and Poland at 24.9. In Slovakia, low inequality is not only the result of strong redistribution through taxes and social benefits, but also of relatively small differences in pre-tax market incomes. Belgium’s result, on the other hand, is strongly tied to a well-developed system of taxes, social transfers, and institutionalised social dialogue.

croatia is below the european union average

Croatia’s Gini coefficient in 2025 was 28.5, which is 0.7 points below the EU average. One year earlier, Croatia stood at 29.8, marking a drop of 1.3 points in just one year. In the longer term, Croatian inequality has also decreased. In 2010, the Gini coefficient was 31.6, and in 2015 it was 30.4. However, the trajectory has not been linear. Croatia was at 28.3 in 2020, after which the coefficient rose again to reach 29.8 in 2024 before last year’s drop. This means that, according to this indicator, Croatia has a more even distribution of disposable income than the EU average, though this alone does not indicate how high those incomes actually are. A country can have relatively low inequality while simultaneously having lower average incomes than wealthier member states.

major economies are above the eu average

Interestingly, all four of the EU’s largest economies are above the Union average. Germany has a Gini coefficient of 30.1, France 30.4, Spain 30.8, and Italy 31.0. In other words, disposable incomes in those countries are distributed more unequally than in Croatia and the EU as a whole. Differences also exist among Nordic countries, which are traditionally associated with relatively equal income distribution. Norway remains among the most equal at 23.7, but Denmark at 28.2 and Sweden at 28.6 are now more unequal than Poland, while Finland stands at 27.1.

poland and romania narrow the gap

A comparison with the average of the previous 15 years shows that income distribution has changed significantly in some countries. The greatest progress among EU members was recorded by Romania, whose Gini coefficient in 2025 was 27.3, a full 6.4 points below its 2010–2024 average. Poland is four points below its own long-term average, Spain 2.5, Portugal 2.3, and Belgium 2.2 points. Economists link part of this reduction in Poland and Romania to strong economic growth and convergence toward the European average.

Between 2015 and 2025, Poland’s GDP per capita adjusted for purchasing power rose from 70 to 81 percent of the EU average, while Romania’s rose from 56 to 78 percent of the European average. Rising minimum wages, the expansion of social programmes, and European Union funds also played an important role.

inequality in hungary and in some nordic nations

The opposite trend is visible in neighbouring Hungary. There, the Gini coefficient in 2025 was 29.5, which is 1.9 points higher than the country’s average over the previous 15 years. Sweden is 1.6 points above its long-term average, and Finland is 1.3 points higher. Denmark also recorded slightly higher inequality than in previous years. This shows that historically even income distributions are not guaranteed and can shift depending on the labour market, unemployment, tax policy, and economic structure.

World.title: Over 80% of Americans Say They Would Visit Croatia After Malkovich Film
World.content:
November the 24th, 2026 – Over 80% of Americans state that they would visit Croatia after watching the hit John Malkovich film.

The first day of the Croatian Tourism Days in Poreč was marked by rain and an awards ceremony, while on Friday the sun shone over the city and the sea in front of Pical. Marina Knezevic-Petkovic reports for Slobodna Dalmacija that the day before at the famed Pical Resort, discussions focused on the competitiveness of European tourism and what reforms and investments mean for the people working in the tourism sector.

The Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ) programme opened with the now very well known six-minute film CROATIA – I hear it’s beautiful. In it, the one and only John Malkovich receives a call from his agent telling him they have discovered where his ancestors are from. When he hears it is Croatia, he responds roughly the way someone who knows just enough about it to be intrigued would: he has heard it is beautiful.

malkovich’s appearance wins over swathes of americans

Dalibor Šumiga, an expert in neuromarketing and consumer psychology and founder of the Promosapiens agency, spoke about what happens after audiences watch those six minutes. How much is a famous face worth in a tourism campaign? And how much of Croatia actually needs to fit into a single film to make someone want to visit? Šumiga discussed how story and emotion can capture an audience’s attention even when a film does not try to cover every landmark that could possibly fit into the frame.

According to the results of an American market study he presented in Poreč, more than 80 percent of respondents said they would visit Croatia after watching the film. During the presentation, this result was described as a 20 percent increase compared to the travel intent expressed before watching. More than 88 percent of respondents rated the film with John Malkovich as standing out from other promotional materials.

how did john malkovich end up promoting croatia?

The journey from the initial idea to filming was shared by Pete Radovich, an American television and sports producer of Croatian roots and the film’s creative director. The winner of 45 Emmys across 18 categories spoke about his own connection to Croatia, why he took on the project, and what it was like working with Malkovich. The talk also covered how the actor reacted to the film and opened up the question of where the story might go next. At the end, behind-the-scenes footage was shown, giving a glimpse into what work on set looked like.

HTZ Director Kristjan Staničić recalled that Croatia has already brought together famous names in previous campaigns, from Luka Modrić and 2Cellos to Zrinka Cvitešić and Maksim Mrvica. Regarding the campaign with Malkovich, he highlighted its multi-million reach and the City Nation Place Award, which HTZ won in London for the best promotional strategy in tourism. Viewership results to date and a selection of domestic and foreign media coverage were also presented in Poreč. Minister of Tourism and Sport Tonči Glavina emphasized that through such campaigns, Croatia aims to build recognition in international markets even after the initial wave of attention surrounding the film passes.

World.title: Maarja Vaino: Mental complacency can be hidden between the rows of an Excel spreadsheet
World.content:
Cultural policy in Estonia is poorly thought out and seems focused primarily on counting money. Increasingly, it feels as though we are being nudged toward fanaticism and servitude, Maarja Vaino writes.

The Estonian Education Grand Forum was recently held, and this weekend the cultural congress Kultuuritahe will take place under the message: "The best defense is culture." What is happening in both education and culture is a matter of national importance, and there can be no doubt about that. The foundation of the Estonian state was the will to pursue education, to paraphrase the title of Juhani Salokannel's biography of Jaan Kross. We were able to achieve our own state only through, and as a result of, a commitment to education and culture.

Between these two important events came the news that Theatrum had once again been denied state funding. This fits neatly into the broader context. Large, attention-grabbing events are needed precisely to signal that things are not going well in education and culture. More accurately, in the way decisions about them are made. The Theatrum case is symbolic in many ways.

Theatrum is not merely a theater but a phenomenon that engages deeply and broadly with the spiritual dimension of being human. It does so primarily through great literature and literary classics, which in itself gives the theater a special position in culture. No other theater has made such systematic use of works with profound philosophical depth while masterfully connecting them to the present day. And it does so not through day-to-day politics or fashionable topics, but through the human inner world, which changes very little and is what connects different eras.

We have no other theater devoted to this kind of spirituality and consistent exploration. In a small cultural space, it is precisely this kind of theater that keeps alive the deep currents of Estonian and world culture, which otherwise risk being buried beneath noise seeking quick effects. Preserving Theatrum means preserving the spiritual balance of our own deeper culture.

"Too often, mediocrity and mutual back-patting are readily accepted."

Yet it seems that this is precisely what the state neither wants nor knows how to preserve. If the criticism is that the theater offers nothing innovative or that its artistic quality is uneven, those words sound like a classic case of searching for a justification. More likely, Theatrum is unwelcome because its spiritual demands and different value system make it seem too — what is the opposite of innovation again? — old-fashioned.

Fear of appearing old-fashioned, combined with a tendency to confuse the strength of tradition with being left behind by the times, unfortunately characterizes both our education and cultural policies. Hence the constant scrambling under the banner of innovation.

The education provided in Estonian schools, previously regarded as among the best in the world, could continue to hold that status through the strength of that same tradition, with only smaller necessary adjustments to make life easier for teachers and students. Instead, tradition has been broken, valuable things have been discarded, and school life has been thrown into disarray. Throughout all these reforms, what should be the main concern has long been forgotten: the content of education and the aforementioned intellectual rigor. We should seek more of that in culture as well. Too often, mediocrity and mutual back-patting are readily accepted.

Theatrum has undoubtedly been one of the reminders of these problems and one of the standard-bearers of spirituality, both through its educational work and its artistic repertoire, as well as through its broader presence in our cultural landscape.

What becomes of a nation and a state where mental complacency can be hidden between the rows of an Excel spreadsheet? One somewhat harsh but nonetheless truthful line of thought goes like this: the person who does not want to think is a fanatic; the person who does not dare to think is a slave.

We speak a great deal about freedom and independence, yet neither can endure without the courage to engage with the deeper content of education and culture and to treat them as true national treasures and guarantees of our identity.

Current education policy works directly against this. Cultural policy, meanwhile, is poorly thought out and seems focused primarily on counting money. Increasingly, it feels as though we are being nudged toward fanaticism and servitude.

World.title: Defense minister in parliament: Ukraine not using Estonian airspace to attack Russia
World.content:
Defense Minister Martin Herem said in Riigikogu that Ukrainian drones are not using Estonian airspace to attack Russia and that Ukraine has never asked Estonia for permission to do so.

Herem explained that Ukrainian drones have entered Estonian airspace because of technical issues or as a result of Russian electronic countermeasures.

Unaffiliated MP Varro Vooglaid stated as fact that Ukrainians are using Estonian airspace for drone attacks against Russia and expressed the view that Russia could eventually respond forcefully.

"If one state allows its airspace or other territory to be used to attack another state, thereby enabling such attacks, it is regarded as a participant in that military attack," Vooglaid said.

"What has the government actually done, or what does it intend to do, to draw a line against the use of our airspace for carrying out such attacks?" Vooglaid asked.

Herem replied that Estonia has not made its airspace available to Ukraine.

"Moreover, Ukraine has never asked for it. Secondly, we have told Ukraine to avoid using our airspace," Herem said.

"You are presenting your hypothesis as a fact. You claim that we have granted access — we have not. Out of the hundreds and thousands of drones Ukraine launches against targets in Russia, only a few have strayed into our airspace or that of our allies. That in no way proves that we permit it. Otherwise, considering the number of drones and the time they spend in the air, one would also have to accuse Russia of allowing it all to happen, because far more of them fly there for much longer periods. As for sensors and air defense systems, Russia does not always detect them and cannot shoot all of them down either. Therefore, the occasional overflight cannot be used to claim that we have made our airspace available," Herem said.

Varro Vooglaid. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

"I never claimed that"

Vooglaid then said that he had never claimed Estonia had authorized the use of its airspace for Ukrainian military attacks.

"I never claimed that we had authorized it. You attributed that claim to me yourself. The question is not whether we granted permission or not, although I also suspect that perhaps permission has been given, but I cannot claim that because I do not have such information. The fact remains that our airspace is being used to carry out these attacks. There can be no dispute about that. This was not a one-time incident, nor a second or third incident. It has happened many times already. I don't even know how many times anymore. Our airspace has repeatedly been used for carrying out these attacks," Vooglaid said.

Vooglaid asked again whether telling Ukraine not to use Estonian airspace was the only thing the government had done to stop "the use of Estonian airspace for this kind of warfare."

"They shrug their shoulders and use it again and again and again. What happens next? Do you simply tell them once more that they may not use our airspace for warfare, or are there additional measures? Some actual expression of protest, summoning the Ukrainian ambassador, issuing an ultimatum, or military measures to prevent Ukrainian war drones from flying through our airspace?"

"And if you say the problem is limited sensor and air defense capabilities, then I would ask why we are investing money in national defense at all if we cannot stop drones. If drones were to come from Russia toward Estonia, would our capability then be any greater, or just as inadequate as it is now?" Vooglaid added.

Drone threat alert for the morning of Saturday, November 21, 2026. Source: EE-ALARM

"Individual drones enter Estonian airspace for technical reasons"

In his response, Herem again stated that Ukraine is not using Estonian airspace.

"These drones enter our airspace for technical reasons, human reasons, countermeasure-related reasons or weather-related reasons. That does not mean anyone is deliberately using it. How do we know that? We simply observe the trajectories of these aircraft. They fly mainly through Russian airspace, while only a few enter ours," Herem said.

"If you say Ukrainians are using it and we are doing nothing about it, then once again look at what is happening in Russia. Many more drones fly there unhindered and without being stopped. We cannot somehow blame ourselves for the fact that these aircraft occasionally end up here. We have discussed this with the Ukrainians. They maintain that the few drones that enter our airspace out of thousands do so unintentionally," Herem said.

"Why do we invest in defense at all? To be better prepared against threats like these. If we knew such investments would have absolutely no effect should drones start coming from Russia, then there truly would be no point in making them," Herem added.

MP Varro Vooglaid has repeatedly argued on social media that Ukraine uses Estonian airspace for drone attacks against targets in Russia and that Estonia has enabled Ukraine to do so.

World.title: Narva Mayor to Minister: Are border residents being sacrificed for security?
World.content:
Narva Mayor Jaan Toots (Center) said closing the Russian border punishes Estonia's own people, while Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eest 200) said the threat from Russia warranted the move.

Last Friday, the government decided to close the road border crossings between Estonia and Russia, in response to the mid-November attack on defense company Threod.

Speaking to "Otse uudistemajast" Wednesday, Toots said he took no issue with the government's security decisions but opposed closing the border to Estonia's own residents. He said many people in Narva and southeastern Estonia have relatives and family members living on the other side of the frontier, adding the government could make an exception for them, given they are Estonian citizens and residents. "We certainly don't see any danger in letting them cross. It would be very strange to see our own people as a source of danger," Toots said.

"Our own Estonian citizens simply want to visit their relatives. I don't see any danger in that. And if people say there's a danger on the other side, that danger is the same if they go through Latvia. We're making life difficult for our own people by not keeping that route open for them," Toots went on.

Taro response was that Russia carries out intelligence operations targeting Estonians at border crossings and that its security services have been attempting to recruit many of them. Toots said people living near the border are aware of the risks, and many leave their phones in Estonia when they cross for that reason.

Toots said Latvia's border with Russia would remain open and that Estonia should therefore introduce temporary checks at its border with Latvia – some of those involved in the Threod incident reported earlier this month had crossed from that border and not from Russia.

Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs criticized Estonia's decision on Wednesday, saying it had been made in haste.

Jaan Toots (left) and Igor Taro on Wednesday's edition of "Otse uudistemajast". Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Taro responded that Latvia could always follow Estonia's lead and close its own border crossings with Russia. "I think we share the same security space, and they'll have to consider whether to leave an opening that could let all sorts of things through or take a different course," the minister said.

"I don't deny that this decision affects people, but Russia's aggression affects a great many people in very different ways. Some people are killed, some lose loved ones, and some are inconvenienced because they can't visit their loved ones for a while. That's how it is," Taro said.

"This is a result of Russia's military actions. The Estonian government isn't trying to give its own people a hard time or make their lives more difficult," he went on.

"As for visiting family members, that is an unfortunate consequence, and I understand how painful it is for these people. I'm from a region where cross-border ties are very close, too. But this is a consequence of Russia's war and its hostile actions against Ukraine, Estonia and other European countries," Taro added.

Toots said he believes Latvia and Lithuania will keep their borders with Russia open, however, and that Estonia may very well suffer economically as a result. "What happens if Russia shuts down rail traffic in retaliation? There are rumors to that effect. The rare earths plant in Sillamäe would immediately grind to a halt. It supplies raw materials to the magnet factory in Narva, where 380 people work, but that would shut down too. So this is a very grave matter," Toots said.

Taro stressed that the government must consider the security of all in Estonia, including people with family members on the other side of the border. He added that the border with Russia would have been closed long ago had the government given no thought to those people, and attack on Threod's drone factory was the last straw, he said.

"The interior minister's duty is to make decisions based on security considerations. Sometimes that means making difficult and painful decisions. That is the responsibility that comes along with the job," Taro said.

Jaan Toots, Igor Taro and show host Merilin Leetna on Wednesday's "Otse uudistemajast". Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Taro noted the government is discussing measures to improve the economic situation in border regions. "We're discussing measures to help businesses adapt to the situation, find new workers and retrain them. We know Narva and Setomaa municipality may lose some revenue. That also has a wider impact on people who may never cross the border but rely on municipal services. In the coming weeks, the government will discuss measures to help municipalities and businesses deal with these effects."

Both Toots and Taro linked each other's conduct and rhetoric to the upcoming Riigikogu elections in March. Taro asked Toots whether the elections were also the reason he did not consider Estonia's security important.

On being asked whether closing the border would lead to fewer attacks on Estonian defense industry sites, Taro said the government had reduced certain risks.

"The risks that came from keeping border traffic open or partially open will go away. That means our domestic security services can focus more on other areas. They won't have to devote as much counterintelligence work to monitoring who crosses the road border between Estonia and Russia," Taro continued.

At the close of the show, Toots reiterated his call for the government to make an exception allowing residents of border regions to cross. "Our people are writing to Santa now, hoping the government might give them a way to cross the border by Christmas. That's our request to the government," Toots said.

"Some children are writing to Santa asking that a drone not fall on their heads at Christmas or New Year's. The effects vary greatly, and a great many people are affected," Taro responded.

World.title: Estonia opens €110M hybrid solar-battery park to stabilize Baltic power grid
World.content:
The Kirikmäe facility stores cheap midday solar electricity and feeds it back during peak demand, providing critical frequency reserves to stabilize Estonia's electricity grid.

Estonia has needed to maintain its own frequency reserves since disconnecting from Russia's power grid in February 2025 to synchronize with the Continental European network.

The hybrid park combines the existing Kirikmäe solar farm — which was Estonia's largest when completed in October 2024 — with a newly built 55-megawatt battery storage system, forming a single integrated power asset.

"The more solar and wind power we have in the electricity system, the more flexibility we need to keep generation and consumption in balance. A solar farm generates electricity when the sun shines, which isn't necessarily when demand and market prices are highest," said Evecon CEO Karl-Joonatan Kvell.

The new Kirikmäe hybrid energy park near Lihula. Source: Verner Vilgas/ERR

"Battery storage is essential to making solar power more controllable. The battery stores energy during hours when prices are lower and feeds it back into the grid when demand is higher. Because it can respond quickly, the battery also provides frequency reserves that help keep the power grid stable," Kvell explained.

Mirova and Evecon developed the site through their joint venture, Baltic Renewable Energy Platform (BREP), backed by a nearly €85 million financing package from Swedbank. BREP also signed a 10-year flexibility and power purchase agreement with German firm Pure Energy — the first of its kind in the Baltic states — covering the battery alongside the Kirikmäe, Imavere and Lohu Metsa solar farms.

Main contractor WiSo Engineering built the battery facility after starting construction in January 2026.

"The battery storage system is technically ready, and the final grid and market tests are nearing completion. In a couple of years, we have helped complete nearly 700 MWh of battery storage capacity, including the Sipa battery park. Almost half of that capacity came from adding battery storage to existing solar farms," said WiSo Engineering CEO Risto Virveste.

Estonia has rapidly expanded grid-scale battery storage since disconnecting from Russia's BRELL grid and synchronizing with Continental Europe in February 2025. Earlier in 2026, Evecon, Mirova, and Corsica Sole opened the 200-megawatt, 400-megawatt-hour Hertz 1 and Hertz 2 battery parks in Harju County, continental Europe's largest such complex. These facilities compete on the Baltic frequency reserve market, helping curb balancing price swings as renewable generation grows.

World.title: Argo Ideon: In a troubled world borders are crossed in strange ways
World.content:
In a normal world, state borders are like the dividing line between Valga and Valka on the Estonia-Latvia border, where you can swing across from the Konnaoja bridge. There is nothing like that on the Estonia-Russia border, nor will there be, writes Argo Ideon.

Ivalo is a settlement of a few thousand residents in northern Finland, in Inari Municipality in Lapland. About ten kilometers away is an airport that is described as the northernmost in the European Union.

When Estonia's three land border crossings with Russia close on December 1, snowy Ivalo may become a transit point for more than a few travelers who, despite everything, are still trying to reach Russia.

Everything has already been calculated in social media groups. There are three flights a day from Helsinki to Ivalo, and on some days even more. The flight takes around two hours. Someone taking an early-morning flight can reach the Norway-Russia border at Storskog by minibus around 1 p.m. and be in Murmansk by 6 p.m., from where flights depart for St. Petersburg and Moscow.

Another route runs through Kaliningrad Oblast. Transfers from Riga through Lithuania are advertised for €90, for example, and from Kaliningrad there are both flights and transit trains into Russian mainland. One  promises to take a passenger from the Port of Tallinn to the Lithuania-Russia border for just €390, with a travel time of seven hours and a distance of 620 kilometers.

A third option remains the Latvia-Russia border, which is still open.

Of course, all of this is far more inconvenient and expensive for an Estonian resident than spending a few hours in line at the Narva border crossing. Yet for those who absolutely need to visit Russia, there appears to be no shortage of alternatives. There is not even any need to go through Istanbul, which is another option.

People's circumstances vary greatly, which is why I do not want to lecture anyone that there is no reason at all to travel to Russia right now.

"In fact, I came to the realization several years ago that I will never visit Russia again in my lifetime."

I would not go myself, even if all border crossings were open and the line at Narva was nonexistent, because Russia does not currently seem like a place that is either pleasant or safe to visit. Estonia's Foreign Ministry advises against travel to Russia, and that should really be sufficient. And for anyone who does not regard Estonian state institutions as enough of an authority, they can read the travel advice issued by the United Kingdom's Foreign Office, which says much the same thing.

In fact, I came to the realization several years ago that I will never visit Russia again in my lifetime. Is that disappointing to some extent? Perhaps mostly because I never properly explored the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg. I visited once on a school trip and barely remember any of it.

Some nostalgic memories of visiting Russia remain. In 1989, a classmate and I traveled there three times. In February, Yngwie J. Malmsteen's Rising Force performed in Leningrad at the Lenin Sports and Concert Complex. In June of the same year, Pink Floyd performed in Moscow at the Olimpiyskiy sports complex. Then in December, the road led once again to Leningrad, which was not renamed St. Petersburg until 1991, to see and hear Black Sabbath.

But the world was very different back then. No Estonia-Russia border existed in the sense of border controls. You could easily travel to Leningrad by train. At the same time, visiting Finland was an unattainable dream for many people. The Soviet system did not envision people simply traveling to Finland. You needed approval from your workplace or school and an exit visa. Finland itself required an entry visa, which could be obtained only after waiting in line at an apartment building stairwell in Mustamäe, where the consulate was located.

For an ordinary tourist to be willing and able to visit Russia in the future, conditions on the other side of the border would have to change considerably. There is no reason to believe that will happen in the next few years. One can always rewatch Oleg Kuvaev's animated series Masyanya, specifically Episode 165, "Masyanya 2050," where St. Petersburg and the surrounding region have become the independent state of Ingria, which has belonged to NATO for years. It is entertaining viewing, but it belongs in the realm of fantasy.

In a normal world, state borders are like the dividing line between Valga and Valka on the Estonia-Latvia border, where you can simply swing across from the Konnaoja bridge. Europe has many borders like that and I think it is worth being happy that the part of the world that matters most to us is still like that.

There is nothing comparable on the Estonia-Russia border, nor will there be.

Yet it will not remain completely closed forever either. Even the Hundred Years' War eventually came to an end.

World.title: Slippery road warning issued across Estonia until Thursday afternoon
World.content:
There is a risk of slippery roads across the country throughout Wednesday and Thursday and temperatures are set to dip below 0 degrees (C), the Environment Agency has said.

The agency issued a level one "yellow" warning for glazed ice in every county until 2 p.m. on Thursday.

"Nov 25 by day and Nov 26 at night remains air temperature near 0°C and will be sleet, snow and rain showers. Risk of slippery roads," the warning says.

A level one warning defines the weather condition as "potentially dangerous."

"Be attentive if you intend to practice activities exposed to meteorological risks. Keep informed about the forecast of meteorological conditions," the agency advises.

A level one alert for slippery roads is in place across Estonia until November 26, 2026. Source: Estonian Environment Agency

World.title: Andres Jõesaar: Estonia's media landscape one of strong journalism and fractured trust
World.content:
The 2026 Media Survey highlights tensions in Estonia's information space. Professional journalism reaches the vast majority of Estonia's population, with Estonian Public Broadcasting (ERR) playing a central role. At the same time, people's perceptions of media credibility vary significantly depending on the language spoken at home and their political preferences. These differences are most pronounced in how Estonian- and Russian-speaking residents assess coverage of the war in Ukraine.

The survey points to a central challenge for Estonia's media policy: How can we maintain strong and diverse professional journalism while also reaching those who have drifted away from the shared information space?

Professional journalism reaches most people in Estonia

Two opposing claims are often made about Estonia's media landscape. On the one hand, traditional news outlets are said to be losing an increasing share of their audiences to social media. On the other, questions are raised about whether Estonia's small market has room for several strong news organizations. The 2026 media survey, conducted by Turu-uuringute AS and commissioned by the Ministry of Culture, helps shed light on both debates.

According to the survey, 71.8 percent of Estonian residents aged 15 and older follow the news through at least one ERR channel at least once a week. Some 55.9 percent do so through Delfi's Estonian- or Russian-language outlets, while 43.9 percent use Postimees' corresponding outlets. Some 62.4 percent of respondents get their news from social media at least once a week, while 8.4 percent follow Russian media channels with the same frequency.

Some 82.3 percent of the population, or approximately 952,000 people, turn to at least one of Estonia's three largest media organizations — ERR, Delfi or Postimees — for news at least once a week. Among those who follow Postimees for news on a weekly basis, 83.9 percent also use ERR channels at least once a week. The corresponding figure for Delfi's audience is 83.3 percent.

Some 17.7 percent, or around 204,000 people, do not follow any of the three at least once a week. Approximately half of them follow the news through other media outlets, but a significant proportion have become disengaged from the media.

Four different attitude groups in place of a single audience

While overall figures on media consumption provide an overview of the reach of Estonia's information space, they do not reveal significant differences in people's media habits and attitudes. These can be better understood through cluster analysis, which groups people with similar behavioral patterns and attitudes.

The analysis identified four clusters of media users. The largest group, accounting for 51.6 percent of the population, comprises those who trust Estonia's professional media. People in this group rate ERR's credibility highly, consider professional journalism important to democracy and distrust Russian media. Approximately 84 percent of this group speak Estonian at home.

The second cluster comprises people with relatively little exposure to the media who are uncertain in their assessments (21 percent). Negative attitudes toward journalism are not necessarily the defining factor for these individuals. This group is also characterized by a frequent reluctance to make definitive assessments of media outlets. Just over half of the group speak Russian at home.

The third cluster comprises people with varied media consumption habits and moderate levels of trust (20.4 percent). They consume a diverse range of media and follow Russian media and alternative information channels more than those in the first group. Their trust in ERR and private media is moderate. Approximately half of this group also speak Russian at home.

The smallest but socially significant cluster comprises skeptics who have become disengaged from the media (7.0 percent). Their trust in ERR and Estonia's private media is very low and they question professional journalism's contribution to democracy. Approximately three-quarters of this group speak Russian at home. This does not, however, mean that the Russian-speaking population as a whole falls into the skeptic category: People who speak Russian at home are represented in all four groups.

The four clusters demonstrate that Estonia's media landscape cannot be characterized in terms of a single average media user. How should we assess this situation? Is the glass half full or half empty? The data suggest both. Half of Estonia's population actively follows and trusts Estonia's professional media, while the other half of the audience is more doubtful, has limited exposure to Estonia's information space and is consequently less informed about what is actually happening in Estonia.

Trust gap clearest in Ukraine war coverage

Across the population as a whole, ERR is Estonia's most trusted media organization, with 77 percent of respondents considering it trustworthy. The corresponding figures for Postimees and Delfi are 59 percent and 57 percent, respectively. However, these overall figures mask substantial differences between Estonian- and Russian-speaking residents.

Among respondents who speak Estonian at home, 89 percent trust ERR, compared with 53 percent of those who speak Russian at home. The corresponding figures are 70 percent and 38 percent for Postimees and 66 percent and 39 percent for Delfi. The gap is considerable, but it is equally important to note that respondents who speak Russian at home do not automatically place their trust in Russian media outlets: 22 percent consider them generally trustworthy, while 40 percent distrust Russian media.

The differences in perceptions become even more pronounced in responses to the question: "How trustworthy do you consider the following media outlets to be in their coverage of the Russia-Ukraine war?"

While trust in Estonian media outlets remains strong on this issue among respondents who speak Estonian at home, those who speak Russian at home have considerably lower levels of trust in all media outlets — Estonian, Western and Russian alike. A large proportion of people who speak Russian at home do not trust any media outlet's coverage of the war in Ukraine.

Is political bias in the media or the way it's perceived?

Trust in the media is also linked to respondents' political preferences. The survey asked respondents to assess how ERR, Postimees and Delfi cover the activities of political parties registered in Estonia. The results do not directly measure actual media bias, but rather how people perceive coverage of political parties.

An analysis of the responses reveals a reciprocal asymmetry: Supporters of both the governing coalition and the opposition tend to perceive coverage of their political opponents as more favorable than coverage of their own political camp. For example, coalition supporters considered Postimees' coverage of the opposition to be markedly more favorable than its coverage of the coalition. Among opposition supporters, the reverse pattern emerged in the case of both ERR and Delfi.

What sets ERR apart in this comparison is the higher proportion of respondents who consider its coverage neutral. Among coalition supporters, 47.4 percent considered ERR's coverage of the coalition neutral, compared with 25.9 percent for Postimees and 32.1 percent for Delfi. Among opposition supporters, 31.6 percent considered ERR's coverage of the coalition neutral, compared with 22.2 percent for both Postimees and Delfi. ERR also had a higher proportion of respondents who considered its coverage of the opposition neutral.

Respondents consider ERR the most balanced media organization in its coverage of political parties' activities.

At the same time, high ratings for balanced coverage do not mean that ERR's work is beyond criticism or that all segments of society consider its coverage equally trustworthy. The existence of linguistic and political differences demonstrates how difficult it is to achieve a widely shared perception of journalistic impartiality across society.

The influence of political attitudes is also borne out by differences in overall trust in media outlets among supporters of different parties. Supporters of some parties are more distrustful of Estonia's professional journalism and consider social media more trustworthy than other groups do. However, percentages for supporters of smaller parties should be interpreted with caution: These subgroups contain few respondents and individual assessments have a considerable impact on the results.

Analyzing assessments of the overall trustworthiness of media outlets according to respondents' party preferences reveals the following picture.

It is important to note that not using a media outlet does not preclude assessing its political bias. The survey also included assessments from people who do not follow the outlet in question at least once a week. Their opinions may have been shaped by past experiences, other people's views or the public image of media organizations. The issue, therefore, is not just what the media publish, but also how perceptions of journalism take shape in society.

Audience views of ERR activities

Although international research confirms the important role public service media play in supporting the development of democratic societies, it is entirely legitimate to ask whether this also holds true for Estonian Public Broadcasting.

High levels of news consumption and trust alone do not fully answer the question of whether public service media are meeting society's expectations. To answer this, we must also examine how people assess the content, quality and importance of ERR's work.

Some 80.0 percent of respondents consider ERR very or fairly important to Estonian society as a whole. The corresponding figure for Estonian-language private media is 71.4 percent and for Russian-language private media 44.4 percent. The latter difference cannot be interpreted solely as an assessment of media quality: An outlet's language focus inevitably influences how important the population as a whole considers it to be.

Particularly highly rated aspects of ERR's work included showcasing achievements in Estonian cultural life (72.2 percent), giving a voice to people from different walks of life (62.3 percent) and covering developments across Estonia's regions (61.7 percent). Survey participants also positively assessed ERR's role in supporting the development of democracy (59.5 percent) and critically examining developments in society (51.8 percent). In its coverage of important societal issues, thoroughness (62.9 percent), expertise (60.1 percent) and diversity of viewpoints (55.7 percent) received higher ratings.

Differences between language groups must also be taken into account when assessing the extent to which ERR's channels help people understand Estonian society. Among people who speak Estonian at home, 87.4 percent consider the information provided by ERR's Estonian-language channels useful in this regard, compared with 38.3 percent of respondents who speak Russian at home. At the same time, 46.6 percent of respondents who speak Russian at home consider the information provided by ERR's Russian-language channels useful. This demonstrates that public service media's ability to create a shared information space also depends on whether the content they offer is accessible and meaningful to different segments of the population, both in terms of language and substance.

What does all of it mean for Estonia's media policy?

Debates about the funding and role of culture in Estonia intersect with several of the tensions described by Nico Carpentier and Jeffrey Wimmer in the relationship between media and democracy. One such tension arises from competing interests in the regulation of media and, more broadly, culture.

In Estonia's media landscape, this tension manifests itself primarily, though not exclusively, in the search for a balance between the commercial interests of private media and the scope of Estonian Public Broadcasting's activities. Research shows that free media in general and public service media in particular play an important role in the functioning of democratic societies. Claims that public service media undermines the operations of private media have not been substantiated by research.

The purpose of public service media is to serve the public interest, including by informing the population and creating a shared information space (public sphere) — a platform for discussion and the exchange of ideas. Serving the public interest is defined in the Estonian Public Broadcasting Act through ERR's objectives and responsibilities. Does what lawmakers stipulated two decades ago still meet society's needs today?

To answer this question, numerous meetings have been held with representatives of various interest groups and experts over the past four years. The feedback revealed two very clear and opposing demands — expansion versus reduction.

A wide range of stakeholders, communities and institutions want ERR to expand its role, including the volume of content it produces and distributes. They want more stories from different parts of Estonia and the world — more correspondents and a greater permanent presence, including in local municipalities; more commissions for domestically produced television series and films (independent production companies); more coverage of various events (celebrations, award ceremonies and the like); coverage of a wider range of sports (sports enthusiasts and associations); more broadcasts and recordings of theater performances and concerts; more children's programming; greater attention to children and young people; more programs catering to niche audiences; greater use of works by Estonian creators (composers, writers and others) and more commissions for original works; more coverage and in-depth analysis of developments in various cultural fields (art, literature, design, architecture, fashion, subcultures and so on); more high-quality entertainment; more discussions about the problems we face in our lives; better accessibility of media content, including more programming with audio descriptions for visually impaired audiences, better-quality captions for hearing-impaired audiences and sign language interpretation for current affairs and children's programs; more programming in different dialects and languages; more boldness and experimentation; more innovation; greater experimentation with new technologies and platforms; the development and deployment of new apps; greater public access to archives (and, in doing so, adequate remuneration for the creators of the works); more educational media content supporting the full spectrum of lifelong learning; more popularization of science...

The list is far from exhaustive. Does the current Estonian Public Broadcasting Act prohibit fulfilling these wishes? The answer is no. All these expectations are consistent with ERR's statutory objectives and responsibilities. If anything, one could argue that the law requires ERR to fulfill them. The extent to which these wishes can be met is determined by editorial choices, which in turn are constrained primarily by financial resources. ERR already does much of this to some extent in its day-to-day operations and, as demonstrated by the survey results, audiences are fairly satisfied with its work.

Opposing the "expansion" of ERR is a firm demand from representatives of private media to significantly restrict ERR's activities. Above all, they want ERR to stop publishing original written content online — its websites should carry only news and content reflecting what has already aired on radio and television — and to stop producing entertainment. The reasoning behind this is the assumption that ERR's activities weaken the financial performance of private media and, consequently, Estonia's entire information space.

There were also calls for ERR's responsibilities to be defined in greater detail. To illustrate this issue, I will describe the two extremes of the spectrum. At one end, public service responsibilities are defined very broadly — public service media must inform, educate and entertain. At the opposite end are specific responsibilities rigidly prescribed for an extended period (for example, requiring children's programming to be broadcast on Tuesdays). Regulations governing European public service broadcasters predominantly define their responsibilities in similarly broad terms to those used in Estonian law.

Both camps' hopes hinge on the legislature

The biggest problem facing Estonia's information space is not a lack of people who follow professional journalism. News from at least one of Estonia's three largest media organizations reaches more than four-fifths of the population every week. The more serious challenge is how to reach people who encounter news but do not trust its sources and how to engage those whose connection to professional journalism is weak.

Addressing this challenge requires high-quality journalism that is accessible in different languages and across different platforms and that can resonate with diverse groups in society. This includes those who feel left out and whose voices go unheard in public debate. Bridging this divide should be one of the central tasks of media policy and journalism in the years ahead.

This article is based on the "2026 Media Survey," commissioned by the Ministry of Culture and conducted by Turu-uuringute AS. The survey was conducted from September 21 to October 2, 2026. There were 1,010 respondents, of whom 882 participated in an online survey and 128 in telephone interviews. The survey covered Estonian residents aged 15 and older.

World.title: Estonia drafts prisoner of war regulations
World.content:
Regulations governing the conditions and procedures for the detention of prisoners of war in Estonia have been drawn up by the government and the Ministry of Defense and sent for consultation. Minister of Defense Martin Herem said this is a natural development.

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Estonia has boosted its eastern border security, defense spending, crisis preparedness, and legislation in preparation for a potential future conflict.

The draft regulation governs procedures for detained prisoners of war, including the principles of short- and long-term detention, the duties of institutions involved in detention, and inter-agency cooperation.

However, it does not outline arrangements for the transfer and exchange of prisoners of war between countries.

The Prison Service and the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) are responsible for organizing prisoner detentions, it states.

The draft specifies that the short- and long-term detention and treatment of prisoners of war must comply with the principles laid down in the Geneva Convention relative to the Treatment of Prisoners of War of August 12, 1949.

"Prisoners of war must be treated humanely throughout their detention and must not be discriminated against on the grounds of race, nationality, gender, religious beliefs, political views or other such characteristics. Humane detention conditions must be guaranteed for prisoners of war at every place of detention," it reads.

Under the draft, prisoners of war have the right to submit requests and complaints concerning detention conditions to the competent authority responsible for organizing their detention.

The legislation also sets out requirements and responsibilities for both the short- and long-term detention of prisoners of war.

Defense minister: We must be prepared

Minister of Defense Martin Herem. Autor/allikas: Siim Lõvi / ERR

Minister of Defense Martin Herem told ERR that the issue of prisoners of war has been dealt with for two years already.

"While until now this was regulated primarily within the Defense Forces, starting with how prisoners are captured, how they become prisoners and how they are transported to rear areas, keeping them somewhere for an extended period required a division of responsibilities within the state. That means dividing responsibilities with the Ministry of Justice and detention institutions, assigning them tasks and regulating their obligations. We have also drawn on and learned from Ukraine's experience," said Herem, who is the former commander of the Estonian Defense Forces.

He said there is nothing extraordinary about preparing such a draft regulation and that it is simply a natural development.

"We are developing our national defense step by step and addressing increasingly detailed issues. Should we find ourselves in a military conflict, there will undoubtedly be prisoners of war, and we must be prepared for that," Herem said.

Earlier this year, the Dutch armed forces tested a new new prisoner-of-war camp design capable of of holding up to 2,000 captured Russian soldiers in the event of a large-scale conflict, Dutch media reported in June.
