“CMFR has closed, but the mission continues with you, present and future journalists,” she said. “I can only hope our efforts have seeded the ground with principles and ideas that will help journalists build a stronger democracy for the people, in a kinder season, in a brighter future.” /cb

World.title: Economist takes issue with Cayetano’s debt payment proposal
World.content:
Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano —Screengrab from Senate of the Philippines/YouTube

MANILA, Philippines — Filipinos do not need to be asked to pay an additional P170,000 each to help settle the national debt because they are already shouldering its cost through taxes and deteriorating public services, an economist said on Wednesday.

Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, meanwhile, took exception to Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano’s sweeping characterization of public servants as thieves, saying honest officials should not be lumped together with corrupt ones.

Rosario Guzman, head researcher of the think tank Ibon Foundation, said Cayetano was treating the estimated per-capita debt as a personal bill for every Filipino, overlooking how ordinary people, particularly the poor, already shoulder the government’s financial obligations.

Article continues after this 

READ: Lacson to Cayetano: Don’t drag us into your sweeping corruption claims

The national debt is a government obligation that should be serviced through tax revenues, nontax government earnings or refinancing, not additional direct contributions from ordinary Filipinos, she said.

“The people, especially the poor majority, are already repaying the debt, which was not even incurred on their behalf in the first place,” Guzman said.

READ: Palace on Cayetano’s call for the generous to pay nat’l debt: You first

She pointed to consumption taxes, which account for more than one-third of government tax revenues and disproportionately burden poorer households, while tax reductions have benefited the wealthy, corporations and foreign capital.

Article continues after this 

Debt burden

Cayetano raised the idea of voluntary contributions during Senate deliberations on the proposed 2027 national budget on Monday, citing the P19.66-trillion national debt as of the third quarter and an estimated P170,598.03 share for each of the country’s 114.93 million people.

“[Because] I was going to ask, if every Filipino owes P170,000, where can I go if I wanna pay my share? If I wanna pay my share of the P170,000, how do I go about doing that?” he asked.

Article continues after this 

He wanted to know if a mechanism existed for citizens willing to contribute beyond paying taxes.

Senate finance committee chair JV Ejercito said none was in place, adding that paying the correct taxes was already the biggest contribution Filipinos could make.

Not a personal bill

Cayetano also suggested wealthy businesspeople could pay for themselves and their families, while overseas Filipino workers could make smaller contributions over time.

But Guzman said the per-capita figure should not be treated as a personal bill each Filipino must settle.

“Cayetano took the debt per capita indicator literally,” she told the Inquirer.

The better way to repay debt and prevent it from becoming unpayable, she said, is to strengthen the economy, “but only very few legislators are talking about this.”

Filipinos are already contributing heavily to government revenues, Guzman said.

More than one-third of tax collections come from consumption taxes, which disproportionately burden poorer households.

At the same time, tax breaks have reduced the burden on the wealthy, corporations and foreign capital, she said.

She also said people paid for government borrowing when it failed to translate into adequate social services.

Guzman cited dilapidated public schools, children holding classes under trees, shortages of textbooks, overworked teachers and overcrowded hospitals, where patients may wait as long as 24 hours for a stretcher.

“The people, especially the poor majority, are already repaying the debt, which was not even incurred on their behalf in the first place,” she said.

Not all thieves

Cayetano also warned that donors would be reluctant to give money if the government kept borrowing and funds were stolen.

“There is a deep sense of distrust toward the government. The prevailing sentiment is that we are all thieves—all of you, all of us—in the government are thieves, so no one wants to donate,” he said.

Lacson took issue with the sweeping characterization, warning Cayetano against dragging honest government workers into his description of widespread public distrust.

“I speak for myself and other public servants, elected or appointed, who don’t steal public funds or take bribes: HUWAG NAMAN SANA NIYA KAMI IDAMAY (Leave us out of this),” Lacson said in a post on X on Wednesday.

Cayetano’s office said the graphic circulating with the quote omitted context. The full statement, it said, described public distrust, not an accusation that all public servants were stealing.

“He was describing public distrust, not accusing all public servants of stealing. That distinction matters,” his office said, urging media organizations and social media pages to verify quotes and preserve context. /cb

World.title: Ex-DOE chief: Tap flood infra funds for Visayas power
World.content:
Leyte Gov. Carlos Jericho Petilla —Leyte Gulf Landings Commemoration Facebook

TACLOBAN CITY, LEYTE, Philippines — Leyte Gov. Carlos Jericho Petilla has urged the national government to consider redirecting part of its flood control budget to the energy sector, warning that the Visayas could face tighter electricity supply in the coming years as power reserves in Luzon and Mindanao dwindle.

Petilla, a former secretary of the Department of Energy (DOE) during the administration of the late President Benigno “Noynoy” Aquino III, said ensuring adequate and reliable electricity should be an immediate priority, particularly amid uncertainties in global energy markets due to the Middle East conflict and the looming effects of El Niño.

“The national government would say there is no budget for power, but there is money for flood control projects. Can we take a portion of the flood control budget because this is an immediate concern now?” Petilla said in an interview.

Article continues after this 

READ: Visayas Grid on red, yellow alert anew

His proposal comes amid the controversy surrounding billions of pesos in government flood control allocations, following allegations of ghost, substandard and overpriced projects, as well as questionable procurement practices and kickbacks involving contractors and public officials.

The issue has prompted calls for closer scrutiny of infrastructure spending.

During deliberations on the proposed 2027 national budget, Sen. Panfilo Lacson raised concerns over alleged duplicate appropriations for flood control projects and called for their removal.

READ: Bishop calls for accountability, RE shift amid Visayas power crisis

Article continues after this 

The Department of Public Works and Highways has proposed P107.4 billion for flood control works next year under its over P644 billion budget for 2027.

Shortfall

Petilla warned that the Visayas could no longer rely on electricity supplies from Luzon and Mindanao as both regions are projected to face their own power supply deficits.

Article continues after this 

“Next year, Mindanao will have a shortfall, so they will no longer export power to us. In 2028, Luzon will also have a shortfall, so they will no longer be able to sell power to us,” he said.

The situation could pose a challenge to Eastern Visayas, where almost all of the region’s 11 electric cooperatives obtain their power requirements from suppliers in Luzon and Mindanao.

The lack of available energy capacity has led the National Grid Corp. of the Philippines to issue red and yellow alerts in the Visayas, resulting in rotational brownouts. This situation has been going on for at least five months already.

Petilla said the country’s energy outlook was becoming increasingly uncertain, with geopolitical tensions in the Middle East potentially affecting fuel supplies and prices, while El Niño could add pressure to electricity generation and demand.

He acknowledged that addressing the country’s power requirements would entail substantial investments, with major energy projects costing billions of pesos.

Storage

One way to improve supply, Petilla said, is to rehabilitate aging power plants to restore their generating capacity and improve their efficiency. However, he noted that building new facilities or undertaking major rehabilitation works could take as long as five years before additional power becomes available.

As a more immediate intervention, Petilla proposed installing battery energy storage systems in existing power plants and charging them using solar energy. The stored electricity could then be dispatched during peak demand periods, particularly in the afternoon and evening when power interruptions frequently occur.

He estimated that the Visayas would need at least 600 battery units, each costing around P2.5 million, with a cited capacity of 50 megawatts and four hours of storage, although the technical configuration would depend on the units’ specifications.

Petilla said installing the proposed battery systems could take approximately 18 months.

The Visayas has more than 100 power plants, but some are already aging or experiencing operational problems, contributing to recurring power interruptions even before the onset of El Niño, he said.

“Even without El Niño, we will experience brownouts because the only reason we are managing to get by now is that some of the plants are operating, while others have gone offline,” Petilla said.

World.title: In Zamboanga Sur, ‘mountain teachers’ brave perilous trek
World.content:
DANGER LURKS In this photo taken last month, teachers and villagers risk injury as they negotiate a landslide-hit road and pathways scoured by heavy rains at Sitio Glab in the mountain village of Cogonan in Labangan, Zamboanga del Sur. The danger has become a normal part of the teachers’ lives as public servants. —Photo by Joel Arnejo/Contributor

PAGADIAN CITY, ZAMBOANGA DEL SUR, Philippines — At the start and end of every school week, teachers assigned to Glab Integrated School at Barangay Cogonan in Labangan, Zamboanga del Sur, brave a landslide-prone road just to reach their classrooms and back to the lowlands.

The journey is perilous. They have to walk narrow, crumbling paths along steep slopes where a single misstep could send them plunging downward.

Their ordeal drew renewed public attention after Gleen Rañoa, a teacher formerly assigned to the school, posted on social media a plea highlighting the hazardous road conditions and urging the Department of Education (DepEd), local governments and concerned agencies to intervene before a tragedy occurs.

Article continues after this 

“One wrong step could cause them to fall down the slope, putting their lives at serious risk,” Rañoa wrote on Nov. 11, noting that severe recurring landslides have left the access route barely passable, with soft soil continually eroding beneath one’s feet.

READ: Teachers guard pupils crossing river in Zamboanga del Sur

While teachers already endure the strain of weekly travel, he said the danger they confront to perform their duties is heartbreaking.

“Their safety and lives should never be put at risk simply because they want to serve our learners,” Rañoa wrote in his appeal. “Our teachers deserve safe roads and safe working conditions. Their dedication to education should never come at the expense of their lives.”

Becoming normal

Allan Torres, Glab Integrated School head teacher, told the Inquirer on Monday that the school had yet to submit a formal incident report to DepEd on the latest landslide, largely because such incidents have become a usual occurrence during heavy rains.

Article continues after this 

READ: Teacher Randy: Community’s bridge where there is none

“Landslides have become a normal event here in our area. Every time it rains, a landslide happens due to the sandy and hilly nature of the soil,” Torres said.

Article continues after this 

He said landslide-prone spots in Sitio Glab are outside the school and should be under the responsibility of the municipal government.

Torres recalled a previous incident when a landslide struck right beside the school and swept away some of their makeshift classrooms. The incident was reported to the barangay council, the Labangan municipal government, and the school division’s disaster risk reduction and management coordinator but no action was taken.

According to him, the barangay’s proposed remedy was to wait until heavy equipment could enter to push rocks toward the river to serve as buffer from floodwaters that trigger the landslides.

Torres stressed the school is endangered by potential landslides every time strong rains pour.

Joel Arnejo, former Glab Integrated School head, recalled that road work in the area began in 2022—around the time he was set for transfer to another assignment—under projects undertaken by the National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-Elcac)

While dry weather makes the roads passable for motorcycles, Torres said conditions deteriorate rapidly once rains set in. Steep ascents and descents turn into rushing streams during downpours, scouring the road surface alongside landslides.

“The scenario happens repeatedly. The road is fixed through bulldozing, but then in less than a month it is damaged again because when it rains. The same thing happens,” Torres said.

Response

At the start of this school year, cracks and slides were already present, though residents and teachers could still pass. Continuous rains from September through the first two weeks of November further damaged the road, worsened by toppled trees and loose soil brought down from upper elevations. This left the damaged stretch as the sole access for teachers and residents.

Zamboanga del Sur Gov. Divina Grace Yu told the Inquirer that this year, P20 million was earmarked to fund the first phase of road repairs, committing to allocate additional funds in 2027 should further work be required.

Describing the soil in the area as soft, Yu said the Provincial Engineering Office is still also studying technical options suited to the terrain.

“We are still studying if we could convert it to a national road, if we could connect it to another municipality, especially since the provincial government could not allocate enough funds for its concreting,” she said.

Yu said the provincial government was waiting for the engineering assessment to determine whether national government support could be sought to address the long-standing access problem affecting both Glab Integrated School personnel and residents of Sitio Glab. /cb

World.title: Sarangani earthquake victims to help build shelters
World.content:
Displaced families stay under a makeshift shelter in an upland area of Barangay Burias in Glan, Sarangani, after leaving their coastal homes following the earthquake. —Pia Piquero/CDN Digital

GENERAL SANTOS CITY, Philippines — Hundreds of victims of the string of earthquakes that struck Glan, Sarangani, in June are trying to rebuild their lives with the help of the very same catastrophe that devastated them.

The Department of Labor and Employment (Dole) tapped them to construct some 164 temporary shelters, five months after the magnitude 7.8 quake brought the coastal town, a major tourism destination, to its knees.

Sarangani Gov. Rogelio Pacquiao said the temporary houses for quake victims, with the project cost reaching P13.12 million, would be constructed in Barangay Margus, Glan, by residents who are beneficiaries of the Tulong Panghanapbuhay sa Ating Disadvantaged/Displaced Workers (Tupad) program.

Article continues after this 

READ: Phivolcs: Ground deformation observed in parts of Sarangani, GenSan

Administered by Dole, the program enlisted 810 earthquake victims to be part of the construction crew during a signing ceremony last week.

Pacquiao said the temporary shelters were part of the 1,020 housing units targeted to be built across Glan and neighboring Malapatan, the province’s hardest-hit municipalities, under the provincial government’s comprehensive earthquake rehabilitation and recovery plan.

READ: Magnitude 7.8 earthquake leaves 35 dead, 200 injured in Mindanao

Milbie Daguro, supervising labor officer of the Public Employment Service Office in Sarangani, said the provincial government tapped Dole to mobilize Tupad workers to build the temporary homes after thousands of families were displaced by the June 8 powerful earthquake and subsequent flash floods.

Article continues after this 

The quake left at least 32 people dead in Glan town, out of the nearly 100 fatalities recorded across Soccsksargen (South Cotabato, Cotabato, Sultan Kudarat, Sarangani, General Santos) and Davao regions.

Tupad beneficiaries will be paid the minimum wage of P476 per day.

Article continues after this 

AFP, Tesda assistance

Pacquiao said each temporary shelter that quake victims would construct in Barangay Margus costs P80,000, rising in a relocation site purchased by the Glan government after the disaster.

The houses are scheduled for completion within a month.

They will augment the 100 houses currently being built by the Armed Forces of the Philippines at the same site. AFP volunteers began work on the project after the provincial government held a sendoff ceremony for troops deployed to Glan and Malapatan on Oct. 12.

The Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (Tesda) was tapped to train the Tupad beneficiaries in carpentry and masonry.

The training will allow them to earn certificates they can use to pursue future employment, said Hernane Forro, administrator of Tesda Sarangani Provincial Training Center-Malapatan.

Forro said the agency was working closely with the provincial government to fulfill its mandate of delivering technical education and skills development.

World.title: Myanmar Records Worst Landmine Casualties in the World for 3rd Year
World.content:
Myanmar recorded the highest number of casualties from landmines and unexploded ordnance in the world last year with nearly 1,900, according to the Landmine Monitor report released Tuesday.

The group’s research shows that Myanmar was the country worst affected by deaths from landmines and so-called “explosive remnants of war” for the third year running.

Worldwide, some 6,929 casualties were recorded in 2025, counting both civilians and military personnel. Myanmar accounted for a massive proportion of over 27 percent or nearly one-third with 1,891.

The military has regularly used antipersonnel mines since 1999 and increased their use notably after the coup in February 2021, the report pointed out.

Casualties soared as a result, from just 368 in 2021 to 1,003 in 2023 before doubling to 2,029 the following year.

They are regularly planted around military bases and outposts as well as mobile phone towers, mining operations and fuel pipelines.

One regime combat engineer reported that he was ordered to plant mines in Kachin and Rakhine states near populated areas, marked only by “Danger Do Not Enter” signs without mentioning mines.

“Often there are no signs,” said Thet Oo of the resistance Yinmabin–Salingyi Strike Committee in heavily mined Sagaing Region.

He said the regime frequently plants landmines when launching offensives or raiding villages, placing them at the entrance of houses.

They are designed to sever legs.

He admitted that the heartland resistance People’s Defense Forces (PDF) also used remote-controlled handmade landmines across the country after the coup. But when resistance governing bodies were formed, they banned mines near settled areas except for military purposes that require their authorization.

“The mines are meant to injure or delay the enemy,” he added. But he claimed they are always cleared before residents return.

The report says ethnic armed organizations reported seizing regime landmines almost every month between January 2022 and this September 2026, showing how prevalent their use is.

Regime-aligned ethnic Border Guard Forces (BGF) and the militias under the regime’s command also use landmines, it says.

“We urge all states to reject the production and use of antipersonnel mines, by any actor, under any circumstances,” Tamar Gabelnick, director of the International Campaign to Ban Landmines (ICBL) told AFP.

Syria was the second-most affected country with an equally massive 1,602 casualties, trailed at a substantial distance by Afghanistan with 497.

World.title: Myanmar’s China Dilemma: Turning Beijing’s Need Into Leverage Requires Legitimate Leaders
World.content:
Anyone seeking clarity on China-Myanmar relations must first ask one crucial question: does China need Myanmar, or does Myanmar need China?

Some argue that Beijing’s often-cited desire for access to the Indian Ocean through Myanmar is overstated. Others contend that China barely needs Myanmar at all, and that the relationship matters far more to Naypyitaw than to Beijing.

The reality is more complicated.

The Malacca Dilemma

Some analysts state that China needs Myanmar to secure overland access to the Indian Ocean, bypassing the Malacca Strait chokepoint. Others dismiss this view, saying the chokepoint is no longer a problem for a country which now boasts the world’s largest navy.

Chinese leaders began wrestling with the “Malacca Dilemma” in the early 2000s under President Hu Jintao. Around the same time, Beijing and Myanmar’s previous junta began talks on pipelines to transport oil and gas from the Bay of Bengal to Yunnan Province. Agreements were reached in 2007-2008, and construction began in June 2010.

At that point, China had yet to commission a single aircraft carrier. Its first carrier — a Soviet-made ship bought from Ukraine in 1998 and modified — did not enter service until 2012. Today, China operates three aircraft carriers and is reportedly building a fourth, which is expected to be nuclear-powered.

In other words, the strategic calculations underpinning the China-Myanmar energy corridor were made before Beijing emerged as a major naval power.

More than one energy corridor

In reality, China has never relied on a single route to meet its vast energy needs. Myanmar’s gas and oil pipelines provide a direct energy corridor from the Indian Ocean, but are only one piece of a much larger network. Beijing also imports oil through the Kazakhstan-China pipeline and receives oil and gas from Russia via overland routes. Meanwhile, the Central Asia-China pipeline network pumps natural gas from Turkmenistan and other Central Asian states into western China. Additional pipelines from Central Asia and Russia are planned or under construction.

For a country the size of China, a single pipeline or supply source is never enough. Beijing’s strategy is diversification.

Why Myanmar matters

Those who argue that China does not need Myanmar often point to Beijing’s expanding network of rail, road and pipeline connections across Eurasia.

China has rail links with Laos, Vietnam, Russia, Mongolia and Central Asia. It has energy corridors stretching north into Russia and west into Central Asia. On paper, Myanmar is only one route among many.

Yet, China is not an economic monolith; its interests vary sharply from province to province. Here is where geography gives Myanmar a unique advantage.

For inland provinces such as Yunnan, Sichuan and Guizhou, Myanmar provides the most direct route to the Indian Ocean. It is also the closest overland entry for energy imports arriving from the Middle East and Africa.

A railway or trade corridor through Myanmar would offer southwestern China a global shipping link that is shorter, cheaper and likely more efficient than ports to the east.

It would also help bridge the yawning gap between the country’s wealthy coastal provinces and its underdeveloped inland regions. Coastal provinces like Guangdong have prospered through direct access to ports, global shipping networks and export markets, outpacing inland neighbors facing higher logistics costs and weaker international connectivity.

For Beijing, plugging southwestern China into international markets is not simply a foreign-policy objective, but part of a broader strategy to reduce economic inequality inside China itself.

This is where Myanmar enters the picture.

The China-Myanmar Economic Corridor, Kyaukphyu projects, road links, railways and pipelines are not intended for China as a whole. They are aimed at accelerating development in China’s southwest including Yunnan, Sichuan and other inland regions seeking easier access to the Indian Ocean and global markets.

A relationship of mutual interests

When it comes to foreign investment, countries only inject capital where they see strategic or economic returns.

During the so-called reform period between 2011 and 2020, Myanmar failed to attract large-scale investment from Western countries despite their stated commitment to the country’s democratization. They were reluctant to invest because the prospects of economic returns were low.

Beijing invests because it sees a tangible benefit — access to the Indian Ocean that will integrate China’s landlocked southwest into global trade networks.

In return, Myanmar gains infrastructure, jobs, technology transfer and improved connectivity. The ousted National League for Democracy government recognized the benefits in 2020 when it signed agreements for the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor.

A well-governed Myanmar could turn China’s need for access into an opportunity, negotiating terms that serve its national interests, and ensuring a win-win situation for both. The question is whether military-ruled Myanmar is in a position to do so today.

The real question

The argument over whether China needs Myanmar or Myanmar needs China misses the point. Both need each other.

China needs Myanmar as an Indian Ocean gateway, a trade partner and a critical link in the development of its southwestern provinces. Myanmar needs investment, infrastructure and access to the world’s second-largest economy. The ingredients for a mutually beneficial relationship are in place.

The real question is whether Myanmar has leaders capable of translating that potential into national gains rather than debt, dependency and unequal agreements.

A military regime lacking a public mandate, mired in corruption, and facing war crime accusations cannot negotiate from a position of strength — or ensure that Chinese investment serves Myanmar’s national interests.

China’s need for Myanmar is real. The challenge for Myanmar is ensuring that need works in its favor.

World.title: Arakan’s Next Battle Is for Legitimacy, Not Territory
World.content:
The International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) November 19 ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during its 2017 military operations marks a historic moment for international justice. But its implications extend beyond Myanmar’s military and the courtroom in The Hague.

For the United League of Arakan/Arakan Army (ULA/AA), which now controls most of Arakan (Rakhine State) in western Myanmar, the judgment raises a fundamental question: Can a movement that has achieved remarkable military victories build a political system that protects the rights of all communities, including the Rohingya?

The ICJ judgment is legally binding on Myanmar, not directly on the ULA/AA, which was not a party to the case. Nevertheless, the organization now controls much of the territory from which hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. Its policies will influence the prospects for reconciliation, refugee repatriation and Arakan’s international engagement.

The ULA/AA’s next challenge is therefore not simply territorial control, but establishing political legitimacy through responsible governance.

The politics of identity

One of the most sensitive issues facing the ULA/AA concerns the terms “Rohingya,” “Bengali” and “Muslim.”

For Rohingya communities, their name represents ethnic identity, historical belonging and the right to recognition. Arakan political actors and the people of Arakan, however, reject the term “Rohingya,” preferring “Bengali” because of competing interpretations of the region’s history and migration.

The ULA/AA has sometimes encouraged the use of “Muslim” as a less politically contentious term in efforts to improve relations between communities.

Such an approach may help reduce tensions, but it cannot resolve the underlying disagreement. “Muslim” describes religious affiliation, while “Rohingya” represents ethnic self-identification. The terms are not interchangeable, and not all Muslims in Arakan identify as Rohingya.

The ICJ’s treatment of the Rohingya as a protected group under the Genocide Convention underscores the significance of their collective identity.

Yet peaceful coexistence does not require every community to agree on a single historical narrative. It requires accepting that disagreements over identity cannot justify discrimination or the denial of fundamental rights.

For the ULA/AA, respecting ethnic self-identification while ensuring equal treatment would demonstrate political maturity rather than weakness.

Social harmony requires more than symbolic gestures

Decades of discrimination, communal violence and displacement have created deep mistrust between Arakanese (Rakhine) and Rohingya/Muslim communities.

Some local initiatives under ULA/AA administration, including intercommunal meetings, sporting activities and limited Muslim participation in local governance, suggest efforts to rebuild relations.

These developments may be constructive, but genuine social harmony requires more than symbolic gestures.

It depends on freedom of movement, access to education and healthcare, protection of property, fair administration and meaningful participation in decisions affecting communities.

The ULA/AA also faces serious human rights scrutiny. United Nations reporting has raised allegations of abuses against Rohingya civilians in areas under Arakan Army control, including arbitrary detention, forced labor, forced recruitment and restrictions on movement.

The organization has disputed allegations of wrongdoing, while citing security threats from armed groups operating near the Bangladesh border.

Such threats require legitimate security responses, but they cannot justify collective punishment or discrimination against civilians. The actions of Rohingya/Muslim armed organizations must be distinguished from the rights of Rohingya/Muslim communities.

Credible investigations, accountability and transparent administration would do more to build trust than political assurances alone.

International engagement is not recognition

The ULA/AA’s territorial advances have transformed the political landscape along the Myanmar-Bangladesh border.

Bangladesh, which hosts more than a million Rohingya refugees, has publicly acknowledged communicating with the AA as part of efforts to address the refugee crisis.

This creates opportunities for practical engagement with regional governments, the United Nations and international humanitarian organizations.

China and India also have strategic interests in Arakan, particularly concerning regional stability, trade and infrastructure development.

However, practical engagement and formal diplomatic recognition are fundamentally different.

Governments and international organizations may cooperate with authorities exercising effective territorial control without recognizing them as sovereign governments.

The ICJ judgment does not confer international recognition or political legitimacy upon the ULA/AA. Nor does it guarantee that regional governments or the United Nations will recognize the organization.

Nevertheless, the ULA/AA could strengthen its international standing by demonstrating respect for human rights, facilitating humanitarian assistance and establishing credible policies for all communities.

The opportunity is significant, but international credibility must be earned through conduct rather than military victories alone.

Preparing for the Rohingya challenge

The Rohingya issue remains one of the most complex long-term challenges facing the ULA/AA.

Refugees in Bangladesh continue to face uncertainty over citizenship, security, freedom of movement, destroyed homes and the possibility of renewed persecution.

Although the ULA/AA cannot independently resolve Myanmar’s citizenship framework or confer internationally recognized Myanmar citizenship, it exercises considerable influence over local security, administration and conditions affecting eventual refugee returns.

Rather than waiting for formal international recognition or a nationwide political settlement, the ULA/AA should develop a comprehensive and transparent policy addressing the Rohingya issue.

Such a framework should prioritize equal protection, respect for ethnic self-identification, intercommunal dialogue and safeguards against discrimination.

It should also establish credible mechanisms to investigate alleged abuses, protect housing and land rights, preserve residency records and consult Rohingya representatives, including refugees in Bangladesh.

Cooperation with Bangladesh, relevant UN agencies and humanitarian organizations could help prepare the groundwork for future repatriation.

Any return process must be voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable. Premature repatriation without adequate security and rights protections would risk repeating past failures.

These steps would not immediately resolve historical grievances or guarantee international recognition. But they would demonstrate that the ULA/AA is preparing to govern a diverse society rather than merely administer territory captured through war.

The real test of Arakan’s future

The ICJ judgment concerns Myanmar’s legal responsibility for genocide. It does not determine Arakan’s constitutional future or confer recognition upon the ULA/AA.

Yet it presents the organization with an important political opportunity.

For decades, Arakanese communities have pursued greater autonomy, political rights and self-determination. Those aspirations remain central to Arakan’s political struggle.

But self-determination becomes more credible when it respects the rights and identities of other communities sharing the same territory.

The ULA/AA has demonstrated its military capabilities. Its next challenge is to establish institutions capable of protecting people regardless of ethnicity, religion or political affiliation.

International engagement may expand as the organization becomes increasingly relevant to regional security, humanitarian operations and the Rohingya refugee crisis.

However, lasting legitimacy will depend on whether it can translate territorial control into inclusive governance, accountability and peaceful coexistence.

The ULA/AA has won control of territory. Its next battle is to earn the trust of all the people who live there.

Aung Marm Oo is the editor-in-chief and executive director of Development Media Group, a news agency based in Arakan. He faces charges under Myanmar’s Unlawful Associations Act and has been in hiding since May 2019.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Leader to Attend Regional Talks in Vietnam
World.content:
HANOI, Vietnam—Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing will attend regional talks in Hanoi on Saturday, Vietnam said. It will be his first multilateral meeting since taking civilian office this year.

The event comes days after the UN’s International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar committed genocide with its 2017 crackdown on the mostly Muslim Rohingya minority.

Min Aung Hlaing was head of the armed forces at the time, before leading a 2021 coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and plunged Myanmar into civil war.

The prime ministers of Cambodia, Thailand, Laos and hosts Vietnam will also take part in the talks held under two regional cooperation mechanisms, ACMECS and CLMV, the Vietnamese Foreign Ministry said in a statement late Tuesday.

Min Aung Hlaing was installed as nominally civilian president in April following widely criticized elections in which pro-military parties won a landslide.

He has since been touring regional capitals, including in neighboring Thailand, Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia, in what analysts say is a quest for legitimacy.

The four nations are part of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which has frozen Myanmar out of high-level summits since the coup, but which agreed this month to seek “calibrated engagement.”

ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn will attend Saturday’s talks in Hanoi alongside Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung and Laotian Prime Minister Saleumxay Kommasith.

According to Vietnamese state media, the discussions are expected to focus on economic connectivity, notably infrastructure, logistics, trade and supply chains as well as the environment.

The meetings will comprise the 12th Cambodia-Laos-Myanmar-Vietnam (CLMV) summit and the 11th Ayeyawady-Chao Phraya-Mekong Economic Cooperation Strategy (ACMECS) summit.

Myanmar’s regime has always denied genocide, saying its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents, and described the ICJ ruling as “a great disappointment” and “not fair”.

World.title: Malaysia to Repatriate Thousands More Myanmar Migrants
World.content:
KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia—Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Tuesday the country will send more than 6,500 migrants back to Myanmar in a new round of repatriations.

The Southeast Asian Muslim-majority country has historically offered safe haven to those exiled from Myanmar by persecution or conflict but has been keen to resolve a long-running refugee challenge involving foreign asylum seekers.

Malaysia already sent back around 1,500 migrants back to war-torn Myanmar in late September in an opaque scheme that rights groups have raised concern about.

The fresh repatriation comes five days after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority.

“The foreign minister has approved three naval ships to transport back on December 6 and 7, 1,500 Myanmar citizens,” Anwar told the Malaysian parliament.

“And for the month of December, 5,303 will be brought back by aircraft at the expense of the Myanmar government,” he added.

The UN’s highest court, based in The Hague, has ruled that Myanmar authorities must “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of refugees displaced either within Myanmar or abroad.

Kuala Lumpur said in late October it would seek clarification from Myanmar over reports that hundreds of migrants recently returned to the country were being held in military detention.

Anwar did not mention the request for clarification, but he said Malaysia reiterated its stance over concern about the Rohingya and other ethnic groups, which was also underscored by the ICJ’s ruling.

Rohingya, a persecuted Muslim minority, make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the United Nations.

Malaysia, which shelters one of Southeast Asia’s biggest refugee populations, is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention and does not formally recognize their status.

AFP fact-checkers have found that Rohingya refugees in Malaysia have been targeted by online disinformation campaigns that rights advocates say are fueling xenophobia and intimidation.

Turkey rebuffs Rohingya resettlement

Separately, Anwar said Turkey was not prepared to consider taking in 10,000 Rohingya refugees from Malaysia, following an announcement by his deputy that was later rowed back.

Malaysia said Friday it was seeking to resettle the refugees in Turkey through a structured skills training program, but the statement was subsequently deleted from Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi’s Facebook page without explanation.

In his initial statement, Ahmad Zahid said the proposal aimed to address Malaysia’s Rohingya refugee situation in a more “coordinated, effective and humane” manner.

“So if they [Turkey] say that ‘we are not ready,’ I respect that decision,” he said.

In response to a lawmaker’s question on whether Ankara had agreed to take in 10,000 Rohingya refugees from Malaysia, Ahmad Zahid said Turkey “is not ready to consider [the request].”

He added that Turkey is currently hosting “more than 4 million refugees from Gulf countries, Arab countries and several neighboring countries.”

Malaysia will explore third-country resettlement options, including among members of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, he continued.

World.title: UK Sanctions 5 Regime Generals Following ICJ Rohingya Genocide Ruling
World.content:
The United Kingdom on Monday sanctioned five more senior Myanmar military officers after the United Nations’ top court ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya community in 2017.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) announced its ruling in the case on November 19.

The UK stated on Monday that it formally recognized the ICJ ruling and announced a major package of measures in response, imposing sanctions against five Myanmar military officers for atrocities against civilians since the 2021 coup.

The new UK sanctions target Brigadier General Myo Htut Hlaing, Major General Myo Min Tun, Major General Myat Thet Oo, Major General Kyaw Soe and Major General Kyaw Swar Oo.

The UK announced asset freezes, travel bans and director disqualifications in response to ongoing violence and repression against civilians across the country.

“Today, we are imposing new sanctions on those suspected of involvement in repression of the civilian population and other serious abuses of human rights in Myanmar,” UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said.

The UK claimed that Brig-Gen Myo Htut Hlaing, deputy commander of Northwestern Regional Command, is responsible for serious cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment of detainees in Chin State.

Maj-Gen Myo Min Tun, Eastern Military Command chief in Shan and Karenni states, was involved in repression of the civilian and threatens the peace, stability and security of Myanmar, it said.

Former head of the Northern Command in Kachin State and ex-ambassador to Laos Major General Myat Thet Oo, who was reportedly removed and jailed in 2024, was sanctioned for his role in enabling military authorities to repress civilians.

Maj-Gen Kyaw Soe, commander of the Western Command in Rakhine State, was sanctioned for involvement in airstrikes on civilians and medical infrastructure.

The UK said Maj-Gen Kyaw Swar Oo, former head of the Western Command, was responsible for repression of civilians including through an airstrike on Mrauk-U General Hospital that killed 33 civilians, including a baby, and left many others injured.

London also intends to introduce legislation targeting the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar.

Alongside the sanctions, the UK is providing £5 million (US$6.53 million) in new aid for about 350,000 people, including Rohingya and other communities in Rakhine State, while a further £3 million will go towards strengthening accountability and justice for survivors of human rights abuses across Myanmar.

The United Kingdom has already imposed sanctions on 42 individuals and 39 entities, including individuals responsible for atrocities against the Rohingya, since the 2021 coup.

The UK earlier welcomed the ICJ ruling and ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defense attaché, Captain Soe Aung, from London.

World.title: 2 More Chinese Scam Syndicates Raided on Military-Linked Land in Yangon
World.content:
The Myanmar regime has raided two more Chinese scam syndicates operating at sites on military-owned land or believed to have military-linked ownership in the commercial capital Yangon.

The regime raided two residential houses in Mayangone Township and a Golden City Condo in Yankin Township on November 20 and November 22 respectively, arresting over 120 people, according to regime reports.

Observers believed the series of scam raids was prompted by tip-offs provided by Beijing.

On Sunday night, the regime raided Golden City Condo in Yankin Township and arrested 16 people on suspicion of involvement in an online gambling scam, the regime reported on Monday.

During raids on four condo rooms, the regime seized 15 laptops, 26 smartphones and three Wi-Fi routers. All four units were linked to Chinese national Jiang Hong Feng, who allegedly operated online casino and sports betting platform Zaw Play.Com.

Golden City condo sits on military-owned land leased in 2013 under a long-term Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) agreement with the military’s Office of the Quartermaster General.

In 2016, Singapore-based Emerging Towns & Cities Singapore (ETC) entered the development by taking a 70-percent stake. The other 30 percent is held by a military-linked local partner, Nature Link. The project generates revenue for the Myanmar military through land-use premiums and ongoing lease payments.

In 2023, two years after the coup, ETC took steps to sell its stake in a subsidiary linked to the project to Grand Ally Pte Ltd, which is owned by Li Bo, a Chinese citizen who is the vice president of sales and marketing for ETC, and the company’s regional sales and marketing director for Myanmar.

Justice For Myanmar (JFM), a rights watchdog, pointed out that ETC’s related-party sales risk maintaining ties to the military through personnel and stakeholders.

Nature Link belongs to Yangon-based Jewellery Luck, a group owned by regime crony Kyaw Sein with interests in real estate, hospitality, mining and forestry.

This scam syndicate not only sits on military-owned land, but is also just 500 meters from police housing compounds, a local resident told The Irrawaddy. The condo sheltering the scam center also shares a compound with the military-owned Myawaddy Media Center, formerly the Military Records Department. It is also located 600 meters from the regime’s No. 2 Police Security Command Headquarters located at the corner of No. 1 Industrial Road and Sayar San Road.

Following Sunday night’s raid, word spread in real estate circles, with agents warning other agents who had rented properties to Chinese nationals to flee the area, a local resident noted.

Real estate agents have a lot of incentive to rent to Chinese nationals in the Golden City condo, she added.

“To enter the condo, you have to pass a security gate and do a face scan,” she said.

Prior to Sunday’s raid, some media—citing resident accounts—had reported a previous regime raid on the condo on November 13, in which suspected scammers were also detained. But the regime has not made any public announcement about the earlier raid.

On the night of November 20, the regime raided suspected Chinese scam syndicates based in two residential buildings in Mayangone Township’s Ward No. 5, arresting 33 Chinese, two Thai and 70 Myanmar nationals.

The two compounds at 19/A and 43/1 Ma Soe Yein Street were just under 1 km from military bases including Military Intelligence Assistant Unit 1. Military defectors claimed the land housing the scam centers is linked to retired military officers and others in military circles.

A Chinese analyst claimed this raid, too, came in response to a tip-off from China.

Although the regime has pledged to keep fighting scam operations and act in accordance with the law, online critics are widely questioning how authorities could remain unaware of large numbers of people living in such compounds while Myanmar nationals face strict overnight guest registration rules and constant surveillance.

“When we register overnight guests, we have to provide the regime ward administrators with portrait photos of guests with their personal identities,” a Yangon resident said.

“Why don’t the ward administrators and authorities know about that?” he said.

Online critics urged authorities to check the many other places in Yangon where Chinese nationals live or rent together, alleging they could be running online scams.

On the night of November 12, the regime raided nine rooms at Golden River Residence condo in Thaketa Township and arrested 52 Chinese nationals, including Su Fu Quan, who was wanted by China, along with eight Vietnamese and 46 Myanmar nationals.

According to the regime’s reports, the syndicates targeted Chinese, Japanese, South Korean and Indian nationals with romance and investment scams.

The regime reported the arrest of 323 people—302 Chinese nationals and 21 Myanmar women—during a raid on a makeshift online scam and gambling compound in southern Shan State’s Kyethi Township on Monday morning.

In a January 2026 report, the Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar (ISP-Myanmar) said scam syndicates in Shan State were relocating from the China-Myanmar border to central Shan State and major urban centers such as Yangon and Mandalay.

ISP-Myanmar also said crackdowns on scam compounds in Karen State had pushed syndicates to relocate to other areas.

On November 19, the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army’s Commander-in-Chief General Saw Shwe Wah and Phaya Thonezu town commander Colonel Saw A One, accusing them of operating and facilitating cyber-scam centers on the Myanmar-Thailand border.

World.title: After the Genocide Verdict, Myanmar’s ‘Foreign Intruder’ Scare Returns
World.content:
Since November 3, when the International Court of Justice (ICJ) announced the date for its judgment in Myanmar’s Rohingya genocide case, one word has surged across Burmese-language social media: “khoe win”, meaning “illegal entrant.” It is routinely paired with “Bengali,” the label Myanmar’s military establishment uses to deny the Rohingya their chosen identity. Sometimes it comes with “kalar,” a slur against Muslims and people of South Asian descent.

The message is familiar. The timing should worry anyone who remembers where it led.

On November 19, the ICJ ruled, by nine votes to six, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during the military’s 2017 operations in northern Rakhine State.

Rather than reckon with that finding, pro-military nationalist circles are again urging Myanmar people to look for “Muslim outsiders” in their own neighborhoods.

Over the past three weeks, I have been monitoring Facebook and TikTok, Myanmar’s most-used social media platforms, and found hundreds of posts demanding that “Bengali intruders” be expelled, questioning Muslim businesspeople’s identity cards or calling for household members’ lists or guests’ lists inspections.

Some propose an Operasi-style campaign, borrowing the Malay term for enforcement operations against undocumented migrants, including Myanmar workers. An old video of former spy chief Khin Nyunt denying Rohingya identity has resurfaced on TikTok. None offers evidence of an influx from Bangladesh.

From social media to parliament

The posts are not all anonymous. On Facebook, veteran pro-military journalist Myat Khine encouraged guest-list checks, suggesting they would expose intruders.

Since November 19, the day of the ruling, Ashin Agga Dhamma, a famous nationalist Buddhist monk, has posted at least 12 interview videos featuring two Muslim businessmen. One of them, Htay Aung, claims Yangon is seeing an influx of illegal Muslim immigrants and rejects Rohingya identity. The monk and Htay Aung are widely seen as close to Ma Ba Tha, the ultranationalist Buddhist movement, and have previously appeared at anti-Rohingya rallies.

On November 15, the Burma Human Rights Network warned that Ma Ba Tha-backed groups were reportedly preparing nationwide protests against the ICJ ruling. It documented threats demanding that Myanmar Islamic organizations deny Rohingya identity, backed by calls to boycott Muslim-owned businesses if they refused.

Separately, UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar Kelley Currie warned on October 29 that groups behind earlier anti-Muslim agitation were becoming more active online and in political spaces under military control. On November 18, citing reports from inside Myanmar, she told journalists in Dhaka that authorities in Naypyitaw were acting alongside Ma Ba Tha and other Buddhist nationalist organizations previously involved in spreading hatred and inciting violence.

On November 10, before the judgment, the inflammatory language reached the military-controlled parliament. Lawmaker Hla Swe accused the Arakan Army of letting undocumented entrants cross from Bangladesh. Deputy Immigration Minister Lin Zaw Tun outlined plans for inspections and arrests of people described as undocumented “Bengali” migrants. No independently verified evidence of the alleged influx was presented, but online demands to “check papers” had acquired an official counterpart. On November 20, the regime rejected the judgment and again called Rohingya “Bengalis.”

The road to 2017

This same deadly playbook has unfolded before. A UN fact-finding mission cited a government inquiry recording 192 deaths during the 2012 Rakhine violence, which displaced more than 140,000, mostly Rohingya. Anti-Muslim mobs killed at least 44 in Meiktila in 2013, according to Human Rights Watch. False online rape allegations helped ignite Mandalay riots that killed two in 2014, according to the US State Department.

These attacks occurred under former General Thein Sein’s military-backed government. Military hardliners and nationalists exploited religious fears during the political opening, presenting the army as the country’s protector. They used the same message against Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy before its 2015 landslide.

The violence of 2012–2014 was part of a broader campaign of hatred and discrimination that culminated in the military’s far larger assault on the Rohingya in 2017. By then, Aung San Suu Kyi led a civilian government, but the military still controlled security operations. The generals carried out the atrocities while her government bore much of the international backlash. That outcome also served the military’s political interests.

The ICJ’s judgment now shows how far the military took this approach. Citing UN investigators, it noted that 36 military-linked Facebook pages posted 10,485 anti-Rohingya hate-speech items, including repeated material, during six months of 2017.

Why revive the rhetoric now?

Min Aung Hlaing, president since April after a military-dominated election, faces pressure on several fronts. On the battlefield, while Chinese pressure helped Naypyitaw secure fragile ceasefires in parts of northern Shan State, major regime counteroffensives in Rakhine and Kachin states have stalled against fierce ethnic and resistance forces.

Diplomatically, ASEAN still bars the junta’s political representatives from summits, while Ambassador Kyaw Moe Tun, who is loyal to the pro-democracy parallel government, still holds Myanmar’s UN seat. At home, the economy is in deep distress, with the kyat plunging toward 5,000 to the U.S. dollar and driving severe inflation.

The ICJ judgment brings another humiliation for a military establishment that has long portrayed itself as the sole defender of Myanmar’s sovereignty. Inciting public anger toward supposed foreign infiltrators is a tactic used by successive generations of generals. But repeating it today carries a far deadlier risk. Myanmar is far more heavily armed than during the communal riots a decade ago. Since the 2021 coup, the military has equipped and mobilized local militias, including Pyithu Sit and Pyu Saw Htee groups, to fight the resistance. In Meiktila in 2013, mobs carried machetes and petrol bombs. Today, the same crowd has access to guns and grenades. Another massacre is not inevitable, but hatred in a country with so many armed groups could be harder to contain.

The opposition has responsibilities too. The National Unity Government and Karen National Union welcomed the ruling. Yet some democracy supporters still reject Rohingya identity. Opposing military rule is not enough if we still deny the minorities’ rights and identity.

Rohingya civilians are not the enemies of Rakhine Buddhists, nor are Rakhine civilians the enemies of the Rohingya. Neither community is the enemy of Myanmar’s people. Their grievances and rights cannot be settled by another campaign of suspicion and hatred.

Myanmar’s generals have spent decades teaching people to fear one another, and those divisions have repeatedly helped the military justify its grip on power. Myanmar’s people have seen where campaigns against supposed outsiders can lead. The genocide judgment should be a reason to confront that history, not repeat it. A demand to inspect someone’s identity card must not become the first step toward another burning village.

Nyein Chan Aye is a Burmese journalist based in Washington, D.C., who previously worked for the BBC and Voice of America. He writes on Myanmar, U.S. policy, China and regional affairs.

World.title: Orazak Smagulov: Scientist Who Traced Anthropological History of Kazakh People
World.content:
ASTANA – In a fast-changing world, where achievements can fade with time, knowledge and contributions to society remain long after a person’s lifetime. Kazakhstan remembers Orazak Smagulov, a scientist who devoted decades to understanding the origins, biological history and anthropological development of the Kazakh people. The country’s first Kazakh anthropologist and founder of its national anthropology school died on Nov. 24 at the age of 96.

His death was announced by Ziyabek Kabuldinov, director of the Valikhanov Institute of History and Ethnology. Smagulov’s research helped establish anthropology as an independent field of scientific inquiry in Kazakhstan and contributed to a deeper understanding of the historical continuity of its population.

A scientific approach to the history of the Kazakh people

Smagulov was a Doctor of Historical Sciences, professor and academician of the National Academy of Sciences of Kazakhstan. His research focused on the anthropological history of the Kazakh people, including their biological characteristics, origins and development across historical periods.

He noted that understanding the history of a population required studying not only written records and archaeological artifacts but also human remains and biological evidence. His research sought to trace connections between ancient populations who lived in the territory of present-day Kazakhstan and contemporary Kazakhs.

“Science, like mathematics, loves precision. It does not accept mere guesswork or assumptions,” Smagulov said in a 2023 interview with National Geographic Qazaqstan.

To establish these connections, he used five systems of anthropological research: somatology, odontology, serology, dermatoglyphics and craniology. These examine human body measurements and physical characteristics, dental morphology, blood-related markers, skin ridge patterns and skull measurements, respectively.

By combining these methods, Smagulov sought to establish a scientific picture of the population’s anthropological development rather than relying on assumptions or accounts written by outside observers.

Tracing 50 centuries of history

One of Smagulov’s central scientific contributions was his research into the biological continuity of populations in the territory of Kazakhstan over several millennia. His studies compared skeletal remains recovered from ancient burial sites with anthropological data collected from contemporary populations. The research examined characteristics of skulls, teeth, blood systems and other physical markers to identify similarities and changes across historical periods.

Smagulov argued that the results demonstrated the continuity of the Kazakh population’s biological history over approximately 4,000 to 5,000 years, placing its origins and development far beyond the period of the Kazakh Khanate.

His findings contributed to research on the ethnogenesis of the Kazakh people, the historical process through which an ethnic community forms and develops, and challenged interpretations that overlooked the long history of populations inhabiting the region.

Challenging the term “nomad”

Smagulov also questioned the use of the term “nomad” to describe the Kazakh people and their historical development. He highlighted that the word was frequently used too broadly, reducing the history and culture of the Kazakh people to nomadic pastoralism and overlooking the diversity of their economic, social and cultural life. In his view, the term was often applied without sufficient scientific consideration of its meaning or the historical realities of the region.

The word “nomad” is commonly associated with populations that move from place to place, often in connection with pastoralism. Smagulov objected to treating it as a comprehensive description of the Kazakh people or as a synonym for their historical identity.

He also criticized interpretations that portrayed the population of Kazakhstan as exclusively nomadic over the past several centuries, arguing that such descriptions neglected other forms of economic activity, settlement, trade, agriculture and urban development.

For Smagulov, the terminology used to describe a people mattered because it shaped how their history was interpreted. He believed historical concepts should be grounded in scientific evidence and should not simplify the complex development of a society.

Expeditions and the development of anthropological research

Born on Oct. 1, 1930, in the Mendykarinsky district of the Kostanai Region, Smagulov graduated from the Mendykarinsky Pedagogical College in 1950 before entering the history faculty of Kazakh State University, graduating in 1955.

His interest in anthropology developed while he was participating in archaeological expeditions and observing that human remains discovered during excavations often received less scientific attention than artifacts.

In 1958, he began postgraduate studies in anthropology in Moscow at the Institute of Ethnography of the Soviet Academy of Sciences. His studies were supported by prominent Kazakh scientist Kanysh Satpayev, who helped him pursue research into the anthropological history of the Kazakh people.

Smagulov recalled that researchers in Moscow initially questioned whether sufficient materials existed to conduct such research in Kazakhstan. He insisted that a comprehensive study should compare skeletal remains from ancient populations with those of contemporary Kazakhs.

With support from Satpayev, he began collecting materials during expeditions to Central Kazakhstan, including the area around the Beghazy archaeological site. The remains were documented, numbered and sent to laboratories in Leningrad for research, as Kazakhstan lacked the necessary laboratory facilities at the time.

Over his career, Smagulov participated in 36 scientific expeditions and worked with researchers from Kazakhstan and abroad. His research included archaeological materials from Otrar, Kok-Mardan, Kuyryktobe and Mardan-Kuik, among other sites.

In 1973, he established Kazakhstan’s first ethnic anthropology laboratory, laying the institutional foundation for the country’s anthropological research school.

Research that faced Soviet censorship

Smagulov’s scientific work also encountered ideological restrictions during the Soviet period. His 1977 book, “Ethnic Genogeography of Kazakhstan,” which examined the genetic markers and biological unity of the Kazakh population, was reportedly destroyed after publication under accusations that it contradicted Soviet national policy.

In a 2023 interview, Smagulov recalled that the book was burned shortly after it was published. He said support from international researchers helped his work reach audiences abroad, including in Italy, Germany, India and the United States.

Despite the obstacles, he continued his research for decades, maintaining that scientific evidence would remain an important foundation for understanding the history of the Kazakh people.

Academic legacy and recognition

Smagulov authored hundreds of scientific works, including monographs on the anthropological history of the Kazakh people and the population of Kazakhstan from the Bronze Age to the present. His research contributed to broader academic studies of ethnogenesis, historical population development and the formation of national identity.

He also participated in international scientific cooperation, including Indian-Soviet, Kazakh-Mongolian and Kazakh-Italian anthropological expeditions. In 1993–1994, he worked with the University of Bologna on research examining adaptation among highland populations in Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan and related ethnocultural processes.

His academic achievements were recognized throughout his career. He received the Chokan Valikhanov Prize in 1991, became a corresponding member of the National Academy of Sciences in 1994 and an academician in 2004. He was awarded the title of Honored Worker of Science and Technology in 1998, the Order of Kurmet in 2010 and the Golden Star medal of the International Turkic Academy in 2019.

Smagulov also contributed to the seven-volume academic History of Kazakhstan as an author and member of its editorial board. He mentored researchers and helped establish a foundation for future generations of anthropologists in Kazakhstan.

A legacy that will continue

Kazakhstan’s Minister of Science and Higher Education Sayasat Nurbek called Smagulov’s death an irreparable loss for the country and the scientific community.

“He devoted his entire life to science and made an invaluable contribution to the study of the anthropological history and ethnogenesis of the Kazakh people. His scientific legacy and merits in the development of national science will never be forgotten,” Nurbek wrote on his official Telegram channel.

Smagulov’s legacy extends beyond the publications, expeditions and institutions he left behind. His work sought to establish a scientific foundation for understanding the history of a people, showing how evidence preserved in human remains could help tell a story spanning thousands of years.

World.title: Kazakhstan Takes Bigger Role in Global Chess, Turlov Says
World.content:
ASTANA – The youngest world championship match in chess history began in Geneva on Nov. 24, pitting 20-year-old reigning champion Gukesh Dommaraju of India against Uzbek challenger Javokhir Sindarov, as Kazakhstan highlighted its growing role in the sport’s global development.

Speaking at the opening ceremony, President of the International Chess Federation (FIDE) and Kazakhstan Chess Federation Timur Turlov said Kazakhstan was increasingly contributing to the international chess agenda through initiatives, major tournaments and efforts to promote the sport worldwide, Kazinform reported.

“Today, Kazakhstan is taking on increasing responsibility for the development of chess around the world. We are putting forward initiatives and effectively shaping the global chess agenda,” he said.

Turlov also described chess as a universal language of diplomacy, highlighting the significance of holding the ceremony at the United Nations in Geneva. Kazakhstan’s Permanent Mission to the UN and other international organizations in Geneva supported the event.

The first game, played on Nov. 24 at the Martin Bodmer Foundation near Geneva, ended in a draw after three hours and 37 minutes.

The 14-game match carries a $2.5 million prize fund. The second game is scheduled for Nov. 25, with Gukesh playing White. If the scores are tied after the classical games, the title will be decided in a tiebreak on Dec. 12.

World.title: Kazakhstan Opens Oil and Gas Sector to Domestic Digital Solutions
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s oil and gas producers will be able to use part of their mandatory annual funding allocations to introduce digital technologies at industrial facilities, creating new opportunities for domestic IT companies.

The Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development and the Ministry of Energy have approved new rules allowing hydrocarbon license holders to direct their existing funding obligation, equal to 1% of their previous year’s extraction costs, towards digitalization projects alongside research and development (R&D). The overall obligation will remain unchanged, and the rules took effect on Nov. 22.

Astana Hub will administer the mechanism, connecting oil and gas companies with Kazakhstan’s IT developers and supporting projects from technical assessment and contractor selection to implementation, the ministry reported on Nov. 24.

The initiative will draw on Astana Hub’s ecosystem of more than 2,700 IT companies and experts, whose solutions include artificial intelligence and industrial technologies.

Applications will be submitted through the national innovation system’s Single Window platform. The Ministry of Energy’s Scientific and Technical Council will review proposals, while Astana Hub and representatives of both ministries will conduct expert assessments. Contractors will be selected competitively from among Astana Hub members.

The mechanism is expected to help producers modernize operations, improve efficiency and industrial safety, while giving domestic technology developers greater access to the industrial market. Authorities also plan to extend the approach to other extractive industries.

World.title: Tokayev to Visit Moscow for Talks with Putin and AI Journey 2026 Conference
World.content:
ASTANA – President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev will pay a working visit to Moscow on Nov. 25-26 at the invitation of Russian President Vladimir Putin, Aibek Smadiyarov, the president’s press secretary, announced on his Telegram channel.

During the visit, the two leaders are scheduled to discuss strengthening the strategic partnership and alliance between Kazakhstan and Russia.

Tokayev will also participate in the AI Journey 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence.

World.title: IEA Says Hormuz Shock Could Reshape Oil Trade for Years
World.content:
ASTANA – The crisis in the Strait of Hormuz has triggered the largest energy supply shock in history and could reshape oil trade long after tankers can again move freely, the International Energy Agency said in its World Energy Outlook 2026 released on Nov.19.

As of November, disruptions in the Gulf had cost the world a cumulative 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic meters of gas supply, according to the IEA. Before the crisis, approximately 80% of the oil that passed through Hormuz went to Asia.

“We have already seen a multitude of short-term responses to lessen the impacts on energy systems, economies, businesses and households. Energy producers both inside and outside the Gulf stepped up to bring additional supplies to market via alternative routes and expanded production. China, the world’s largest oil importer, massively reduced its purchases from international markets,” IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote in the report’s foreword.

Longer-term responses from governments included change in policies or changes in “perceptions of risk.” Birol also noted the countries’ efforts to build new pipelines to avoid the Strait of Hormuz.

Oil production in Kazakhstan dropped by 8.3% in nine months of 2026, reaching 69.4 million tons, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin said at a government meeting in October. This decline, he noted, is among the factors hindering the country’s economic growth.

“This year, the economy is facing a number of headwinds. First, there is a decline in oil production and a negative contribution from the oil sector to GDP growth,” Zhumangarin said.

The decline in production was recorded in Kazakhstan’s largest fields. The Tengiz field on the Caspian shores posted a 12% decrease to 26.7 million metric tons. Kashagan’s output fell by 6% to 12.8 million metric tons and Karachaganak by 18% to 7.5 million metric tons.

For Kazakhstan, the most important oil route runs through the Black Sea. The Caspian Pipeline Consortium, which carries Kazakh crude to a terminal near Russia’s Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, repeatedly suspended flows after attacks on tankers near the terminal. The pipeline handled around 81% of Kazakhstan’s crude exports in 2025, according to KazMunayGas national oil and gas company.

The Caspian Pipeline Consortium, which carries Kazakh crude to a terminal near Russia’s Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, repeatedly suspended flows after attacks on tankers near the terminal.

Askar Ismailov, an independent oil and gas analyst and founder of PACE Analytics, counts eight attacks on CPC facilities and tankers carrying Kazakh oil since January. According to him, storage tanks could absorb a one-day export halt with little effect on annual production. In his scenarios published in a Telegram post, he estimated a weeklong shutdown could cut output by as much as 650,000 metric tons. A three-week shutdown could cost two million tons.

Ismailov expects Kazakhstan to produce 94 million to 95 million tons of oil and gas condensate this year, below the government’s November target of 96 million tons.

“A high Brent price can’t make up for the oil that Kazakhstan will physically be unable to produce and export in the remaining 40 days,” he wrote.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin told a government meeting in October that lower oil production was already weighing on economic growth. Export disruptions were one of several pressures on producers. A January fire and power outage temporarily halted production at Tengiz, Kazakhstan’s largest oilfield.

Rough seas can also keep tankers from loading. By late May, the CPC had recorded 680 hours of weather-related downtime at its tanker terminal near the Russian port of Novorossiysk. Even after a tanker leaves the terminal, it must pass through the Bosporus and Dardanelles to reach the Mediterranean. Dense fog regularly halts traffic in the Turkish Straits, usually for hours and there is no other sea passage out of the Black Sea.

Kazakhstan can bypass the Black Sea by shipping crude across the Caspian from Aktau to Baku and sending it by pipeline to Türkiye’s port of Ceyhan. KazTransOil shipped 1.16 million tons toward the Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline in January–September, up 24% from a year earlier. By the end of October, shipments had reached 1.32 million tons, exceeding the 1.26 million tons shipped in all of 2025.

Overall, the IEA projects that oil output across the Caspian region stays flat at around three million barrels a day through 2050 in its Current Policies Scenario.

Why a gas producer is buying more gas

Kazakhstan imported 6.4 billion cubic meters in the first nine months of 2026, more than the 4.7 billion it bought in all of 2025, according to the Energy Ministry. The ministry cited rising domestic consumption.

In 2025, total natural gas production in Kazakhstan reached a record high of 68.1 billion cubic meters but only 27.4 billion cubic meters was ready for sale, according to the Energy Ministry. Much of the country’s gas comes from the Tengiz, Kashagan and Karachaganak fields, where it is produced alongside oil and condensate. Domestic processing capacity limits how much of that raw gas can be treated and piped to homes, factories and combined heat and power plants.

Producers reinjected 52% of the gas they extracted in January–September to maintain pressure in oil reservoirs, according to the ministry.

IEA also expects Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to take a larger share of extra Russian gas exports as domestic demand rises and output from mature fields declines.

Writing on his Tradereport Telegram channel, a trading and investment analyst Yernar Serik put gas imports at $1.08 billion and exports at $812 million in January-September. Kazakhstan also spent more than it earned on petroleum products and electricity. Russia supplied around 80% of the country’s energy imports by value, according to his analysis.

Overall, Serik indicated Kazakhstan exported $35.5 billion of energy goods in the first nine months of 2026 and imported $2.6 billion. However, when removing crude oil, exports of everything else fell 25% to $1.8 billion while imports rose 44% to $2.6 billion, leaving a deficit of $832 million, according to calculations by Serik.

World.title: EDB Plans to Invest at Least $500 Million in Uzbekistan in 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – The Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) plans to invest at least US$500 million in Uzbekistan in 2027, with its total investment volume in the country potentially reaching US$3 billion by 2031.

The plans were discussed during a Nov. 25 meeting in Tashkent between EDB Chairman Nikolai Podguzov and Uzbekistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Jamshid Khodjaev. According to the bank, the talks focused on expanding investment cooperation, implementing prospective projects and the bank’s country strategy for 2027-2031.

The EDB is currently considering 10 potential projects in Uzbekistan with a combined investment volume that could exceed US$1 billion, Podguzov said.

“Uzbekistan is one of the EDB’s key investment destinations. In 2027, we intend to invest at least US$500 million in projects in Uzbekistan,” he said.

He added that using non-sovereign financing instruments could help attract private and international capital without increasing the country’s direct sovereign debt burden.

The officials identified five priority areas for cooperation: transport and logistics infrastructure, water and energy resilience, industrial development and production cooperation, digitalization, and financial instruments. The latter includes support for small and medium-sized enterprises, export financing, green finance and Islamic finance.

The meeting also covered opportunities to expand cooperation with state-owned companies and private investors through project financing and syndicated lending.

Uzbekistan joined the EDB in 2025, becoming the bank’s third-largest shareholder with a 10% stake. In May, the bank opened its representative office in Tashkent and began operations in the country.

The EDB is a multilateral development bank investing in Eurasia. By the end of June, its cumulative portfolio comprised 348 projects worth US$22.1 billion, covering transport infrastructure, digital systems, green energy, agriculture, manufacturing and mechanical engineering.

World.title: Rybakina Named ESPN’s Best WTA Player of 2026 After Historic Season
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina has been selected as the WTA Player of the Year in ESPN’s review of the 2026 professional tennis season. ESPN, a U.S.-based sports media company covering major sporting events worldwide, published its selection following a remarkable year in which Rybakina won two Grand Slam titles and finished as world No. 1.

The 27-year-old won the Australian Open in January and the US Open in September, bringing her career Grand Slam tally to three. She defeated Belarusian Aryna Sabalenka in both finals.

According to ESPN’s season review, Rybakina stood out for her powerful serve, composure under pressure and consistent performances against the world’s leading players.
