World.title: Azerbaijan, Uzbekistan sign 2027-28 parliamentary roadmap (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 25. Azerbaijan's Parliament (Milli Majlis) and Uzbekistan's Oliy Majlis have signed a roadmap for developing interparliamentary cooperation in 2027–2028 during the Second Azerbaijan-Uzbekistan Interparliamentary Forum, according to the Azerbaijani Parliament's Press and Public Relations Department.

The document, titled the “Plan of Practical Measures for the Development of Interparliamentary Cooperation for 2027–2028,” was signed by the Chairperson of the Azerbaijani Parliament, Sahiba Gafarova, on behalf of Azerbaijan, and the Chairperson of the Senate of Uzbekistan's Oliy Majlis, Tanzila Narbayeva, on behalf of Uzbekistan.

The roadmap provides for expanding bilateral and multilateral cooperation between the two countries' legislative bodies, strengthening the exchange of experience in lawmaking, developing parliamentary diplomacy, and advancing other priority areas.

World.title: Cancelled flight forces man to drive 1,000km to 'lifesaving' appointment
World.content:
A West Australian man was forced to drive more than 1,000 kilometres to make a "lifesaving" medical appointment after his commercial flight was cancelled earlier this month.

Wyndham resident John Barnes was due to fly from Kununurra in the remote Kimberley region to Perth on November 11, but Airnorth cancelled his flight at the last minute.

Instead, Mr Barnes embarked on a 1,000km, 11-hour drive to Broome to catch a flight to Perth the next day.

Mr Barnes said it was a family effort just to get to Broome, with his wife and brother-in-law taking turns driving throughout the night.

"I take things in my stride, and I like challenges, but that's just not a fair challenge," he said.

John Barnes prepares to fly to Perth from Broome after driving over 1,000km overnight. (Supplied: John Barnes)

'A time bomb'

Mr Barnes said he made it to Royal Perth Hospital just in time for his appointment.

He has suffered from gallstones and sepsis in recent months.

As a result, Mr Barnes said he could not risk rescheduling his medical review to the following week.

"I'm basically a time bomb waiting to go off," he said.

"If another gallstone goes where it shouldn't … they've saved my life once, and I don't exactly need that to happen again."

John Barnes says he almost missed a "lifesaving" medical appointment due to a flight cancellation in Western Australia's north. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

Mr Barnes said he understood flight cancellations happened, but the regularity in the East Kimberley was unsettling.

"I felt really let down. It took the mat from underneath my feet," he said.

" 'I sincerely apologise for this inconvenience' … I mean, are they going to reschedule my doctor's appointment? Are they going to reschedule my accommodation? "

Half the journey, double the price

Kununurra resident Sharon D'Aietti said she factored flight unreliability into her travel planning.

"We always go [to Perth] at least a day in advance just to be sure we can take other [onward] flights … sometimes two days in advance," she said.

Ms D'Aietti said her parents visited her in Kununurra earlier this year but were shocked by the cost of flying to the Kimberley region.

When booking, a flight from Darwin to Broome that stopped in Kununurra cost about $500; the Broome to Kununurra leg alone cost nearly $1,000.

Sharon D'Aietti says expensive and unreliable flights are taking a toll on her young family. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

"It's half of the kilometres … but costs double the money," Ms D'Aietti said.

"It was the same plane. The same flight that is stopping here [in Kununurra].

"So why would you add $500 to the price? It just didn't make sense to me."

The WA government has extended a scheme to cap airfares for regional residents to Perth until 2031.

Flight delays and cancellations at the East Kimberley Regional Airport in Kununurra have had an impact on residents. (ABC Kimberley: Rebecca Nadge)

But Ms D'Aietti said in Kununurra people were "limited on the flights you can get," with residents still forced to buy full-price fares for specific travel dates.

She said expensive fares and cancellations were putting her and other families in the East Kimberley under strain.

"We love the place," Ms D'Aietti said.

"But I understand why people don't want to come and don't want to live here."

'End of the line'

Airnorth has a monopoly on flights to and from Kununurra, after rival airline Nexus halted services last year.

Shire of Wyndham East Kimberley president David Menzel said flights were crucial for the region's development.

"Livability, retention of staff, attracting new staff … it's near impossible if you're this far from anywhere and people haven't got confidence in the air service," he said.

"People are just losing confidence in the air service we've got.

"It feels like we're at the end of the line and get the leftovers."

David Menzel says more competition and government support are needed to rectify unreliable air travel in WA's north. (ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic)

Cr Menzel said he hoped to restart conversations with carriers and the government to find better solutions.

"The market is broken, really," he said.

Airnorth was contacted for comment.

WA Transport Minister Rita Saffioti earlier this year labelled the East Kimberley Regional Airport as a gateway to the region, while also providing a critical supply chain link for local communities and industry.

World.title: Breaking: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
World.content:
Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran, has died aged 65.

Taylor's death was confirmed by his family and bandmates in a statement posted on social media and Duran Duran's website.

He died after a "long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", the statement said.

"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music," the band said.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."

Andy Taylor, seen here circa 1985, died following a prostate cancer diagnosis. ( Getty Images: Vinnie Zuffante)

On the night he was inducted in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, Taylor revealed that he had been battling stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years and was unable to attend.

"I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band," he wrote.

"You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one's own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible."

The band's pop hits include Hungry Like the Wolf, The Reflex and Rio. The rise up the charts of Hungry Like a Wolf was inextricably linked to the launch of MTV.

The two-time Grammy Award-winners had nine gold and six platinum records, with 20 top-20 singles in the UK and 18 in the US.

The two-time Ivor Novello Award winners are also MTV Video Visionary Award recipients.

Duran Duran's Andy Taylor reveals stage 4 cancer diagnosis "Many families have experienced the slow burn of this disease and of course we are no different," Taylor wrote.

The band's imperial stage came through a trio of hit albums between 1981 and 1983 that delivered dance-floor anthems as Girls on Film and Union of the Snake, and the moody ballads The Chauffeur and Save a Prayer.

Their cemented their popularity when they recorded the James Bond theme song A View to a Kill and earned a slot at Live Aid in 1985.

Mixing fashion, pioneering synthesisers and glam-pop swagger, the telegenic band were all over radio and young people's walls, with bassist John Taylor and singer Simon Le Bon becoming heart-throbs and the band being labelled part of the New Romantics.

Princess Diana was known to be a fan, and that meant a lot to the band.

"It worked well for us," drummer Roger Taylor told Rolling Stone.

"It was genuine. I don't think it was some sort of PR stunt. It was massive for us because she was the number one icon of the early 80s."

MTV success and love from Princess Diana propelled their profile. Seen here in 2004, with Andy Taylor on the far left. (AP: Lo Sai-hung/ File)

Success in the MTV era

The band's success was in large part to their videos, including their Antigua-set song Rio, which featured shots of the band in pastel suits sailing confidently on a yacht.

For the album Rio, they shot three music videos in Sri Lanka and two in Antigua, feeding MTV's need to have a stream of visuals, something classic rock did not have.

Loading...

"A lot of the success of the album is down to the power of the videos and the way it made the band omnipresent around the globe," Le Bon told The Daily Beats in 2012.

Andy Taylor agreed: "I don't think we could have done it without MTV."

New wave's 'Fab Five'

John Taylor and keyboardist Nick Rhodes started the band as teenagers in the northern city of Birmingham in 1978.

The group's name was inspired by a character in the Jane Fonda-starring sci-fi movie Barbarella.

Roger Taylor, Le Bon and Andy Taylor joined soon after, with the British press referring to them as the Fab Five.

Andy Taylor answered an ad in Melody Maker music magazine for a live-wire guitarist. (None of the Taylors were related.)

"We all grew up on the same vinyl records and live gigs, from David Bowie to Roxy Music, The Sex Pistols and, of course, Chic," Andy Taylor wrote in a letter read by the band during their Rock Hall induction.

"I could go to all those places as a player and developed a hybrid guitar style that fitted this amazing concept of a band."

AP

World.title: Renegades WBBL player bowled without facing a ball
World.content:
The Melbourne Renegades have pipped Brisbane Heat by three wickets in a last-ball thriller highlighted by a bizarre diamond duck to Deandra Dottin.

Chasing 138, Dottin came in at 4-97 and was adjusting her helmet strap and was gloveless on arrival at the crease outside the allotted 75 seconds time limit.

She was ordered by umpires to stand aside while Heat spinner Sarah Glenn had a free bowl at the stumps. She was on target and Dottin departed without facing a ball.

The drama preceded a tense final over when the Renegades required nine runs from Lucy Hamilton's bowling.

Annie Wikman smacked the first ball for four, and five singles followed, including Wikman's winning run from an inside edge.

Tess Flintoff top-scored in the chase with 30 from 32 balls and Georgia Wareham made a valuable 29 from 26 against a Heat bowling attack led by Glenn's 2-15 and Sienna Ginger's 2-13.

The Renegades (nine points) replaced the Heat (eight points) in fourth spot and, if they beat the Melbourne Stars on Saturday, will feature in the finals.

Renegades captain Sophie Molineux was instrumental in Wednesday night's win at Melbourne's Junction Oval, taking 4-20.

Earlier, Molineux produced her superb bowling spell to stymie the Heat batters.

The Australian captain claimed a wicket in her first over, bowling dangerous opener Grace Harris for a golden duck, and another in her second.

Molineux returned to bowl the 13th over and took two more wickets in three balls, while Orla Prendergast top-scored with 23 from 15 balls, and Lucy Hamilton (21 from 15) and Sienna Ginger (21 from 21) played handy knocks.

Sophie Molineux ripped through the Heat's top order. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Brisbane must now hope the Renegades are defeated by the Stars on Saturday to have any hope of reaching the play-offs.

The Heat will know their fate by the time they host the Perth Scorchers on Sunday.

Sydney Thunder, on six points, remain the only other chance to reach the finals. They meet the finals-bound Adelaide Strikers on Thursday and the Sydney Sixers on Saturday.

The Thunder must win both games but, even then, they're relying on the Renegades and Heat to both lose their respective last matches.

AAP

World.title: Copper theft costing SEQ ratepayers a small fortune
World.content:
Bikeways, neighbourhood streets, sporting fields, and community facilities are being plunged into darkness across south-east Queensland as copper thefts cost ratepayers about $1.7 million last financial year.

Brisbane, Ipswich, Logan, Redland and Moreton Bay City councils are experiencing a big rise in copper thefts, with incidents in one area quadrupling from the year before.

The Greater Brisbane councils are being forced to replace the stolen copper with aluminium cabling, and at least one is even considering proactive replacements to prevent thefts.

It comes as the Queensland government accelerates rectification works through a $40 million investment and progresses legislation to disrupt the theft and sale of stolen scrap metal.

Brisbane darkness takes away 'feeling of safety'

Brisbane City Council had 44 copper cable thefts in 2025–26, more than double the 15 in 2024–25, with estimated repairs costing a whopping $1.2 million.

Infrastructure chair Ryan Murphy (LNP) said the 2025–26 thefts spanned parks, sports fields and public spaces, and the council was installing CCTV in high-risk locations.

He said 17 thefts from the past financial year are still awaiting repair, with most expected to be complete by March next year.

Ryan Murphy says the Brisbane council has considered proactively replacing copper wire with aluminium cables. (ABC News)

"Right now, we've got 109 lights out across the city, in Rochedale, Calamvale, Boondall, Deagon, Carina, Wynnum, there's no rhyme or reason to where these copper thieves strike," he said.

"Copper theft has been happening on and off since 2023, but the rise of copper theft has tracked pretty neatly with the rise of the copper price.

"As organised crime makes this a focus of their money-making schemes, there are also other people opportunistically copying."

He said there was a particular problem of bikeways and paths, which had less surveillance than community facilities.

"Some paths are really important local connections between schools, businesses, public transport and losing the lights takes away that feeling of safety, particularly for people using public transport to get home in the evening," he said.

He said that, as well as the direct cost of replacing the copper wire with aluminium cables, there was the indirect cost of delayed new projects.

"We don't want to have these lighting sites become an ATM for copper thieves. We want them to have so much less value that thieves won't bother going back," he said.

"We'll also likely start proactively replacing copper on the city's bikeways with aluminium. It's something we've thought about, but it's not something we'd like to do.

"It's not an upgrade. The best thing we could do is leave the copper that's in existing lights in place."

Developers using aluminium wire in new builds

Ipswich Mayor Teresa Harding said the council had already spent more than $100,000 on copper streetlight theft in the 2025–26 financial year up to April.

"Over the past five years, that figure has exceeded $1.25 million," she said.

"Council is fighting back against copper thefts by progressively replacing copper streetlight cabling with aluminium, and we're already seeing positive results.

"Developers are also increasingly using aluminium cabling in new estates from the outset, which has helped reduce thefts in areas that were previously being targeted repeatedly."

Teresa Harding says the Ipswich council has spent $1.25 million on copper theft over the past five years. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)

She said while this was helping, thieves were still targeting isolated copper cable sections, with recent thefts from Mount Juillerat Drive in Redbank Plains, and repeated thefts in some of the newer estates in Redbank Plains.

Cr Harding said people attempting to steal copper were often accessing or cutting into live electrical infrastructure and placing themselves in "serious danger".

"To help reduce that risk, council has installed signage in a number of locations identifying where aluminium cabling has been installed," she said.

Earlier this year, in March, a man in Toowoomba attempted to steal copper wire from an Ergon Energy site and received life-threatening injuries; the irony was that there was no copper wire, only aluminium.

Logan copper thefts quadruple in just one year

In Logan City, copper thefts from streetlights more than quadrupled from three incidents costing $53,379.61 in 2024–25, to 13 in 2025–26 costing $234,633.88.

Redland City Council has spent more than $152,000 on copper wiring theft from pathways and sports fields in 2025–26 and this financial year.

"Council now installs aluminium cabling instead of copper cabling at sports fields and uses lockable electrical pits for pathway lighting," a spokesperson said.

A Moreton Bay spokesman said the council had spent about $500,000 on copper wire theft since 2021.

"This obviously does not consider the costs incurred by clubs, schools, shopping centres and the like across City of Moreton Bay who have also paid for repairs or received insurance payouts," he said.

"City of Moreton Bay welcomes the recent passing of new state anti-copper theft laws following councils' push for legislative change."

Increasing rates of copper theft costing Qld taxpayers millions a year Experts say cost of living pressures, and the ability to make money quickly, is behind a surge in copper thefts which are leaving highways and sporting fields in the dark.

Hundreds of thefts on Queensland-owned roads

Multiple councils noted they did not control all streetlights in their local government areas, with many of them the responsibility of Energex or the Department of Transport and Main Roads.

Throughout Queensland, more than 350 incidents of copper theft affected lighting on state-owned roads from July 2024 to June 2026.

A Transport and Main Roads spokesperson said: "The Queensland government is committed to cracking down on metal theft, recently passing legislation that delivers stronger protections, tougher enforcement powers and increased penalties for those committing copper theft."

World.title: 18yo bailed following alleged home invasions, thefts and police pursuit
World.content:
An 18-year-old allegedly involved in 17 criminal incidents and filmed driving in a police pursuit in Mildura on Sunday has been bailed to attend a funeral.

Rupert Clark, of Gol Gol, New South Wales, was arrested alongside a 17-year-old, a 15-year-old, two 14-year-olds and a 12-year-old.

The group of six is alleged to have stolen a white Volkswagen Tiguan from a Merbein South address at around 7am on November 22.

Mr Clark faced the Mildura Magistrates' Court charged with a range of offences including dangerous driving while pursued by police, conduct endangering life, conduct endangering serious injury and theft of a motor vehicle.

The Mildura Magistrates' Court heard the group drove the car at speeds of up to 225km/h, before police engaged in a pursuit from Red Cliffs to Mildura at about midday.

An alleged youth offender films police pursuing a stolen vehicle in Mildura. (Supplied: Sunraysia Crime Watch)

Stop sticks were deployed at an Irymple intersection, slowing the car to a top speed of about 50km/h.

The court heard the Volkswagen then struck a 2026 MG wagon at a nearby roundabout, drove on footpaths, and damaged four police vehicles before stopping in a Mildura paddock where arrests occurred.

Parts of the pursuit were allegedly filmed by one of the boys from the front passenger seat and posted on social media.

Seventeen distinct criminal incidents were described in court during Clark's bail hearing, which began on Monday.

The court heard Mr Clark was already on bail in NSW over charges including reckless driving at speeds of more than 45km/h above the limit

Since August, he had been subject to a curfew, a driving ban, and was not to associate with the 12-year-old arrested alongside him on Sunday.

The court heard Mr Clark allegedly committed offences in the company of two distinct groups of young people.

The offences allegedly committed by the groups included home invasions, vehicle thefts and dangerous driving, with several interactions filmed and shared on social media.

Rupert Clark, 18, features in videos of alleged criminal activity that circulated on social media on Sunday. (Supplied: Sunraysia Crime Watch)

Posting and boasting

Detective Senior Constable Jake Gale said Mr Clark was an unacceptable risk of being released on bail due to the "extremely serious nature" of the offending.

He said the teenagers did not gain anything "other than entertainment and notoriety" and were emboldened by community attention by posting and boasting online.

Rupert Clark is alleged to have been driving the green vehicle in this video, uploaded to social media on November 15. (Supplied: Sunraysia Crime Watch)

Senior Constable Gale said the alleged offences had been escalating in severity and risk, and police were concerned someone would be killed as a result.

Five videos were played in court to demonstrate Mr Clark's driving offences.

The first was of Sunday's police pursuit.

Video Two was from 7am that morning, showing the car being driven at about 205km/h on the wrong side of the road on Eleventh Street, near Nichols Point.

Another video was taken at 825am on Eleventh Street near the Old Aerodrome Ovals in Mildura, showing the car travelling on the wrong side of the road at 165 km/h in a 60km/h zone.

Police prosecutor Kristen Simm said the video demonstrated "incredible risk", as little athletics and baseball events take place on the adjacent ovals on Sundays.

The fourth video, taken at 910am near Mildura Airport, showed Mr Clark being egged on by the car's occupants to attempt to ram a family of emus.

The final video was taken at 10am on the outskirts of Mildura, where the car reached speeds of 225km/h.

Mr Clark was shown driving with a phone in his lap.

Loading...

Bail granted

Mr Clark's lawyer, Tyra O'Neill, requested her client's temporary release, to attend the funeral of his grand-uncle on Thursday.

His grand-uncle has passed away on November 3.

He was deemed unsuitable for a Court Integrated Services Program and the court heard he was midway through a youth justice assessment, which would be ready by Friday.

The prosecution argued Mr Clark should not be allowed to attend the funeral, as the formal assessment had not been completed.

Magistrate Greg Thomas granted Mr Clark temporary bail, on house arrest-like conditions.

He will not be allowed to leave his home, unless in the company of his mother and step-father.

For 48 hours Mr Clark will not be allowed to attend Mildura, except for medical, youth justice or court matters.

He is also not allowed to drive a motor vehicle, and cannot associate with any of the five co-accused from the police pursuit.

Upon his bail ruling, Magistrate Thomas said it appeared Mr Clark was encouraged, controlled and egged on by his co-accused, and if the other people were removed, he doubted Mr Clark would be involved in offending behaviour

"A number of people have been seriously injured or killed in the community this year, it's caused terrible grief," Magistrate Thomas said to Mr Clark.

"It's very important you don't add to that."

The matter will return to court on Friday.

World.title: Star quarterback Rodgers released after stunning tirade against coach
World.content:
Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers came to Pittsburgh in a Chevy. He left it sitting atop a flamethrower.

The four-time NFL Most Valuable Player torched Steelers coach Mike McCarthy during a staggering appearance on ESPN's The Pat McAfee Show overnight, barely 12 hours after the team said it planned to bench him on Friday, local time, against Denver.

Not long after that, Rodgers was released by the team.

In the interview, Rodgers accused McCarthy of falling asleep in meetings, arriving late and in one case, saying "one, two, three, Packers" instead of "Steelers" after a huddle. McCarthy and Rodgers won a Super Bowl with the Packers in 2011.

Rodgers told McAfee he found out about the surprise decision to bench him while on the phone with teammates, including tight end Pat Freiermuth.

The team announced late on Tuesday, local time, that Rodgers would be inactive for Friday's game against the Broncos, with Mason Rudolph set to start, a shock announcement coming hours after McCarthy had publicly committed to Rodgers remaining the starter after an ugly offensive showing in a loss to Philadelphia.

The club excused Rodgers from Wednesday's practice, and Rodgers wasted little time going on the offensive, painting the picture of a 63-year-old coach who was out of touch, would fall asleep during team meetings, and struggled to put together a coherent game plan in the modern NFL.

Rodgers said he had discussed McCarthy's inattentiveness with the coach and had talked to him about changing play-calling duties.

Aaron Rodgers and Mike McCarthy speak during the game against the Eagles. It would be the last time the two were seen on the field together. (Getty Images: Michael Owens)

"If you try and bench me or don't change the play-calling then you should just release me, because I feel like at this point, I'm doing what's right for the organisation," Rodgers said.

"He responded with, 'I'm going to do what's right by the organisation,' which in his mind was getting rid of me," Rodgers added.

"Now obviously he got the owner and the GM on his side."

The scene played out bizarrely during Rodgers's extended appearance on the show in which he has been an occasional contributor.

McCarthy waded through a throng of assembled reporters at Steelers headquarters, most of them huddled over their phones listening to Rodgers, after practice ended.

Minutes later in a subdued locker room, the Steelers players and coaches who were left to pick up the pieces declined to get into specifics about Rodgers's accusations but did not dismiss them either.

Asked if he was confident McCarthy could lead the team going forward, Freiermuth responded with a simple, "I'm confident", but little else.

Wide receiver Marquez Valdes-Scantling, who played alongside Rodgers and under McCarthy as a rookie in Green Bay in 2018, acknowledged there was general frustration about the team's recent performance but allowed: "I didn't think it was this."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AP

World.title: Fuel tanker crash on major Cairo highway kills at least 30
World.content:
A fuel tanker crash ignited a massive fire on a major highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday and killed at least 30 people, according to Egyptian authorities.

The blaze on Ring Road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, injured at least 25 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, the public prosecutor's office said in a statement.

The crash occurred on a stretch of the highway at Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in the Greater Cairo area, according to the health ministry.

Rescue workers were seen pulling people out of burning cars and an Associated Press video showed firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among vehicles.

Hundreds of people gathered in the aftermath of the Cairo crash. (AP: Mohammed Salah)

Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi has issued a statement expressing his condolences and the public prosecutor’s office says DNA investigations are underway to identify the victims.

Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that he would head to the scene himself.

He said the death toll was preliminary.

Deadly traffic accidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transport safety record.

Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.

In January 21 people were killed and 16 injured in a massive multi car pile-up on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

AP

World.title: Man threatens partner with handgun while screaming 'I will kill us both'
World.content:
A man who pointed a handgun at his partner's face while screaming "I will kill us both" and told her he was "prepared to get in a shootout with police" has been jailed for more than seven years.

Kyle Robert Wilson pleaded guilty in the Northern Territory Supreme Court to assaulting the woman and threatening to kill her and burn her house down outside Darwin last year.

Wilson, 27, also pleaded guilty to a string of drug offences after being caught supplying a commercial quantity of methamphetamine during his subsequent arrest.

'What do I have to do, cut your f***ing head off?'

The court heard in February 2025, Wilson lent his partner his ute, which she drove to her mother's house — before he started texting her, demanding the vehicle back and threatening to kill himself.

Wilson followed her in a "buggy" to the house, where he pulled up alongside her and told her to "get the f*** in the buggy now".

When she got in, he then drove down a dirt track and started screaming at her about calling the police.

In sentencing, Justice John Burns said Wilson then pulled out a .45 calibre handgun and pointed it at his partner's face while driving at high speed into a swampy area near Girraween Road and screaming "I will kill us both".

"You told the victim that you did not give a f*** what happens and that you were prepared to get in a shootout with police," he said.

After the vehicle became bogged in the swamp, nearby police approached the couple, but left after they declined their offer of assistance.

John Burns said Kyle Robert Wilson's offending was "a confronting, protracted episode of domestic violence" over more than two days. (ABC News: Tiffany Parker)

As the woman then tried to leave, the court heard Wilson told her "if you walk away, I will shoot you in the back", and ran after her, knocked her down and kicked her in the back.

Now "too afraid to leave", Wilson's partner helped him unbog the buggy, and they eventually drove back to her house while he continued to threaten her life, before he ultimately left her at home.

What has changed in the year since a landmark DV inquest? A year after NT Coroner Elisabeth Armitage handed down 35 recommendations from a landmark domestic violence inquest, those on the frontline say things are getting worse.

The following day, the court heard Wilson, his brother and another man went to the woman's house to collect some of his property and he demanded she "give up the stuff".

"What do I have to do, cut your f***ing head off?" he said.

The woman managed to hide in some bushes, where she overheard Wilson ask his brother "where the f*** is she?" and "did you let her leave?".

"What do you think she’s doing right now, going to the police?" he said.

Justice Burns said Wilson then threatened to burn the house down and "kill her or her dog", while calling for a jerry can of fuel.

"During this, the victim felt petrified, she thought she was going to die, she had never seen you like this before," he said.

"She managed to jump her fence and ran as fast as she could to a neighbour’s address but there was nobody home.

"She then remained hiding at her neighbour’s address until you and your brother left."

The court heard after finding some workers at a nearby shed who called a friend for her, the woman was picked up and stayed with the friend until the next day, when she decided to call the police.

Offender's 'poor choices'

In setting a non-parole period of three years and 10 months, Justice Burns said Wilson's offending was "a confronting, protracted episode of domestic violence" over a period of more than two days.

But Justice Burns said he also took into account Wilson's "difficult" upbringing, including his use of methamphetamine from the age of 14.

"Your father was involved in substance misuse, violence and gang associations, including affiliations with the Hells Angels," he said.

The court heard the woman "felt petrified" and "thought she was going to die" during the ordeal. (ABC News: Tiffany Parker)

"You said that your substance use had escalated in the lead-up to the offending and that you were associating with others involved in drug use and criminal activity.

"You acknowledge responsibility for your offending and describe your actions as poor choices."

In relation to the drug charges, Justice Burns said he was satisfied that Wilson's dealing was "a reasonably small enterprise for your own benefit".

He sentenced Wilson to a total of seven years and eight months in prison for the combined offences.

Wilson will be eligible for parole in April 2029.

World.title: ‘Very dark’: Rescuers battle tough conditions in race to save 17 trapped miners
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaMining ‘Very dark’: Rescuers battle tough conditions in race to save 17 trapped miners Zach Hope and Karuni Rompies Updated November 26, 2026 — 9:19am ,first published 10:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Singapore/Jakarta: Indonesian rescuers have now pulled nine bodies from a flooded gold mine south of Jakarta and are struggling to reach at least 17 other fossickers who have been trapped since Monday. The abandoned mine’s terraced shaft was so narrow and slippery teams could not immediately get down oxygen tanks, according to Desiana Kartika Bahari, the head of the Jakarta branch of the nation’s search and rescue agency, BASARNAS. A rescue worker entering the narrow passage, which may stretch 100 metres below the ground. BASARNAS “We also need to bring lamps as it is very dark – and right now the rain is pouring in heavily,” she said. She said it was still unclear if diving experts would be needed from overseas, like in this year’s Laos cave rescue and the Thailand rescue of the Wild Boars youth football team in 2018.



The mine used to be operated by state-owned company PT Antam, Desiana said. The fossickers were searching for gold illegally in one of the “thousands” of closed shafts in Bogor, West Java, when the nearby Ciseureuh River overflowed. She said the shaft was possibly 100 metres deep. Rescuers prepare to put the body of miner recovered from the flooded gold mine into an ambulance. BASARNAS via AP “We don’t know for sure [how many people were down the mine] but we talked to illegal miners here and they gave 26 names, so maybe there are 26 people,” she said. “We don’t know for sure because they are illegal. They are quite stubborn, these illegal miners, because they have been warned frequently for not doing what they are doing.”



Monday night and most of Tuesday went by before rescue crews from Bogor arrived and attempted to pump the water out. “In fact, they found pumps inside the pit believed to be belonging to the illegal miners. It means these people know that it is dangerous to go down there,” Desiana said. The first three bodies were recovered on Wednesday afternoon at a depth of between 30 and 40 metres, according to a press release from BASARNAS. The toll continued to rise through the afternoon and evening as rescuers moved through the shaft. Rescuers are working through tough conditions. Police told Kompas TV they were investigating who might have financed or directed the illicit mining. Authorities in Indonesia have struggled to contain such operations, often carried out by impoverished family breadwinners risking their lives to find scraps of gold left behind by departed mining companies.

Stocks on Wall Street closed moderately lower after another punishing pullback in AI stocks lost momentum as the day went on, reversing much of the market’s losses. The S&P 500 index fell 0.3 per cent after having been down as much as 3.2 per cent earlier in the day. The Nasdaq composite finished 0.6 per cent lower. At one point, it had been down as much as 4.6 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.3 per cent. After a respite following the return of Jensen Huang to Nvidia, AI stocks are falling again. AP Photo/Richard Drew The ASX is set to brush off the negative lead and open higher, with futures pointing to a gain of 58 points, or 0.7 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.4 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US66.27¢. Wall Street pared its losses even as a report raised more worries about high inflation and as President Donald Trump plans to escalate the US trade war with major trading partners.



Related Article Exclusive

Fashion retail ‘It was our baby’: General Pants isn’t the same trend-setting denim store its founders built AI stocks lost ground for a second day following Monday’s relief rally over the surprise reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Stocks have been generally falling since setting an all-time high last month as worries grow that AI stock prices have grown unjustifiably high. The market turnaround came as some of the biggest tech companies bounced back from steep drops. Nvidia, which was down more than 9 per cent at one point, closed with a 3.9 per cent loss. Broadcom, which had dropped more than 6 per cent, ended just 0.1 per cent lower, while Microsoft came back from a more than 3 per cent slide to finish down 1.2 per cent. There were some gainers among tech stocks: Meta climbed 3.4 per cent and Salesforce rose 2 per cent.



Gains in financial services stocks also helped temper the market’s losses. Visa rose 1.8 per cent, Mastercard gained 1.9 per cent and American Express rose 1.2 per cent. Anthropic bounced back from an early drop to close with a 1.1 per cent gain. Still, since soaring to $US115 per share on the day it became the first major frontier lab to go public, Anthropic shares have tumbled by about 28 per cent. Roughly three quarters of the stocks in the S&P 500 rose, although the pullback in technology stocks kept the index in the red. Technology companies, particularly those focused on AI, have large market values that give them a dominant influence over whether major indexes rise or fall. Nvidia is among the most valuable companies on Wall Street and its surge on Monday led a tech sector rally. It is now one of the biggest weights pushing the market lower. The S&P 500 index is down 5.2 per cent for November, after losing some ground in October and September.



“At this point, between the AI angst and the newly announced tariffs, it doesn’t look like the Santa Claus Rally is in store for us this year,” said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management, in a research note. Questions about Nvidia’s corporate governance, as well as the influence of a US president who owns millions of dollars’ worth of shares in the company, have added to concerns surrounding the artificial intelligence sector. Relief over Huang’s return as CEO is fading because of worries that AI might not produce enough profit to justify the large investments and stock values. That dynamic is running up against stubbornly high inflation. The latest update on inflation showed that prices rose at a more aggressive 3.8 per cent rate in October from the same period last year, and followed a 3.6 per cent rate in September. The data is from the Federal Reserve’s preferred measure of inflation, the personal consumption expenditures price index. Aside from potentially stifling economic growth, high inflation could mean higher interest rates, with the Fed likely to raise its benchmark interest rate at its December policy meeting to try to tame inflation. The rate of inflation is well above the central bank’s target of 2 per cent. The economy has been resilient, though, even as inflation squeezes households and businesses and consumers grow increasingly anxious about spending and finances. The government said that the economy grew even faster in the July-September quarter than previously estimated, with growth revised upward to a 4.3 per cent annual rate, the fastest in three years.



Much of the spending that is driving the economy, though, has been from large tech firms building out AI infrastructure and from upper-income households. There are signs poorer Americans are relying more on credit to sustain their spending. Higher oil prices, fuelled by the US war with Iran and its impact on the world’s oil supply, have also contributed to inflation. The price of a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 3.5 per cent to settle at $US94.61 on Wednesday. The price has swung between $US72 and $US114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. Energy companies mostly gained ground Wednesday, including a 1.1 per cent rise for Chevron. The wide-ranging and often uncertain US trade conflict with much of the world also added to rising costs. The US plans to hike tariffs on China, the European Union and other trading partners after the US Supreme Court struck down broader tariffs that were set last year. Businesses tend to pass along some or all of the cost of tariffs to consumers. Anger over stubbornly high prices was a factor in pushing voters to punish Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats. Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.87 per cent from 4.91 per cent late Tuesday.



All told, the S&P 500 fell 18.31 points to 7,182.78. The Dow gained 164.25 points to 50,182.95, and the Nasdaq dropped 147.73 points to 23,585.80. Related Article Opinion

AI Trump saved his billionaire mate but the walls may start closing in Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Markets fell throughout Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi lost 6.2 per cent as Samsung Electronics fell 9.9 per cent and SK Hynix plummeted 11.1 per cent. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8 per cent. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group slumped 14.8 per cent. US financial markets will be closed Thursday for Thanksgiving. One Nation treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce said new recruit Leah Blyth would bring some “dynamism” to South Australia’s representation.

Asked whether Blyth was only leaving the Liberals because she was unlikely to get a winnable seat on the party’s Senate ticket, Joyce said it was “sort of hypothetical question”.

“I don’t believe that people join One Nation for that reason. They join One Nation because they are a conservative, they have a conservative view of the world and they want to be part of what is a genuinely conservative party,” he told Radio National.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce. Alex Ellinghausen

Asked about Nationals leader Matt Canavan’s concession, when asked if more people had been considering defecting, that it had been a hard time for those in the Coalition, he said that was a “fair appraisal”.

World.title: ‘Quasi-legal nonsense’: Judge scolds Uber driver’s AI spiral
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceAI ‘Quasi-legal nonsense’: Judge scolds Uber driver’s AI spiral Elias Visontay November 26, 2026 — 8:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A federal court judge has berated a sacked Uber driver who relied on AI-generated “quasi-legal nonsense” to formulate his appeal seeking to get his job back, despite AI having failed him at earlier attempts to be reinstated. The driver - who must now foot the bill for Uber’s legal costs - had been fighting to overturn his deactivation from the rideshare giant after it booted him from the app in September 2025 following four complaints against him from customers. An Uber driver has been scolded for his repeated reliance on AI in his legal quest to get his job back. Marija Ercegovac / Stephen Kiprillis While three prior complaints received in the years since 2021 alleged aggressive behaviour, Uber decided to sack the driver after two 21-year-old female customers claimed he called them “pretty girls” and spoke of conspiracy theories of being stalked and bugged. In the September 2025 incident, the women alleged he asked his ChatGPT to recite to them his employment history and reasons he was fired from his previous job, and that he asked the AI chatbot to give them his medical history, including that he had been sent to a “psych ward”.



After he was told about the complaint, the driver sent Uber about 82 documents outlining why he should keep his job, including one titled The Anatomy of a Systemic Attack: A Forensic Analysis and Accountability Report on the Digital and Institutional Persecution of [the driver’s name]. Related Article Exclusive

Unfair dismissal Sacked worker forced to pay for using ‘plain wrong’ AI in landmark case Uber proceeded to axe his account. He then sought to overturn the decision via the Fair Work Commission’s unfair deactivation code – an unfair-dismissal-style appeals avenue for gig economy workers introduced by Labor last year. He was unsuccessful, with the commission finding Uber had complied with the code and acted to protect rider safety. The driver then appealed this decision to the full bench of the commission – a panel of at least three members put together to hear significant matters or appeals – which shot down his claims alleging errors of fact and improperly handled evidence in his initial case. Hours after his appeal was refused, the driver “began sending lengthy emails to the commission complaining about the decision”. “He was asked to refrain from sending emails – a request he ignored. He sent many more emails,” the full bench noted. “It is clear that his emails were drafted by AI … They are, by and large, incoherent,” it found.



Among the documents with which he flooded the commission was an application to revoke the full bench’s refusal of his appeal, and for it to be considered by a different panel. This request was thrown out because he failed to argue mistakes in the previous decision, instead relaying his initial arguments about his overall deactivation. “The directions sought … are largely unintelligible,” the full bench said. “There is much to be said for the view that what has perpetuated the present absurdity is a large [AI] language model.” Federal Court Justice Nye Perram Dissatisfied, the driver then went to the Federal Court, seeking to quash the commission full bench’s decision against him. However, Justice Nye Perram dismissed his application, finding he did not establish judicial errors. One of his arguments also focused on a procedural fairness claim related to his initial unfair deactivation case before the full bench hearing – a decision the Federal Court was not reviewing. “[His] underlying argument is therefore quasi-legal nonsense,” Perram said. “The large language model which [he] has very properly disclosed that he utilised in the preparation of the submissions is the source of this nonsense. “Whilst this reads well, what it is saying does not make any sense,” he said.



Related Article Workplace How AI is helping workers take on their bosses in workplace disputes Perram said the driver’s repeated legal actions relying on AI “raises several red flags as to whether [he] may be a vexatious litigant” and should be barred from filing new lawsuits. “However, whilst the proceeding is misconceived from top to bottom it is also contained in a single dispute with Uber and there is much to be said for the view that what has perpetuated the present absurdity is a large language model,” the judge said. “This is a case which was commenced without any reasonable cause,” Perram said. The driver has been ordered to pay all of Uber’s legal costs. The rise of artificial intelligence has led to an explosion of nonsensical Fair Work Commission cases lodged by workers against their employers, generating frustration among judges and tribunal members and routinely backfiring on workers who are left to foot their employer’s legal costs.



In a presentation to the Victorian Bar Association earlier this year, Fair Work Commission president Justice Adam Hatcher said it has become clear that the tribunal’s operations are being “significantly disrupted” by the widespread availability and use of AI tools. World.title: ‘Turncoat town’: Liberal senator defects to One Nation
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOne Nation ‘Turncoat town’: Liberal senator defects to One Nation Brittany Busch and Michelle Griffin Updated November 26, 2026 — 7:44am ,first published 5:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Liberal senator Leah Blyth has joined One Nation, one year to the day after Barnaby Joyce quit the Nationals to defect to Pauline Hanson’s party. The South Australian had only been appointed to the Senate in February 2025 to replace retiring leading moderate Simon Birmingham, and was not expected to secure a winnable spot on the Liberal ballot for next year’s election. The opposition spokeswoman for defence infrastructure and former state president said in a joint press release with Hanson on Thursday morning that she believed One Nation was the only viable choice. One Nation defector Leah Blyth. Alex Ellinghausen “The Albanese government is running this country into the ground. But I can no longer in good conscience tell Australians that the Liberal Party can save this country,” Blyth said.



“One Nation has never shied away from confronting the uncomfortable truths facing our nation. They are the only party with the bold ideas needed to turn this country around.” Hanson said Blyth had approached her to defect, and that the decision would resonate with former Liberal supporters who felt the party had abandoned them. Pauline Hanson told reporters she would hold a press conference later on Thursday morning. Dominic Lorrimer The minor party leader had teased the defection in a video released on Wednesday night showing her preparing a steak in a sandwich press, as she had done for Joyce a year previously. “I have never, ever, ever approached Leah or any other member of parliament here to come across to One Nation,” she told 2GB on Thursday morning, saying Blyth had had a “gutful” of Coalition infighting.



“She said, ‘I don’t leave my husband and three children to come to this place and feel that I’m wasting my time being away from them’,” Hanson said. “She said, ‘I want to make a difference. I got into this to make a difference to the people.’ She said, ‘You, your party, your team, that’s what you’re constantly doing.’ She said, ‘You’re not frightened to call it out. You stand and fight all the time.’ She said, ‘That’s what I want to be a part of.’” The defection is a blow to Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, who had overseen 10 months of relative stability in the Coalition and had told his party room on Tuesday that they could win the next election as Labor struggles with grim economic results and the fallout from tax hikes introduced at the last federal budget. Blyth’s former Coalition colleagues were scathing on Thursday. Federal party president Tony Abbott said Blyth had left because she lost an internal vote.



“This has got nothing whatsoever to do with principle, nothing whatsoever to do with the national interest. I think the public will see through what this is,” he said in a video posted to Instagram. Blyth’s time as a Liberal senator has been marked by the internal struggles of the South Australian branch and her break with hard-right powerbroker Senator Alex Antic, who seized the presidency from her in September. Conservatives in Canberra have long feared that Antic himself wants closer ties with One Nation. Antic was pictured shaking hands and smiling with Hanson in the Senate in September, and has never ruled out defecting to One Nation when asked. Shortly after winning the presidency in a fight so bitter the federal executive considered intervening, Antic told podcaster Reality Check Radio he believed the Liberals and One Nation would need “some sort of understanding in some format” to form government.



Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume denied internal divisions were to blame, and said the move surprised everyone because Blyth had never raised her discontent in the party room. “She wasn’t a big contributor to the party room,” the senator said as she arrived at parliament for the final sitting day of the year. Nationals leader Matt Canavan said One Nation was turning into “turncoat town” and Blyth’s defection smacked of self-interest. “Leah went to the election last year supporting net zero. She didn’t oppose the hate speech laws earlier like we did, the Nationals,” Canavan told Radio National.



“To turn around now, a few months later, say ‘my principles and policies are more aligned with One Nation’ – I mean, give me a break. Smacks of self-interest to me. Good luck to her.” Canavan insisted he was not concerned about any further defections, but when asked whether he had talked anyone out of leaving the Coalition, conceded it had been a tough time. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership ‘He used me’: Nationals veteran accuses Barnaby Joyce of hypocrisy and misleading party faithful “There was always going to be a bit of bloodletting over the past year or so. But as I say, I’ve tried very hard to keep people together.” Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie said the Coalition would not be distracted by Blyth’s move and accused her of acting in self-interest.



“Australians are struggling with some really significant and serious challenges, and people deciding to defect for their own personal political reasons is pretty sort of self-interested,” she told Nine’s Today. Blyth’s defection brings the number of One Nation senators to five, with two MPs in the lower house. While Hanson had regularly fanned speculation throughout the year that other members of parliament had approached her to join the party, Blyth is the first federal politician to make the switch since Joyce. David Farley became the party’s second MP in May, when he won the Farrer byelection following the resignation of former opposition leader Sussan Ley. One Nation’s popularity has surged in all the polls this year and was the first preference of one in four voters in the latest Resolve Political Monitor. But Hanson’s party has also attracted closer scrutiny. The party’s general manager, appointed in February to professionalise the party, has gone on leave and may not return to Pauline Hanson’s outfit after claims he downplayed sexual assault and lied in his CV. Labor frontbencher Pat Conroy said Blyth’s defection revealed the disunity of those in the Liberal Party, who were “eating each other alive”.



“I think the sort of hatchet job they’ve now put on about her, about how she wasn’t making her contribution, well, she was in their shadow ministry, so obviously they thought highly enough of her,” he told Radio National. World.title: Darwin’s waterfront park is more than a green space, it’s a trip through time
World.content:
InspirationNorthern Territory Darwin’s waterfront park is more than a green space, it’s a trip through time Brian Johnston November 26, 2026 — 7:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This article is part of Traveller’s guide to the Best of the Northern Territory. See all stories .

The obvious and glamorous in travel can distract us with razzle-dazzle. Yet modestly presented attractions sometimes relate astonishing human stories if only we seek them out, as I discover on my fourth visit to Darwin. The city has several museums that address its bombing in 1942, complete with salvaged planes, talking holograms and virtual-reality recreations. The Bombing of Darwin exhibition is excellent. Bicentennial Park is not merely a pretty green space, it’s a journey through history. Alamy This time, however, I discover Bicentennial Park, and realise that old-fashioned sightseeing is sometimes best. No virtual reality or swelling music to sidetrack me. I stand and read signboards as blossoms twirl from trees, and soon become absorbed. Between Darwin’s Indigenous art, Crocosaurus Cove and Mindil Beach Sunset Market, I’m glad I’ve taken a walk in the park. This larrikin city tells various great Australian stories, but none are more compelling than the one recounted on its modest signboards.



They provide a detailed account of Darwin’s bombing by Japanese forces on February 19, 1942, but in ways I haven’t heard before. What first strikes me is their considered criticism of Australia’s political and military decision-making. 



Bicentennial Park shows that war is no abstraction but a lived experience. Other signboards recount the thoughts of an army nurse, a Chinese-Australian businessman, and Tiwi Islander who took a crash-landed Japanese pilot prisoner. I read about a cable the telegraph supervisor sent off, informing distant politicians that bombs were “falling like hailstones.” He was one of nine people killed after taking shelter in a makeshift trench near the postmaster’s residence after a direct bomb hit. I look up from this board and the Arafura Sea, from which the bombers came, is pale blue as steel. Bicentennial Park is a long green strip between low ocean cliffs and the city centre, and one of Darwin’s most pleasant places. Its wiggly pathways are popular with joggers. Picnickers flop underneath banyan trees. Locals read books on benches beneath cascades of bougainvillea, lipstick-pink against emerald lawns. Yet I’m always drawn back to more signboards, which run north-westwards chronologically. Something else that sets them apart is that they present war as a visceral experience. No sugarcoating history’s pill here.



“Incendiaries slammed into the galley and amidships, creating fire and more smoke,” recorded Dallis Widick, a lieutenant aboard USS Peary. “The men from the forward fire room, burnt and injured, climbed up the airshafts.” Related Article Northern Territory The two must-do day trips from Australia’s smallest, wildest capital Owen Griffith, an observer on nearby HMAS Platypus, reported of USS Peary that “she finally pointed her nose up to the sky and disappeared in a ball of black oily smoke with her machine guns firing to the bitter end.” The harbour was aflame with burning oil. The descriptions are cinematographic, but no images or sound effects distract me. There’s only USS Peary’s salvaged naval gun, pointing to the spot where the warship sank. And the Darwin Cenotaph, which stands where an anti-aircraft battery was mounted. There are many memorial plaques too. But mostly, there are only old-fashioned words from eyewitness accounts about the day Darwin was flattened, eleven ships sunk, 30 aircraft destroyed, and at least 235 people killed.



They remind me of the exhibit in the excellent Museum and Art Gallery of the Northern Territory about Cyclone Tracy, which wrecked Darwin again in 1974. This city knows how to tell thumping stories from personal perspectives. Slow down, take your time, and Darwin has depth beneath its more immediate attractions. DETAILS Vibe Hotel Darwin Waterfront has large, pleasant rooms and a great location on Darwin’s waterfront dining hub. Rooms from $154 a night. Bicentennial Park is a short walk away. See vibehotels.com; northernterritory.com The writer was a guest of Coral Expeditions.

World.content:
Updated WorldAfricaTragedy ‘No time to get out’: At least 31 killed, dozens of vehicles burned in Egypt fuel tanker crash Enas Alashray and Yomna Ehab Updated November 26, 2026 — 7:22am ,first published 6:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Cairo: At least 31 people have been killed and 21 wounded in a fire after a vehicle carrying petrol products overturned on a major ring road in Cairo, Egypt, authorities said. The fire broke out above a tunnel in Warraq district, just north of central Cairo, the public prosecution said. Preliminary estimates found that 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles, had been burned, it said, adding that casualty figures and damage were still being assessed. Loading The prosecution ordered DNA samples to be taken from the bodies of victims who had not yet been identified to establish their identities. Thirty-nine ambulances took part in rescue operations, the Health Ministry said.



Videos circulating on social media showed thick plumes of smoke billowing from the scene. Reuters verified the location by matching the buildings and road layout to archive and satellite imagery of the area. The date was confirmed through the original file’s metadata. The date was also confirmed through local media reports and a statement from the Health Ministry. Burned cars are seen as firefighters extinguish blazes from a deadly fire on a road in Giza, Egypt. AP Photo/Mohammed Salah “The cars were charred, with people inside them. They did not have time to get out,” Ali Youssef, who was at the scene, said. “The fire burned the vehicles and the people inside.” Ahmed Sameer, who was stuck in traffic as the road was blocked after the accident, saw the fuel truck and many cars on fire. He said he saw at least eight bodies being removed from burned cars.



“It was a huge fire; the cars got stuck together because of the fire,” he told AP, describing the fear and panic that followed. “It was a shocking scene.” The ring road connects key highways across Greater Cairo, linking the governorates of Cairo, Giza and Qalyubia. Citing local media, the London Telegraph reported that a truck overturned after a high-voltage electricity cable fell in front of it, causing the driver to lose control. The vehicle then crossed the concrete median barrier and rolled over, starting a fire which spread to passing cars. Reuters footage from the scene in Giza showed firefighting vehicles, charred cars and minibuses, burnt motorcycles and debris scattered across the major ring road, while people and security personnel inspected the aftermath and a bulldozer moved damaged vehicles.



Rescue workers pulled people from burning cars as hundreds of people gathered at the scene. Local media reported that firefighters had brought the blaze under control. Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. Loading Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the 15 injured were taken to a nearby hospital and that he would head to the scene himself. He said the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further. Deadly traffic accidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.



Egypt has expanded its road network in recent years, building highways and bridges under a broader infrastructure programme aimed at easing congestion and accommodating rapid population growth and urban expansion. The projects have improved traffic flow in some areas, but road safety concerns persist. Crowds gathered at the scene in Giza. AP Photo/Mohammed Salah The number of people killed in road accidents rose 10.8 per cent to 5829 in 2025 from 5260 a year earlier, according to the state statistics agency CAPMAS. In January, 21 people were killed, and 16 were injured in a massive multi-car pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef. World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaMining ‘Very dark’: Rescuers battle tough conditions in race to save 17 trapped miners Zach Hope and Karuni Rompies Updated November 26, 2026 — 9:19am ,first published 10:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Singapore/Jakarta: Indonesian rescuers have now pulled nine bodies from a flooded gold mine south of Jakarta and are struggling to reach at least 17 other fossickers who have been trapped since Monday. The abandoned mine’s terraced shaft was so narrow and slippery teams could not immediately get down oxygen tanks, according to Desiana Kartika Bahari, the head of the Jakarta branch of the nation’s search and rescue agency, BASARNAS. A rescue worker entering the narrow passage, which may stretch 100 metres below the ground. BASARNAS “We also need to bring lamps as it is very dark – and right now the rain is pouring in heavily,” she said. She said it was still unclear if diving experts would be needed from overseas, like in this year’s Laos cave rescue and the Thailand rescue of the Wild Boars youth football team in 2018.



The mine used to be operated by state-owned company PT Antam, Desiana said. The fossickers were searching for gold illegally in one of the “thousands” of closed shafts in Bogor, West Java, when the nearby Ciseureuh River overflowed. She said the shaft was possibly 100 metres deep. Rescuers prepare to put the body of miner recovered from the flooded gold mine into an ambulance. BASARNAS via AP “We don’t know for sure [how many people were down the mine] but we talked to illegal miners here and they gave 26 names, so maybe there are 26 people,” she said. “We don’t know for sure because they are illegal. They are quite stubborn, these illegal miners, because they have been warned frequently for not doing what they are doing.”



Monday night and most of Tuesday went by before rescue crews from Bogor arrived and attempted to pump the water out. “In fact, they found pumps inside the pit believed to be belonging to the illegal miners. It means these people know that it is dangerous to go down there,” Desiana said. The first three bodies were recovered on Wednesday afternoon at a depth of between 30 and 40 metres, according to a press release from BASARNAS. The toll continued to rise through the afternoon and evening as rescuers moved through the shaft. Rescuers are working through tough conditions. Police told Kompas TV they were investigating who might have financed or directed the illicit mining. Authorities in Indonesia have struggled to contain such operations, often carried out by impoverished family breadwinners risking their lives to find scraps of gold left behind by departed mining companies.

Related Article Exclusive

Fashion retail ‘It was our baby’: General Pants isn’t the same trend-setting denim store its founders built AI stocks lost ground for a second day following Monday’s relief rally over the surprise reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Stocks have been generally falling since setting an all-time high last month as worries grow that AI stock prices have grown unjustifiably high. The market turnaround came as some of the biggest tech companies bounced back from steep drops. Nvidia, which was down more than 9 per cent at one point, closed with a 3.9 per cent loss. Broadcom, which had dropped more than 6 per cent, ended just 0.1 per cent lower, while Microsoft came back from a more than 3 per cent slide to finish down 1.2 per cent. There were some gainers among tech stocks: Meta climbed 3.4 per cent and Salesforce rose 2 per cent.



Gains in financial services stocks also helped temper the market’s losses. Visa rose 1.8 per cent, Mastercard gained 1.9 per cent and American Express rose 1.2 per cent. Anthropic bounced back from an early drop to close with a 1.1 per cent gain. Still, since soaring to $US115 per share on the day it became the first major frontier lab to go public, Anthropic shares have tumbled by about 28 per cent. Roughly three quarters of the stocks in the S&P 500 rose, although the pullback in technology stocks kept the index in the red. Technology companies, particularly those focused on AI, have large market values that give them a dominant influence over whether major indexes rise or fall. Nvidia is among the most valuable companies on Wall Street and its surge on Monday led a tech sector rally. It is now one of the biggest weights pushing the market lower. The S&P 500 index is down 5.2 per cent for November, after losing some ground in October and September.



“At this point, between the AI angst and the newly announced tariffs, it doesn’t look like the Santa Claus Rally is in store for us this year,” said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management, in a research note. Questions about Nvidia’s corporate governance, as well as the influence of a US president who owns millions of dollars’ worth of shares in the company, have added to concerns surrounding the artificial intelligence sector. Relief over Huang’s return as CEO is fading because of worries that AI might not produce enough profit to justify the large investments and stock values. That dynamic is running up against stubbornly high inflation. The latest update on inflation showed that prices rose at a more aggressive 3.8 per cent rate in October from the same period last year, and followed a 3.6 per cent rate in September. The data is from the Federal Reserve’s preferred measure of inflation, the personal consumption expenditures price index. Aside from potentially stifling economic growth, high inflation could mean higher interest rates, with the Fed likely to raise its benchmark interest rate at its December policy meeting to try to tame inflation. The rate of inflation is well above the central bank’s target of 2 per cent. The economy has been resilient, though, even as inflation squeezes households and businesses and consumers grow increasingly anxious about spending and finances. The government said that the economy grew even faster in the July-September quarter than previously estimated, with growth revised upward to a 4.3 per cent annual rate, the fastest in three years.



Much of the spending that is driving the economy, though, has been from large tech firms building out AI infrastructure and from upper-income households. There are signs poorer Americans are relying more on credit to sustain their spending. Higher oil prices, fuelled by the US war with Iran and its impact on the world’s oil supply, have also contributed to inflation. The price of a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 3.5 per cent to settle at $US94.61 on Wednesday. The price has swung between $US72 and $US114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. Energy companies mostly gained ground Wednesday, including a 1.1 per cent rise for Chevron. The wide-ranging and often uncertain US trade conflict with much of the world also added to rising costs. The US plans to hike tariffs on China, the European Union and other trading partners after the US Supreme Court struck down broader tariffs that were set last year. Businesses tend to pass along some or all of the cost of tariffs to consumers. Anger over stubbornly high prices was a factor in pushing voters to punish Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats. Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.87 per cent from 4.91 per cent late Tuesday.



All told, the S&P 500 fell 18.31 points to 7,182.78. The Dow gained 164.25 points to 50,182.95, and the Nasdaq dropped 147.73 points to 23,585.80. Related Article Opinion

AI Trump saved his billionaire mate but the walls may start closing in Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Markets fell throughout Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi lost 6.2 per cent as Samsung Electronics fell 9.9 per cent and SK Hynix plummeted 11.1 per cent. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8 per cent. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group slumped 14.8 per cent. US financial markets will be closed Thursday for Thanksgiving. “I don’t believe that people join One Nation for that reason. They join One Nation because they are a conservative, they have a conservative view of the world and they want to be part of what is a genuinely conservative party,” he told Radio National.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce. Alex Ellinghausen

World.title: ‘Quasi-legal nonsense’: Judge scolds Uber driver’s AI spiral
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceAI ‘Quasi-legal nonsense’: Judge scolds Uber driver’s AI spiral Elias Visontay November 26, 2026 — 8:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A federal court judge has berated a sacked Uber driver who relied on AI-generated “quasi-legal nonsense” to formulate his appeal seeking to get his job back, despite AI having failed him at earlier attempts to be reinstated. The driver - who must now foot the bill for Uber’s legal costs - had been fighting to overturn his deactivation from the rideshare giant after it booted him from the app in September 2025 following four complaints against him from customers. An Uber driver has been scolded for his repeated reliance on AI in his legal quest to get his job back. Marija Ercegovac / Stephen Kiprillis While three prior complaints received in the years since 2021 alleged aggressive behaviour, Uber decided to sack the driver after two 21-year-old female customers claimed he called them “pretty girls” and spoke of conspiracy theories of being stalked and bugged. In the September 2025 incident, the women alleged he asked his ChatGPT to recite to them his employment history and reasons he was fired from his previous job, and that he asked the AI chatbot to give them his medical history, including that he had been sent to a “psych ward”.



After he was told about the complaint, the driver sent Uber about 82 documents outlining why he should keep his job, including one titled The Anatomy of a Systemic Attack: A Forensic Analysis and Accountability Report on the Digital and Institutional Persecution of [the driver’s name]. Related Article Exclusive

Unfair dismissal Sacked worker forced to pay for using ‘plain wrong’ AI in landmark case Uber proceeded to axe his account. He then sought to overturn the decision via the Fair Work Commission’s unfair deactivation code – an unfair-dismissal-style appeals avenue for gig economy workers introduced by Labor last year. He was unsuccessful, with the commission finding Uber had complied with the code and acted to protect rider safety. The driver then appealed this decision to the full bench of the commission – a panel of at least three members put together to hear significant matters or appeals – which shot down his claims alleging errors of fact and improperly handled evidence in his initial case. Hours after his appeal was refused, the driver “began sending lengthy emails to the commission complaining about the decision”. “He was asked to refrain from sending emails – a request he ignored. He sent many more emails,” the full bench noted. “It is clear that his emails were drafted by AI … They are, by and large, incoherent,” it found.



Among the documents with which he flooded the commission was an application to revoke the full bench’s refusal of his appeal, and for it to be considered by a different panel. This request was thrown out because he failed to argue mistakes in the previous decision, instead relaying his initial arguments about his overall deactivation. “The directions sought … are largely unintelligible,” the full bench said. “There is much to be said for the view that what has perpetuated the present absurdity is a large [AI] language model.” Federal Court Justice Nye Perram Dissatisfied, the driver then went to the Federal Court, seeking to quash the commission full bench’s decision against him. However, Justice Nye Perram dismissed his application, finding he did not establish judicial errors. One of his arguments also focused on a procedural fairness claim related to his initial unfair deactivation case before the full bench hearing – a decision the Federal Court was not reviewing. “[His] underlying argument is therefore quasi-legal nonsense,” Perram said. “The large language model which [he] has very properly disclosed that he utilised in the preparation of the submissions is the source of this nonsense. “Whilst this reads well, what it is saying does not make any sense,” he said.



Related Article Workplace How AI is helping workers take on their bosses in workplace disputes Perram said the driver’s repeated legal actions relying on AI “raises several red flags as to whether [he] may be a vexatious litigant” and should be barred from filing new lawsuits. “However, whilst the proceeding is misconceived from top to bottom it is also contained in a single dispute with Uber and there is much to be said for the view that what has perpetuated the present absurdity is a large language model,” the judge said. “This is a case which was commenced without any reasonable cause,” Perram said. The driver has been ordered to pay all of Uber’s legal costs. The rise of artificial intelligence has led to an explosion of nonsensical Fair Work Commission cases lodged by workers against their employers, generating frustration among judges and tribunal members and routinely backfiring on workers who are left to foot their employer’s legal costs.



In a presentation to the Victorian Bar Association earlier this year, Fair Work Commission president Justice Adam Hatcher said it has become clear that the tribunal’s operations are being “significantly disrupted” by the widespread availability and use of AI tools.
