World.title: Farmlands appoints new board chair in wake of AgriZeroNZ investment backlash
World.content:
South Otago dairy and beef farmer, chartered accountant and shareholder director Will Clarke has been appointed as Farmlands' new chair, having won 87 percent of the vote at this week's AGM.

But the rural co-op's new chair and board has work to do to win over some of its more than 81,000 farmer shareholders, following pushback against its earlier decision to invest in $1 million in AgriZeroNZ over three years.

About 200 people attended the meeting in person, as well as 700 more online. There were 4554 votes cast, from 5.6 percent of all shareholders.

Some shareholders expressed concerns about the lack of consultation and widening scope of the co-op's spending. Others questioned the merit of investing in emissions reductions tools during an over three-hour long meeting in Gore on Tuesday night.

It comes just days after former Farmlands chair Rob Hewett - also the chair of AgriZeroNZ - resigned. A shareholder proposal to remove him was cited as a "significant factor", alongside personal attacks online.

Not all shareholders were opposed to the AgriZeroNZ investment, with one questioning why Farmlands hadn't invested more in methane emissions reductions tools, and another saying shareholders were talking about an investment worth $12 split equally.

However, a resolution asking the board to explore options for exiting Farmlands' existing investment in AgriZeroNZ and to pursue an exit if commercially reasonable passed with almost 60 percent of the vote.

The resolution was non-binding, meaning it was a recommendation to the board and the board will take it under advisement.

Clarke said the board would independently review shareholder communication, processes around the AGM, and consideration of shareholder proposal.

He said the board would report back to shareholders though this would likely take longer than the three-month timeframe put forward in the proposal, as the board's first meeting is in February.

"We intend to take the learnings from this AGM as an opportunity to work more closely with our shareholders to build a stronger future for Farmlands together. We are a co-operative with almost 65 years of history, and we want to ensure we are ready for the next generation. We want to be a trusted partner that our shareholders can rely on."

Another resolution to require shareholder approval by special resolution "for further investments in AgriZeroNZ or related entities, or in other organisations whose dominant purpose is to develop or supply products that reduce methane by altering livestock digestion" received 54 percent percent of the votes, short of the 75 percent threshold required as a special resolution and did not pass.

Laurie Patterson, of Groundswell and a proponent of an earlier resolution to see Hewett removed from the board, withdrawn following his resignation, told those at the AGM he made no allegation of misconduct of improper decision making.

He said it wasn't about Hewett's character but whether the dual chair roles were an appropriate arrangement for the co-op.

Clarke thanked shareholders for "engaging constructively" with the board on their proposals. He was encouraged to see shareholder participation increase to almost 6 percent, "a significant rise from prior years".

He also thanked Hewett for his many years as the board's chair.

World.title: The floating classroom teaching kids to protect their environment
World.content:
By Karaima Fai'ai, RNZ Pacific

Children on the remote Fijian island of Totoya in the Lau group have been learning from their elders aboard a sailing canoe as part of a programme bringing traditional knowledge back into Pacific Islands classrooms.

The environmental education programme, run by Conservation International, brings teachers and knowledge-holders together to design lessons that reflect their island's culture and environment.

Earlier this month, 45 students from Totoya's four villages took part in a pilot of the programme, weaving food baskets, building a model of their island and sailing on the Uto ni Yalo, a double-hulled voyaging canoe.

Regional project manager Catherina Bolinga said one of the elders on board was the last surviving sailor from Totoya.

"It was really good to see him show the kids and name the parts of the [canoe] while we were on board," she said.

School children on board Uto Nia Yalo. Supplied/ KPHC

Bolinga said the same elder taught the children to weave baskets, which they then filled with food and carried onto the canoe.

She said elders told her it was the first time they had taught the younger generation to weave, because they usually did the weaving themselves.

Totoya District School head teacher Jone Draunidalo said the pilot has changed how his teachers planned to run their classes.

"Experiential teaching is very important, and we have chosen to use that teaching method," he said.

Draunidalo said lessons can be taken outside the classroom, such as measuring the school playground to learn about area and perimeter, which helps students develop confidence.

"So come next year, we will begin to implement what we have learned from those three days."

School children learning to weave food basket as part of the environmental education programme, run by Conservation International. Supplied/ KPHC

Conservation International Fiji director Semisi Meo said the programme is about more than teaching children about nature.

"Knowledge survives only when it is practiced," he said.

Meo said island communities in Fiji are facing climate change, declining fisheries and the gradual loss of traditional knowledge as people migrate and lifestyles change.

"A society can lose biodiversity and cultural knowledge simultaneously because both rely on the transmission of information across generations."

He said children became noticeably more engaged when lessons were connected to their own island.

"When a community begins teaching itself again, one can reasonably conclude that something important is working."

The programme is modelled on Guardians, a project in Samoa launched in 2018, that used a voyaging canoe as a classroom to teach children about looking after the ocean.

Its founder, Conservation International senior director of marine heritage Schannel van Dijken, said voyaging knowledge was not being taught in Pacific schools.

"These canoes were actually our floating classrooms," he said.

Van Dijken said Pacific ancestors had to understand navigation, plants, food and biodiversity to voyage across the ocean and return.

"These were our astronauts," he said.

"You can't teach this intimate understanding of how to live on an island and how to navigate and how to voyage, in a classroom. It needs to be outside. It needs to be experiential."

The Samoan lessons have since been included as supplementary material in the country's primary school curriculum.

The approach is now being adapted for Fiji and the Cook Islands, funded by New Zealand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade through the Manaaki Fund and by the Global Environment Facility.

Van Dijken said those projects end in the middle of next year, and the focus now is finding new partners.

Aotearoa project portfolio manager Dhaneshree Ndebele said the aim is for the lessons to become part of school curriculums rather than a one-off.

"It's been a very colonial curriculum so far," she said.

Ndebele said bringing traditional concepts such as ra'ui, a Cook Islands practice of closing an area so it can recover, into school subjects gives students a reason to care.

"A lot of the time, they see the sign there and they don't know what the sign is for," she said.

"When you start working in an experiential manner, and kids start to see, 'Oh my gosh, pollution affects the fish like this. This affects our food.' They're more likely to care and to say, 'Oh, now I understand why my elders put a [ra'ui] on this place.'"

The programme has already been piloted on Moala in Fiji and on Mauke, Mangaia and Atiu in the Cook Islands.

Matuku, the last of the three Fijian pilot islands, is due to host the programme early next year.

World.title: French tourist Maëlle Favregros' fatal fall in popular alpine area prompts safety warnings
World.content:
Social media is leading some tourists to take risks and venture into the outdoors unprepared, a coroner says.

French tourist Maëlle Favregros died from blood loss after falling while crossing slippery, rocky terrain near the Brewster Glacier in Mount Aspiring National Park in February last year, findings released on Thursday said.

The 23-year-old was not wearing tramping boots or on a managed track and had discovered the Brewster Glacier trip on AllTrails.

Coroner Alexandra Cunninghame urged trampers to plan their routes using official sources - including the Department of Conservation (DOC) and Plan My Walk - be aware of hazards, stay on official marked routes and have the necessary skills and gear for alpine trips.

There were seven search and rescues in the area last year, six in 2024, seven in 2023, as well as another death in 2020.

Mountain Safety Council chief executive Mike Daisley said the coroner's findings aimed to stop such tragedies from repeating.

"Maëlle's death occurred in terrain beyond the managed DOC track network in an alpine environment where significant natural hazards exist and where visitor judgement, preparation and decision-making are critical factors in maintaining safety," he said.

Mountain Safety Council chief executive Mike Daisley. Supplied / Sarah Topliff

The Brewster Glacier area was reasonably quiet and not many people explored it until about six years ago when suddenly there was a spike in visits and a lot of interest, Daisley said.

Trampers should use social media for ideas but not for preparation, he said.

"Social media in itself is not the problem. Use that for inspiration, but don't consider that your plan. Do some investigating and find out about the environment that you've decided just because you've seen a picture of it, and it's great to be inspired by it, but do your research."

The Brewster Glacier is accessed via the steep Brewster Track which climbs about 1000 metres over about 2.8 kilometres.

An interagency group had been set up in April 2024 to help raise awareness of the hazards in the area after a rise in people getting into trouble.

It prompted a new Brewster Track safety video to be released last November highlighting the hazards.

The Department of Conservation carried out a review of Favregros' death and had made several changes to boost awareness of the hazards.

They included installing new signs at the carpark and at Brewster Hut warning of the risks, targeted social media advertising about safety and planning for the track, and working with AllTrails so people were aware of the hazards, risks and skills needed.

"The increasing use has been mirrored by an increase in visitor incidents requiring search and rescue involvement, mainly associated with visitors getting into difficulty when attempting to access areas off the DOC managed experience, such as Mt Armstrong and the Brewster Glacier," the review said.

Coroner Alexandra Cunninghame. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Brewster Hut was traditionally used as a base for alpine adventures and the department said it had been managed with the expectation visitors had the necessary skills, experience and capability.

The area had recently attracted "much lower skilled" visitors who wanted to visit Brewster Glacier, partly due to a surge in social media and visitor numbers, the department said.

The coroner did not make any specific recommendations to the department, saying it had already boosted safety messaging which would hopefully decrease the chance of similar deaths.

A long-awaited trip gone wrong

Favregros and her friend Arthur Boutillier had pitched their tents near the hut after walking up Brewster Track on 21 February 2025, the coroner's findings said.

They set out to explore the lake near the glacier about 5.30pm.

She was wearing shoes, not tramping boots, and carried a backpack and hiking poles.

Boutillier said his friend had grown up in the mountains and had experience hiking and trail running.

He described the area as "all ice and open rock" after arriving above the lake about 6.45pm, before they decided to get closer.

Boutillier took the route closer to the lake shore, while Favregros hiked up a long escarpment, where water flowed through cracks and moss and slime had attached on to smooth rock.

Brewster glacier. RNZ / Claire Concannon

Boutillier told the coroner they were tired but Favregros was happy to be there as she had been looking forward to the glacier trip for a long time.

"For me she was so [taken] by the glacier, she was always talking about, that she had been less vigilant about what she was getting into," he told the coroner.

Then he heard a scream and ran to find Favregros lying on the ground in a patch of water.

She lost consciousness and he tried to carry her, putting her into the recovery position when he could not take her further.

There was no reception and he realised he would have to leave her to go for help but told police she died before he left.

He ran back, taking about 40 minutes to get to the hut while trying to use his phone to call for help.

He called police on 111 at 7.48pm.

A helicopter was sent but low cloud initially prevented the crew from landing.

They were able to retrieve her body when the weather cleared.

World.title: Meridian invests in massive Southland data centre project
World.content:
Meridian Energy is investing around $55 million in Datagrid, the company behind a large 300MW data centre development in Southland.

The investment will see Meridian take an 11.27 percent equity stake in Datagrid Holding Group NZ Ltd.

Meridian CEO Mike Roan has also been appointed as a director of Datagrid.

Datagrid holds a resource consent to build the Southland data centre, although it remains subject to a final investment decision by Datagrid.

In addition to the investment, the two companies have signed a 140MW power purchase agreement.

Meridian said this agreement, if called on, would run for 15 years, beginning sometime between July 2028 and January 2029.

The agreement would be subject to the Electricity Authority providing clearance under its Materially Large Contracts regime.

Roan said backing this projects allowed Meridian to make a further contribution to the Southland region while supporting broader economic growth.

"Meridian has worked with Datagrid since 2020, and by directly investing we are supporting employment and economic development in a region where we have a deep and long-standing relationship.

"The project also represents a significant source of long-term electricity demand, further supporting our ongoing investment in new renewable generation."

The investment matches a similar one made by Mercury.

World.title: NRL beefs up hip-drop penalties but sticks with set restarts
World.content:
Players will be automatically sin-binned for hip-drop tackles in 2027 as the NRL moves to drive the practice out of the game.

Two months after Nathan Cleary's horrific leg injury in Penrith's preliminary final, the league has warned it will come down hard on the illegal play.

In a move discussed by the league's rule panel on Monday, players will face the sin bin for any contact deemed illegal by the bunker or referees.

How set restarts are dominating the NRL season After three rounds of the NRL season the increase in set restarts has left coaches, players and fans alike more confused than ever about the specifics behind rugby league's most controversial rule change.

Stiffer penalties could also apply at the judiciary, with an understanding such tackles are hard to pick up on the run when a player is not injured.

The NRL is expected to circulate videos in coming months to help clubs understand what will be classed as an illegal play.

The crackdown comes after Cleary, Mitch Kenny, Isaiah Iongi, J'maine Hopgood, Tolu Koula and Reece Walsh all suffered serious injury in 2026 as a result of hip-drop tackles.

The NRL adopted a similar approach to head contact in 2021, resulting in a record number of players being sin-binned or sent off.

The latest move is not expected to have the same impact, given the comparatively low number of illegal hip-drop tackles.

The NRL will trial new kick contest rules in the 2027 pre-season. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

The approach was one of several key issues discussed over recent days, with the NRL largely sticking to the same laws as 2026.

A new kick contest interpretation will be trialled in the preseason, with minor knock-ons to be overlooked in aerial contests.

If it is approved for the NRL campaign, the bunker will not intervene in a genuine aerial contest when two players make contact with the ball at the same time.

Knock-ons will still be called if a player catches the ball and loses possession before regathering.

The NRL has ruled out introducing last year's trialled kick-off rule for the regular season, where the team who conceded points could decide whether to receive.

The NRL will not introduce the kick-off rule it trialled last year. (AAP Photos: Jeremy Ng)

A brainchild of Wayne Bennett, the rule was trialled late last year but was widely talked down by fans and players.

There is still some scope for it to be tested again in pre-season, but head office have ruled out using it through the 2027 campaign.

The NRL has ruled out changing the contentious set-restart rule, with six-agains still to be awarded across 80 metres of the field.

Prior to last season, teams were awarded penalties rather than set restarts for infringements as they came out of their own 40-metre zone.

That area of the field was decreased to the 20-metre zone last year, leading to a sharp uptick in set restarts and margins at the start of the season.

Several high-profile players had been critical of the set restart rule at the end of last season, but no changes are expected for 2027.

AAP

World.title: 'All-time' Langer spray shut down ball tampering after Sandpapergate
World.content:
A member of the 2018 Cape Town squad was behind a suggestion to use lollies on the ball in the United Arab Emirates on Australia's first tour after the sandpaper scandal, Usman Khawaja says.

Khawaja on Wednesday confirmed reports of the 2018 drama in Dubai, which had prompted new coach Justin Langer to deliver what he called an "all-time" blow-up over the matter.

A report from veteran broadcaster Gerard Whateley this week suggested a player had asked in Australia's first Test under Langer where the mints or red frogs were, with the ball not swinging.

Khawaja's peace proposal Usman Khawaja reveals he proposed a peace statement to Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg in the hope of ending the war of words tearing Australian cricket apart in relation to Sandpapergate.

Another unnamed player in the side also spoke up, the report said, before new captain Tim Paine put a stop to the conversation and Langer unleashed on the group.

Khawaja would not name the player who suggested the use of mints, but said they had been part of the group that had been involved in the furore in South Africa.

"Especially for that certain player, to do it was very odd," Khawaja told The Grade Cricketer podcast.

"I'll just say that player was in Cape Town, South Africa.

"We were struggling to take wickets … We were desensitised to the whole ball [thing]."

Using sugar-laced saliva to shine one side of the ball had been a regular tactic of teams for years, with players rarely sanctioned despite the practice being illegal.

Usman Khawaja says a player suggested using lollies to shine up one side of the ball. (AP: Kamran Jebreili)

When asked whether the player in question had been joking, Khawaja did not answer directly.

"I remember very well the blow-up [from Langer]," the former opener said. "I remember it was very targeted at one player, then the whole team.

"What I remember from it was like, 'If any of you guys ever even think about this again, you will not play for Australia again.'

"He didn't actually get a hat and [rub it against his backside], but his metaphor was, 'This is what you're doing with the baggy green right now.'"

Khawaja said documentary cameras were ordered to stop filming for the spray.

In the 80-minute interview, Khawaja, who called time on his international career in January, defended his decision to wait until after his retirement to go public with a claim the entire team knew of the 2018 ball-tampering plot in South Africa.

CA says Cummins backing not a sign it is taking sides Cricket Australia insists its backing of Pat Cummins to remain Australia's cricket captain does not mean it does not believe the accounts of other players.

"If I came out and said that while I was playing, I was 100 per cent [certain] my career was over. I couldn't play for Australia anymore," the 39-year-old said.

"I'm not trying to hide from that. I understand that. You can call me selfish, and maybe it was."

Cameron Bancroft and David Warner have backed Khawaja's initial recollection of events, while the third member of the trio banned after the 2018 scandal, Steve Smith, has yet to comment publicly on the latest revelations.

Khawaja has repeated at length that Smith talked him out of going public with his claims of collective responsibility in 2018, preferring to take the fall himself as captain.

"He's a great leader … I've never seen anyone take responsibility like that in my life," Khawaja said.

"I'm really conscious of Smudge dealing with it how he wants to deal with it now, and I'm really respectful of that."

AAP

World.title: NSW hold on for epic draw against Queensland
World.content:
Forgotten Test spinner Mitchell Swepson has outshone Nathan Lyon to almost bowl Queensland to an unlikely Sheffield Shield victory, before NSW held on for a draw with two wickets in hand.

On a frantic final day in Sydney, Queensland raced from 2-106 to 6-306 on Wednesday morning, before declaring and setting NSW 282 for victory.

With rain a constant threat and at times interrupting, the Blues then initially chased after a win before slumping to 6-105 and going defensive in the final hours.

At one stage in the final hour the covers were brought on for 7 minutes, as Queensland players remained on the field and even put stumps back in themselves.

But the Blues ultimately held on, going to stumps at 8-152 after 56.5 overs.

In a match full of Test ramifications, Steve Smith was bowled by a big-turning Jack Sinfield off break on 13 on Wednesday, adding to his first-innings 12.

Sam Konstas charged the first ball he faced from Swepson and was caught at cover for 11, missing a final chance to ram home his chances of a Test recall.

Queensland were desperately close to a famous victory at the SCG. (Getty Images: Mark Kolbe Photography)

For Queensland Jack Clayton did his chances no harm with an unbeaten 84, keeping the innings together alongside Hugo Burdon (98) and Michael Neser (61).

But the most notable aspect were Swepson's 11 wickets for the match and Lyon's four.

Swepson was able to get great turn out of an SCG wicket that he declared on Tuesday was back to its old spinning ways, before his fourth-innings 5-55.

In comparison Lyon was solid but failed to illicit any real turn or significant bite with his finger spin.

His overspin and bounce had Marnus Labuschagne caught behind sweeping on day three, before catching Burdon's edge with one that went straight on on Wednesday.

Lyon also had Neser caught in the deep as Queensland pursued quick runs late in their innings, but otherwise finished with 3-84 to go with his first-innings 1-86.

Lyon's status as Australia's No.1 spinner is not up for debate in the eyes of selectors, but his selection in Perth will likely come down to the nature of the wicket.

Although there have been questions asked of the 39-year-old in recent weeks, including a stinging attack from Stuart MacGill this week.

Swepson, meanwhile, is not in the Test frame but retains hope of earning a recall for the Border-Gavaskar Trophy in India later this summer.

His 11 wickets for the match was the best haul by a spinner in the Sheffield Shield since Stephen O'Keefe in 2014, and the best of his own career.

After producing the ball of the match to bowl Kurtis Patterson out of the rough on day two in first-innings figures of 6-73, he was again the destroyer on Wednesday.

He had a cutting Josh Philippe caught behind, bowled a leaving Ryan Hicks for a duck with one that went straight on, trapped Charlie Stobo lbw and then had Lyon caught low at slip late.

But the leggie was unable to get the two breakthroughs needed in the last over, as NSW held on.

AAP

World.title: Khawaja says he offered Sandpapergate peace proposal
World.content:
Usman Khawaja has revealed he proposed a "middle ground" peace deal to Todd Greenberg that could end the Sandpapergate feud that has ripped Australian cricket apart.

Speaking on The Grade Cricketer Podcast, Khawaja read out a text message he sent to Greenberg, the CEO of Cricket Australia (CA), that he hoped the entire squad could stand behind.

"We accept and acknowledge as a team that we knew we were ball tampering by artificially altering the condition of the ball in South Africa in 2018," Khawaja's proposed statement read.

"Whether it was sandpaper, or by any other means, is irrelevant. We knew what we were doing, and we take full responsibility as a team and squad for our actions, something we should have done eight years ago.

"Furthermore, we would like to acknowledge that Steven [Smith], Cameron [Bancroft] and David [Warner] paid an enormous price for the sake of the team for which we are sorry and eternally grateful."

Khawaja said he wrote the statement after thinking about the situation last Friday.

"I was driving to the mosque on Friday … and I was reflecting and thinking about, can we not just find a middle ground?" Khawaja said.

"I don't even care any more about what they say, what we say.

"Everything is just being drip-fed right now, and it feels like there's no end to it."

He even admitted that he had a "pipe dream" that the entire squad would take accountability one day.

Khawaja said Greenberg was initially receptive to the idea, but was not convinced that the statement would solve the issue, and said he would put it to "the other parties" involved.

In a wide-ranging interview on the cult podcast, Khawaja touched on multiple topics, including the threats he has received that meant he required a security guard at a charity cricket game in Cairns on Sunday.

Usman Khawaja said he still loves Pat Cummins. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney, file photo)

Khawaja said Pat Cummins's comments in his press conference were "really surprising" and that he had texted the Australian captain before his press conference in an attempt to try and find the middle ground.

"I was never expecting him to come out and attack me personally like that," he said.

"Attack what I said? Yeah. Personally, the way he did, for so long and he kept going and going and going I've never seen that side of Pat before.

"I didn't want to watch it, but I had to watch it. I wanted to turn it off so many times.

"I will always love Pat, and as much as he hurt me, I'm not going to judge him on a presser."

Khawaja said that he is "not convinced" that anyone else would have spoken about it when justifying the Sandpapergate chapter of his book, adding that he could understand why some people were angry that he wrote about the topic when some of his teammates were still playing.

"100 per cent, I definitely can. I'm not an idiot, I'm not devoid of empathy," he said.

"I get that side, and that's why I'm so happy now that CA has come out and said there's not going to be any sanctions, nobody's going to get in trouble, Pat Cummins remains as captain — I was actually really happy with that.

"I don't want to hurt anyone individually."

Usman Khawaja says he wants there to be a middle ground found. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

Khawaja said that had he come out and spoken during his career he would have never played for Australia again.

"If I'm being brutally honest, if I came out and said that while I was playing, 100 per cent my career was over," he said.

"I couldn't play for Australia anymore.

"I'm not trying to hide from that. Call me selfish, maybe it was.

"The thing I've tried to do … is talk about Cameron Bancroft. How much longer do I wait? What do I do? Do I make him suffer for another five years?"

Khawaja said that he knew sandpaper was being used on the field in Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha, just by looking at the wear on the ball that was not consistent with normal wear and tear of a game.

Khawaja said he delayed coming on the podcast, he missed two previous appointments, because his appearances clashed with Pat Cummins's press conference and Cameron Bancroft's revealing West Australian article.

"I just thought that, if I came on at that time, I would inflame the situation so much more," he said.

"This was never about me versus Pat [Cummins], and I know that's what the media wanted but that was never my goal.

"As disappointed as I was about that presser, I was just, 'I'm going to stay away from this'.

"The Bancroft situation was the same … it was so deep, it was so full on."

World.title: Matildas keeper reveals career-threatening health scare
World.content:
A neurological disorder threatened to cut Teagan Micah's career short, but the Australian goalkeeper has overcome it with a little help from her Matildas friends.

The 29-year-old was diagnosed with autonomic dysfunction after suffering a concussion in March while training with her current French club, Lyon.

She previously sustained a serious head injury in 2022 with Swedish side FC Rosengård and the latest concussion forced the shot stopper to miss March's Asian Cup.

It also led to her developing the debilitating condition, which stops the nervous system properly regulating automatic body functions.

Micah has recovered and returns to Joe Montemurro's Matildas squad for their two-game series against Colombia, beginning in Canberra on Saturday night.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, the Queensland product revealed the "big health scare" threatened to force her into early retirement.

"I had a lot of chats with my family, with doctors, my best friends … every day about retirement, and it was looking like that for a while," Micah said.

Teagan Micah plays for OL Lyonnes in the French top flight. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Lilou Cassin)

She experienced problems regulating her heart rate, which would rise to 190 beats per minute after walking for 2 minutes.

Micah consulted with specialists in Sydney, Geneva and France in a bid to get healthy and back on the field.

"It was probably about June, July time when I came home to [Australia] for about two weeks and I also saw my doctors here … it was kind of the turning point for me," she said.

"I sat down with my family and spoke a lot with them [about retiring] and it was just a matter of … get back healthy first and then making the decision.

"I didn't want to make a decision before that because I knew it wasn't going to be something I'd be comfortable with … I just knew I wanted to keep going."

Micah, who says she feels "alive again", credited ex-Lyon star Ellie Carpenter and other Australian teammates for getting her back on her feet.

"She got me through so many days," Micah said of close friend Carpenter.

"She sent me food to my apartment when I couldn't get out of bed for days.

"Steph [Catley], Ellie, Ras [Hayley Raso] were the main ones checking in all the time.

Hayley Raso (left) was one of Teagan Micah's key supporters during her lay-off. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

"Also the coaching staff here, the Matildas, were incredible as well … and at Lyon, those girls made me smile on days where I didn't think I had it in me anymore."

Competing with Mackenzie Arnold for the number 1 shirt, Micah said she would do everything possible to nab a spot in Australia's squad for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil.

"I need to probably go back to the drawing board and write down what I want to achieve now with the rest of my career," Micah said.

"Now that I feel good and I'm ready to go it's like where do I want my career to take me … [I want] to use this second chance I have."

The friendlies in Canberra and Geelong are world number 15 Australia's last before the World Cup draw on December 11.

World number 19 Colombia have established themselves as the second-best South American team behind hosts Brazil.

Along with Micah, Australia have regained Mary Fowler, Kyra Cooney-Cross, Alanna Kennedy, Tameka Yallop and Kahli Johnson.

Everton attacker Holly McNamara [hamstring] is out until late December, while Clare Hunt and Charlie Rule remain sidelined.

AAP

World.title: Ireland lose skipper for Wallabies clash while Suaalii relishing centre role
World.content:
Ireland stand-in skipper Dan Sheehan will miss his side's final Nations Championship match against the Wallabies after being given a two-week suspension following his red card for a croc-roll against South Africa at the weekend.

Sheehan's initial yellow card eight minutes from the end of Saturday's 20-17 win was upgraded to a red after the match.

The 28-year-old has captained Ireland in the absence of injured Caelan Doris.

Sheehan, usually a hooker, played at number eight for the first time in his international career against the Springboks as the side were grappling with an injury crisis at the back of the scrum.

Ireland are already without at least three number eights through injury, with Jack Conan and Sean Jansen missing, as well as Doris.

Given the Wallabies' strength at the back of the scrum, the absentees will be cause for concern for the Irish.

Ulster's 23-year-old giant, James McNabney, should be fit to return after missing the Springboks clash after he was knocked out on debut against Fiji, although his Ulster teammate, backrow utility forward Nick Timoney, will likely start.

Ireland, which finished third in the Northern Hemisphere section, will face Australia at Twickenham in a play-off to decide fifth and sixth place.

Meanwhile, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii said he enjoyed the combination at centre with the experienced Len Ikitau as the debate over his best position for the Wallabies continued.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii says he enjoyed playing centre. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Suaalii played at centre in his first 22 starts for Australia, following his high-profile defection from rugby league, but new Wallabies coach Les Kiss moved him to wing for the 42-38 victory over South Africa in Perth in September and the first Bledisloe Cup clash against New Zealand last month.

The absent Hunter Paisami may be expected to challenge him for that outside centre spot, while Ikitau could benefit from a move to 13, with Carter Gordon at 12.

In the Nations Championship this month, he was picked on the wing against England but returned to the midfield against Scotland and last weekend's 29-26 win over Wales.

"I just love playing rugby and, being able to play 13, you get to be both sides of the ball. You can defend and attack and you're in the front line," he said in London.

"Playing alongside Lenny, he's great with his comms. He's quiet off the field but once he goes on the field, he helps you quite a bit."

The 23-year-old Suaalii has also been a regular fullback for the New South Wales Waratahs in Super Rugby but has not been picked at number 15 for Australia.

With the hosting of the World Cup now less than a year away, and where home hopes will rest heavily on his shoulders, where best to use Suaalii's powerful presence has stirred plenty of debate among Aussie pundits.

"I think my biggest thing is just, I'm still learning the game. I'm still trying to get better each week," he added.

"It doesn't matter what number I have on my back; I'm just trying to use the skill sets I have … defence, aerial attacking, ball in hand, breakdown.

"I see myself just growing my game in all that sense: the attack, defence, breakdown, transition. I'm really just focusing on putting my energy towards trying to get better in that sense and then position-wise, it's just up to the coach.

"I've always said that. I'm happy to play anywhere, just always just trusting what the coach is going to do and, at the end of the day, I'm playing for my country, so I'm always grateful for that."

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Indian teen wonder breaks List A record with 200 from 52 balls
World.content:
Indian cricket prodigy Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has broken yet more records, this time with the fastest century and double century in men's List A competitions.

The 15-year-old smashed a century in 28 balls, then 150 in 40 balls, and finally crossed 200 in 52 balls while playing for India A against the United Arab Emirates in the Asia Cup Rising Stars 50-over tournament.

All of those are records for List A competitions, the International Cricket Council confirmed, adding that Sooryavanshi's 200 was nearly twice as fast as the previous record of 103 balls.

The teen was caught soon after on 204 to end an innings boasting 28 sixes. India easily chased down the target of 250 set by the UAE to finish on 3-254. More than 80 per cent of the team's runs came off Sooryavanshi's bat.

List A cricket is the level below one-day international cricket. It covers the top level of one-day domestic cricket around the world as well as international games involving a top nation's development team, such as India A.

The records continue a spectacular year for Sooryavanshi. He scored 175 to win the Under-19 World Cup final for India in February, lit up the Indian Premier League and became the youngest player to represent India in a full international game, beating the record held by all-time great Sachin Tendulkar.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AP

World.title: Players and umpires unite against Super Netball rule changes
World.content:
Super Netball players and umpires have released a joint statement opposing suggested rule changes to the competition.

It is a rare move from the umpires, who typically keep quiet on such matters.

Heading into its 11th season, there is a desire from stakeholders to increase entertainment value and keep pushing the sport forward in order to hold onto its tag as the world's best league.

However, there is a clear divide in how that should be done.

The Vixens and Thunderbirds contested the 2026 Super Netball Grand Final. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

In April, Netball Australia shelved plans for expansion and signed a five-year broadcast deal with Nine to return to free-to-air TV audiences.

These are the kinds of ideas the player and umpire group prefer.

"Netball has a bright future. Getting there will take big ideas and bold thinking," the statement read.

"We don't want less innovation. We want much more of it.

"Why not more teams, more games, new competitions and exciting formats? Why not fresh broadcast opportunities, technology, digital engagement and events that bring new audiences to our sport?"

Ruth Aryang of the Fever looks to block a super shot by Uneeq Palavi of the Mavericks. (Getty: Paul Kane)

The last rule changes fell six years ago when the super shot was announced six weeks before the 2020 season start. The decision was controversial and created distrust between the national governing body and the athletes, who felt their opinions had been disregarded.

Since then, England and New Zealand have also added two-point shots to their top-flight competitions.

Other innovations, such as tactical timeouts and rolling subs, have been much better received.

In May this year, Netball Australia ran a fan engagement survey, asking how they could elevate the 2027 spectator experience. Of the 3,000-plus fan submissions, there were consistent themes around speed, scoring and technology.

That same month, it formed a League Innovation Forum — comprised of Netball Australia staff, as well as Super Netball club, coach, umpire and player association representatives — to discuss potential modifications.

Former Big Bash League boss Anthony Everard is head of the project.

If the competition already has regular sell-out crowds, does it need more rule changes? (Getty: Matt King)

Although the sport has been reluctant to confirm details, three key proposals have been leaked:

Stop the clock: Time will be held when the ball is out of play in the last two minutes of a match.

Time will be held when the ball is out of play in the last two minutes of a match. A shoot-off: If a match is still tied at the end of extra time it will go to a shoot-off. Allowing two shooters each two attempts at a two-point super shot or giving one shooter three attempts at a regular goal.

If a match is still tied at the end of extra time it will go to a shoot-off. Allowing two shooters each two attempts at a two-point super shot or giving one shooter three attempts at a regular goal. The centre pass heist: Players can request two centre passes in a row up until the last two minutes of a match.

The last of the three was trialled in early November in Victoria's men's premier division. Those involved said it did not make a compelling case as it had little impact, interrupted flow, and created confusion and inconsistency in the game.

None of the All Australian umpires that officiate Super Netball were involved in the trials. (AAP: Scott Barbour)

When ABC Sport asked Netball Australia how these trials went, it was told that executives were finalising their recommendations to present at a December board meeting.

The players and umpires have concerns the trial didn't appropriately replicate the demands and standard of Super Netball and that fundamental changes will be made again without proper consultation.

By taking this stance now, they hope it's not too late to change the executive's minds.

"Netball is a team sport … That's it's magic," the statement read.

Loading Instagram content

"Reducing a hard-fought contest to a shootout involving a small number of players moves away from what makes netball great. It also unnecessarily exposes individual players to additional pressure and scrutiny.

"The centre pass heist raises similar concerns. Possession should be earned through the contest, with all players having the opportunity to influence the outcome. Close games should be decided by skill and teamwork.

"Rule changes aren't off the table. But surely we should first ask: What problem are we solving? Will it improve the contest, reward skill, entertain fans and grow the game? And have we considered those who play and officiate it?

"If the answers are convincing, let's get on with it. If not, let's keep exploring."

Tech.title: Google’s patent for custom AI video feeds paints a bleak picture of entertainment’s future
Tech.content:
Last year, Google filed a patent for a system called My Channel that’s designed to create feeds filled with personalized, AI-generated videos and s based on information the company knows about its users. The patent has been rejected, but unfortunately, Google might appeal or resubmit an amended version, and we could see this monstrosity come to market.

First spotted by Patentlyze, the patent — which was filed last May and published last week — describes how My Channel would use a person’s demographic data and viewing history to create its own prompts that would then be fed into an LLM to help generate AI videos tailored to that person’s specific interests. In addition to factoring in what kinds of videos a user tends to watch, the system would capture contextual data from their device like IP addresses, GPS locations, and specific details about the user’s age. My Channel could also base its prompts on current news like sports scores and things happening on social media, and all of the video generation would take place on Google’s servers.

According to the patent, My Channel would be able to churn out entire movies of various genres. If a user watches a lot of videos about Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, the system might serve up something like Ash Koosha’s Odysseus: The Fall. The patent details how My Channel might be able to connect to other streaming services — which would give it even more information about users and, presumably, access to useful training data for video generation. It all seems like a convoluted way to whip up AI knockoffs of professionally produced art, but what’s most unsettling about the patent are its mentions of My Channel creating digital avatars of users and turning them into “the protagonist or lead character” in the content it pumps out.

Image: Google

Setting aside the fact that My Channel would use photos, videos, and audio clips of people to create these avatars, the system sounds like it is designed to generate a form of “entertainment” that is deeply at odds with what makes engaging with art a worthwhile, enjoyable experience. It can be fun to metaphorically project one’s self into fictional narratives to understand how characters feel, but what Google is proposing is giving people access to an endless supply of bespoke content that doesn’t at all encourage them to use their imaginations to empathize with or relate to the characters. The patent makes it seem like Google thinks that viewers would be entertained enough just by seeing themselves onscreen. That’s bleak in and of itself because My Channel sounds very much like an unholy cross between JibJab and the panoptic elements of Google.

My Channel feels like an even more depressing idea when you consider how the service would make it that much easier for its users to avoid broadening their horizons by being exposed to new things that exist outside their comfort zones. If Google were able to strike the right licensing deals with other streaming services, My Channel users could presumably gorge themselves on artless AI regurgitations of preexisting content. That might keep some people glued to the service — a goal that every streaming platform strives for — but it would also discourage them from engaging with entertainment that isn’t expressly crafted to appeal to their assumed tastes.

When people refer to AI-generated videos as “slop,” they’re talking about the fact that generative models are incapable of generating art with the same kind of creative intention that makes human-made stories compelling. Video generation models can mimic visual elements of the data (read: movies and series) they’re trained on, but they cannot truly think or feel in the way that directors, writers, and actors can. This reality is why it has been so baffling to see AI-boosting entertainment companies, streamers, and studios insisting that the technology will fundamentally revolutionize the industry for the better. It feels much more likely that gen AI is going to keep flooding the internet with garbage no one wants to watch.

Tech.title: WhatsApp’s new scheduled messages let you choose the right time to send
Tech.content:
To schedule a message, press and hold the send button and pick the date and time you want it to arrive. It will look like any other message to the person receiving it. You can see all future messages you have lined up, and delete them beforehand if you change your mind.

Even if your phone is off or out of battery, your scheduled message will still show up at the time you chose, and it remains end-to-end encrypted like all your personal messages, so no one else can read it, not even us.

Scheduled messages work with text, photos and videos, and are rolling out globally over the coming weeks. It’s one more way to show up for the people who matter to you, now at exactly the right time.

Tech.title: EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Saying it was necessary to prevent the possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps, the US Army conducted a controlled detonation of over 9,700 pounds of lead azide today at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa. Videos of the detonation showed plumes of smoke several hundred feet high drifting south before quickly dissipating.

Following the explosion, the Army confirmed that all of the barrels at the plant had been destroyed without any secondary explosions or infrastructure damage. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley during a press conference held two hours after the blast, according to the Associated Press.

The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has been monitoring the area around the ammunition plant leading up to today’s event. According to a statement from the EPA following the detonation, “real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region” an hour after the detonation. The data collected by EPA employees, contractors, and monitoring equipment is shared here.

The Army has used lead azide in munitions for nearly a century but began transitioning away from the material around 15 years ago because it can be difficult to transport and store. Over time, the material can degrade and crystallize and eventually become unstable enough to detonate at ambient temperatures. The Iowa ammunition plant housed 68 barrels containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, representing the country’s remaining stockpile. For safety reasons, the material was stored in liquid form embedded in sawdust and burlap bags while water and ethanol were added to prevent freezing. However, the decision was made to detonate the stockpile after an inspection by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms (ATF) discovered “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels” last March.

Ahead of today’s detonation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) supported a recommended, but voluntary, temporary relocation of all the residents of Middletown and immediate surrounding areas that began yesterday. A cone-shaped evacuation zone extends about five miles southwest of the ammunition plant to account for the post-explosion dispersion and deposition path of dust. Displaced residents will be lodged until Friday, November 27th, and can return home once the all-clear has been given.

To reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army said it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation. Walls made of four 16,000-gallon water tanks were installed to capture lead particulate, while the aging earth-covered magazines holding the barrels were covered with tarps and lead containment screens and flooded with foam.

Tech.title: 1Password breach leaked customer names and emails, but not passwords
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

1Password says a hacker stole customer names and email addresses after gaining access to its backend systems. The breach didn’t expose passwords or other information stored in customer vaults, but could put users at risk of phishing attempts, according to a post disclosing the incident. It’s unclear how many users are affected.

The password manager began investigating the incident on November 19th, after an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. Using the compromised account, the hacker accessed 1Password’s source code and pushed malicious code to backend services to download customer data. Along with customer names and emails, the leaked data included public keys, as well as account and user identifiers.

It also included tokens from certain emailed invitation or account recovery links. According to 1Password, attackers can’t use tokens alone to gain access to an account, as they would need to pair them with a single-sign-on method or a six-digit numeric code sent to a user’s email. 1Password has since lengthened the codes it sends to users to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them harder to guess.

Related 1Password lets AI agents use your passwords without seeing them

The password manager also disabled the affected GitHub account, rotated internal credentials compromised by the breach, and added a new detection system for similar attacks. It warns customers about potential phishing attempts as well, saying phony emails, texts, or calls may reference 1Password invitations or account recovery attempts. The company says it will never ask customers for their account password or Secret Key, and that users should only enter this information into the official 1Password app or website.

Tech.title: The Fairphone 6 Plus is modular, repairable, and $100 off right now
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Unlike most smartphones, the Fairphone 6 Plus is designed for home repair, with easily replaceable parts that could help extend its lifespan well into the future. That makes its midrange price point easier to justify, especially now that it’s dropped to a new low of $552.49 (about $98 off) at Amazon as part of the retailer’s ongoing Black Friday sale.

The 6.3-inch Fairphone 6 Plus features 12 user-replaceable parts, including the battery, screen, USB-C port, and cameras, all of which you can swap out with the included screwdriver. Replacement parts are relatively affordable, too; a new battery costs $39.99, which helps offset its middling battery life and lack of wireless charging. It also comes with a five-year warranty and up to six Android OS upgrades, making it a good option if you want a phone you can keep using for years.

Although repairability is its marquee feature, the 6 Plus is also a solid midrange Android device. Fairphone prioritizes ethically sourced materials, making it a strong choice for environmentally conscious buyers who don’t want to sacrifice performance. Its Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 processor handles everyday tasks well, and its cameras take decent photos, though they’re not quite on par with those of pricier phones.

What’s more, it offers a clean, bloatware-free Android experience and modular back panels, which you can swap for optional accessories like a card holder or crossbody strap. Our own Allison Johnson particularly liked the phone’s dedicated switch for turning on customizable focus modes called Moments, which can simplify your homescreen and limit access to distracting apps — something we could all use a little less of.

Tech.title: The loneliest peptide party in New York
Tech.content:
This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.

On a rainy fall evening, an experimental art venue in Chelsea Market had a small line out the door. There are always lines in New York City. Viral food trends, gallery exhibitions, pop-ups, and parties. The folks in line looked like your average joe, ready for a Friday night on the town. You wouldn’t look twice — except, perhaps, for a man with a wizard beard and a laser sword strapped to his back.

Inside, the man with a laser sword stood in the middle of the cavernous bottom floor of a two-story warehouse strewn with large bean bags. On the wall were psychedelic projections of jellyfish, shrimp, and other sea creatures. A bizarre choice, considering peptides won’t induce any trippy vision quests, and not a single person was getting groovy. The industrial beams had posters with QR codes that you could scan to get samples of Afterglow, a new type of peptide product. According to seemingly discarded pamphlets around the venue, Afterglow isn’t a standard injectable or oral peptide. The company makes strips that dissolve under the tongue. The “Afterglow Peptide Field Guide” also described what each sample does, dosing recommendations, and potential side effects. At the upstairs bar, bartenders mixed custom cocktails called Afterburn — complete with bioluminescent veggie nectar — and Margatrutide. (For the record, a bioluminescent veggie nectar cocktail tastes as awful as you think.)

Welcome to a peptide launch party.

Bioluminescent veggie nectar cocktails for the peptide curious.

Peptide parties are old news in San Francisco, but they’re somewhat more novel in New York City. Milling around the edges of the venue were various reporters and photographers. We were all trying to get a sense of why anyone had bothered to come out. Not that many did. Despite the venue’s size, the main floor had plenty of empty space.

One person I spoke to was a fencer with sore joints. They’d heard that one of the peptides might help with recovery. Another had a father in the wellness industry and had heard vague things about how effective peptides could be. One woman, staring at a projected jellyfish, merely shrugged. Her friend was more into “wellness stuff” and she had no plans, so, why not check out a party? A man, staring into his bag of Afterglow samples, was mostly interested in weight loss but scared about the safety of gray market products. A few feet away, another man was furiously reading the Afterglow pamphlet. “I like to know what I put in my body,” he said.

The only problem was he didn’t remember which sample he had tried.

A common refrain: Well, this beats doing research online. This, at least, was a social event where you could theoretically connect with other people. And there were clusters of strangers speaking to each other. Mostly, near the bar. Everywhere else, people stared awkwardly on their phones, their eyes occasionally roaming the room without meeting anyone else’s gaze for more than a second or two. After a while, they’d disappear into the back room and reappear with a goody bag full of peptide samples.

Scanning a QR code got you one of two goodie bags at the Afterglow launch peptide party.

After 90 minutes, I decided to leave. For the umpteenth time that evening, I’d walked up to someone, asked about peptides, and got a noncommittal “I really don’t know anything — I just came to learn more.” (When asked if they had, they invariably shrugged and pointed to the goody bag.) It was clear that the only peptide evangelists here were likely associated with the launch. The whole thing, to me, seemed as if someone had tried to draw a cool party from memory. The last thing I saw was a person draped in a ghost sheet sitting alone in the corner.

As it turned out, the man with the laser sword was a performance artist who’d been invited to attend. Out of journalistic integrity, I asked if he had ever tried peptides. He told me he was more interested in the unifying energy of the universe. When I got up to leave, he waved and said, “Giggles.”

If I were peptide curious, the Afterglow launch party was a pretty awful way to learn anything about these substances. To be fair, Afterglow’s Partiful invitation mostly described this event as “an environment great for aura farming” and the “hard launch of [its] first of many experiments in culture.” Nevertheless, as part of the press, I did walk away with a smattering of Afterglow’s products. In total, I got packets of what Afterglow calls Charge (NAD+), Rejuvenate (glutathione), Wolverine Blend (BPC-157 / TB-500), Strength Blend (CJC-1295 / Ipamorelin), Glow Blend (GHK-Cu / BPC-157 / TB-500), Connect (PT-141), GLP-2 (tirzepatide), and GLP-3 (retatrutide). Or at least that’s what the packaging says. There’s no way to truly verify gray market peptides for safety or efficacy because they’re unregulated products.

First of all, last I checked, GLP-1 medications do not upgrade like iPhone models. Afterglow’s pamphlet correctly lists that your body has “three hormone switches”: GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon. The accompanying descriptors of what each does are broadly correct, though lacking in nuance. For example, there is a hormone called glucagon-like peptide 2, but it’s not tirzepatide. The “real” GLP-2 is a hormone related to intestinal health. Tirzepatide is still considered a GLP-1 medication that’s a dual agonist because it works on two hormones (GLP-1 and GIP.) The GLP-2 moniker is a misnomer popularized by ill-informed influencers. The same goes for retatrutide, which, as of this writing, is still an unapproved GLP-1 medication that works on three hormones (GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon) and is therefore a triple agonist. There is no such thing as GLP-3.

Most partygoers didn’t know a single thing about peptides and had to read the provided pamphlets.

For all the samples, there were no instructions regarding dosing on the packaging — just another QR code leading to Afterglow’s product page. Those pages happen to contain instructions for how to use the strips, and the amount of product within the strips. There are disclaimers about how little studied the compounds are, but nothing about interactions, side effects, or what to expect while taking. Just a throwaway line to talk to your doctor.

All that information, you’d have to find on the pamphlet given at the party. (Ironically, some “important cautions” on the pamphlet state to avoid taking samples with alcohol, at a party where the booze was flowing.) Provided you didn’t throw it out. One would hope that information is on a box if you were to buy directly from the seller. But for all intents and purposes, what I just described is what a clueless partygoer would have to go on.

If everything in that pamphlet were 100 percent factual, perhaps a conscientious partygoer could feel reassured. On that front, I have bad news. The pamphlet calls PT-141 an “FDA-approved peptide that boosts sexual desire for both men and women.”

Several free samples were available at Afterglow’s peptide party.

PT-141, also known as bremelanotide or Vyleesi, is FDA approved. But only for premenopausal women suffering from hypoactive sexual desire disorder. It is not approved for post-menopausal women, men, or for general sexual performance enhancement.

Another concern: How does one evaluate a sublingual peptide strip? Specifically, is this delivery method even scientifically proven effective in humans? Spoiler: It’s not! A collapsible FAQ menu on Afterglow’s site states, “We don’t know yet. Nobody has published how much of most peptides reaches the blood from a strip compared with an injection. We’re funding studies to measure exactly that, and we’ll share what we find.”

As for why you’d want to even try a sublingual strip? Afterglow’s website suggests it’s more convenient than injections or pills. No refrigeration, no needles, and no need for learning how to reconstitute a drug. Just pop a strip under the tongue and go.

And good luck trying to find reputable sources of information on your own. Afterglow says it’s funding its own research, but its site has no reviewable documentation just yet. A Google search brings up a questionable AI overview, a handful of links from dubious med spas, a couple of dead links, and one PubMed study in mice. Most of the links also primarily discuss the difference between oral peptides in pill form and injectables — so not terribly relevant here.

I’d consider it fair game if I were confident that anyone at the party I went to did their due diligence. As it stands, I talked with over a dozen people who were mostly there for vibes, booze, and freebies.

Not all peptide parties are created equal. Some happen on WWII cargo ships, complete with panel discussions about peptide supply chains. Another “peptide 101” talk I attended in New York happened at the back of a bitcoin bar. There, most attendees also knew very little about peptides, but at least they got treated to a PowerPoint presentation about the basics. There was a dubious demonstration of how to inject oneself that would’ve probably made any pharmacist or doctor scream. But at the very least, peptides were defined and attendees could ask questions. (The answers to those questions were on the right track with regard to the dangers of the gray market. They were less reliable about scientific rigor and why “anecdotal evidence” is not the same as clinical evidence of safety.)

A performance artist wearing a laser sword bid me farewell by saying, “Giggles!” He told me he was not familiar with peptides.

But a striking, recurring theme is just how much is unknown. These substances aren’t well-studied in humans, so there’s not much evidence as to long-term benefits or side effects. The peptide curious know shocking little about the substances they’re supposedly interested in. Likewise, it’s incredibly difficult to get reliable, unbiased data on gray market interest or usage, though there have been attempts to quantify this surging demand in recent months. Case in point, telehealth provider Hims & Hers just conducted a consumer survey of roughly 2,000 American adults. Of those surveyed, 68 percent said they had little to no knowledge about peptides. Less than 18 percent were even able to identify that peptides are chains of amino acids. Even so, 40 percent said they were interested or very interested in trying injectable prescription treatments — including peptides — if offered by a telehealth service.

Even so, peptides are everywhere. The word appears in copious ads for skincare creams, weight loss drugs, and supplements. Looksmaxxers, influencers, and celebrities like Gwyneth Paltrow and Joe Rogan talk about them in podcasts, documentaries, and social media as if they’re miracle shortcuts. Hims & Hers has even announced it’s launching a service called Peptide Plus — nevermind that the vast majority of what it’ll offer are not actual peptides.

The last sight I saw before leaving the party.

In this kind of environment, of course more people will become peptide curious. Which makes it even more concerning that the most readily available information sources are not medical or scientific experts well-versed on the topic at hand. There are dubious links online summarized into less-than-critical AI overviews. There are pamphlets handed out at weird parties, where there’s more booze and schmooze than education. Influencers branding themselves as experts as they flash crudely summarized studies in a bar back room. Industry panels that are inaccessible to the average consumer, full of jargon and assumed knowledge of the science at hand.

It’s clear something needs to be done until general knowledge improves. Until then, the parties will continue.

Tech.title: FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In an announcement on Wednesday, the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative. With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites.

The FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satellite milestone by 2040. The FCC also deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits, rather than having them burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, saying the company hasn’t provided “sufficient information” about its disposal process plans.

SpaceX has described its Starmind project as a way to “capture solar energy in space to power” AI capabilities on Earth. The company says Starmind will transmit data to Earth using high-speed lasers that connect to Starlink. It plans to produce chips for its satellites at an upcoming Terafab facility.

Google has already taken its first steps toward putting compute into space, with the launch of a “Project Suncatcher” AI server satellite last month. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher in 2029.
