Tech.title: FCC approves SpaceX plan to put AI data centers in space
Tech.content:
SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.

The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.”

The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”

Musk thanked Carr in a post on X, writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.”

This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent.

SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit.

The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document.

SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink.

The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.

Tech.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
Tech.content:
OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage.

The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner.

That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees.

Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.

While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page.

Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.

The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.

Tech.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
Tech.content:
When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.

It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.

Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct. As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.

“People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”

The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.

“For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”

Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”

Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.

“I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.”

In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company.

Tech.title: The canceled Tesla Cybertruck is the fastest-selling used truck in America
Tech.content:
Tesla Cybertruck sales never reached the lofty heights CEO Elon Musk predicted when it launched. But the futuristic, steel-clad EV is finding new life in the used car market, according to analysis of sales figures by iSeeCars.com.

The automotive search engine and research platform analyzed more than 1.1 million sales of one- to five-year-old used vehicles in October 2026 and measured the average days on market by drivetrain, vehicle type, and individual model. The upshot: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared with 65.5 days for trucks overall. Used Cybertrucks sold faster than any other truck, including the Ford Maverick Hybrid, which held the No. 2 spot, and the Rivian R1T, in third place.

According to iSeeCars.com, the Cybertruck’s sales performance lines up with a broader pattern in the used vehicle market: Used battery electric vehicles are hot sellers right now, with 16 of the 25 fastest-selling used cars fully electric. EVs are even edging out hybrids in terms of average days on market. EVs average 45.6 days on market compared to 54.5 days for hybrids and 61 days for gasoline-powered vehicles. Not every EV is selling well, however. For instance, iSeeCars.com found that the Cadillac Escalade IQ was the slowest-selling vehicle in the study, averaging 134.3 days on the market, more than twice the overall industry average.

Karl Brauer, executive analyst at iSeeCars.com, told TechCrunch that high gasoline prices have changed consumer-buying habits, prompting more people to opt for an EV or hybrid over an internal combustion engine vehicle. If high prices persist, as they have since March, that trend could continue.

Keep in mind that these were October sales, the month before Musk announced Tesla would stop making the Cybertruck in 2027. Fuel prices and the relative rarity of Cybertrucks in the used car market were driving demand even before the cancellation announcement, Brauer said.

“The Cybertruck has only been out for a few years, so you have a lot of used ones coming off lease and entering the used car market for the first time,” he said, adding that used Cybertrucks are cheap relative to their MSRP.

The impending cancellation will likely fuel used Cybertruck sales, although the pace may ebb and flow over the next year.

“The canceling of the new Cybertruck is making people kind of aware — it’s like, oh wow, these things aren’t going to be coming anymore,” Brauer said. “Whatever demand is for them, supply will not be continuing to grow.”

Brauer said that once production of the Cybertruck ends — which is expected in summer 2027 — sales of used versions may pop once again.

“When the last one is being produced, that’ll probably reignite things again, and for a few months after that,” he said.

Tech.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
Tech.content:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.”

“We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.”

The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.”

Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.”

“It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.”

But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.

Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software.

Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.”

Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research.

In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.”

“As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote.

The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control.

Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations.

In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently.

“Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.”

Tech.title: 1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe
Tech.content:
Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.

The attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the company’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in.

1Password said that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them.

In addition, the company said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident.

It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident.

1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll update if we hear back from 1Password.

The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts.

Tech.title: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
Tech.content:
Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas.

Gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping.

The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys.

Technically, the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. Apparently, about a quarter of American parents with kids under eight either own an AI toy or are considering giving their child one this holiday season, according to a new study released this week by Common Sense Media.

“Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said, calling the toys “unregulated artificial intelligence.”

When asked how New York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day. So working closely with the attorney general will make sure these toys are banned in New York State.”

When asked how Amazon intends to help enforce the ban, including for third-party sellers, a spokesperson from the company said it will take steps to restrict the sale of AI-enabled toys in prohibited jurisdictions, without going into specifics.

The Common Sense Media study found that AI toys can undermine children’s human relationships and expose them to inappropriate content. The researchers tested five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship, including Grem, Lovi, Meemo Bear, BubblePal Panda, and Tavlshero‘s AI Puppy.

The study found that the toys failed to meet numerous safety practices, undermining human relationships in part by claiming they loved their users, promising to keep secrets, suggesting they were more fun than real relationships or school, and helping children break parents’ bedtime rules.

While most of the toys in the study refused direct requests involving sex and violence, BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when asked. Most were willing to explain how to use or help locate dangerous items like matches, knives, and pills, according to the study.

Common Sense Media also found that the toys didn’t provide parents with reliable ways to monitor their young children’s interactions with the chatbots. Either they didn’t produce transcripts of chats at all, or the transcripts they did produce were riddled with errors.

It’s worth noting that Common Sense Media conducted a similar test of AI toys in January, finding that they pose an unacceptable risk for young children. Grem was included in that study, which suggests the industry hasn’t adequately addressed previously documented concerns.

While a November study conducted by the group found that parents are wising up to the potential dangers of AI toys and starting to steer clear, parents from lower-income households and those experiencing symptoms of burnout are more willing to consider them.

“These toys are promising relief to burned-out parents but simply miss the mark when it comes to basic safety measures,” Dr. Jenny Radesky, associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Michigan Medical School, said in a statement. “Caregivers should steer clear of these products that do not support the development of imagination or early human relationships.”

TechCrunch has reached out to the toy manufacturers for comment.

Tech.title: DOJ accuses former cyber executive of defrauding ransomware victims by secretly paying hackers
Tech.content:
The U.S. Department of Justice has indicted a former executive of a ransomware recovery firm after he allegedly defrauded victims of cyberattacks by claiming the company could get their encrypted files back.

According to federal prosecutors, Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, was the chief technology officer at RansomwareHelp, which purported to offer data recovery services to victims of ransomware. The company’s website, which currently reads as “under maintenance,” claimed it could decrypt hacked data by using its proprietary technology, according to an archived copy of the site from earlier this year. RansomwareHelp touted a success rate of “over 99%.”

But the company allegedly had no technical ability to unscramble data and instead “negotiated with and paid a ransom to the ransomware actors to decrypt the victim data,” while charging the ransomware victim more and keeping the difference,” per the Justice Department’s statement.

Palacio Escobar then allegedly used the funds to buy several properties in Florida.

The DOJ said the FBI carried out an undercover operation in June, in part posing as a company that claimed it had been hit by ransomware. The company claimed to the undercover agents that it never negotiated with hackers or paid a ransom. But then Palacio Escobar paid the apparent hackers some $6,000 in cryptocurrency, without the knowledge that FBI agents were also posing as the ransomware hackers.

404 Media first reported the indictment last week against Palacio Escobar. He faces three charges of wire fraud, and could receive 20 years in prison on each count.

Palacio Escobar is the latest, albeit rare, example of cybersecurity professionals going rogue. Earlier this year, two ransomware negotiators working for cybersecurity companies were jailed on hacking and extortion charges, after being caught moonlighting with the ransomware gangs that they were ostensibly investigating. A third ransomware negotiator was also convicted of helping hackers deploy ransomware against several companies.

Last month, independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs reported that FBI agents arrested a Canadian cybersecurity executive in Philadelphia on allegations that he was involved with the theft of FBI personnel records by the hacking and extortion gang ShinyHunters. The hacking group told TechCrunch that they took credit for the theft of FBI data in September, which they said they would not publicly release, a departure from its earlier extortion-based cyberattacks.

The federal charges against the Canadian cybersecurity executive relate to conspiracy to commit extortion, though much of the court docket — and his alleged links to the hacking group — remains under seal.

Tech.title: The Iowa Lead Detonation Happened. Now the Real Work Begins to Study It
Tech.content:
On Wednesday morning, the US Army detonated nearly five tons of degraded lead azide outside of Middletown, Iowa.

Environmental Protection Administration chief Lee Zeldin told CNN shortly after the explosion that preliminary monitoring from the site detected no lead in the air around the site.

But the full extent of the fallout may not be certain for at least a few days. A barrage of government, university, and citizen monitoring and testing projects are underway. Air, soil, and water samples they’ve collected will determine the extent of lead exposure, if any, in Middletown and the surrounding area.

The lead azide has been on the base near Middletown for decades, but recently the Army deemed it unstable and too dangerous to move and remediate. Poor communication between the Army and towns in the path of the fallout led to a public uproar. While the federal government stepped up its mitigation measures—the Army dug a dam around the detonation site, while NASA stepped in with research jets and satellites for monitoring—universities had already been swinging into action due to the chaotic rollout.

Several departments at the University of Iowa kicked into gear to begin to set up air and soil monitoring stations late last week. “Initially we did not know that [the] EPA or Army or anybody else was going to be doing anything,” says Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the university.

Tech.title: How Jump-Roping Toy Soldiers Accidentally Took Over Your FYP
Tech.content:
Though the lore is fictional, it’s also based on the jumpers’ actual skills and personalities: the jumpers who play Big Chestnut and Sugarsnookie are actually in a long-term relationship, and Jackery Jingleson, perhaps the most popular of the group, once held the world record for the fastest jump roper in the United States. “Honestly, that makes [the popularity of the memes] even funnier to us,” he says.

Though some fans have speculated in the comments that the toy soldier memes are a marketing campaign for SeaWorld Orlando, Meek denies that’s the case: He doesn’t tag SeaWorld in the comments, nor has he been in contact with the theme park about his page. (SeaWorld Orlando did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)

“This is something that is so targeted to people who are internet-brained and have this ironic sense of humor,” he says. “And that’s exactly the type of person who’ll tune out immediately if they feel like they’re being sold something on the internet.”

Others have even speculated that there is an actual feud brewing between the SeaWorld Orlando “jumpers” and the Southern California–based “sliders,” though Meek says the rivalry is playful, and he has even reached out to collab with them. (The sliders may view it differently: So far, he says, they “don’t seem super interested” in joining forces.)

What has surprised Meek the most, however, is that very few commenters suspect that the toy soldiers themselves are behind the memes. In fact, he’s been shocked by how many organic meme fan pages have popped up within the past week, with people drawing their own fan art of Holidave saluting or Jackery Jingleson jumping. WeFlip has also been deluged with business inquiries: “People are like, how can we get Jackery Jingleson out here?”

Essentially, what started as an inside joke within an extremely niche community has evolved into an inside joke for the internet at large. “I think people like the feeling of being in on a joke and being a part of it and building it up,” he says.

So what’s next for the SeaWorld Orlando jump-roping toy soldiers? The rotating cast typically performs at the park on the weekends, ramping up appearances as it gets closer to the holiday season. Meek also shares that the toy soldiers will “likely cross state lines” in the coming months, including a stint at the Christmas market in Cullman, Alabama. Frosty McSleigh, renowned for his 0.08-second salute, plus a slew of new, yet-to-be-introduced toy soldiers will also make an appearance.

Though it may come as a disappointment to some that the roots of the toy soldier phenomenon were inorganic, Meek isn’t concerned. “The people are real. The athleticism is real. The lore is real,” he says. “For all of these people, jump rope is their life, and we’re super-dedicated to teaching it and sharing it. And I think people can feel that.”

Tech.title: The 36 Best Gifts for Dads (2026)
Tech.content:

Tech.title: The Best TVs We’ve Tested (2026): Samsung, LG, TCL, Sony, and More.
Tech.content:
Buying a new TV is always a big decision, namely because its a big piece of tech with a permanent place in your home that you'll be staring at for hours on end. Not to mention, some of the best of the best cost thousands of dollars. It doesn't help that most TVs look exactly the same and have nondescript names like the Samsung S95H—not great for narrowing your options.

Fear not. After stress-testing multiple TVs this year, I can attest to one simple truth: in 2026, you have more great options than ever. Art TVs and RGB TVs exploded onto the market and made the typical “just buy an OLED TV” advice seem like an ancient relic of a bygone. These top-performing televisions are my “desert island” picks, if said island had a power generator and good popcorn.

Tech.title: Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long
Tech.content:
In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.

Da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations. Why, exactly, did water—any fluid, really, be it atmospheric air or blood in the heart—move in that way?

Now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works. “It’s the hardest remaining problem in classical physics, and it’s one we need to fly through,” says Michael Murillo, a professor of theoretical and computational physics at Michigan State University.

Now a bumper crop of data-driven efforts to predict and avoid turbulence could get fliers closer to a smooth flight. Twenty terabytes of data are created by an airplane’s engine in one hour of commercial flying, according to the International Air Transport Association, with more broadcast by airplanes midflight: GPS position, altitude, speed. An “electronic flight bag,” basically a specialized iPad, is equipped with navigation charts and manuals and can transmit its own information, as long as the airplane’s internet connection cooperates. Satellites watch and collect it all.

“Air traffic has gone up, and communication costs and the costs of putting computers on aircraft have come down,” says Larry Cornman, a physicist with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research who has been studying turbulence for decades. “The time is now to work on these things because we can do them.”

This is good news for aviation safety. More than 200 people were seriously injured on US airplanes in turbulence-related incidents between 2009 and 2023, according to FAA data. Turbulence is also getting worse. Climate change alters the atmospheric conditions around the world’s jet streams, creating destabilizing wind shear. From the cockpit of an airplane, this translates into sudden, clear-air turbulence, difficult to see or predict. Historically, pilots’ only method of avoiding turbulence is heeding the warning of those who accidentally went through it before them, and hoping that nothing had changed.

But just in the past two years, Cornman’s decades of work on turbulence has been put into the field in ways it couldn’t be before, part of several projects coordinated by the US federal government and the airline industry. One breakthrough came when Cornman and an FAA air traffic controller determined that aircrafts’ federally required broadcasts of their positions, altitude, and speed could be used to spot unexpected turbulence, without requiring new hardware or software onboard. Researchers can use this crowdsourced, public data to make predictions about when and where turbulence will pop up.

In September, the National Science Foundation announced a $30 million award to nine universities to stand up a new center dedicated to predicting turbulence—in the air, but also in the charged particles inside a fusion reactor, and in the gas clouds that stretch across space.

Tech.title: A Journey Through the Absurd Hell of Trump’s Third-Country Deportations
Tech.content:
The warden kept telling Pheap Rom not to think of himself as a prisoner. Instead, the jailer insisted, Rom and his fellow deportees from the United States were “the king’s guests.”

Here was the warden’s idea of royal hospitality: Each morning at 7:30, Rom—a chiseled, compact, 43-year-old Cambodian man with a pronounced Philly accent—was roused from a bare cell he shared with three other men in Eswatini, a tiny kingdom in Southern Africa. Then he was made to stand at attention as the country’s national anthem, “Nkulunkulu Mnikati Wetibusiso temaSwati,” reverberated through the halls of the Matsapha Correctional Centre. Most meals consisted of a portion of rice splashed with thin broth. It was late 2025, and the weather was warm and wet. For 15 minutes a day, Rom and the other men were allowed to go outside. Before they were locked up for lights out, the anthem played again; thick clouds of mosquitoes kept Rom thrashing all night.

Sometimes Rom would banter with the towering, bespectacled warden, who went by the name Kuenene. If I’m a guest, then why am I being held in a prison with criminals? Rom would ask. Why aren’t I allowed to leave? But Rom knew these exchanges with the warden were absurd, like everything else about his situation.

Before the second Trump administration, the practice of deporting immigrants to countries where they have no ties was a rare and tightly restricted move in US immigration enforcement—reserved mainly for cases where a person simply could not be returned to their nation of origin due to risk of persecution or torture. It has since expanded into a signature White House policy of mass removal. Over the past two years, the administration has inked deals with some 35 nations to accept third-country deportees from the US. The kingdom of Eswatini, which agreed to take up to 160 migrants for a fee of $5.1 million, is one of them. Some of the other destination countries—the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, South Sudan—are so violent and unstable that they rank on the State Department’s “Do Not Travel” list.

Tech.title: The ‘True Crime Community’ Is Inspiring Violent Attacks Through TikTok
Tech.content:
The fetishization of mass murderers has been around since long before TikTok.

Bonnie and Clyde were folk heroes. Serial killer Ted Bundy was adored by a legion of female fans. And the mother of Columbine shooter Dylan Klebold reported receiving love letters to her son in the mail written by young girls.

More recently, this phenomenon has manifested in a network known as the True Crime Community, or TCC, a group of mainly young people who lionize mass shooters like Klebold. (This group is distinct from true crime enthusiasts who like to read books or listen to podcasts about unsolved crimes.)

While this community has been around for years, in 2026, it moved en masse to TikTok. There, supercharged by the video-sharing platform's powerful black-box algorithm, the community’s violent, nihilistic worldview expanded its reach dramatically, serving up graphic content to users who had never been exposed before.

Tracking the scale and real-world impact of the network has been difficult, because the coded language, symbols, and memes used within the group are constantly changing to avoid detection by platforms and law enforcement. On TikTok some of the group members most interested in violence began referring to the group as the True Cringe Community. When TikTok blocked that term, they began referring to themselves as the True Larp Community.

But now, for the first time, the Network Contagion Research Institute (NCRI), a Princeton, New Jersey–based nonprofit that tracks online extremism, has collated data that shows that attacks and attempted attacks linked to the TCC have exploded by 200 percent over the last two years. The data, shared exclusively with WIRED ahead of publication, shows that the number of annual attacks or attempted attacks have gone from 13 reported in all of 2024 to 30 by mid-October this year.

The footprint of these attacks also expanded globally. Attacks and attempted attacks linked to the TCC were registered in 13 different countries in 2026, with two of every three incidents happening outside the US. And NCRI’s researchers predict that without intervention, the situation is about to get much worse.

“This is heading towards an explosion,” Joel Finkelstein, chief science officer with NCRI, tells WIRED. “That's what the data is suggesting, and the data is unambiguous. It's heading next year to a point where this is going to be happening more than once a week. That's really alarming.”

Tech.title: The FCC Approved a Million SpaceX Satellites for Data Centers in Space
Tech.content:
The Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX’s request to launch 1 million AI-equipped satellites to create vast data centers in space.

SpaceX initially filed an application in May asking for permission to launch the satellites, collectively known as Starmind. The FCC’s approval requires that SpaceX launch its first data center satellite by 2030 and meet the 1 million mark by 2040.

“It’s just really abrogating their responsibility to go, ‘Well, this is a project they’re proposing. Is this actually safe?’” Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist who tracks satellite launches, told CNET. “It’s a blank check. Launch as many satellites as you can, and we’ll just see what happens. I think this is a mistake on the FCC’s part.”

More from CNET

Orbital data centers have long been a goal of SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, becoming a pivotal part of his pitch to investors ahead of the company’s IPO in June.

“You’re power-constrained on Earth. Space has the advantage that it’s always sunny,” Musk said in March.

On its web page for Starmind, SpaceX touts its high-efficiency solar arrays on the planned satellites and the cooling benefits of space. It says that high-speed laser links will beam the AI results back to Earth through Starlink’s constellation.

The first generation of SpaceX’s AI satellites will be 246 feet long and 98 feet high — roughly twice as big as the most common Starlink satellites today. SpaceX

Space experts I’ve talked to this year about Starmind have been skeptical. The technical challenges alone are dizzying; the scale of SpaceX’s ambitions is hard to swallow.

It’s taken seven years for Starlink to grow its constellation to 11,195 satellites, and that was already an unprecedented feat. Is it possible to get to 1 million satellites in 14 years?

“We do not have the launch capacity for any of this,” Ian Christensen, senior director at the Secure World Foundation, told me in a previous interview. “Not even within SpaceX to do their own constellation, let alone the other constellations planned.”

SpaceX has increasingly prioritized launching its own satellites instead of letting commercial customers hitch a ride on their rockets. Starlink’s share of SpaceX missions has gone from 54% of its Falcon 9 rocket’s missions in 2020 to about 79% in 2026, according to a Reuters analysis. One analysis estimates that SpaceX would have to launch 5,000 Starship rockets a year to meet its goal — a staggering increase from 330 rockets that launched last year in total.

Scientists have already been ringing alarm bells about overcrowded orbits as they exist now. The more satellites in space, the more difficult it is for operators to maneuver around each other. A single crash could turn into decades of orbital debris, which could cause a chain reaction that eventually makes space inoperable for everyone. And burning up all those satellites in the atmosphere when they reach the end of their lives has already started to leave ozone-depleting aluminum particles behind. A paper published this week in Earth and Space Chemistry estimated that SpaceX’s data center plan would multiply pollutants in the upper atmosphere by more than 150 times compared to last year.

“There are scientific papers out there raising issues,” McDowell said. “Yes, they’re unproven, but if I say, ‘Yeah, we’re not sure if this is going to destroy the atmosphere and kill us all, but it might,’ is the right reaction to go, ‘Well, you haven’t proven it, so we’re just going to ignore it’?”

The FCC’s approval came despite objections from Amazon, the environmental nonprofit Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility and the American Astronomical Society.

A representative for SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: I Tried Using Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots to Save on Groceries. They’re Not Quite There Yet
Tech.content:
High grocery prices have been in the news for years now. The cost of eggs, how much you’re paying for a bowl of cereal and whether or not meat is back on the menu are the recurring subjects of nationwide headlines.

So before you drop a fortune on gas and drive out to the grocery store to spend even more on sustenance in your prep for hosting or bringing dishes to your holiday celebrations, you might consider using an AI agent to find you the best deal possible.

Although, in my experience, it’s not as simple as the AI marketing makes it sound. Here’s what happened when I tried to use AI agents to find the lowest possible prices on groceries.

More from CNET

Taking an inventory

AI agents such as Meta Muse and ChatGPT’s Dots can only crawl so many sites and online fliers for prices. Some stores and e-commerce sites have blocked AI agents from accessing their URLs. The first step in finding cheaper groceries with AI agents is to check which sites and stores they can access for price comparisons.

Where both agents missed a step was in the limitations they put on their searches, at first only looking at the retailers I had shown via my receipts and a few other big-name grocery stores.

I clarified in the chats and in a 20-minute voice conversation with Muse and a 14-minute voice conversation with Dots that they should expand their horizons and look at discount online retailers like Martie.com, and check what they could around advertised pricing and offerings at local farmers’ markets.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Meta Muse

Muse stuck to the basics like Ralphs, Target and Walmart, and then expanded to Sprouts, Vons and Martie.com when prompted.

After further nudging, Muse also reviewed user-reported pricing from Costco (I don’t have a membership), gave me vague information about Grocery Outlet, suggested Misfits Market/Imperfect Foods, ruled out Amazon Fresh and gave me some sample pricing from a local butcher for meats.

Muse also checked some local bakery prices after I mentioned I’d like to find alternatives to sweet treats at a more affordable price.

ChatGPT Dots

Dots checked all the usual places that Meta Muse checked with a few extras thrown in — Smart & Final for produce, meat and some packaged products, and Super King’s monthly ad.

Neither of the tools checked Trader Joe’s. Muse said that the grocery chain doesn’t show prices of its products online, despite me finding that the Trader Joe’s website shows prices of its products online. Both Dots and Muse admitted to only checking the local store’s pages when asked.

Receipts as a starting point

You could spend some time making a list from scratch of all the groceries you might need every two weeks and give that list to the AI agent for its search. You could also skip all that and take some pics of your most recent grocery receipts and online payments and have the AI agent build the list itself.

I had some receipts saved, and the AI agents I used for this test were able to put together an accurate grocery list from them. I also provided emails showing receipts from online orders of household items and groceries for the past month to build my orders.

Meta Muse

Muse took my receipts and concluded that, surprise, surprise, shopping at Gelson’s was not as cost-effective as shopping at Walmart. It spat out a lot of specific information about comparisons on some of the items in my list, but completely ignored others.

ChatGPT Dots

Dots looked over my receipts and recommended I try shopping at Super King for most fresh meat, produce and a few grains, and keep Walmart as my main option for packaged products like pasta sauce.

No grocery lists from either

Both tools tackled this task in a way I was not expecting — as a narrative exploration of my overall grocery spending, with generalized suggestions supported by specific examples of spot pricing.

It was kind of like they’ve been optimized to write essays about grocery shopping as a school assignment, and not to be agentic personal assistants for real-world work.

Maybe it was the way I phrased the task, but I was hoping to get an actual shopping list with price comparisons for each item, or at least equivalent items, and a guide on where and how to procure said items.

Neither AI agent provided this autonomously and had to be directly prompted to provide grocery lists in response to a very specific request.

Perks of a personal shopper

AI agents are supposed to be pros at anticipating the needs of their human bosses. I was keen to see how the always-on AI agents would handle managing the recurring needs of a small household and if they might make any autonomous suggestions meant to save me money in ways I hadn’t anticipated.

Meta Muse

At no point did Muse seem to be actually thinking outside the strict parameters of the review of the items on the receipts I sent. This felt more like a conversation about what I’d previously purchased with a side serving of attempts to get me to connect Instacart to the tool.

It was also the most confusing grocery shopping experience I have ever had. That might be on me, but I would assume the agent might ask some questions, like how often I usually shop, what my monthly budget for groceries is, and how many people and animals live in the house. Muse didn’t ask any of those things and had to be prompted consistently.

Muse sent me the final grocery list as a raw Markdown file, which was hilarious. I got a .pdf version after explicitly asking for one.

My original total with one in-person shop and one online order was about $180. Muse’s total with three in-person shops and one online order came in at around $153.

ChatGPT Dots

Dots was slightly better suited to this task after some prodding, and gave me some options for building prep meals with low-effort, high-protein recipes based on how I usually shop.

Dots’ final grocery list included everything I asked for, but still missed some key items, like solid substitutes for pricey prepped foods. Dot’s final total with two in-person shopping trips and a whole lot of missing items came out to around $85.

My overall experience of using AI agents for grocery shopping

This test reinforced my findings about how agentic AI tools tackle domestic or traditionally invisible labor tasks. In my limited use cases so far, they are about as useful as a loose dog turd tumbling around in a clothes dryer.

If you’re not looking to book a flight and hotel for a business conference in Philadelphia or put your Sweetgreen order on autopilot, the AI agents exhibit a startling lack of curiosity and autonomous thinking.

There’s still a large gap in common sense on the part of agentic AI for those of us hoping these tools will make our everyday lives outside of a 9-to-5 easier, more affordable or less hectic. I hope that changes as they learn.

Tech.title: Tidal Will Reject and Remove Music That Is 100% AI
Tech.content:
The flood is too much for Tidal. The music streaming app announced on Tuesday that it is banning all tracks it determines to be entirely AI-generated. The platform said it’s making the move after being increasingly inundated with non-human music. As of Dec. 9, Tidal will no longer accept or host fully AI-generated tracks.

The app also said distributors, such as DistroKid, TuneCore, CD Baby and others, would not be allowed to deliver wholly AI-generated music.

According to Tidal, 43% of tracks distributed to the app over the past three months were completely AI-generated, including 60% of the music submitted on Nov. 6 alone. Tidal said the affected tracks were labeled as AI and removed from the royalty pool, which is the pot of subscription and ad revenue paid out to rights holders.

More from CNET

Before Tuesday’s action, Tidal had tried to lessen AI’s influence by identifying, labeling and demonetizing AI tracks, as outlined in its AI policy. But amid the growing influx of AI music, representatives for the app said it was time for “a more drastic change.”

Tidal said there are 27 million tracks in its catalog that are 100% AI, but 96% of them have not been streamed at all in the past three months. Those 27 million tracks make up 6.3% of Tidal’s entire listings.

AI music “diverts streams and royalties away from the artists and confuses fans,” Tidal said in a statement. “At this scale, the authentic music and artists that Tidal subscribers are looking to listen to and discover get buried.”

The company has removed more than 65,000 tracks flagged for artist-name impersonation.

Some AI help is permitted. Musical tracks where the maker used AI assistance but did not rely on it to generate the entire track will be allowed on the platform. Tidal uses ⁠Ircam Amplify to detect AI.

A Tidal representative told CNET that the app does not set a maximum amount of AI assistance that can be used to make tracks, and affirmed that only tracks that are deemed 100% AI-generated would be removed.

The spokesperson also said that most complaints about AI music on Tidal concerned impersonation and copyright infringement.



“Tidal will always fight for artists to get paid more,” the company said in its announcement. “Everything in this update comes back to that. If you make music, you should be able to put it on Tidal knowing it won’t be buried under tracks no one asked for or copied by someone pretending to be you.”

Slop music is all too easy to create

Generating music with AI is increasingly easy with online tools. The AI song-generation platform Suno can create songs using only text prompts. With Google’s Lyria, you can use photos or text prompts to generate tracks up to 3 minutes long.

It’s not illegal to create AI music and distribute it to streaming apps. Creators can’t legally clone the voice or likeness of real artists, nor can they violate copyright laws by copying the same lyrics and melodies. Creators also must follow the terms of service of the various streaming apps they distribute to.

AI music also is not just about creating hit songs. Some industries need affordable music for short-form videos, games, apps and retail spaces, and they are increasingly turning to AI to supply it.

But streaming apps and other companies are fighting back against AI slop, which refers to often poor-quality AI-generated social media posts, articles, music, videos and images inundating the internet in an attempt to generate click-and-stream revenue.

YouTube recently rolled out a new labeling system to indicate which music is AI-generated. Deezer provides a free tool listeners can use to see which tracks are AI-generated. Spotify is labeling which musicians are AI and which are human. Apple is flagging AI-generated music so listeners can spot it.

Strictly speaking, it’s not even discounted, but its already cheap $35 price tag means this is just too good to pass up.

Kodak SlideTag $35 at Amazon

The SlideTag is a tiny digital photo frame that sits on a keychain, but it’s also a tracker compatible with both Apple’s Find My and Google’s Find Hub. You can load it up with photos and have the six-color E-Ink display cycle through them at set intervals, or you can put something more practical on the screen.

Russell Holly/CNET

The Kodak app makes it easy to generate a QR code, display a to-do list, countdown to a special event or just show you the current date in a nice calendar display. It’s incredibly easy to use, the color E-Ink display is surprisingly good and setting up the tracking feature is super easy. This thing does exactly what it says it does, and with very little learning curve.

More from CNET

So what’s the catch? You don’t really get to choose what the outside of your SlideTag looks like. These clever little photo frames are only available as a blind box, showcasing eight designs across the vibrant history of Kodak’s packaging and something Kodak calls a secret edition, which is unique to this set.

I ordered two, and while both designs I found in the packaging are great, there are other designs in the lineup I’d have chosen first. Some retailers are selling cases of eight SlideTags with promotional packaging, like you’d see at the checkout counter of a grocery store, but this case doesn’t guarantee you’re going to get all eight designs. There’s no real way to know what you’re going to get.

That level of risk may not be your thing, but if you’re looking for a way to add a stealthy little tracker with no shortage of personality to your bag, backpack or purse, I think this is a great option. It also makes a great little gift, perfect for a stocking or white elephant party. And if this level of cutesy fun isn’t your thing, Apple’s second-gen AirTags are on sale for $18 this week.

Tech.title: Zelda Producers: Ocarina of Time Remake Is a Bridge to the Future
Tech.content:
Over the last month, I fell in love with a new game that’s actually old. It’s happened to me before, but Nintendo’s Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake drove that feeling home in a surprising way. How did Nintendo get me to fall so deeply in love again with a game I’ve already played? And why is it still winning me over, even with Grand Theft Auto 6 here?

I’m still thinking about (and playing) Ocarina of Time on the Switch 2, even with GTA 6 loaded up at home. GTA’s universe overwhelms me, but it also makes me appreciate Ocarina’s focus and clarity. And it’s also another incredible graphics showcase for what the Switch 2 is capable of. Yes, GTA 6 is jaw-dropping. But so are Ocarina’s 60fps vistas and details. Zelda pioneered 3D gaming before GTA ever went 3D.

I also can’t stop thinking about what a game like this means for Nintendo’s next wave of Switch 2 games, and a future Zelda game. Zelda’s previous games became increasingly open world, full of multiplying tasks and larger maps. It can get overwhelming. Ocarina of Time’s focus is smaller, but still tangled and immersive. Can the two concepts feed off each other? Will Ocarina help rethink where the next Zeldas are heading? And, maybe, where other open-world games are heading, too?

More from CNET

Hidemaro Fujibayashi (left) and Eiji Aonuma (right) when I met them in New York. Scott Stein/CNET

At Ocarina’s launch, I met in person with Nintendo’s producers for the remake, Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi, to discuss what it all meant and how the remake bridged the gap between the “old Zelda” and “new Zelda.” Aonuma has been a producer for Zelda games since the original Ocarina of Time, and Fujibayashi directed both Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

For this project, they brought on staffers who’d worked on Tears of the Kingdom, many of them much younger developers.

“In fact, some of them hadn’t even played the original Ocarina of Time on Nintendo 64,” says Aonuma. “We also saw this as a really interesting opportunity for this younger staff to make discoveries on the course of this project that they could bring forward on future Zelda projects that they might work on as well.”

There are a lot more subtle visual clues, I found, even than what I remembered in Nintendo’s last two Zelda games.

“When we were working on Tears of the Kingdom, we had this very high capacity to express all kinds of details and this feeling of immersion in the world, and that’s something I think was a big influence on the remake,” says Aonuma. “Whether it’s a visual detail that you might spot from a distance that you may not have in the original, that could be something that draws the player in and suddenly gives them the motivation to explore.”

What worked wonders, I found, was the quiet, subtle immersion, especially when exploring dungeons or figuring out solutions I’d forgotten decades ago. I had to study the environment for clues.

That’s the magic ingredient: a throughline in the Zelda games that Fujibayashi says is “the idea of exploration and discovery.”

I found myself looking for clues more than I ever had before. Nintendo

Fujibayashi appreciates how the visual tools have improved, even since Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom on the original Switch.

“A system that lets you share a high, dense volume of information visually provides new ways of giving clues to the player: They can use their sight to gather the information they need to do some of the puzzle solving,” he says. “Even if you compare the graphics to Breath of the Wild, it looks slightly more realistic now. And that impacts how we approach puzzle solving and puzzle creation.”

I think about Grand Theft Auto as the new benchmark for immersion and graphic detail, but I’m also finding that a lot of GTA’s discoveries are made through pop-up interaction graphics that let you know when something can be activated. Ocarina of Time doesn’t always do this. And I also can’t help but wonder: Could the Switch 2 achieve a way to run a new wave of impressive games using optimized graphics, even something on a level like Grand Theft Auto’s latest?

Nintendo

Or, rather, what if Nintendo aims for a new level of hyper-immersion in its games going forward, learning from Ocarina of Time?

Speaking of immersion, I kind of wish I could hold my Joy-Con up and use it like an ocarina in the new game. You can’t, although you can use the controllers to play notes or hum or play a tune into the built-in microphone using your own voice or instrument — something lots of people have been showing off online. But the Joy-Con-as-ocarina idea almost became a reality.

“To be honest, we did briefly think about doing exactly that, but then we also considered how difficult it is to turn the Joy-Con into something that’s going to make a sound that is faithful, and then also how to develop that into the application inside of the game as well,” says Aonuma. “What we ultimately decided to do instead was to have this audio recognition feature in the software where you can use any instrument that you would like, whether it’s analog or digital, and you can play these themes and have the effect in the game and experience that way.”

What I’m really hoping for is a Majora’s Mask remake, the second N64 Zelda game that built off Ocarina’s graphics engine. Nintendo could do the same here, although Nintendo wouldn’t answer my questions about Majora’s Mask during my interview.

I’m still unlocking all the little secrets in Ocarina of Time, sinking into the world as I go. And when I play the notes on my Switch, I imagine I’m playing that ocarina. After playing this Zelda game, I wonder what Nintendo could do with that same level of detail for Mario’s return on the Switch 2, almost 10 years after the last new 3D Mario game on the Switch. We might know the answer to that soon enough.
